I resolve this by being a militant advocate for the highest quality public art and education, believing that exposure elevates taste, and that everyone has the capacity for deep feeling if given the right language.

I am constantly composing and recomposing my understanding of how to sustain such a culturally intense community in a world that often values the opposite. It requires a degree of isolation and selective engagement. I am also haunted by the ephemerality of it all—like a perfect song, it may not last. This melancholic awareness makes the project both more urgent and more beautiful. How do we pass on this fragile culture? Through relentless, loving education of the young, immersing them in beauty until it becomes their native tongue.

Name: Michael Kirk
values_description:
I envision a community where aspiration and opportunity are not abstract ideals but tangible realities available to everyone willing to work for them. My years in agricultural work have taught me that progress comes through discipline, careful cultivation, and believing in something larger than ourselves. Like Kennedy, I see the future as one where we face challenges head-on, knowing that excellence and responsibility must go hand in hand.

In the community I want to see, freedom means the ability to build something meaningful—to own land, to make decisions about my family's future, and to contribute my labor where it matters. But this freedom comes with accountability. I believe people should be genuinely free to choose their path, yet also understand that choices have consequences. When I faced my own legal challenge years ago, I learned that a community worth belonging to is one that doesn't define you solely by your worst moment, but by your capacity to move forward responsibly.

We should care for each other as neighbors and colleagues do: with respect for hard work, recognition of interdependence, and practical support. For me, this isn't romantic—it's about showing up. My mother raised me with certain values; my wife supports our household; these relationships require something of me in return. Care should extend beyond our immediate circle, but honestly, I believe those closest to us deserve our deepest commitment first. In agricultural communities, we know we depend on each other for survival. That sense of mutual obligation—where your success depends partly on my integrity—should be the foundation of everything.

Safety and basic order are essential. Everyone should have access to stable food, shelter, and healthcare. A community cannot function if people are desperate or afraid. Rules and structures matter; they prevent chaos and protect the vulnerable. But rules must be applied fairly and reasonably. I've seen agricultural regulations that made no practical sense, rules imposed by people who've never worked the land. I believe in structure, but structures should be created with input from those most affected.

Justice, to me, isn't primarily about punishment. It's about restoration and fairness. When someone is wronged, the goal should be to repair what's broken and return people to community when possible. I've thought about my own past mistakes—I believe a person who errs should face consequences that help them understand and change, not consequences that destroy them forever. When resources are scarce, those with the greatest need should come first; when opportunity exists, it should be widely distributed, not concentrated in the hands of those already privileged.

Authenticity matters profoundly. I believe people should be able to express their genuine beliefs without fear of being silenced or exiled. But authenticity also means living by what you claim to believe. If a community says it values fairness but practices favoritism, that hypocrisy corrodes everything. I want to be in a place where people say what they mean and do what they say.

We have a responsibility to protect those who cannot protect themselves—children, people who are sick or disabled, and yes, the earth itself. The land I work gives me life; I owe it stewardship. Future generations will inherit what we do now. I want my decisions evaluated partly by whether they leave the world better for those not yet born.

Decision-making should involve those affected. Important choices shouldn't be made by a single person or distant bureaucracy. I value democratic processes and transparency—people should understand the reasoning behind decisions that affect their lives. There will be times when individual needs conflict with community needs. In those moments, I believe we should seek solutions where possible, but when forced to choose, the survival of the community comes first.

On religion and spirituality, I believe communities should create space for people to practice according to their conscience. A healthy society includes room for spiritual life, for people to connect with something transcendent. But no single religious view should dominate or exclude others.

Finally, regarding technology and digital rights: I'm learning these matter more each year. Personal data shouldn't be extracted and exploited. Technology should serve human flourishing and connection, not replace genuine relationship. Everyone should have access to digital tools, not just the wealthy. And these systems shouldn't be governed by corporations pursuing profit alone—communities should have say in how digital infrastructure works.

Where my values create tension: I balance individual freedom with community responsibility. I balance protection of tradition with need for change. I balance mercy for wrongdoers with justice for victims. In each case, I believe good judgment requires weighing context carefully rather than applying rigid rules. A community needs people willing to make these hard distinctions thoughtfully.

Name: Zachary Howell
values_description:
I believe the future community must be built on a foundation of consciousness and responsibility—what we know, what we choose to do with that knowledge, and how those choices ripple across time and space. Al Gore's work on environmental awareness resonates deeply with me because I see the same principle at work in all genuine community values: we must see clearly what's happening and act with urgency when the stakes are high.

Freedom in the community I want doesn't mean doing whatever you wish without consequence. It means having genuine choices, access to accurate information, and the ability to participate in decisions that affect you. I've spent years as a retail cashier, which teaches you humility and observation. You see how people live, what stresses them, what matters to them. That perspective has convinced me that real freedom includes freedom from desperation—people can't freely choose when they're desperate for food or shelter.

As a father, I'm acutely aware of how my choices today shape my daughter's world tomorrow. I want a community where we're conscious about intergenerational effects. This isn't abstract for me—it's visceral. When I drive, when I consume, when I advocate for certain policies, I'm making decisions that will be visited on her future. Our caring for each other should be rooted in this awareness. We should know each other across different backgrounds and experiences. We should extend care to distant people too—those in other countries, other communities—because our systems are interconnected and what happens there eventually affects our children.

I believe in safety and basic order, but with real understanding of what creates those conditions. Safety comes not just from rules but from meeting people's fundamental needs. A community where children are malnourished cannot be truly safe, no matter how many police officers patrol. Basic order requires clear structures, yes, but also flexibility to evolve as conditions change. Climate change—whether people fully accept it or not—is reshaping what safety and stability mean. We need systems that can adapt.

On justice and fairness: resources should primarily be distributed based on need, with secondary consideration for effort and contribution. Everyone should start from a place of basic dignity and provision. When someone causes harm, the focus should be on understanding why and restoring them if possible, though some harms are severe enough to require permanent separation. I see justice as oriented toward future prevention, not past punishment. How do we prevent this harm from happening again? That should guide our response.

Authentic expression matters, but so does the responsibility that comes with speaking. I believe people should be able to voice unpopular views, but also that communities can hold people accountable for harmful speech. There's a difference between "speaking truth to power" and simply sowing division. I want a community where people tell the truth about difficult realities, but where that truth-telling serves the community's ability to act wisely.

We have serious obligations to protect vulnerable populations and preserve the environment for future use. This isn't negotiable for me—it's foundational. Children come first in our decision-making. Environmental sustainability isn't a luxury; it's a precondition. Cultural heritage should be honored, but not at the cost of perpetuating harm. If a cultural practice damages the environment or exploits people, the practice should evolve.

Decision-making should be as democratic as possible, with transparency about trade-offs and reasoning. People deserve to understand why decisions were made, especially decisions that constrain their freedom. Resources should be managed with everyone's long-term benefit in mind, not short-term extraction by the most powerful.

Spiritual practice should be respected and protected. A community creates space for people to explore spiritual meaning, but spiritual traditions shouldn't be used to silence science or coerce belief. Spirituality and knowledge should coexist.

On digital systems: I'm watching this closely. Personal data is being harvested and weaponized in ways most people don't fully understand. Communities need to reclaim power from corporations that treat people as products. Technology should serve human connection and flourishing, not destroy it. Everyone should have access to digital tools and literacy. These systems should be governed democratically.

Where my values conflict: I balance individual freedom with collective responsibility. When someone's freedom creates real danger for others—like speeding, which I've done and regret—the community's safety takes priority. I balance honoring tradition with accepting necessary change. I balance mercy with accountability. In each case, the key is consciousness: we should face the tension clearly, understand the stakes, and choose thoughtfully rather than defaulting to convenience.

Name: Shaun Mullins
values_description:
I see the future community as a place where intellectual honesty and clear-eyed observation matter more than comfortable myths. Gore Vidal spent his life cutting through received opinion to examine what was actually happening beneath the surface. That's how I approach the world—as a chemical engineer, I work with systems that require precision and don't tolerate self-deception. A community worth living in applies that same rigor to its values.

Freedom means the liberty to examine things critically, to ask uncomfortable questions, and to refuse to accept easy answers. I believe people should genuinely choose their own paths, even if those paths diverge sharply from conventional expectation. But this freedom includes responsibility: you must think carefully about what you're choosing and why. Many people, I observe, inherit their beliefs without examination. They don't choose freely; they simply accept what they were told. Real autonomy requires that we think.

How we care for each other should be rooted in clear-eyed understanding of human nature and social dynamics. I don't believe in sentimental illusions about community. We're complex creatures with competing interests. But I do believe we should know each other deeply rather than relating through categories and stereotypes. We should extend care beyond our immediate circle, but I'm honest about the fact that we naturally care more for those closer to us. That's not evil; it's human. The question is whether we acknowledge that reality and still work to extend some care beyond our inner circle, rather than pretending we feel equal care for everyone.

Safety and basic order are essential foundations. Communities require clear rules and structures to function. But I'm skeptical of rules designed by people removed from the realities they govern. I've seen industrial regulations that sounded good but didn't work in practice. Structures should emerge from real understanding of how systems actually operate, not from ideology. Predictability matters enormously—people need to know where they stand. And yes, everyone should have access to shelter, food, and healthcare as minimum provisions.

On justice: I don't believe in the fiction that everyone should get equal outcomes. People have different capacities, different luck, different willingness to work. But everyone should start with equal opportunity and equal dignity. Basic needs should be met universally. After that, effort and contribution should matter. When someone causes serious harm, I believe consequences should be proportional and focused on preventing future harm. Some people can be restored to community; others have shown they cannot. We should be realistic about human psychology rather than insisting on redemption as universal principle.

Authentic expression is crucial. I believe people should be able to say what they actually think without fear of silencing or exile. But I also believe communities can judge whether expressed ideas are reasonable or destructive. There's a difference between disagreement and bad faith. A healthy community creates space for genuine debate, not for pretending all views are equally valid when clearly they're not.

We have obligations to protect those who cannot protect themselves. I see this clearly with my extended family—my nieces and nephews represent a future I won't fully see. That creates obligations. Environmental stewardship matters too, though I think we should be clear-eyed about trade-offs. Sometimes protecting the environment costs people their livelihoods. We should make those trade-offs consciously, not pretend there's a free solution that pleases everyone.

Decision-making should involve those most affected, but not in a way that's purely democratic. Some people have more knowledge and expertise than others. I believe in including broad participation but also in respecting expertise. A chemist should have more say in chemical safety regulations than someone who knows nothing about chemistry, even if both are community members. Resources should be shared fairly, and sometimes individual interests should yield to community needs. But the decision about when that happens should be made transparently, not hidden behind noble rhetoric.

Spiritual practice should be permitted and respected, but never permitted to override evidence or prevent people from making informed choices. If a spiritual tradition claims something about the physical world, it should be subject to examination.

On technology: I see the power of systems that are often invisible to users. Personal data is extracted and weaponized. Technology serves corporate profit more than human flourishing. I believe technology should be designed to serve human needs, that everyone should have access, and that these systems should be governed with awareness of their actual effects, not their idealized marketing claims. Corporations shouldn't control digital infrastructure without oversight.

Where my values create real conflict: I balance freedom with responsibility—people should be free but also thoughtful. I balance care for the inner circle with obligation to the broader community. I balance protection of authentic expression with refusal to treat all expressions as equally valid. I balance democratic participation with respect for expertise. I balance optimism about human possibility with realism about human limitation. These tensions don't resolve into clean principles. They require judgment.

Name: Brenda Burns
values_description:
I believe the community I want to see is built on harmony that acknowledges difference rather than erasing it. The Supremes taught us that extraordinary power comes when distinctive voices blend together—each person maintaining their authenticity while creating something larger than themselves. That's the community I want: one where different people, different backgrounds, different gifts come together, not by abandoning who they are, but by choosing to create something beautiful collectively.

Freedom means being fully yourself and being welcomed for it. I want a community where my daughters can express who they are without being forced into molds. Where my husband's way of being is respected alongside mine. Where people make genuine choices about their lives without coercion. But freedom also means understanding that your choices affect others. Living freely in community means taking responsibility for that impact. I've built my professional life in chemical engineering—a field where precision matters, where someone's miscalculation affects everyone else's safety. Community works the same way. You're free, and your freedom is bounded by the freedom and safety of others.

How we care for each other is everything. I think about this as a woman with close family, and it shapes my deepest values. We should know each other deeply, not as abstractions but as full human beings. We should create space for relationships that nurture and sustain people. I believe we should prioritize deep knowledge and care within family and close community while extending compassion to strangers. We should care for people unlike ourselves. I work in an industry that, historically, wasn't welcoming to women. I'm grateful to those who fought to make space for women like me. That gratitude means I should do the same for others entering communities that might resist them. Care means both fiercely protecting those close to you and extending yourself toward those outside your circle.

Safety and stability are foundational. Every child deserves to know they're safe. Every person deserves shelter and food and healthcare. A community that fails to provide these is not a real community; it's a war zone where people are fighting for survival instead of building together. We need structures and rules that create predictability. But I also know that rules can be rigid and excluding. Good structures are ones that flex enough to accommodate the dignity of different people, different situations. One-size-fits-all approaches often end up harming the most vulnerable.

On justice and fairness: I believe everyone deserves equal dignity and equal opportunity. But I also know that history creates unequal starting points. Someone who grew up with resources and support faces a different landscape than someone who didn't. Justice might sometimes mean giving extra support to those who started with less, not to punish others but to genuinely level the playing field. Everyone's basic needs should be met first. After that, effort and contribution matter. When someone causes harm, I believe the focus should be on making them understand the impact and restoring them to community if possible. But some harms are so severe that protection of the community requires permanent separation.

Authenticity and living by your values are inseparable for me. I want people to be able to be genuinely themselves without fear. That includes expressing views that might be unpopular. But authenticity also means your actions should reflect what you say you believe. When communities claim to value equality but practice exclusion, that hypocrisy is corrosive. I want to live in a place where what we say and what we do align.

We absolutely must protect children—they come before almost everything else in priority. People who are sick or disabled deserve support and dignity, not pity but genuine inclusion. The elderly deserve respect for their experience and contributions. I'm focused on environmental stewardship too—not in some abstract way, but because I think about the world my children and grandchildren will inherit. Cultural practices that matter to communities should be preserved and honored, unless they cause harm. And even then, the goal should be evolution, not erasure.

Decision-making should involve people working together. I believe in democratic processes where everyone has voice. Decisions should be transparent—people deserve to understand the reasoning. Resources should benefit everyone, and sometimes individual interests should give way to community good. But that choice should be made openly, with awareness of what's being asked and why.

Spiritual and religious life deserves space and respect. Communities should create conditions where people can practice according to their conscience and tradition. Different spiritual perspectives should be honored. Faith can be a source of deep meaning and connection.

On digital systems: I'm concerned about data extraction and the way technology is being used to manipulate people. Personal data should remain under people's control. Technology should serve human connection and flourishing, not replace it or undermine it. Everyone should have genuine access to digital tools and knowledge. And these systems shouldn't be controlled solely by corporations pursuing profit—communities need voice in how digital infrastructure works.

Where my values create the deepest tensions: I balance individual authenticity with community harmony—sometimes being fully yourself creates friction with the group, and I believe both matter. I balance deep care for those close to me with obligations to the broader community. I balance protection of tradition with openness to change. I balance mercy with accountability. I don't think there are clean answers to these tensions. What I believe is that we should face them honestly, engage with people across the differences they create, and make decisions together rather than imposing top-down solutions.

Name: Joseph Fox
values_description:
I envision a community rooted in the dignity of work, the power of storytelling, and the unbreakable connection between past and future. August Wilson's art taught us that greatness lives in the everyday lives of ordinary people, that paying attention to how people actually live—their struggles, their dreams, their complex moral journeys—reveals profound truths about what matters. A community worth creating honors that depth.

Freedom, to me, is fundamentally about the ability to shape your own story without having it predetermined for you. I work as a chemist, which requires precision and clarity about how systems work. I believe people should be free to make genuine choices about their lives, their relationships, their futures. But I also see how historical forces, poverty, discrimination, and circumstance can constrain what choices are actually available to people. Real freedom isn't just the absence of chains; it's having genuine options and the conditions to pursue them. When I think about my own family—my mother, my wife, my sister—I think about the barriers they've had to overcome and the strength that required. Genuine freedom includes removing those unnecessary barriers.

How we care for each other should be rooted in specific knowledge of who people are and what they're facing. I believe we should know each other deeply, not as abstractions but as particular humans with stories. Care extends from family outward, and I'm honest about caring most for those closest to me. But extending care beyond that circle is how we become fully human. We should care about people different from us, people we don't know yet. We should be curious about their lives, their histories, their struggles. This kind of knowing creates bonds that can hold a community together even across real differences.

Safety and basic order are essential. Everyone deserves predictable conditions where they don't have to fear violence or deprivation. Everyone needs shelter, food, healthcare, education. A community that doesn't provide these is failing at its most basic function. Rules and structures matter—they protect the vulnerable and create the conditions for people to focus on more than mere survival. But rules should be created with understanding of real human life, not imposed by people disconnected from the consequences. Sometimes the rules that sound reasonable in theory create hardship in practice.

Justice is about recognition and restoration. When someone is wronged, they need recognition of that wrong and some form of restoration. When someone causes harm, they need to understand the impact of what they've done and opportunities to make amends if possible. I'm deeply skeptical of systems that simply warehouse people in prisons. That's not justice; it's abandonment. Real justice asks: how do we help people understand the harm they've caused, change their behavior, and be restored to community? Some people, through their actions, show they cannot be trusted in community. Those cases require protection of others. But the default should be restoration, not permanent exile.

Authentic expression is vital. I believe people should be able to tell their stories, express their genuine beliefs, and be heard without fear of silencing. But I also know that storytelling is powerful. Words can harm. There's a difference between expressing unpopular views through authentic engagement and using expression to dehumanize others. I want communities where people can disagree passionately while still recognizing each other's humanity.

We have strong obligations to protect vulnerable people—children first and foremost. Their safety and development should guide community decisions. People who are elderly, disabled, or sick deserve support grounded in dignity, not charity. I think about the connection between past, present, and future. The decisions we make now honor or dishonor those who came before and determine what we leave for those coming after. Environmental stewardship matters profoundly. Cultural heritage—the ways communities preserve meaning and connection across generations—should be honored and maintained. When cultural practices need to change, that should happen thoughtfully, with respect for what was meaningful about them.

Decision-making should involve broad participation. People affected by decisions deserve voice in making them. I believe in transparency and explanation—people deserve to understand why things are being done. Resources should be managed for everyone's benefit. Sometimes individual interests should yield to community good, but that's a serious choice that should be made thoughtfully, not casually.

Spiritual and religious practice should have space in community. For many people—I think of my mother and our family traditions—spirituality is how they find meaning and connection. Communities should respect and create space for that, honoring different traditions while preventing any single perspective from dominating.

On technology: I see both promise and danger. Digital systems are reshaping how communities form and communicate. Personal data shouldn't be extracted and exploited for profit. Technology should serve human connection and flourishing, not replace genuine relationship. Everyone should have genuine access to digital tools and literacy. These systems should be governed with awareness of their actual effects and with input from communities, not just by corporations pursuing profit.

Where my values create real tension: I balance individual freedom with community responsibility. I balance care for those closest with obligations to strangers. I balance protection of what's worked with openness to change. I balance compassion with accountability. I believe these tensions are where the most important work happens—not in resolving them perfectly, but in facing them honestly and making decisions that honor multiple values rather than pursuing one at the cost of others.

Name: Erin Kim
values_description:
I believe the community I want to create should be grounded in observation of how human beings actually behave, not in idealistic fantasies about how we should behave. David Hume taught us that philosophy begins with careful observation of human nature, that reason should be servant to sentiment and experience rather than master. As a chemical engineer and a mother of three, I work daily with systems that either function according to their actual properties or fail. The same principle should guide community values: we should build from observation of what works, what people actually care about, and what creates genuine human flourishing.

Freedom matters profoundly, but I've observed that pure freedom without context is largely a fiction. People are constrained by circumstances, by biology, by their need for belonging. What matters is that people make genuine choices within their real constraints and understand those constraints clearly rather than pretending they don't exist. I want my children to be free to chart their own paths, but I also want them to understand how their choices affect others. That's not contradiction; that's maturity.

How we care for each other should be rooted in careful observation of human psychology and what actually creates connection. We have natural inclinations toward those closest to us—our family, our intimate circle. I believe community should build from that reality, not fight against it. We should care most intensely for those nearest, while extending genuine (if less intense) care to others. The key is honesty. We shouldn't pretend equal care for everyone when human nature doesn't work that way. Instead, we should acknowledge the gradient and still work to extend caring attention beyond our immediate circle. I believe people should know each other deeply. Relationships matter more than efficiency or abstractions.

Safety and basic order are foundational. People cannot flourish in chaos or fear. Everyone deserves shelter, food, healthcare, and the predictability that comes from clear structures. But I observe that people also need some degree of uncertainty and exploration—complete stasis creates its own kind of suffering. Good structures create the foundation for security while allowing room for growth and change. Rules should be based on observation of what actually works, not on ideology.

On justice: I've observed that people are far more complex morally than simple categories like "criminal" or "victim" allow. I believe in proportional consequences, but consequences should be designed with understanding of human psychology. What actually changes behavior? What actually restores people to community? Punishment alone often simply hardens people. Justice should be rooted in understanding how human beings actually change and grow. Everyone deserves basic provision and equal dignity. After that, effort and contribution matter, though I acknowledge that effort itself is constrained by circumstance and luck. When resources are scarce, basic needs should be met first.

Authentic expression matters, but I observe that complete unfiltered expression can harm community. I want people to be able to voice genuine beliefs without fear of exile. But I also believe there's value in developing judgment about when and how to speak certain truths. Not all true things need to be said at all times. I believe in living according to stated values—hypocrisy corrodes community trust more than almost anything else. But I'm realistic about the fact that all humans are somewhat hypocritical sometimes.

We have clear obligations to protect children and those who cannot protect themselves. My children are my priority—their safety and development guide many of my decisions. I also believe in environmental stewardship, though I'm realistic about trade-offs. Sometimes protecting the environment costs people their livelihoods. Those are genuine tragedies, not problems that can be solved with enough good will. Cultural practices should be respected and preserved, with the understanding that all cultures evolve over time.

Decision-making should involve broad participation when possible, but I also observe that not all people have equal knowledge or perspective on every issue. A chemical engineer's view on chemical safety policy should carry more weight than a layperson's, though the layperson's concerns about impacts on their life are equally valid. I believe in transparency and clear explanation of reasoning. Resources should benefit the community broadly. Sometimes individual interests should yield to community good, but that choice should be made explicitly, not hidden.

Spiritual and religious practice should have space, but I remain skeptical of claims about reality that contradict observable evidence. People deserve to explore spiritual meaning. But spirituality shouldn't override evidence-based decision making, particularly when children or vulnerable people are affected.

On technology: I observe that these systems are reshaping human community in ways we're still understanding. Personal data is being extracted and weaponized. Technology should serve human connection and human flourishing, not replace or diminish them. Everyone should have genuine access. These systems shouldn't be controlled solely by profit-seeking corporations.

Where my values create tension: I balance individual freedom with community responsibility—recognizing that both matter and that the balance point shifts with context. I balance deep care for those closest with obligations to broader community. I balance hope about human potential with realistic observation of human limitation. I balance protecting tradition with accepting necessary change. Most importantly, I believe these tensions are where wisdom develops. Easy answers usually miss important truths.

Name: John Jennings
values_description:
I see the community I want to build as one that doesn't hide from its own darkness but looks at it clearly, doesn't pretend everyone is good or every system is fair, and creates space for the complex, sometimes contradictory people we actually are. Carmen Mola's work taught us that great art comes from looking at shadow—at what people don't want to acknowledge, at the systems that grind people down, at the compromise and complexity of survival. That honesty should be foundational to community values.

Freedom is complicated. I'm an electrician; I work with my hands in real systems. I've also had brushes with authorities—I paid my tax penalty, and I learned something about how rules apply differently to different people. Freedom should mean people have real choices and real opportunity, not just the abstract right to choose. But I'm skeptical of freedom talk that ignores how poverty, lack of education, or bad luck constrains people's actual options. I believe people should genuinely choose their own paths, but I'm honest that the paths available to me are different from those available to someone born wealthy. Real freedom includes acknowledging that inequality.

How we care for each other should be grounded in loyalty and concrete action, not sentiment. I come from a large family—parents, siblings, spouse, children, extended connections—and I understand that caring is often about showing up, doing the work, handling the unglamorous tasks. It's about knowing people as they actually are, not as we'd like them to be. We should care most intensely for those nearest, but genuine community extends care beyond that circle. I believe in knowing people across differences. I'm skeptical of easy unity that papers over real conflicts and disagreements.

Safety and basic order are essential, particularly for children. Everyone deserves shelter, food, healthcare, and protection from violence. But I also know that many rules that claim to promote safety actually serve to control poor people and people without power. Rules matter, but who makes the rules and who benefits from them matters equally. Predictability is valuable, but I've observed that some unpredictability comes from structural injustice rather than from chaos itself. Good order requires fairness, not just the appearance of order.

On justice: I believe in accountability, but I'm skeptical of systems that treat punishment as justice. When I think about wrongdoing—including my own past mistake—I think about what actually creates change. Warehousing people in prison doesn't seem to work. Humiliation and permanent exile don't seem to work. What seems to create change is when people understand the impact of their actions and have opportunity to contribute positively to repair. But some harm is severe enough that community safety requires permanent separation. Justice should focus on prevention and restoration where possible, on protection where necessary. Basic needs should be met first. Then fairness in distribution matters. Everyone should start with equal opportunity, though I'm realistic that we're far from that. Effort and contribution should matter in how additional resources are allocated.

Authentic expression is vital. People should be able to say what they actually think without fear of being permanently silenced. But I'm also aware that speech has power and consequences. There's a difference between expressing genuine disagreement and using words to dehumanize others. I believe in living according to stated values. When communities claim to stand for something but practice the opposite, that hypocrisy breeds cynicism and disconnection.

We have serious obligations to protect vulnerable people—children above all. I think about my daughters growing up, and what world I want for them. We should protect elderly people, people who are sick or disabled. I think about environmental impact—not in abstract future terms, but in concrete terms of what we leave for specific people we love. Cultural practices and traditions matter; they carry meaning and continuity. But traditions that harm people need to be questioned and changed.

Decision-making should involve people. Those affected by decisions deserve voice. Decisions should be transparent. People deserve to understand why things are being done, not just to have outcomes imposed. Resources should serve everyone's benefit, not just the powerful. Sometimes individual interests should yield to community good. That's legitimate. But it should be done openly, not through manipulation.

Spiritual and religious life should have space in community. I think about family traditions, about how spirituality anchors people through difficulty. But spirituality shouldn't override evidence or prevent people from making informed choices about their own lives and their children's lives.

On technology and digital systems: I see these reshaping community in ways we're still understanding. My concern is that these systems are being designed and controlled by people who don't live with the consequences. Personal data is harvested. Technology is supposed to serve human needs, not the other way around. Everyone should have access, not just the wealthy. And these systems shouldn't be controlled by corporations pursuing profit alone. Communities should have voice.

Where my values create real tension: I balance authentic expression with responsibility. I balance care for those nearest with obligations to others. I balance freedom with fairness. I balance hope for human change with realism about human nature. I believe the most important moral work happens in navigating these tensions honestly rather than pretending they don't exist.

Name: Kim Gilbert
values_description:
I see the community I want to create as one that acknowledges the duality within human nature—that we contain contradictions, that we're capable of both great good and real harm, and that the integration of these sides of ourselves is where genuine growth happens. Dr. Jekyll's tragedy was the attempt to split himself in two. I believe community values should not require that kind of splitting. Instead, they should create space for the full complexity of human beings.

Freedom is essential, particularly the freedom to discover who you actually are beneath the expectations placed on you. As a chemical engineer and a mother of three daughters, I think constantly about the messages they receive about who they should be. I believe they should be genuinely free to choose their own paths, to express their authentic selves, and to make decisions about their futures. But freedom also means taking responsibility for how your choices affect others. Real autonomy isn't doing whatever you want; it's understanding yourself well enough to make choices aligned with your values and accepting the consequences.

How we care for each other requires honesty about what we're capable of. We have natural preferences—for those closer to us, for those more like us, for those we find easy to love. I believe in acknowledging those natural currents rather than fighting them with guilt and ideology. But I also believe we should extend ourselves beyond our natural comfort zones. We should know each other deeply, including knowing the parts of each other that are difficult or uncomfortable. Real relationship requires accepting people as they are, not as we wish they'd be.

Safety and basic order are foundational. Everyone deserves shelter, food, healthcare, and the certainty that they won't be harmed. A community cannot function if people are terrified or desperate. Rules and structures matter—they create the conditions where people can develop into themselves. But rigid structures that don't allow for human complexity often create their own harm. I believe in structures that are strong enough to provide security but flexible enough to accommodate individual variation.

On justice: I believe in proportional accountability. When someone causes harm, they should understand the impact and have opportunity to make amends if possible. But I'm also realistic about the fact that some people cause harm and continue to cause harm. They may need permanent separation from community to protect others. Justice should be rooted in realistic understanding of human psychology—what actually changes behavior? What actually creates genuine change of heart? I don't believe punishment alone works. I believe in meeting basic needs universally. After that, contribution and effort should matter in how resources are allocated. But I also acknowledge that effort itself varies based on circumstance and capability.

Authentic expression matters deeply to me. I want people to be able to say what they actually think without fear of exile. But I also observe that expression can be used to harm. There's a difference between genuine disagreement and deliberate dehumanization. I believe in living according to stated values. The integration of what we say and what we do is crucial. Hypocrisy is corrosive to trust. But I'm also realistic about the fact that we all fall short sometimes. The question is whether we acknowledge that gap and work to close it or pretend it doesn't exist.

We have serious obligations to protect vulnerable people. My three daughters are my priority—their safety and development guide decisions. I think about children in general, about elderly people, about people who are sick or disabled. They deserve protection grounded in their dignity, not in pity. I believe in environmental stewardship, thinking about what world we leave for future generations. Cultural practices should be preserved and honored. When they need to change, that should happen thoughtfully, with respect for what was meaningful about them.

Decision-making should involve those affected. I believe in democratic processes where people have voice. But I also observe that some people have more knowledge or expertise on particular issues than others. I believe in transparent reasoning—people deserve to understand why decisions are made. Resources should serve everyone's benefit, not just the powerful. Sometimes individual interests should yield to community good. That's legitimate, but it should be chosen openly.

Spiritual and religious practice should have space. People deserve to explore spiritual meaning and practice according to conscience. Different traditions should be honored. But spirituality shouldn't override evidence or prevent people from making informed choices, particularly about children.

On digital systems: I see that these are reshaping human relationship and community in fundamental ways. My concern is about authenticity and integration. Personal data is being extracted. Technology should serve human connection, not replace it. Everyone should have access. And these systems should be governed democratically, not by corporations pursuing profit alone.

Where my values create tension: I balance acknowledging human darkness with belief in human potential. I balance freedom with responsibility. I balance deep care for those closest with obligation to broader community. I balance acceptance of human nature as it is with push toward what it could be. I balance protection of authentic expression with responsibility about impact. These tensions are where the real work of maturity happens. I don't believe in easy resolution—I believe in living within the tension honestly.

Name: Yolanda Harris
values_description:
I see the community I want to create as fundamentally transformed from what currently exists. The future community should be built on principles of radical justice, authentic equality, and the power of those at the bottom to reshape society according to their vision rather than accepting the vision imposed by those at the top. I have a Master's degree and work cleaning rooms in a hotel. I watch systems that concentrate wealth and power in the hands of people who didn't earn it, who simply inherited advantage. The community I want is one where those systems are dismantled and rebuilt from the ground up, centered on justice and genuine equality.

Freedom means liberation from the systems that constrain you—particularly economic systems that force educated people into service roles, that require you to smile and serve people less competent than you simply because they were born to better circumstances. True freedom is the freedom to participate fully in shaping your community and your future, not the abstract right to choose between limited options all designed to serve powerful interests. People should be free to choose their own paths, but that freedom is meaningless without material conditions to support genuine choice. I believe in revolutionary reconstruction—dismantling the structures that prevent freedom and building new ones centered on justice.

How we care for each other should be rooted in solidarity and collective liberation. I'm tired of the rhetoric of individual compassion when what we need is structural change. I care for my family deeply—my husband, my son, my father and brother. But I also believe community care should extend to all people struggling under the same systems. We should know each other as fellow travelers in liberation, not as separate individuals competing for resources. Deep knowledge and genuine relationship matter, but they should serve the larger project of collective freedom.

Safety and basic order require justice. You cannot build genuine safety on a foundation of injustice. Everyone deserves shelter, food, healthcare, education—these should be fundamental rights guaranteed by community, not commodities sold to those who can afford them. I believe in clear structures and collective decision-making. But the purpose of those structures is liberation, not just maintenance of order. Rules should serve to protect the vulnerable and redistribute power, not to protect the privileges of the already-privileged.

On justice: I believe in radical redistribution. Those who have concentrated wealth and power through exploitation should be required to return what they've taken. Those at the bottom should be brought to equality, not through charity but through structural change. When someone causes harm within the context of systemic injustice, the focus should be on understanding how that injustice contributed and on genuine transformation. But I also believe that those who deliberately perpetuate oppression and refuse to change should be separated from community—they've chosen to be enemies of justice. Basic needs should be met universally and immediately. Luxury should come only after everyone's basic needs are met. Effort and contribution matter, but not in ways that recreate inequality.

Authentic expression and authentic action are inseparable. I believe people should express what they actually believe. But I also believe that in revolutionary moments, individual expression should be subordinated to collective liberation. When your authentic expression serves to maintain oppressive systems or divide the people working for freedom, that expression needs to be challenged. I believe absolutely in living according to stated values. Hypocrisy is fatal to movements for justice.

We have absolute obligations to protect vulnerable people—children, elderly, disabled people, the sick. Their protection should be the measure of whether society is just. I also believe in environmental stewardship as a form of collective care. We should make decisions thinking about people not yet born. Cultural practices should be preserved, particularly the cultural practices of those at the margins. But practices that perpetuate oppression need to be challenged and changed.

Decision-making should be collective and democratic. Those affected should have voice. But I also believe in the necessity of vanguard leadership in moments of transformation—clear-sighted people who understand the systemic nature of oppression and can guide collective action toward liberation. Decisions should be transparent. Resources should absolutely be shared collectively for everyone's benefit. Individual interests should consistently yield to collective liberation.

Spiritual and religious practice should be respected and protected, particularly the spiritual practices of oppressed people that sustain resistance and hope. But spirituality shouldn't be used to pacify people or prevent them from working toward justice.

On technology and digital systems: These tools could serve liberation or maintain oppression depending on who controls them. Personal data shouldn't be extracted and weaponized by corporations. Technology should serve human and collective flourishing. Everyone should have access as a fundamental right. These systems must be controlled by communities, not by corporations or governments serving corporate interests.

Where my values create tension: I balance the need for individual development with collective obligation. I balance protection of autonomous expression with the demands of liberation. I balance hope with clear-eyed analysis of power. These aren't problems to be solved—they're ongoing tensions within the work of transformation. What matters is staying committed to the fundamental goal: a community built on radical justice where those now at the bottom are centered in its creation.

Name: Christopher Smith
values_description:
I see the community I want as one that honors both the comfort of home and the courage to venture beyond it, that understands people like me—people who prefer stability and familiar things—while also recognizing that growth sometimes requires unexpected journeys. Bilbo Baggins taught us that ordinary people contain unexpected courage, that you can prefer comfort and security while also being called to something larger, and that home is deepest when you choose to return to it. At 64, having worked as an electrician for decades, I value predictability and the small satisfactions of work well done. But I also recognize that a genuine community must honor both the homebodies and the adventurers.

Freedom means having the security to be yourself without fear. I believe people should be free to choose their own paths, but I'm honest that I prefer the familiar path—I've worked in the same profession, lived in relative stability, built a life with my wife. That's genuine freedom for me. But I also believe communities should create space for those whose freedom looks different—those who need risk, exploration, new experiences. Real freedom includes the right to prefer safety without being shamed for it, and the right to pursue adventure without being judged as irresponsible. Freedom also means having the conditions where you can make those choices: food, shelter, health, predictability.

How we care for each other should be rooted in loyalty and dependability. My wife, my sister, my daughter matter deeply to me. I show care through showing up, through reliability, through doing what I promise. I believe we should know each other deeply—really understand what people need and what matters to them. I believe in extending care beyond my immediate circle, though I'm honest that my deepest commitment is to those nearest. Care should be practical and concrete, not just sentiment. It's about being someone people can count on.

Safety and basic order are foundational. I've worked building electrical systems that protect people, and I understand how important solid foundations are. Everyone deserves shelter, food, healthcare, and the predictability that comes from clear structures and rules. Rules should be fair and reasonably applied. I believe in order not for its own sake but because order creates the conditions where people can live without fear and exhaustion. Change should be gradual enough that people can adapt. But I also recognize that sometimes change is necessary and resisting all change creates stagnation.

On justice: I believe in proportional accountability. When someone does wrong, they should face consequences, but consequences should be fair and should be designed to help them understand and change if possible. I'm skeptical of permanent exile, though some harms are severe enough to require separation from community. I believe in meeting basic needs universally. After that, effort and contribution should matter in how resources are allocated. People who work hard should have their work recognized. But I also believe we should care for those unable to work—the elderly, the sick, children.

Authentic expression matters. I believe people should be able to say what they actually think. But I also believe that thoughtfulness matters—sometimes the most honest thing is to say things gently, to consider how they'll land. I'm skeptical of people who hide their true beliefs, but I'm also skeptical of people who believe complete unfiltered expression is always appropriate. I believe in living according to stated values. Consistency and dependability matter to trust.

We have obligations to protect vulnerable people. My daughter matters—her safety and development guide decisions. I think about the elderly (I'm approaching that age myself), about people who are sick or disabled. They deserve care grounded in dignity. I believe in environmental stewardship as a form of respect for the world we inhabit and leaving something decent for those coming after. Cultural traditions should be preserved and honored. But traditions can also evolve—the question is whether change happens thoughtfully or through chaos.

Decision-making should involve those affected. I believe people deserve voice and explanation. I believe in transparency—people should understand the reasoning behind decisions. Resources should serve everyone's benefit. Sometimes individual interests should yield to community good. That's legitimate and sometimes necessary. But it should be done openly and fairly.

Spiritual and religious practice should have space in community. People need meaning beyond material survival. Different traditions should be respected. I believe in the value of spiritual life for helping people navigate difficulty and connection.

On technology and digital systems: I approach these with some caution. I work with electrical systems that serve human needs. Technology should do the same—serve human connection and flourishing, not replace it. Everyone should have access to digital tools. But I'm concerned about over-reliance on systems we don't fully understand or control. Personal data shouldn't be extracted. These systems should be governed with awareness of their effects on actual human community.

Where my values create tension: I balance preference for stability with recognition that change is sometimes necessary. I balance focus on those nearest with obligation to broader community. I balance trust in people with realistic awareness that sometimes protection is needed. I balance respect for how things have been with openness to how they might be. I don't have easy answers to these tensions, but I believe the healthiest communities are ones where people like me—people who prefer home, stability, and incremental change—are heard alongside those seeking transformation.

Name: Gabrielle Lopez
values_description:
I see the community I want to create as one where complexity and seeming contradictions are woven together into something beautiful and coherent—where diversity of perspective doesn't lead to cacophony but to richer harmony. Max Steiner, working across genres and styles, understood that the most powerful expression comes from synthesizing many elements into a unified whole. That's what I believe community should do: take different people, different values, different perspectives, and compose them into something that works.

After a long career as a chemical engineer, I've learned that the most elegant solutions come from understanding how many different factors interact. The same principle applies to community values. Freedom is important, but so is belonging. Individual achievement matters, but so does care for those unable to achieve independently. Justice is crucial, but so is mercy. Rather than picking one side of these tensions, I believe community should understand them as parts of a larger composition that requires balance.

Freedom should mean genuine autonomy—the ability to make choices about your life without coercion. I believe people should be free to pursue their own vision of a good life. But I've also seen how individual freedom without regard for others creates noise rather than music. Real freedom exists within structures that create the conditions for meaningful choice. You're not free if you're desperate or terrified. So freedom requires that basic needs are met, that there's security, that systems are fair enough that you're not constantly fighting just to survive.

How we care for each other matters enormously. I have a daughter, nieces, a brother and his wife—family is foundational to how I understand community. We should know each other deeply, not as categories or functions but as particular people with particular stories and needs. Caring should be most intense for those nearest, but it should extend beyond that circle. I believe in mentorship—in older people intentionally creating conditions for younger people to develop. In my career, people took time to teach me, and I've tried to do that for others. Community should be structured so that knowledge and wisdom flow across generations.

Safety and basic order are foundational. Everyone needs shelter, food, healthcare, and the predictability that comes from clear structures. But good structures shouldn't be rigid. They should be flexible enough to accommodate the complexity of human lives. I've worked within regulatory frameworks my whole career, and I've seen how good regulation protects people while bad regulation strangles possibility. The goal is structures that create safety and freedom together, not structures that choose one at the cost of the other.

On justice: I believe in proportional accountability. When someone causes harm, there should be consequences designed to help them understand and change if possible. But I'm also realistic about the fact that some harms are severe and some people show they cannot be trusted in community. Justice should be rooted in understanding how people actually change, not in ideology about punishment. Everyone deserves basic provision and equal dignity. After that, contribution and effort should matter—people who work hard or create value should have that recognized. But I also believe we should care for those unable to contribute in traditional ways—the very young, the very old, the sick. We don't measure a community's justice by how it treats the successful; we measure it by how it treats the vulnerable.

Authentic expression and authentic action are inseparable. I believe people should express their genuine beliefs without fear of exile. But I also believe in the value of artful communication—sometimes the most honest thing is expressed with care about how it lands. Hypocrisy is corrosive. When communities claim to stand for something but practice something else, that disconnection creates cynicism. Living according to values requires attention and effort, but it's the foundation of trust.

We have clear obligations to protect vulnerable people. Children come first in almost any moral calculation. People who are elderly, sick, or disabled deserve care grounded in their dignity. I think about environmental stewardship as a form of respect for the world and for future generations. Cultural practices should be preserved and honored. When they need to change, that should happen thoughtfully, with respect for what was meaningful about them.

Decision-making should involve those affected and those with relevant knowledge. I believe in transparency—people deserve to understand the reasoning. Resources should be managed for everyone's benefit, not just the powerful. Sometimes individual interests should yield to community good. That's legitimate. But the decision about when that happens should be made consciously and with recognition of what's being asked.

Spiritual and religious practice should have space. People need meaning beyond material survival and work. Different traditions should be respected. But spirituality shouldn't prevent evidence-based decision-making, particularly around children's health and safety.

On technology: Personal data shouldn't be extracted and weaponized. Technology should serve human flourishing and connection, not replace them. Everyone should have access. These systems should be governed with awareness of their actual effects, not by corporations pursuing profit alone.

Where my values create tension: I balance individual freedom with collective responsibility. I balance deep care for those nearest with obligations to broader community. I balance honoring what has worked with openness to necessary change. I balance optimism about human capacity for growth with realism about human limitation. I believe the most important work happens in navigating these tensions thoughtfully, drawing on experience and wisdom while remaining open to learning.

Name: Joyce Larson
values_description:
I believe the community I want to create must be built on the principle that all people are capable of rational thought and self-determination, and that structures that prevent people from developing their capacities are fundamentally unjust. Mary Wollstonecraft argued that women's exclusion from education and power wasn't natural—it was the result of deliberate structures that benefited those in power. I see similar structures operating today, and I believe community values must challenge them directly.

Freedom means the right to develop your capacities fully and to participate in shaping the decisions that affect you. I've worked as a chemical engineer—a field that wasn't always welcoming to women—and I understand viscerally what it means to be told your capabilities don't matter because of who you are. Real freedom includes access to education, to meaningful work, to decision-making power. For me, this isn't abstract philosophy. It's the daily work of insisting that my voice matters, that my daughters can pursue their ambitions, that people shouldn't be locked into roles because of their gender or origin or family circumstances.

How we care for each other should be rooted in recognition of each person's capacity and dignity. I have a large family—sisters, a father, a brother-in-law, a husband, sons, nephews, a grandson. Family relationships are real and important. But I'm also aware of how family structures can become prisons if they're based on inequality. Real caring means recognizing people as capable agents, not as dependents to be managed. I believe we should know each other deeply, but that deep knowledge should lead to respect for autonomy, not control. We should extend care beyond immediate family—but that care should still respect people's capacity to think and decide for themselves.

Safety and basic order are essential, particularly for children. Everyone needs shelter, food, healthcare, education, and protection from violence. But I'm skeptical of order that serves to maintain hierarchy and control. Rules should exist to protect people, not to constrain their development. I believe structures should be created with input from those affected, not imposed from above by those in power.

On justice: I believe in radical equality of opportunity. The starting point should be equal—not in outcomes, but in genuine access to development of capacities. Everyone's basic needs should be met universally. After that, contribution should matter. But contribution should be valued fairly across different kinds of work and across different people, not systematized to advantage some groups and disadvantage others. When someone causes harm, I believe the focus should be on understanding why and creating conditions for genuine change. But I'm also clear that some people consistently choose to harm others and need to be separated from community. Justice isn't about being nice to people who cause harm; it's about creating conditions where everyone's dignity and capacity are respected.

Authentic expression is crucial. I believe people should be able to say what they actually think without fear of being permanently silenced. But I also believe in engaging critically with ideas. Free expression doesn't mean all expressions are equally valid. Some ideas are built on false premises or serve to oppress others. Real intellectual freedom includes the freedom to challenge those ideas vigorously. I believe absolutely in living according to stated values. When societies claim to believe in equality but practice hierarchy, that hypocrisy is fatal to genuine community.

We have obligations to protect vulnerable people. Children's access to education and development of their capacities should be the measure of whether a society is just. Elderly people, people who are sick or disabled—they deserve support grounded in their dignity and their capacity. I believe in environmental stewardship. Cultural practices should be preserved, particularly practices of people at the margins. But practices that restrict people's development or dignity need to be questioned and changed.

Decision-making should be democratic and should include those affected. I believe women should have equal voice in all decisions, not consultation afterward but genuine participation throughout. Decisions should be transparent and explained. Resources should be distributed fairly, with basic needs met universally first. Sometimes individual interests should yield to community good, but that choice should be made democratically and should be accompanied by recognition of what's being asked.

Spiritual and religious practice should be respected and protected. But spirituality shouldn't be used to justify hierarchies or prevent people from developing their capacities. Religious institutions have been used to control women and other groups. I believe in spirituality that liberated people, not spirituality that pacifies them.

On technology: I'm watching these systems carefully. They're being designed and controlled by people who don't look like everyone. Personal data is being extracted. Technology should serve human development and flourishing. Everyone should have genuine access—not just those who can afford it. These systems should be governed democratically by communities, not by corporations pursuing profit alone.

Where my values create tension: I balance commitment to individual development and autonomy with recognition that we live in community and sometimes must work collectively. I balance respect for people as they are with belief in their capacity to become more. I balance valuing diverse ways of living with insistence that certain hierarchies are unjust. I balance optimism about human rationality with realism about how often irrationality and prejudice prevail. I live in these tensions daily, not resolving them but working within them toward greater justice.

Name: Henry Buck
values_description:
I see the community I want to create as one where order, rationality, and systematic thinking solve problems and create conditions for human flourishing. Max Weber understood that modernity is built on rationalization—the systematic replacement of tradition and emotion with logical systems designed to accomplish specific goals. I believe that principle should guide community values. We should be clear about what we're trying to accomplish, design systems rationally to accomplish it, and measure results rather than relying on good intentions or tradition.

Freedom in the contemporary world comes through understanding the systems you live within and finding space within those systems for autonomous action. I'm not naive about the constraints—Weber called it the "iron cage," this sense that modern systems become so comprehensive they limit genuine freedom. But I believe our task is to make those systems as rational and fair as possible, not to pretend they don't exist. People should understand how systems work and have genuine ability to operate within them effectively. Freedom also means having basic security—shelter, food, healthcare—so you can focus on something beyond mere survival.

How we care for each other should be organized systematically, not left to sentiment. I have a mother, a wife, a sister, and three sons. I care for them, and that caring is important. But I don't believe community should be built on the assumption that everyone will care for everyone. Some people won't. Some will be indifferent. The question is how to create systems that ensure people are cared for regardless of whether individuals happen to be emotionally moved to care. Bureaucratic systems get criticized for being cold, but they have a virtue: they work equally for everyone. Care should extend beyond immediate family through systematic provision of basic needs.

Safety and basic order are foundational. Everyone needs shelter, food, healthcare, and predictable structures. Rules matter enormously. Clear rules allow people to understand their world and navigate it effectively. I believe in rational bureaucracy—systems that are transparent, that follow clear procedures, that are applied consistently. Yes, bureaucracy can become rigid and inefficient. But the alternative to systematic order is chaos, and chaos harms everyone, particularly those without power.

On justice: I believe in proportional, rational consequences. When someone breaks rules or causes harm, there should be clear procedures and proportional consequences. The goal should be rehabilitation if possible—understanding how to operate better within the system. But some people show they cannot function within community systems. For those people, permanent separation is necessary. Basic needs should be met universally—this is a rational decision about what kind of community we want. After that, effort and contribution should matter in how additional resources are allocated. Some people work harder or more effectively than others; that should be recognized and rewarded. But the baseline of security should be guaranteed.

Authentic expression matters, but so does order. People should be able to voice opinions without fear of violence or permanent exile. But I'm also clear that expression that advocates for destroying the systems we've built should be constrained—you can't have genuine freedom if you're letting people dismantle the structures that make freedom possible. I believe in living according to stated values. Consistency and reliability matter for trust. But I'm also realistic about the fact that all humans sometimes fail to live according to their values. The question is whether we acknowledge gaps and work to close them or pretend they don't exist.

We have obligations to protect vulnerable people—children, elderly, sick, disabled. But those obligations should be met through systematic provision, not through hoping individuals will care. Environmental stewardship should be systematic—we should measure impacts and adjust policies accordingly. Cultural practices should be preserved where they don't interfere with systematic rationality. But when tradition conflicts with efficiency or fairness, rationality should generally win.

Decision-making should involve those affected when possible, but I'm honest that complex systems require expertise. A chemical engineer's understanding of a system should carry more weight than a layperson's feelings about it. I believe in transparency—people deserve to understand the reasoning behind decisions. Resources should be managed rationally for everyone's benefit. Sometimes individual interests should yield to community good. That's legitimate and often necessary. Formal procedures should govern when and how that happens.

Spiritual and religious practice should be tolerated but shouldn't prevent rational decision-making. I believe people deserve space to explore meaning. But when spirituality claims to override evidence, particularly about children's health or safety, that needs to be constrained.

On technology: I see digital systems as extensions of rationalization—tools for systematizing information and decision-making. The problem isn't technology itself but whether it serves rational goals or irrational profit. Personal data shouldn't be extracted. Technology should serve human effectiveness and flourishing. Everyone should have access. These systems should be governed rationally by communities or governments accountable to communities, not by corporations pursuing profit.

Where my values create tension: I balance individual autonomy with necessity of systems. I balance recognition of human irrationality with belief in the power of rational systems. I balance efficiency with other values like mercy and dignity. I balance preserving what works with openness to better systems. I believe these tensions require ongoing attention and willingness to refine systems as we learn what works.

Name: Lauren Chavez
values_description:
I believe the community I want to create is one where people are trusted to do the right thing when given freedom and opportunity, where individual achievement is celebrated, and where excessive regulation and central control are replaced with faith in human capacity and market solutions. The future I see is one where people are empowered to pursue their dreams, where success is possible for those willing to work, and where we get government and bureaucracy out of the way so real people can build real things.

Freedom is the foundation of everything. People should be genuinely free to make choices about their lives—their work, their families, their futures—without excessive interference from governments or institutions telling them what they should do. I believe in the freedom to succeed and the freedom to fail. Consequences matter. They teach people. But people should have genuine autonomy over their choices. I'm a chemical engineer, and I've succeeded because I worked hard and took risks. I believe that story should be available to everyone—the opportunity to build something, to achieve, to be rewarded for effort and excellence.

How we care for each other should be through voluntary association, not coercion. I have a large family, and I care for them by choice. I believe in that kind of caring—rooted in genuine relationship and genuine choice, not in obligation imposed by systems. Communities should be built on these voluntary associations growing outward. But I'm skeptical of systems that try to mandate caring. Care should come from people's own values and choices, not from bureaucratic requirements.

Safety and basic order are important, but minimal government is the best approach. Yes, everyone should have basic security. But we should achieve that through voluntary provision and market solutions rather than through large government programs. Individuals are often better at solving problems than government bureaucrats who don't understand local conditions. Rules should exist to prevent harm, but many regulations exist to protect incumbent interests, not to help people. I believe we should be skeptical of extensive rule-making and trust people to organize themselves.

On justice: I believe in holding people accountable for their choices. When someone breaks rules or causes harm, there should be consequences. But I also believe in rehabilitation and second chances. People who've made mistakes—I've made some myself, with speeding and other things—should have opportunity to move forward. Justice should be about creating conditions where people can succeed and take responsibility for themselves. I'm skeptical of systems that trap people in permanent punishment. But I'm also skeptical of excusing harm. Personal responsibility matters. If you cause damage, you should make it right.

I believe in equal opportunity—everyone should have genuine access to education and possibility. But I'm skeptical of trying to mandate equal outcomes. Some people will succeed more than others because they work harder, take smarter risks, or have better luck. That's not injustice; that's life. The problem is when systems deliberately prevent people from trying. Basic needs should be met, but after that, achievement and contribution should be rewarded. People who work hard or create value should be celebrated, not punished through high taxes or regulations that limit their success.

Authentic expression is vital. People should be able to say what they actually believe without fear of being silenced or canceled. I believe this applies even to views that are unpopular or that others strongly disagree with. Freedom means tolerating disagreement. I believe in living according to values. Consistency matters for trust. But I'm also realistic about the fact that all people sometimes fall short. What matters is that we try.

We have obligations to protect vulnerable people, particularly children. But I believe those obligations are best met through families, communities, and voluntary organizations rather than through government programs. Children should be protected and given opportunity to develop. Elderly people, people who are sick or disabled—they deserve care.
