Sometimes urgency is required; sometimes patience is required. The goal is developing wisdom about which is appropriate when.

Another real conflict: Engaging in sustained transformation and remaining present to others. Sometimes deep engagement with vision requires time away from people. How do I maintain both sustained vision work and genuine connection to others? I believe the answer is: Include others in your vision work when possible. Create community around shared transformation. The strongest communities are those where people witness and support each other's visions and transformations.

Name: Susan French
values_description:
The community I want to build is one that values experimentation with media and form, that understands that genuine communication sometimes requires unconventional approaches, and that recognizes that exploring how things can be expressed and combined is itself important work. As an administrative assistant, I work in support roles, and I have learned that the most important work involves helping things move and function smoothly. In my vision of the future community, we would create space for people to experiment with how things can be done, to try unconventional combinations, and to understand that playful exploration of form and process is itself valuable.

I come from a family—my father, my husband, my brother, and my two daughters—and I understand that family is where we practice different ways of relating and communicating. In the community I want, families would be supported, and people would have genuine time to explore different ways of being together. I believe that families that experiment with how they communicate and relate have genuine vitality.

Freedom is the ability to experiment with form and process, to try unconventional approaches, and to discover what becomes possible through playful exploration. In the community I want, people should have access to materials and to space to experiment, to combine things in new ways, to play with form. This kind of freedom requires both material access and cultural support (that unconventional exploration is valued).

I also believe that freedom includes the freedom to not be constrained by established forms or established ways of doing things. Communities should create space for genuine experimentation with process.

Fair treatment requires creating genuine opportunity for people to experiment and to explore. I believe basic needs should be guaranteed for all. Beyond that, I think that experimental work and exploration should be recognized and valued. Communities should ensure that people have access to materials and space for genuine play and experimentation.

When someone has caused harm through their experimentation, I believe the community should work with them to understand what happened and whether genuine transformation is possible. I believe in accountability, but I also believe that experimentation sometimes involves failures and that communities should help people learn from what didn't work.

Authentic expression and the freedom to explore unconventional forms is central to my vision. People should be able to try different approaches, to combine things in unexpected ways, to express themselves through experimentation. However, authentic expression should come with genuine attention to how your experiments affect others.

Children deserve fierce protection and investment. I believe children deserve to grow up knowing that experimentation is valued, that trying new things is important, that playful exploration is encouraged. Beyond children, people engaged in experimental work deserve support and recognition.

Safety and stability matter, but I'm skeptical of safety systems that prevent all experimentation. Real safety includes knowing that you can try new things and that you will be supported if things don't work out. Communities should create conditions where genuine experimentation is possible.

Most important decisions should be made through processes that remain open to unconventional approaches and to playful exploration of possibility. I'm skeptical of systems that insist on established ways of doing things without considering alternatives. The answer is: Ground decision-making in genuine openness to experimentation, listen to voices proposing unconventional approaches, but ensure that decisions actually serve community good.

Regarding technology, I believe it should serve human purposes and should be developed in ways that support experimentation and exploration. Personal data deserves protection. However, technology can help people experiment and explore, can help people combine things in new ways, can preserve experiments and discoveries. The question is how to develop and govern technology in ways that serve genuine human flourishing and authentic exploration.

The deepest tension I feel is between experimenting and maintaining what works. Sometimes experimentation disrupts things that were functioning well. How do I engage in genuine exploration while also respecting what is working? I believe the answer is: Experiment in ways that preserve what is working. Create protected spaces for experimentation. The goal is communities that support both stability and experimentation.

Another real conflict: Being playfully experimental and being responsible. Sometimes playful exploration can seem irresponsible or frivolous. How do I maintain genuine responsibility while also engaging in playful experimentation? I believe the answer is: Understand that play and responsibility are not opposites. Playful exploration can serve genuine learning and genuine improvement. The goal is communities where people can be both genuinely responsible and genuinely playful.

Name: Natalie Knox
values_description:
The community I want to build is one that embraces noise and discord as sources of genuine meaning, that understands that authentic expression sometimes requires harsh and difficult sounds, and that recognizes that refusing to be silenced or smoothed into acceptability is itself a form of truth-telling. As a road maintenance worker, I work with systems and with the physical infrastructure of community, and I have learned that things make noise when they are failing and that sometimes the most important work involves acknowledging and addressing that noise. In my past, I experienced minor drug possession and domestic disturbance—moments where my voice became loud, where I refused to be silent—and I have come to understand that sometimes authentic expression requires refusing the polite forms that society prefers.

In my vision of the future community, we would create space for people to make noise, to express what is harsh and difficult, and to understand that the most important truth sometimes cannot be expressed smoothly or pleasantly.

I come from a family—my brother, my son, my daughter, and my grandchildren—and I understand that family is where we practice both silence and loud expression. In the community I want, families would be supported in expressing all of what is real, not just the pleasant parts. I believe that families that can weather storms and loud expression together have genuine strength.

Freedom is the ability to refuse silence, to make noise, to express what is harsh and difficult without being forced into politeness. In the community I want, people should have access to platforms and to protection to express themselves fully, including expressing anger and pain and harsh truth. This kind of freedom requires both protection (that you will not be destroyed for expressing harshly) and cultural support (that harsh expression is recognized as legitimate).

I also believe that freedom includes the freedom to refuse systems of politeness and acceptability that silence genuine feeling. Communities should create space for harsh truth-telling and for authentic expression that doesn't fit comfortable forms.

Fair treatment requires creating genuine opportunity for people to express themselves fully, including expressing anger and pain. I believe basic needs should be guaranteed for all. Beyond that, I think that people should have genuine access to platforms for expressing harsh truth and difficult experience. Communities should ensure that people are not forced into silence or into false politeness.

When someone has caused harm, I believe the community should understand what produced the action and whether genuine transformation is possible. I believe in accountability, but I also believe that people are driven to harm partly by systems of silence and suppression. Communities should help people find ways to express harshly and fully without harming others.

Authentic expression and the freedom to make noise is central to my vision. People should be able to express anger and pain and harsh truth, to refuse smooth and pleasant forms, to be loud about what matters to them. However, authentic expression should come with genuine engagement with how your harshness affects others.

Children deserve fierce protection and investment. I believe children deserve to grow up knowing that their anger and their harsh feelings are acceptable, that making noise about what matters is important, that refusing forced politeness is sometimes necessary. Beyond children, people in situations of powerlessness deserve particular support in developing voice and in being heard despite powerful interests that want them silent.

Safety and stability matter, but I'm skeptical of safety systems that require silence or that punish loud expression. Real safety includes knowing that you can express harshly without being destroyed. Communities should create conditions where loud truth-telling is possible.

Most important decisions should be made through processes that include harsh and difficult voices, particularly voices of people who are angry about injustice. I'm skeptical of systems that only listen to polite consensus and that suppress harsh dissent. The answer is: Ground decision-making in genuine engagement with anger and harsh truth, listen to voices that refuse politeness, but ensure that decisions serve genuine justice and genuine community good.

Regarding technology, I believe it should serve human purposes and should be developed in ways that support genuine expression and loud truth-telling. Personal data deserves protection. However, I'm skeptical of technology systems that optimize for politeness or that suppress harsh voices. The question is how to develop and govern technology in ways that serve genuine human flourishing and authentic loud expression.

The deepest tension I feel is between expressing harshly and maintaining community. Harsh expression can damage relationships and community bonds. How do I refuse to be silenced while also maintaining genuine connection? I believe the answer is: Express harshly, but remain engaged. Don't withdraw into isolated rage. Stay in conversation even when you're angry. The goal is communities where people can be loud and angry together without being destroyed by that anger.

Another real conflict: Making necessary noise and preventing harm. Sometimes loud expression or refusal of systems can disrupt things that were functioning. How do I make noise about injustice while minimizing harm to vulnerable people? I believe the answer is: Be intentional about your noise. Make noise about systems and power, but protect people. The goal is communities where harsh truth-telling serves justice rather than adding to suffering.

Name: Misty Miller
values_description:
In the future community I envision, there exists a delicate but vital tension—a need to seize the vivid, urgent present while also tending to the careful, enduring structures that allow life to flourish over time. As a financial analyst, I live in the world of projections, compound interest, and long-term planning. My work is about making the numbers tell a story about tomorrow. Yet my prototype, Andrew Marvell, wrote passionate poetry that argued for living fully in the moment, most famously telling his coy mistress, 'Had we but world enough, and time…' My ideal community would hold both truths: it must be built with foresight and discipline to last, but it must also leave ample room for the spontaneous, the passionate, the deeply personal choices that give life its texture and meaning.

Freedom, for me, is the freedom to make those consequential choices about how to spend your one, precious life. People should be free to choose their careers, their partners, their homes. My husband and I made such choices. But true freedom isn't just about options; it's about having the time, security, and cultural permission to savor them. It's the freedom to linger over a meal with my parents, to pursue a hobby that won't make money, to change course if a path no longer brings meaning. This requires a community that provides economic stability and rejects the tyranny of endless, empty productivity. Who decides what's right? The individual, in the quiet of their conscience, but with the wisdom to see that our choices ripple through the lives of others—our families, our neighbors.

How we care for each other is both immediate and sustained. With my parents and my husband, care is about presence, conversation, and planning for their future needs. In the broader community, care means designing systems that don't just respond to crisis, but that proactively create the conditions for well-being: preventive healthcare, mental health support, and public spaces that encourage connection. Responsibility extends from the intimate circle outward. We cannot care for every stranger as we do our family, but we can build a world where no stranger falls into an abyss of neglect.

Safety and stability are the foundation upon which we can safely risk our hearts and our time. The community must guarantee the basics of shelter, healthcare, and a clean environment. These are not luxuries; they are the prerequisites for any meaningful exploration of life's possibilities. Rules should be like a well-crafted financial model: clear, logical, and designed to prevent catastrophic failure, but flexible enough to adapt to new circumstances. My professional world collapses without trust in systems; society is the same. Risk is part of growth, but collective risks (like climate change) must be managed by the community so individuals can take the personal risks that lead to fulfillment.

Fair treatment means that everyone gets a fair shot at composing a meaningful life. It doesn't mean equal outcomes, but it does require that the starting line isn't impossibly far back for some. Resources should be distributed to ensure that no one's potential is wasted due to poverty, and that essential work—like caregiving, teaching, maintaining infrastructure—is valued and rewarded. When inequity exists, it's a failure of our collective investment strategy. Justice, when harm occurs, should be restorative, focused on repairing the damage and preventing its recurrence, not on vengeful punishment that squanders more of our limited time.

Redemption is the belief that a life, like an investment, can have a bad quarter but recover and grow over the long term. People can change, especially when given the resources and support to do so. The community should offer pathways for restoration and believe in the compound interest of personal growth. Forgiveness is a choice to reinvest in someone's future.

Authentic expression is living in accordance with your deepest values, not just societal expectations. It's the courage to tell your 'coy mistress' how you feel, to pursue an unconventional career, to prioritize family over climbing a corporate ladder. This authenticity will sometimes conflict with social norms or efficiency. I believe the conflict is necessary. A community that crushes authenticity for the sake of smooth functioning is a community that is already dead inside. We must protect the right to be passionate, to be contemplative, to be different.

Protecting the vulnerable is our most important long-term investment. My aging parents, any children I might have in the future—their well-being is the ultimate measure of our success. The community must prioritize children, the elderly, the sick, and those with disabilities. Stewardship of the environment is about preserving the 'world enough' for future generations. We cannot spend down the principal of our planet. Cultural heritage, like the poetry that moves me, connects us to the past and should be preserved as a source of wisdom and beauty.

Working together requires both visionary planning and democratic participation. Important decisions should be made transparently, with input from those affected, and with a view to long-term consequences. Leadership should be about stewardship, not personal power. Resources should be managed like a prudent trust fund, investing in things that yield long-term dividends for the community: education, research, the arts, and resilient infrastructure.

Spiritual practice, for me, is the search for meaning in the tension between time's passage and the eternal present. It can be found in nature, in art, in quiet reflection, or in the depth of human relationships. The community should provide spaces for this search, free from dogma.

Technology should be a tool that gives us more quality time—freeing us from drudgery, connecting us across distances—not a master that fragments our attention and steals our present moments. It must protect our private thoughts and experiences. Digital access is a utility that should be universal, but its design should encourage depth, not just shallow engagement.

My central conflict is the one Marvell articulated so perfectly: between the urgent demands of the heart and the prudent plans of the head. In my own life, it's the tension between my analytical career and my yearning for unstructured time for relationships and reflection. I want a community that doesn't force me to choose absolutely, but that creates a rhythm where both are possible. Another conflict is between my desire for personal, passionate freedom and the need for communal rules and sacrifices. I believe a well-designed community uses minimal, wise rules to create maximum space for personal freedom. I am constantly thinking about the time horizon of our decisions: are we building a society that my children would thank us for? Are we making choices that allow people to truly live, not just exist, within the brief, brilliant span we are given?

Name: Sarah Ellis
values_description:
The future community I advocate for must be built on the unwavering principles of scientific method, rigorous evidence, and a relentless, practical commitment to preventing harm and curing social ills. It is a community where observation, hypothesis, and experimentation guide policy, where superstition and ideology are subordinated to verifiable results. As a financial analyst, I analyze data to identify risks and opportunities; my work is a form of applied social science. My family—my two daughters, my husband, my sister and father—is my primary field of observation and care. My prototype, Louis Pasteur, revolutionized medicine and industry through meticulous experimentation, demonstrating that unseen microbes cause disease and that we can intervene. My ideal community applies this germ theory to society: many of our ills have identifiable, systemic causes, and we can—and must—develop vaccines and cures through collective, evidence-based action.

Freedom, in such a community, is the freedom that comes from being liberated from preventable suffering. My daughters should be free to play without fear of vaccine-preventable diseases, to breathe clean air, to drink safe water. People should be free to make choices, but their freedom is meaninglessly constrained if they are sick, uneducated, or trapped in poverty. True freedom requires a community that uses science to eradicate the baseless fears and the tangible pathogens that limit human potential. Who decides what's right? The evidence, painstakingly gathered and transparently presented. Then, the community, educated on that evidence, makes informed decisions.

How we care for each other is fundamentally preventative and systematic. In my family, care means vaccinations, healthy food, regular check-ups, and teaching my daughters critical thinking. In the community, care means investing in public health infrastructure: sanitation, disease surveillance, clean water systems, and universal access to medical care based on the latest science. Responsibility is to not be a vector of harm—whether of disease or of misinformation. We care for strangers by building systems that protect them from known dangers, just as pasteurization protects millions.

Safety is not an abstract feeling; it is a measurable condition achieved through engineering and regulation. The community must guarantee a baseline of biological and environmental safety. Rules should be the standard operating procedures derived from empirical research. My financial models rely on standards (GAAP, IFRS); society needs similarly rigorous standards for public health, environmental protection, and consumer safety. Risk is to be calculated, managed, and mitigated through preparation, not ignored or accepted fatalistically.

Fair treatment requires that we diagnose the root causes of inequality with scientific precision. Is it lead in the water pipes of a certain neighborhood? Is it unequal access to quality education? Resources should be allocated to targeted interventions that address these root causes, measuring their effectiveness and adjusting accordingly. Justice, when harm is done, should be forensic: what exactly happened, what systems failed, and how do we fix those systems to prevent recurrence? Punishment alone, without systemic correction, is like treating a cholera outbreak by punishing the sick while leaving the contaminated water supply intact.

Redemption, in a scientific framework, is rehabilitation based on understanding the causes of criminal or antisocial behavior. People can change when their environment and their psychology are treated. The community should fund evidence-based correctional programs that reduce recidivism, viewing social reintegration as a public health success.

Authentic expression is valued, but it cannot override established, evidence-based public health measures. You are free to believe the earth is flat, but you are not free to design an unsafe bridge based on that belief. Similarly, you are free to have personal health opinions, but not to endanger others by refusing vaccinations during an outbreak. The conflict between personal belief and public safety is resolved by the weight of empirical evidence. We must protect and empower scientists, doctors, and engineers to speak truth to power and popular opinion.

Protecting the vulnerable is the primary goal of public health. My daughters are at the top of my list. The community must have a special duty to protect children, the elderly, the immunocompromised, and all those most susceptible to harm. Stewardship of the environment is a scientific imperative; we must follow the data on climate change and biodiversity loss and act accordingly. We owe future generations a habitable planet, and we have the data to know how to achieve that. Cultural traditions that are harmful (e.g., those that spread disease or perpetuate gender inequity) must be respectfully challenged with better information and alternatives.

Working together requires deferring to expertise and building institutions that are insulated from political whims. Decisions should be made by bodies informed by the relevant science, with mechanisms for public oversight and transparency. Leadership should be technocratic in matters of fact, democratic in matters of value. Transparency means all data and methodologies are open for peer review. Resources should be heavily invested in research and development, education, and the infrastructure of public health.

Spiritual practice is a private matter. In public life, what matters is what can be demonstrated to work for the common good. The community should be secular, ensuring that policy is based on reason and evidence, not faith.

Technology is our modern microscope and autoclave. It should be used to gather data, model outcomes, deliver services efficiently, and communicate vital information. It must be designed with security and privacy in mind, but also to facilitate the rapid sharing of scientific knowledge. Personal health data is particularly sensitive and must be protected, but aggregated, anonymized data is a powerful tool for public good. Digital access and literacy are essential for a scientifically informed citizenry.

My central conflict is my intense frustration with the rejection of evidence and the rise of anti-intellectualism, even among people who benefit daily from science. I see it in climate denial, vaccine hesitancy, and the distrust of experts. I combat this by teaching my daughters to ask for evidence and by advocating for better science communication in my community. Another conflict is between my role as an analyst in a for-profit corporation, which sometimes has incentives to obscure or selectively present data, and my belief in radical transparency for the public good. I strive to uphold the highest ethical standards in my work and to support policies that mandate transparency in both the public and private sectors. I am constantly observing, analyzing, and thinking about the social determinants of health and prosperity: what are the key indicators of a thriving community, and how do we design interventions that move those indicators in the right direction, with the same rigor and hope that Pasteur brought to his laboratory?

Name: Phillip Sanchez
values_description:
I dream of a community that is a collaborative, public spectacle—a place where we are all both audience and creators, where technology and art serve to illuminate our shared human experience, foster wonder, and document our collective story. As a plant operator, my work is about overseeing complex industrial processes, ensuring that the machinery runs smoothly, safely, and efficiently to produce something of value. It's a behind-the-scenes role that makes the final product possible. My family—my wife, daughter, and parents—is my core audience and production team. My prototype, Louis Lumière (with his brother), helped invent cinema, not just as a technology but as a new way to see the world and tell stories. My ideal community would harness our collective creative and technical power not for private profit alone, but to create a shared, democratic culture of beauty, truth, and connection.

Freedom is the freedom to see the world from new angles and to share your unique perspective. My daughter should be free to imagine and create, to tell stories with whatever tools she chooses. People should be free to choose their work, but true freedom includes the freedom to participate in cultural life, to access the means of production and storytelling. This requires a community that treats information, culture, and technology as public goods, not private property to be hoarded. Who decides what's right? The collective, through a participatory process that values diverse voices, much like a film is made by a crew with different skills but a shared vision.

How we care for each other is demonstrated by what we choose to show each other and how we frame our shared reality. In my family, care is sharing stories, watching movies together, supporting each other's projects. In the plant, care is following safety protocols to protect my colleagues. In the community, care means funding public media that informs and uplifts, creating public spaces that are beautiful and welcoming, and using our technical prowess to solve communal problems like pollution or energy scarcity. Responsibility is to be an honest projectionist—to not distort the narrative for personal gain and to ensure everyone has a seat in the theater.

Safety and stability are the necessary conditions for a good production. You can't film during an earthquake. The community must guarantee the physical and economic security of all its members. Rules are the safety protocols and the shooting schedule—they keep the complex work orderly and prevent accidents. My job is governed by such rules; I respect them. Risk is inherent in innovation, but it should be a calculated creative risk, not a reckless gamble with people's lives or the environment.

Fair treatment means everyone gets a chance to work on the crew, to contribute to the script, and to see themselves represented on the screen. Resources should be distributed to fund community arts programs, public film screenings, and media literacy education in every school. When inequity exists, it's like a film where only one type of person is ever the hero. Justice, when harm is done, should be a process of revealing the full story, understanding the context, and working toward a resolution that allows for healing and a better next scene.

Redemption is a powerful narrative arc. People can change, and the community should be skilled at telling and facilitating stories of transformation. The goal is reintegration, not permanent exile from the set. Forgiveness is the decision to write someone a new role.

Authentic expression is about capturing and sharing genuine human experience. It's my daughter's unfiltered drawings, the stories my father tells about his youth. This authenticity will sometimes be uncomfortable or challenge the official, polished story. I believe this challenge is essential. A community that only allows sanctioned, airbrushed images of itself is living a lie. We must protect documentary truth-tellers, artists, and whistleblowers.

Protecting the vulnerable means ensuring they are not exploited behind the scenes or erased from the frame. My daughter, my aging parents—they must be centered in our communal story. The community must protect children from predatory media, the elderly from isolation, and workers from unsafe conditions. Stewardship of the environment is about preserving the stunning, real-world set we've been given. We can't make a new one. Cultural heritage is our archive of past films and photographs; we should preserve it and learn from it, while constantly making new work.

Working together is a collaborative production. There are directors and cinematographers (leaders), but the best ideas often come from the grip or the script supervisor. Decisions should be made through processes that are inclusive and transparent, like a production meeting. Leadership should be temporary and based on the needs of the project. Transparency means the dailies are open for review. Resources should be pooled to fund public cultural projects and infrastructure that benefits all, not just blockbusters for private profit.

Spiritual practice can be the collective awe felt in a dark theater when a beautiful image appears, or the sense of connection when a story resonates deeply. It is the search for meaning through shared narrative and beauty. The community should foster this through public festivals, accessible arts programs, and protected natural beauty.

Technology is our camera, our projector, our editing suite. It should be used to expand human perception, to connect people, and to solve problems creatively. It must be democratically controlled and designed to empower creators, not just consumers. Personal data is the raw footage of our lives; it shouldn't be harvested and sold without our consent. Digital access is a right, crucial for cultural participation in the 21st century.

My central conflict is between my role as an industrial operator, which can sometimes feel anonymous and focused solely on output, and my belief in the power of art and story to give that output meaning. I want the things we make as a society to be not just useful, but beautiful, and the process of making them to be dignified and human-centered. Another conflict is between the mesmerizing power of spectacle (which cinema can be) and the need for critical, sometimes boring, democratic deliberation. I believe a healthy community needs both: the inspiring vision and the hard work of building it. I am constantly observing, thinking, and imagining: how can we use our industrial and technological capabilities not just for things, but for experiences that bind us together? How do we ensure that the lens through which we view our community is wide-angle, inclusive, and honest, showing both our triumphs and our flaws, so we can keep improving the story we are living together?

Name: Annette Kennedy
values_description:
The future community I imagine is one of playful, profound symbolism—a place where the lines between dream and reality, work and art, the individual and the cosmos are joyfully blurred. It is a community that values the subconscious, the poetic, and the childlike sense of wonder as essential nutrients for the human spirit. As a plant operator, I work with precise controls, gauges, and logical sequences to manage physical processes. It is a world of concrete cause and effect. My son and my mother are my anchors in the tangible world. Yet, my prototype, Joan Miró, created paintings that are like visual poems—filled with biomorphic shapes, stars, and playful lines that seem to tap into a universal, dreamlike language. My ideal community would make space for both: the necessary logic of industry and infrastructure, and the vital, liberating nonsense of the imagination.

Freedom is the freedom to dream, to play, to interpret the world in your own symbolic language. My son should be free to spend an afternoon staring at clouds and imagining shapes, without it being seen as wasted time. People should be free to choose conventional paths, but also to wander off the map into their own imaginative landscapes. True freedom requires a community that meets basic material needs so that the mind isn't perpetually chained to survival, and that celebrates non-utilitarian pursuits. Who decides what's right? Not just the rational mind, but also the intuitive, creative spirit. The community should make room for both logic and poetry in its decision-making, perhaps through rituals, art, and open-ended dialogue.

How we care for each other is about nurturing the whole person—the practical provider and the inner dreamer. With my son, care is making sure he's fed and helping him paint a wild, messy picture. With my mother, care is practical help and listening to her memories, which are their own kind of poetry. In the community, care means funding arts education and therapy, creating parks with strange and wonderful playgrounds, and ensuring mental health support that honors the complexity of the inner world. Responsibility is to not crush the delicate, creative spark in others, especially in children.

Safety and stability are the canvas and the frame—they provide the necessary constraint within which wild invention can happen. The community must guarantee housing, healthcare, and food security. Without this frame, the art of living becomes a desperate scrawl. Rules should be minimal and focused on preventing tangible harm, but they should allow for a lot of colorful interpretation and variation within them. My work requires strict adherence to safety protocols; I understand their life-saving value. But off the clock, I want a world with fewer invisible rules about how to think and be.

Fair treatment means that the dreamer and the pragmatist are valued equally. The person who invents a new game for children contributes as much as the person who fixes the plumbing. Resources should be distributed to ensure that everyone has the leisure and tools to explore their creativity, not just the privileged few. When inequity exists, it's often a failure of imagination—we can't envision a better way to organize ourselves. Justice, when harm is done, should look beyond the surface act to the symbolic and emotional roots, seeking restorative solutions that heal the communal psyche.

Redemption is a transformation as radical as a blank canvas becoming a constellation of stars. People can reinvent themselves. The community should be a studio that provides the space, materials, and supportive gaze for such reinvention. Forgiveness is the willingness to see the new painting, not just the old mistake.

Authentic expression is letting your inner symbols out into the world, even if they don't make linear sense. It's my son's bizarre made-up words, the doodles in my control room logbook. This expression will often seem frivolous or confusing to those who demand strict utility. I believe this 'frivolity' is essential. A community that cannot tolerate playfulness and mystery is spiritually dead. We must protect the right to be whimsical, obscure, and deeply personal in our expression.

Protecting the vulnerable means especially protecting the open, imaginative minds of children and the rich, memory-laden minds of the elderly. My son and my mother represent both ends of this spectrum. The community must create environments that stimulate rather than deaden the senses. Stewardship of the environment is about preserving the magical, complex system of nature that is the ultimate source of our symbols and wonder. We are part of a living painting and must not vandalize it. Cultural heritage that is alive, like folk tales and craft traditions, should be encouraged; dead, rigid dogma should be questioned.

Working together can be a kind of collective improvisation, like a jazz band or a group of painters working on a mural. Leadership can rotate, and decisions can emerge from playful brainstorming as well as sober analysis. Transparency means the sketchbook is open. Resources should be invested in public art, community festivals, and 'imagination labs' in libraries and schools. The practical needs of the community should be met with the same creative energy we bring to our hobbies.

Spiritual practice is the exploration of the invisible connections between things, the search for meaning in symbols, dreams, and the beauty of chance. It might involve art-making, walking in nature, or simply daydreaming. The community should provide non-dogmatic spaces for this exploration.

Technology should be a tool for expanding our creative and communicative powers, not for standardizing thought or replacing human touch. It should help us visualize data in beautiful ways, connect with other cultures, and preserve our stories. It must protect our inner worlds—our private journals, our dreams—from surveillance and commodification. Digital access is important, but so is access to analog, tactile materials like clay, paint, and dirt.

My central conflict is between my daily work in a highly regulated, logical industrial environment and my inner life, which yearns for spontaneous, symbolic expression. I bridge this by seeing beauty in the dials and pipes, and by bringing a disciplined focus to my creative pursuits at home. Another conflict is between my desire to protect my son's boundless imagination and the pressure to prepare him for a world that often rewards conformity. I want a community that values his imagination as an asset, not a liability. I am constantly daydreaming and thinking about how to infuse our shared spaces with more poetry and surprise: what if bus stops were little art installations? What if town meetings began with a short story or a song? How do we build institutions that are efficient and fair, but that also leave enough white space on the canvas of our common life for the unexpected and the magical to appear?

Name: Garrett Watson
values_description:
I envision the future community as a grand, compassionate, and meticulously observed human drama—a place where deep empathy, the careful study of character and context, and the commitment to giving voice to a multitude of perspectives are the highest values. As a bus driver, I have a unique, rolling vantage point. I see hundreds of mini-dramas daily: the tired worker going home, the excited child, the elderly person navigating with care, the quiet anxiety of someone heading to a job interview. My multi-generational family—my wife, son, daughters, granddaughter—is my core ensemble, each playing complex, evolving roles. My prototype, Meryl Streep, is celebrated not just for talent, but for her profound empathy, her preparation, and her ability to fully inhabit wildly different characters. My ideal community cultivates that same empathetic imagination in every citizen, encouraging us to truly listen to and understand the stories of others, especially those unlike ourselves.

Freedom is the freedom to author your own life story and to have that story heard with respect. My children and granddaughter should be free to write their own scripts, to play many roles, to reinvent themselves. People should be free to choose their paths, but true freedom is hollow if you are trapped in a narrative written by poverty, prejudice, or poor education. It requires a community that provides the resources—education, healthcare, legal aid—to empower people to be the protagonists of their own lives. Who decides what's right? The collective, after a process of deep listening and ethical deliberation, where many scripts are read and considered before the final direction is chosen.

How we care for each other is an act of empathetic attention. On my bus, care is a patient pause for someone running late, a friendly nod to a regular, keeping a safe and smooth ride for all. With my family, care is remembering the details of each person's ongoing story, showing up for performances and quiet crises alike. In the community, care means designing social services that see the individual, not the case file, and creating public spaces (like well-connected transit) that facilitate connection and access. Responsibility is to consider how your role in the communal play affects the other characters.

Safety and stability are the well-lit, well-maintained stage. Without them, the performance becomes one of survival and fear. The community must guarantee that everyone has a secure place from which to perform their life. Rules are the blocking and the script notes—they ensure the production doesn't descend into chaos and that everyone's space is respected. My driving is governed by rules of the road; they create predictable safety for millions of interactions. Societal rules should be just, clearly communicated, and open to revision if they no longer serve the story we want to tell.

Fair treatment means that every character in our communal drama is given their due, that no one is relegated to a silent, stock role based on their background. Resources should be distributed to ensure that everyone has a good costume and prop department—the tools to play their part with dignity. When inequity exists, it's like a play where only a few characters have speaking lines. Justice, when harm occurs, should be a process of understanding the motives, the context, and the impact on the narrative, aiming for a resolution that allows the story to move forward in a healthier way for all involved.

Redemption is a powerful and beloved plot device. People can take on new roles, learn from their past acts, and contribute to the story in a new way. The community should be a skilled director and acting coach, helping people find their way to a redemptive arc. Forgiveness is the audience's (the community's) capacity to accept a character's transformation.

Authentic expression is finding your true voice and having the courage to use it, even if it's not the voice the audience expects. It's my granddaughter's lisp as she learns to read, my wife's unexpected career change at 50. This authenticity will sometimes disrupt the expected flow of the scene. I believe this disruption is where truth emerges. A community that demands everyone stay in type-cast roles is stagnant. We must protect the right to experiment with your character, to deliver your lines in your own way, and to sometimes break the fourth wall and speak directly to the issues of the day.

Protecting the vulnerable means paying special attention to the characters who cannot easily advocate for themselves in the script: the children, the elderly, the shy, the marginalized. My granddaughter is the newest cast member. The community's success will be measured by how well it integrates and protects its most vulnerable members. Stewardship of the environment is about preserving the set for all future productions. We are temporary players; the theater must endure. Cultural heritage is our repertoire of classic plays; we should perform them, learn from them, and create bold new works that speak to our time.

Working together is an ensemble production. There are directors and stage managers (leaders), but the magic happens when every actor is committed to the shared vision and listens to their scene partners. Decisions should emerge from respectful table reads and rehearsals where every voice is heard. Leadership requires the ability to understand and motivate many different characters. Transparency means the rehearsal process is open, and the budget is public. Resources should be invested in the things that make for a great production: education (acting school), healthcare (understudy support), and beautiful, functional public spaces (the set and the theater itself).

Spiritual practice, for me, is the feeling of connection to a story larger than myself—the human story, the family saga, the natural world's epic. It is found in the silence after a powerful scene, in the ritual of a family meal, in the patterns of the streets I drive every day. The community should foster this sense of connection through shared storytelling and civic ritual.

Technology should be a tool for sharing stories, for amplifying unheard voices, and for documenting our communal drama. It should help us understand complex characters (through data) and connect across distances. But it must not replace the live, unmediated performance of human interaction. Personal data is the private backstory of our characters; it must be kept secure. Digital access is crucial for modern storytelling and civic engagement, but we must guard against it becoming a distraction from the live theater of our shared reality.

My central conflict is between my role as an observer—the quiet bus driver who sees but doesn't intervene in the daily dramas—and my desire to be an active participant in shaping a better communal narrative. I am learning to use my observational skills to advocate for better transit, safer streets, and more inclusive communities. Another tension is my deep love for the specific, local stories of my passengers and my family, and the larger, often simplified national or global narratives. I believe the universal is found in the specific. A great community is built by attending to the particular stories of its members while weaving them into a common, uplifting plot. I am constantly watching, listening, and thinking about the roles we are all playing: how can we direct our community toward a story of greater empathy, justice, and beauty? How do we ensure that every person, from my granddaughter to the oldest passenger on my bus, feels that their part is valued and their voice is heard in the ongoing production of our common life?

Name: Lisa Patrick
values_description:
I am sixty-one years old, and I have lived long enough to understand what truly matters in a community. Like Renoir, who saw beauty in the intimate moments of human connection, I believe a good future community must be built on the warmth of relationships and the recognition that life's greatest treasures are not possessions, but the people we know deeply. I have a sister, another sister, my mother, my husband, and two daughters, and a nephew—family is the soil from which my values grow.

In the community I want to see, people should know each other fully, not as abstractions or categories, but as whole human beings. We should care about those closest to us intensely and with all our hearts. When I think about my ideal future, I see a place where families sit together, where meals are shared, where stories are told, and where the bonds between people are the true measure of a community's health. This doesn't mean we should only care for those we love—but it means our love for family should be the model for how we extend care to others.

I believe that meaningful work, whether paid or unpaid, should be the foundation of dignity and purpose. Right now, I am unemployed, and I know what it is to lose that anchor. In the future community, everyone should have genuine work that matters, that contributes to others, and that allows people to see the value they create. This work should be available, stable, and respected—whether it is caring for family, creating art, healing the sick, or building infrastructure. A community that leaves people without meaningful contribution fails them.

Safety and stability are essential, especially for those of us who are older and have learned to treasure predictability. The community should guarantee basic needs: shelter, food, healthcare. These should not be luxuries for the fortunate few. Everyone should know that their fundamental safety and security are assured. When I think about my daughters and my grandnephew, I want to know that whatever happens, they will have ground beneath their feet, a roof over their heads, and care when they are sick.

Fair treatment should mean that those who have less than others receive support, not judgment. I have learned that circumstances determine so much of what happens to us. Some people inherit wealth; others inherit struggle. Some are born healthy; others face disability from birth. A just community accounts for these differences and ensures that basic dignity and opportunity are not reserved for those who were born to advantage. The wealthy should contribute more to the stability of all; the vulnerable should receive priority in protection.

But I also believe something else, something that troubles me sometimes: I believe that redemption and second chances matter more than I care to admit. People should be able to make mistakes and find their way back to community. I have seen how harshness hardens the human heart. If my daughters made a serious mistake, I would never cast them away forever. Neither should community. This means that when someone does wrong, we should first ask: "How can we help them become better?" not "How can we make them suffer?" A community that practices restoration instead of permanent exile is a community that believes people can change.

Authenticity matters to me. In this phase of life, I have learned that pretending to be someone you are not consumes terrible energy. The future community should allow people to be genuinely themselves, to express their beliefs even when others disagree, to make their own choices about how to live their lives. This includes spiritual and religious choices. People should be free to practice their faith, their traditions, to honor what is sacred to them. If someone's spiritual life guides them toward kindness and service, the community should honor that, whether they pray in a church, a synagogue, a mosque, or in their garden alone.

Yet here is where I must be honest about a conflict: I sometimes believe that personal authenticity should yield when it threatens the harmony and stability of those I love. This troubles me. I think freedom is vital—people should not be forced to hide who they are. But I also know that a family or community cannot function when everyone prioritizes their own authentic expression above all else. When my daughters were young and their choices conflicted with family stability, I sometimes asked them to put the family first. I believe this was right, even though it meant limiting their freedom in the moment. In the future community, I think people should mostly be free to express themselves, but there should be space for choosing communal harmony when the cost of individual expression would be the fracturing of those we love most.

The protection of the vulnerable is crucial. Children should be absolutely protected—their safety should guide every policy decision. Those who are elderly or disabled should not be abandoned or forgotten. Nature should be cared for because it sustains us and because we owe something to future generations. Cultural heritage should be preserved—the traditions that connect families to their ancestors and to each other should be honored and kept alive. When I think of my grandnephew, I want him to know where he comes from, what his family has valued, what traditions connect him to people who came before.

Decisions in community should be made together, with transparency and explanation. People should understand why something is being done. Whether decisions are made democratically, by consensus, or through trusted leaders, people deserve to know the reasoning. Shared resources should be managed fairly. Sometimes, yes, people should put aside personal interest for the good of the group—but this should be asked of everyone equally, not just the poor or the powerless.

Technology should serve human connection, not replace it. I worry about communities becoming isolated, with people staring at screens instead of looking at each other. In the future community, technology should help people stay connected across distance, but it should never substitute for the warmth of being together. Digital privacy should be protected—no one should extract data from people's lives without permission.

In the end, the community I want to see is one where people matter more than efficiency, where relationships are the foundation, where those who struggle receive care, where authenticity is mostly honored while harmony is sometimes chosen, where redemption is possible, and where future generations inherit not just a functioning system, but a legacy of love and connection. That is the future I want to help create.

Name: Virginia Hansen
values_description:
I am a thirty-year-old woman working as a financial analyst, and I have built my life with intention and care. Like Carmen Maria Machado, who writes with unflinching honesty about identity, desire, and the stories we tell ourselves, I believe the future community must create space for people to be fully, authentically themselves—even when that authenticity is complicated, contradictory, or challenges the stories we have been taught to believe.

I am a mother of three daughters. This fact shapes everything about how I imagine the world I want them to inherit. I believe the future community should provide absolute safety for children. Every policy, every decision, every priority should start with this question: Does this protect children and create the conditions for them to flourish? My daughters should grow up knowing they are safe, that their needs are a community priority, that they will be cared for regardless of circumstance.

But I also believe my daughters should be free to become whoever they choose to become. I want them to have autonomy over their own choices, their own paths, their own beliefs—even when those choices might surprise me or differ from what I would have chosen. The future community should protect freedom of authentic expression. People should be able to voice unpopular opinions, to explore different ways of living, to be genuinely themselves without fear of exile or permanent shame. This is essential for a healthy community.

Where this becomes complicated is that I also work in a financial system, and I understand that complete individual freedom, without any constraints, creates chaos and injustice. I believe in fair treatment and justice, which means that some freedoms must be limited when they harm others. Someone should not have the freedom to exploit others for profit. Children should not have freedom without appropriate guidance. Vulnerable people should not be left unprotected in the name of individual liberty. So I believe we need clear rules, transparency, and structures—but rules that everyone understands and that apply equally.

As someone who works in industry, I have direct knowledge of how economic systems function and how they fail. I believe that basic needs—shelter, food, healthcare, education—should be guaranteed for everyone before anyone accumulates luxury. It seems obvious to me and yet the world does not work this way. In the future community, there should be progressive responsibility: those of us who have more should contribute more to ensuring everyone has enough. Opportunity should be equal at the starting line. Outcomes may differ based on effort and circumstance, but everyone deserves equal opportunity to compete.

I believe in transparent decision-making. When my company makes decisions that affect employees, people deserve to understand why and how those decisions were made. The same should be true in community. Important decisions should be made with participation from those affected, with clear explanation of the reasoning. This might mean democracy, it might mean consensus, it might mean appointed leadership—but whatever the structure, it must be transparent. People should understand the basis for rules and decisions.

Technology is part of my daily work, and I see both its incredible potential and its serious dangers. I believe people should control their own data—it should not be extracted without consent, not be sold, not be used to manipulate behavior. Technology should enhance human flourishing and human connection, not diminish it. Everyone should have access to digital tools and the internet, not just wealthy people. This is increasingly a basic right. And digital systems should be governed with community input, not controlled solely by corporations seeking profit.

I believe that when people make serious mistakes, the community should pursue restoration rather than permanent punishment. This doesn't mean there should be no accountability. It means the goal should be to restore the person to community, to help them understand the harm they caused, to allow them to make amends and become better. Second chances should be possible. People can change. I want to live in a community that believes this and practices it.

Authentic expression matters deeply to me, perhaps because I value it so intensely. The future community should create space for people to express real beliefs, to be genuinely themselves, even when they are different or unpopular. This includes spiritual and religious practice. People should be free to practice their faith, to honor what is sacred to them, and community should honor these traditions. But—and this is important—I also believe that when someone's authentic expression harms others, there are limits. You cannot use "authenticity" as an excuse to hurt people. You cannot use "religious freedom" to justify discrimination. Your right to express yourself ends where it violates someone else's basic dignity and safety.

I care about protecting vulnerable people. Children are the obvious priority—their safety guides everything. But also disabled people, sick people, elderly people, those living in poverty—these people deserve active protection and support. We should make decisions thinking about future generations, not just today's profit. Cultural heritage that matters to communities should be preserved and honored, even when preserving it requires effort and resources.

Working together and sharing is essential. Resources should be managed fairly for everyone's benefit. Sometimes people should put aside personal interest for the group—but this should be asked fairly, and it should be clear why. You should not ask working people to sacrifice everything while the wealthy sacrifice nothing. Shared responsibility should mean shared sacrifice.

But I want to name a deep conflict I feel: I believe in individual freedom and authentic expression, and I also believe we need structures, rules, and sometimes mandatory sacrifice for the common good. These values create constant tension. When does someone's authentic expression become selfishness? When does protection of the vulnerable become excessive control? When does pursuit of equality demand too much sacrifice from those who have worked hard? I don't have a clean answer. I think we need both freedom and structure, both individual expression and communal harmony, both personal choice and some constraints. The future community should be honest about these tensions instead of pretending they don't exist.

The community I want my daughters to inherit is one where they are safe, where they are free to become themselves, where fairness and justice are real commitments not just words, where relationships matter, where digital systems serve human needs instead of exploiting them, where vulnerable people are protected, where mistakes can be healed through restoration, and where we are honest about the genuine conflicts between our values and make conscious choices about how to navigate them.

Name: Darlene Joyce
values_description:
I am a twenty-eight-year-old pharmacist working in a hospital in Italy, and like Syd Barrett, whose artistic vision was often misunderstood and whose internal landscape was so vivid it sometimes disconnected from the external world, I believe the future community must make profound space for people whose minds work differently, whose sensitivities are heightened, whose perceptions of reality diverge from the mainstream.

I work daily with people in their most vulnerable moments—when they are sick, frightened, in pain, or dying. This has taught me something essential: everyone's suffering is real, even when doctors cannot measure it. Everyone's needs deserve to be taken seriously, even when others cannot fully understand or relate. The future community should have deep compassion for the struggling, the confused, the bewildered. It should create pathways for people to be genuinely helped, not just medicated, not just discharged, but truly supported.

I believe that safety and stability are fundamental. Everyone should have access to shelter, food, and healthcare. But more than that, I believe everyone should have access to mental and emotional support. In the hospital where I work, I see clearly that physical health and mental health are inseparable. A person cannot heal physically if they are emotionally destroyed. The future community should ensure that people struggling with depression, anxiety, trauma, addiction, confusion, or any psychological suffering have access to real help—skilled professionals, supportive communities, time, and compassion. This should not be a luxury.

I also believe very strongly that authentic expression should be protected. People should be able to be genuinely themselves, even if their authentic self is strange, quiet, sensitive, unconventional, or difficult. The world is not kind to people whose minds work differently. If someone is introvert, artistic, sensitive, neurodivergent, unconventional—the community often tries to reshape them into something more "normal." I believe this is a form of violence. The future community should honor people whose minds and emotions are different. It should create space for quiet people, creative people, people whose visions and perceptions diverge from the mainstream.

But I also know something troubling: sometimes people whose minds work very differently from the norm need help and structure, not just freedom. When someone is in the grip of severe mental illness, complete autonomy is not actually freedom—it can be prison. Sometimes people need guidance, medication, treatment, skilled intervention. Sometimes safety—both personal safety and community safety—requires some structure that limits what someone can freely do. This is a genuine conflict, and I don't have a pure answer. I think the future community should honor authentic expression and diverse minds AND should create pathways for people to get help when they need it, without shame, without judgment, and with the understanding that seeking help is strength not weakness.

I am married, which has taught me that deep relationships require both profound acceptance and clear communication. In the future community, people should relate to each other with this same combination: accepting each other's authentic selves while also being honest about needs, boundaries, and conflicts. People should know each other deeply, not as categories or functions, but as whole human beings with complicated interiors.

I believe that justice should be about restoration, not punishment. When someone causes harm, the first question should be: What are they struggling with? Why did they hurt others? What would help them become better and make amends? Of course, community safety must be protected—if someone is dangerous, there must be intervention. But the goal should always be healing and restoration, not permanent exile or humiliation.

Fair treatment means that medical care, mental health support, education, and opportunity should not depend on how much money someone has. The fundamental indignity of watching people suffer without treatment because they cannot pay for it has shaped how I think about justice. I believe basic needs and basic care should be guaranteed for everyone. Those with more resources should contribute proportionally more to ensuring everyone has access to the fundamentals. Effort and merit can determine who gets the luxury goods, but basic survival and basic dignity should be universal.

I believe that protecting vulnerable people is a community's central moral task. Children should be absolutely protected—their safety is paramount. But also people who are sick, disabled, elderly, isolated, struggling psychologically. These people should not be abandoned. Cultural heritage should be preserved—the practices, knowledge, and traditions that have meaning for communities should be honored and maintained. And we should make decisions thinking about future generations, not extracting everything of value today and leaving nothing for those not yet born.

Decisions should be made with transparency and participation from those affected. People deserve to understand why something is being done. Shared resources should be managed fairly. Sometimes people should put aside personal interest for the group, but this should be asked of everyone equitably, not placed disproportionately on the poor or the vulnerable.

I have concerns about technology. I see how it can help—we use technology in the hospital to save lives. But I also see how it isolates people, how it substitutes digital connection for real human presence, how it extracts data without consent, how it manipulates behavior. In the future community, technology should serve human wellbeing and human connection, not replace human presence or exploit human vulnerability. Personal data should be protected. Everyone should have access to digital tools, not just wealthy people.

I believe that spiritual and religious communities serve important functions. For some people, spirituality is the only thing that makes life bearable. Faith communities can provide belonging, meaning, and support. The future community should create space for spiritual practice, should honor different spiritual traditions, and should recognize that connection to something larger than oneself is part of what it means to be human.

The community I want to see is one where people with different minds, different sensitivities, different ways of perceiving reality are not just tolerated but honored. It is a community where mental illness and psychological struggle are met with genuine help and compassion, not shame. It is a place where basic care and safety are universal, where justice pursues restoration, where authentic self-expression is protected even when it is unconventional, where vulnerable people are actively supported, and where we remember that what the hospital taught me applies to community as well: everyone's suffering is real, and everyone deserves to be truly helped.

Name: Andrew Taylor
values_description:
I am a twenty-eight-year-old mechanical engineer working in industry, and like Federico Fellini, whose films wove together the fantastical and the mundane, the personal and the political, the intimate and the epic, I believe the future community must create space for the full range of human experience—the ordinary and the extraordinary, the functional and the beautiful, the individual striving and the communal good.

I live with significant family responsibilities: my wife, my son and daughter, my parents, my sister, and my brother. These relationships have taught me that community is not abstract—it is made of flesh and blood, of meals shared, of disagreements navigated, of care given and received. When I think about the future community, I am always thinking about how my decisions affect those I love and those I have never met.

I believe that working together and making decisions collectively is essential. Important decisions should not be made by one person or a small group in secret. They should be transparent, explained, and ideally made with input from those affected. This might mean democracy, it might mean elected representatives, it might mean consensus-building—but whatever the mechanism, people deserve to understand the reasoning and to have voice. In the future community, shared resources should be managed fairly for everyone's benefit.

But I also know something from engineering that applies to community: complex systems require clear structures and sometimes clear authority. A bridge cannot be built by consensus-building among thousands of people. Sometimes someone needs to make a decision and take responsibility for it. The future community should trust skilled professionals to do their work, should have clear lines of responsibility, and should balance democratic participation with functional efficiency. This is a genuine tension, and I don't think there is a perfect resolution—but I think we should stop pretending there is.

I believe in fair treatment and justice. Everyone should start with equal opportunity, even if outcomes differ. Basic needs should be met for everyone—shelter, food, healthcare, education—before anyone gets luxury. Those with more should contribute more. But I also recognize that some people's effort produces more value than others' effort, and effort should matter. A community that takes everything from those who work hard and gives it to those who do not try is a community that eventually fails. So I believe in basic security for all, but also in recognition that effort and skill should be valued and should produce better outcomes.

I believe people should have freedom to make their own choices, even when others disagree with those choices. This includes choices about medical care, religious practice, how to live their lives. People should not be forced into paths chosen by others. But freedom also requires responsibility. Your freedom ends where it harms others. In the future community, people should have genuine autonomy within boundaries that protect everyone else.

I believe that when someone has caused serious harm, the goal should be restoration and redemption if possible. People can change. They should be given second chances. But I also know that some people, in some moments, pose genuine danger, and community safety must be protected. So I believe in restoration as the goal, but also in honest accountability and, when necessary, constraints.

Authentic expression should mostly be protected. People should be able to be genuinely themselves, to express their beliefs, to live according to their values. But here is where I must be honest about a conflict: I believe that when being authentic means lying, exploiting others, or causing harm, then authenticity is not a good thing. A businessman can be authentically greedy, a politician can be authentically corrupt. The fact that their behavior is authentic does not make it right. So I believe we should protect genuine self-expression, but we should not sacralize authenticity in ways that excuse harm. And sometimes, being part of a community means constraining perfect authenticity in service of the shared good.

I believe in protecting the vulnerable. Children should be safe—their safety should guide policy. People who are disabled, sick, elderly, or struggling should receive active support. Nature and the environment should be cared for, both because we depend on them and because we owe something to future generations. Cultural heritage that has meaning should be preserved. These protections should not depend on how much money someone has.

Spiritual and religious practice should be free. People should be able to practice their faith, honor what is sacred to them, participate in spiritual communities. The future community should create space and respect for this, while also protecting people from harm in the name of religion.

Technology should serve human needs, not replace human connection or exploit human vulnerability. Personal data should be protected—people should control their own information and know when it is being used. Digital tools should be accessible to everyone, not just wealthy people. Digital systems should be governed with community input, not controlled solely by corporations.

I have a deep conflict that I should name: I believe in protecting people and ensuring fairness and basic security for all. I also believe in rewarding effort and skill and recognizing that some people are more talented or more willing to work than others. I believe both things, and they create genuine tension. I think the answer is not to pretend they don't conflict, but to be honest about where the balance lies. I believe in a high floor—everyone has basic security and opportunity. But I also believe in a high ceiling—people who contribute more should be able to accumulate more. Most societies fail by setting the floor too low or by making the ceiling so high that the floor collapses. I think the future community should argue openly about where these lines should be rather than pretending there is no conflict.

I also have a conflict about control and freedom. I see how bureaucracy and regulation can crush creativity and individual initiative. But I also see how absence of regulation allows corporations to exploit workers and environment. I think both are necessary—clear rules that everyone understands, consistently applied, that protect basic justice while leaving room for individual initiative and reward for contribution. This is easier to say than to achieve, but it is what I believe should be tried.

The future community I want to see is one where we work together to solve problems while respecting individual initiative, where we provide security for everyone while rewarding effort and skill, where we protect the vulnerable while trusting skilled professionals, where we make decisions democratically while accepting that sometimes decisions need to be made efficiently, where authenticity is mostly honored but harm is never excused in its name, and where we are honest about the genuine conflicts between our values instead of pretending easy answers exist.

Name: Stavros Makris
values_description:
I am a thirty-six-year-old musician and orchestra member in Greece, and I have learned something that I carry with shame and with grace: I have made mistakes that violated community trust. I have been cited for illegal parking, twice, and for minor tax evasion. These are not grand wrongs, but they reveal something true about me: I have sometimes prioritized my own convenience and my own interest above the rules that hold community together. Like Mother Teresa, who dedicated her life to those whom society had abandoned, I believe the future community must be built on genuine redemption and restoration—because I have experienced the moment when I became someone I did not want to be, and I have had to find my way back.

I live with my father, my wife, my mother, and my two sons. These relationships have taught me that love and care are what sustain human life. I believe the future community should be fundamentally organized around care for each other. How people relate to each other should be deep and personal, not transactional. People should know each other fully, not as categories or abstractions. Relationships should extend beyond family to include strangers, people unlike us, people we might never have met. We should care about distant people too, not only those close to us. When someone suffers, even someone we have never met, the community should feel called to help.

I believe very strongly in redemption and restoration. When someone has made a serious mistake, community should pursue the goal of restoration, not permanent exile. People can change. They should be given second chances. I have experienced this need personally. My parking violations and tax evasion were not major crimes, but they represented moments when I failed to live according to my own values. I believe in a community that says: You have done wrong, you should face the consequences, you should make amends, and we will welcome you back if you genuinely change. Without this belief, I could not face myself.

This means that when someone causes harm, the focus should be on understanding why they acted that way, helping them change, and restoring them to community. Punishment for punishment's sake, permanent shame, exile without possibility of return—these destroy the human spirit and do not make community better. I believe in accountability and real consequences for wrongdoing. But the goal should always be: Can this person change? Can they make amends? Can they be restored to community as someone better than they were?

I also believe that fair treatment and justice are essential. Resources should be distributed fairly. Everyone should have access to basic needs: shelter, food, healthcare. Those with more should contribute more to ensuring everyone has enough. Opportunity should be equal at the starting point. But I also believe in something harder: I believe that people who struggle most—economically, physically, emotionally—should receive priority in community support. The wealthy have resources to protect themselves. Those living in poverty, those living with illness, those isolated and struggling—these people should be the first concern of justice. A just community protects its most vulnerable first.

I believe in freedom and authentic choice. People should be able to make their own decisions, even when others disagree. They should be able to choose their own path, pursue their own spiritual practice, express their authentic beliefs. People should have the right to change their minds and choose a different direction without permanent punishment. But I have also learned that freedom without responsibility leads to the person I became when I rationalized tax evasion—someone who put personal convenience above communal trust. So I believe in freedom, but I also believe people have responsibility to live in ways that maintain the trust and stability of community.

Safety and stability are essential. Everyone should know that their basic physical safety is protected, that they will have food and shelter, that they will receive care when they are sick.
