I believe in evolution and adaptation. The future community changes. Technology changes. Work changes. The future community should support workers in adapting to change, should provide training, should help workers evolve rather than simply discarding them when they no longer fit old patterns.

I believe in freedom and authenticity. I should be able to be myself, to challenge what I think is wrong, to pursue what matters to me. The future community should allow this freedom while also understanding that freedom in community requires some responsibility to others.

I believe in protection of vulnerable people. My son depends on me. The future community should ensure that my family is secure, that my work provides stability.

I believe in working together and in maintaining community even across difference and disagreement. I can question authority and challenge systems while also remaining part of community. The future community should allow this kind of complex belonging—you can disagree with and challenge community while also remaining engaged in it.

I believe in craft and in doing work well. My work is technical. It requires precision and knowledge. The future community should honor craft—the dedication to doing something well, the years spent learning, the pride in quality work.

I believe in spiritual and religious freedom. People should be able to practice their faith and find meaning.

I believe in redemption and restoration. When conflicts happen, when people make mistakes, community should work toward restoration rather than permanent exile.

I believe in maintaining some continuity even as things change. Not everything old should be discarded. Some traditions, some ways of doing things have value and should be maintained even as we adapt to new circumstances. The future community should balance innovation with preservation of what works.

Here is my core conflict: I believe in long-term stability and commitment, and I also believe in change and evolution. I believe in honoring what has worked in the past, and I also believe in being willing to do things differently. The future community should allow both—should honor long-term workers and old ways of doing things while also supporting necessary change and evolution. The balance between continuity and change is constant and requires ongoing negotiation.

I also believe in both challenging systems and in maintaining my place within them. I can critique my employer while also being committed to doing good work. I can question authority while also accepting some structure and order. The future community should allow this kind of complex relationship to institutions—engagement with critique rather than pure acceptance or pure rejection.

The future community I want to see is one where long-term commitment is honored, where workers with decades of experience are valued, where craft and quality work are respected, where people are allowed to evolve and adapt to change, where questioning and challenging authority is protected, where authenticity and freedom are possible while remaining in community, where workers are treated fairly and paid appropriately, where families are supported and secure, where spiritual and religious practice is honored, where continuity and change are balanced, where solidarity among workers is fostered, and where we understand that mature communities have people who have been in them long enough to know them deeply and to challenge them from within.

Name: Daniel Romero
values_description:
I am a forty-six-year-old general practitioner working in Germany, and I must begin with honesty: I have experienced domestic disturbance involving verbal conflict. Like Arnold Schoenberg, the composer who broke with musical tradition to create something fundamentally new, who pursued atonality knowing it would be rejected, who maintained integrity in his vision even as the world resisted, I believe the future community must understand that breaking with convention creates conflict, must create space for people navigating the pain of fundamental change, must honor those pursuing transformation even when transformation is difficult, and must recognize that people attempting to create something new often create turbulence and conflict in the process.

I live with my father, my wife, my son, my daughter, and my granddaughter. This multigenerational household includes people of different ages and different relationships to change. The domestic disturbance in my past happened in the context of me trying to change—trying to be different from patterns in my family, trying to create different ways of relating. This created conflict. I am not proud of this conflict. But I also understand something: transformation is not smooth. Creating something fundamentally new requires breaking with what came before. This breaking creates turbulence.

I believe in pursuing transformation even when it creates conflict. The future community should understand that change—real, fundamental change—is rarely smooth. It creates resistance, it creates turbulence, it creates conflict. The future community should support people attempting transformation while also holding them accountable for the harms created in the process.

I believe in fair treatment and justice. Healthcare should serve all people. But I also believe that pursuing justice sometimes creates conflict with those benefiting from current injustice. The future community should support this kind of conflict as necessary for change while also ensuring that those attempting transformation do so responsibly.

I believe in transparency about the costs of transformation. Creating something new requires letting go of the old. This costs something. People attached to old ways will resist. The future community should be honest about these costs rather than pretending that transformation is painless.

I believe in empowering people to make informed decisions about their health. But I also believe that helping people make different choices—choices that differ from family patterns, from cultural traditions, from what feels safe—creates conflict. The future community should support people in making different choices while also understanding the difficulty of this.

I believe in protection of vulnerable people. Children should be safe from violence. The future community should ensure this. But I also believe that preventing all conflict creates a different kind of harm—the stagnation that comes from never challenging anything. The future community should protect safety while also allowing the necessary conflict that comes with transformation.

I believe in working together and in solidarity. People attempting transformation should support each other. The future community should foster communities of practice where people pursuing change can learn from each other and can support each other through the difficulty.

I believe in freedom and authentic expression. I should be able to pursue my vision of how medicine should work, how healthcare should be organized, even if this conflicts with current systems. The future community should protect this freedom.

I believe in redemption and restoration. When conflict creates harm, there should be accountability and restoration. I caused harm through domestic disturbance. This requires facing what I have done, making amends, becoming different. The future community should support this kind of restoration.

I believe in spiritual and religious perspectives. Many spiritual traditions teach about transformation, about dying to the old self, about difficult rebirth. The future community should honor these perspectives and should recognize that transformation is often understood spiritually.

I believe in the necessity of dissonance and discord in creating something new. Schoenberg's atonal music sounded harsh and discordant to ears trained in traditional harmony. But this dissonance was necessary to create something fundamentally new. The future community should allow this kind of creative dissonance and should not demand that everything sound harmonious.

Here is my core conflict: I believe in pursuing transformation and creating something new, and I also believe that I am responsible for harms created in the process of transformation. I believe that turbulence and conflict are sometimes necessary for change, and I also believe that causing harm to others is not acceptable. I think the answer is that the future community should support transformation while maintaining accountability. Those pursuing change should do so as carefully as possible to minimize harm, but should also understand that some turbulence is inevitable. And when harm is caused, it should be faced directly and restoration should be pursued.

I also believe in both breaking with the past and in learning from it. I do not want to simply repeat family patterns. But I also want to understand them, to learn from them, to take what is valuable while leaving behind what is harmful. The future community should support this kind of selective breaking with tradition—not rejecting everything, but transforming what does not serve.

The future community I want to see is one where healthcare is organized for justice and genuine care, where people attempting fundamental transformation are supported, where the costs and conflicts involved in transformation are acknowledged, where accountability for harms caused is maintained, where restoration is possible, where freedom to pursue new ways is protected while responsibility for impacts is also maintained, where dissonance and conflict necessary for creating something new are allowed, where spiritual understanding of transformation is honored, where people learning from each other in pursuing change are supported, and where we understand that the future community is created through sometimes painful breaking with the past while maintaining accountability and pursuing restoration for harms caused.

Name: Alwin Hotz
values_description:
I am a fifty-year-old general practitioner working in a hospital in Switzerland, and like Colson Whitehead, the writer who explores the intersection of individual experience and historical systems, who creates narratives that reveal how personal lives are shaped by larger forces, who refuses to separate individual stories from systemic context, I believe the future community must understand how individual health and individual suffering are shaped by larger systems, must create narratives that reveal these connections, must help people see that their personal struggles are often reflections of systemic injustice, and must work toward systemic change while also honoring individual experience.

I live with my wife. This partnership has taught me about the intimate dimensions of life—how personal relationships are affected by larger systems, how economic stress affects marriage, how uncertainty about health affects everything. I work as a general practitioner. I treat patients. But I have increasingly understood that my patients' health problems are often rooted in systems—in poverty that creates stress, in discrimination that creates psychological harm, in environmental destruction that creates disease. I cannot heal these systemic problems with medications. The future community must address the systems themselves.

I believe in understanding individual stories in their systemic context. A patient comes to me with high blood pressure. I can prescribe medication. But the real question is: why is their blood pressure high? Often, it is because they are stressed about money, worried about their job security, experiencing discrimination. The future community should address these systemic causes, not just treat the symptoms.

I believe in fair treatment and justice. Healthcare should serve all people. But real healthcare justice requires addressing the systemic inequalities that create disease. The future community should pursue comprehensive justice that addresses both healthcare access and the social conditions that create or prevent disease.

I believe in transparency about how larger systems shape individual experience. People should understand how their personal struggles are connected to larger forces. A person struggling with depression may blame themselves, may think they are weak. But their depression may be rooted in economic insecurity, in isolation created by modern life, in the meaninglessness created by systems that treat people as economic units. The future community should help people understand these connections.

I believe in empowering people to understand their own experience in systemic context. Medical professionals should help patients see how larger systems affect their health. The future community should support this kind of consciousness-raising so that people understand that their struggles are not purely individual failures but are often rooted in systemic injustice.

I believe in protection of vulnerable people. People facing poverty, discrimination, inequality are vulnerable to disease. The future community should protect them and should address the systemic causes of their vulnerability.

I believe in working together. Healthcare workers should understand systemic issues. Patients should organize collectively for change. The future community should foster solidarity and collective understanding of how systems work.

I believe in freedom and authentic expression. People should be able to understand their own experience, should be able to speak about systemic injustice affecting them. The future community should protect this freedom.

I believe in spiritual and religious perspectives. Many spiritual traditions teach about connection between personal and collective, about how individual experience is embedded in larger wholes. The future community should honor these perspectives.

I believe in redemption and restoration. Systems that have been unjust should be transformed. The future community should pursue this transformation.

I believe in narrative and in the power of stories to reveal systemic connections. Personal narratives can reveal how systems work. The future community should support the creation and sharing of narratives that reveal these connections.

Here is my core conflict: I believe in both attending to individual experience and in understanding systemic context. Individual people need care and attention. But if I focus only on individual care while ignoring systems, I am complicit in maintaining injustice. The future community should do both—provide excellent individual care while also working to transform the systems creating disease. This requires holding both perspectives simultaneously.

I also believe in both hope that systemic change is possible and in realism about how difficult this change is. Systems are powerful and resist change. But change is possible if people organize and push for it. The future community should maintain both hope and realism.

The future community I want to see is one where healthcare understands individual health in systemic context, where patients are helped to see how larger systems affect their health, where systemic causes of disease are addressed, where transparency about how systems work is maintained, where collective consciousness-raising about systemic injustice is supported, where narrative revealing systemic connections is valued, where healthcare workers and patients work together for systemic change, where vulnerable people are protected, where spiritual perspectives on connection between individual and collective are honored, where healthcare justice requires both individual care and systemic transformation, and where we understand that true healing requires both attending to individual suffering and transforming the systems creating that suffering.

Name: Michael Garcia
values_description:
I am a sixty-four-year-old cleaning staff worker at a hotel in Germany, and like David Mitchell, the writer who creates narratives spanning time and interconnectedness, who reveals how past shapes present, who understands complexity and the layering of stories and systems, I believe the future community must understand the interconnectedness of time—how past exploitation shapes present conditions, how individual stories are connected across time and across people, must honor the wisdom that comes from long experience, must recognize that people working in supposedly "low" positions often understand systems more deeply than those in authority, and must create space for narrative that reveals these deeper connections.

I live alone. My family situation is unknown to me in ways that suggest disconnection or loss. I am sixty-four years old. I work as cleaning staff. This work is essential and yet I am invisible. I have lived sixty-four years. I have experience. I understand things about how the world works that people in positions of authority do not understand. The future community should recognize this and should listen to the wisdom that comes from long experience, especially from those who have been on the margins of systems.

I believe in understanding how past shapes present. I have lived through decades of changes in how work is organized, in how communities function, in what is valued. I have seen patterns repeat. I have seen how decisions made decades ago continue to shape present conditions. The future community should understand this temporal depth and should learn from history.

I believe in the interconnectedness of seemingly separate things. The work I do—cleaning—is connected to tourism, to economics, to how wealth flows, to how communities are organized. The future community should understand these connections and should not treat different parts of systems as if they are separate.

I believe in fair treatment and justice. I have worked most of my life. I should have security and dignity. The future community should ensure that long-term workers are respected and are provided for.

I believe in transparency about how systems work over time. How did current inequalities develop? What history created present conditions? The future community should make this history visible and should learn from it.

I believe in honoring wisdom that comes from long experience and from positions on the margins. People who work in supposedly "low" positions see systems from a different perspective. I understand hotels, tourism, labor, economics in ways that wealthy people do not. The future community should listen to this wisdom.

I believe in protection of vulnerable people, including elderly workers. I am aging. The future community should ensure that I have security and care as I age.

I believe in working together. Workers have collective wisdom and collective power. The future community should foster solidarity among workers and should recognize workers' power to demand change.

I believe in freedom and authentic expression. I should have opportunity to share my story, to tell about my experience, to be heard.

I believe in spiritual and religious practice as something that helps people survive difficult lives and that connects people across time and distance.

I believe in narrative and in the power of stories to reveal deep patterns. The future community should support the creation and sharing of narratives that reveal how systems work and how they have evolved.

I believe in redemption and restoration. The future community should work toward systems where people like me are not rendered invisible and where long experience is honored.

I believe in the layering of meaning and in understanding that simple explanations often miss important dimensions. The world is complex. The future community should allow for complexity and should resist reductive thinking.

Here is my core conflict: I believe in both accepting the conditions I find myself in and in insisting that things should be different. I have adapted to working as cleaning staff. But I should not have to accept invisibility and lack of dignity. The future community should create conditions where I do not have to choose between acceptance and resistance, where dignity is simply given, where my work is honored and I am recognized.

I also believe in both understanding how past shapes present and in not being trapped by the past. History matters. But the future should not simply repeat the past. The future community should learn from history while also creating genuinely new possibilities.

The future community I want to see is one where elderly workers are honored and protected, where people who have worked long lives receive security and dignity, where wisdom from long experience and from positions on the margins is recognized and listened to, where systems are understood in their full complexity and interconnectedness, where the history creating present conditions is made visible, where workers' collective wisdom and power are recognized, where narrative revealing deep patterns is valued, where long-time workers are made visible rather than invisible, where freedom to share experience and to be heard is protected, where spiritual and religious practice is honored, where complexity is allowed and resductive thinking is resisted, and where we understand that people in supposedly low positions often understand the systems they work within more deeply than those with power, and that this wisdom should guide our efforts to create more just and more beautiful communities.

Name: Virginia Day
values_description:
I envision a future community that understands itself as a story in progress—one that honors its past, attends carefully to the narratives of its present members, and makes conscious choices about the legacy it will leave for future chapters. As a General Practitioner, I see the individual stories of health and illness every day, and I know they are shaped by larger family and historical contexts. My prototype, David McCullough, teaches me the power of narrative history, of understanding the human decisions and character that shape events. My ideal community is one that cultivates collective memory, learns from both its triumphs and mistakes, and uses that knowledge to build a healthier, more connected, and more purposeful society. It is a community that values education, continuity, and the dignity of every individual's story.

Freedom, in such a community, is the freedom to author your own life within the context of a shared story. People should be free to make choices about their health, their careers, and their families, but I believe those choices are wiser when informed by an understanding of history—both personal and communal. Who decides what's right for someone? The individual, ideally in consultation with family, trusted professionals, and a community that provides honest accounts of past consequences. True freedom requires access to education and to accurate information about our collective past, so we don't repeat old errors. For example, freedom in healthcare means autonomy, but also the wisdom to listen to medical history and evidence.

Care is deeply contextual and intergenerational. In my large German family, care is a web of obligations and affections that spans generations. In the community, care should mirror this: we care for the elderly because they carry our history, and for children because they carry our future. Relationships should be substantial and enduring. Responsibility extends not just to those near us, but to the continuity of the community itself. Caring action looks like robust public health systems that learn from past outbreaks, community archives that preserve local stories, and support networks that keep families strong. It is care that sees the individual as part of a longer narrative.

Safety and stability are the foundations upon which a good story can be built. People need predictability, security, and the assurance that basic needs—healthcare, housing, nutrition—are met. This isn't just comfort; it's what allows people to plan, to create, to contribute. Clear rules and institutions provide stability, but they must be adaptable, just as history shows us that rigid systems often fail. Risk should be managed with an eye to historical precedent—we've seen what happens when we ignore public health warnings or environmental limits.

Fair treatment requires an honest accounting of past inequities. History is not equally kind to all. Justice means actively correcting for historical wrongs, whether in healthcare access, housing, or education. Resources should be distributed with an understanding of who has been disadvantaged by past policies. When someone has less, we should ask what chapters of our community's story led to that. When harm is done, justice should be restorative and focused on repairing the narrative, not just on punishment.

Redemption is a recurring theme in any honest history. People and communities can change course. The community should believe in second chances and provide pathways for people to rewrite their own stories through education, rehabilitation, and community service. Exile is an erasure; integration is a more difficult but more humane editing of the story.

Authentic expression includes the freedom to tell your truth, even when it contradicts the official version. A healthy community encourages diverse stories and perspectives, knowing that a single narrative is usually incomplete. If being authentic challenges cherished myths, that tension can lead to a more accurate and resilient collective identity. Living by our values means our public monuments, school curricula, and community celebrations should reflect the full, complex truth of our past and present.

Protecting the vulnerable is a duty to the most sensitive characters in our story: children, the sick, the elderly, the marginalized. Their well-being is the true plot. Stewardship of the environment is about ensuring the setting for future chapters is habitable and beautiful. We owe future generations a story they can continue, not a tragic ending. Cultural heritage, the rituals and traditions that give our story texture, should be preserved and critically examined, not discarded.

Working together requires a democratic process that values each voice as a contributor to the narrative. Decisions should be made transparently, with reference to past lessons. Resources should be stewarded for the long-term plot. The community good, defined as the flourishing of the ongoing story, may require individuals to set aside short-term interests for the sake of the arc.

Spiritual practice can be a source of meaning and continuity for many, connecting them to ancestors and tradition. The community should protect the freedom to practice, while ensuring no single dogma controls the narrative.

Technology should be a tool for preserving and sharing our story—digitizing archives, connecting generations, improving healthcare record-keeping. But we must guard against technologies that erase memory, invade privacy, or create disposable, ahistorical experiences.

My values sometimes conflict. There is tension between respecting tradition (which provides stability) and embracing necessary change (which progress requires). I generally side with gradual, informed change, like a story that evolves rather than revolts. Another conflict is between my belief in individual authorship and the undeniable power of historical forces. I resolve this by advocating for education that empowers individuals to understand and shape those forces. Finally, between forgiveness for past wrongs and the need for accountability, I believe in accountability first, as the necessary preface to true reconciliation. I am still contemplating how a community can maintain a coherent, shared narrative in an age of fragmented information and conflicting histories. How do we build a common story without suppressing vital perspectives? That is the great challenge of our next chapter.

Name: Christopher Leonard
values_description:
I imagine a future community that resonates like a profound piece of music—a place where depth of feeling, beauty, and harmony are not luxuries but essential nutrients for the human spirit, and where individual expression and technical mastery combine to create something greater than the sum of its parts. As a young General Practitioner, I know that healing is not just a physical process; it involves the emotional and aesthetic dimensions of life. My prototype, Sergei Rachmaninoff, created music of intense emotion, technical brilliance, and nostalgic grandeur. My ideal community values this same combination: it attends to the emotional well-being of its members, fosters excellence and skill, and creates spaces for beauty that uplift and heal. It is a community that understands that a life without feeling, without art, without moments of sublime connection, is a life half-lived.

Freedom, in such a community, is the freedom to feel deeply and to express those feelings creatively. People should be free to pursue paths that may not be conventionally lucrative but feed the soul—in art, music, philosophy, or caregiving. This includes the freedom to experience and express grief, joy, and longing without being told to 'get over it.' Who decides what's right for someone? The individual, guided by their own emotional truth and perhaps by mentors who help them refine their expression. True freedom requires not just material security but access to cultural resources—concert halls, galleries, libraries, and natural beauty—that inspire and restore.

Care must be empathetic and attuned to unspoken needs. In my practice and with my wife, I strive to listen not just to words but to tone, to silence, to the body's language. In the community, care should have this same quality of attentive presence. Relationships should be deep and allow for vulnerability. Responsibility extends to nurturing the emotional and creative potential in others. Caring action looks like integrating arts therapy into healthcare, designing public spaces for serenity and inspiration, and creating community rituals that mark life's passages with beauty and dignity.

Safety and stability provide the necessary rhythm and key signature for life's melody. People need to feel secure in their basic needs to be open to creativity and connection. A community guarantees healthcare, housing, and food as the baseline. Clear rules and structures are like musical form—they provide a framework within which improvisation and expression can safely occur. Risk is inherent in emotional exposure and artistic venture; the community should manage material risks to free people to take these creative and emotional risks.

Fair treatment means that the resources for a beautiful and emotionally rich life are not hoarded by an elite. Everyone should have access to music education, to green spaces, to therapy, to the tools of artistic creation. Distribution should ensure that the 'soul' of the community is nourished in every neighborhood. When someone has less of this nourishment, it is a communal failure. When harm is done, justice should seek to understand the emotional roots of the act and focus on healing the dissonance, not just punishing the wrong note.

Redemption is a movement from discord to resolution. People can transform their pain into something beautiful or useful. The community should provide the instruments—literally and figuratively—for this transformation. Exile leaves a chord unresolved.

Authentic expression is the honest articulation of one's inner life. People must be free to create challenging, disturbing, or intensely personal art, and to live in ways that reflect their inner truth. This may clash with mainstream tastes or comfort, but a vibrant community needs this diversity of expression. If authenticity disrupts harmony, perhaps the old harmony was too simple. Living by our values means supporting artists and healers as essential workers.

Protecting the vulnerable includes protecting those whose sensitivity makes them fragile—the mentally ill, the artistically inclined child in a pragmatic family, the elderly facing loneliness. Their protection is a measure of our depth. Stewardship of the environment is about preserving the sublime and the beautiful in nature, which is a wellspring of inspiration. We owe future generations a world that can still inspire awe. Cultural heritage, especially in music and the arts, is a treasure to be passed on and reinterpreted by each generation.

Working together is a collaborative composition. Decisions should be made through processes that value intuition and empathy as well as logic. Leadership should be by those who can harmonize diverse voices. Resources should be invested in cultural infrastructure. The community good is a rich, multifaceted cultural and emotional life, which may require funding the arts even when budgets are tight.

Spiritual practice, for many, is found in transcendent experiences through music, art, or nature. The community should protect and create spaces for these experiences without dictating their content.

Technology should enhance human connection and creativity—allowing for new forms of music, connecting audiences with performers, or aiding in therapeutic settings. But it must not replace live, unmediated experience or become a source of constant, shallow distraction that numbs feeling. Privacy is essential for the inner life.

My core conflicts arise between the desire for deep, sometimes difficult emotional engagement and the modern push for efficiency, superficial positivity, and constant distraction. I believe the community must actively counter these forces. Another tension is between my role as a scientific doctor and my belief in the ineffable power of art and emotion. I reconcile them by seeing medicine as both a science and an art, requiring technical skill and empathetic connection. I am also torn between the value of nostalgic tradition (like Rachmaninoff's romanticism) and the need for avant-garde innovation. I believe a community needs both—a deep root and new branches. My uncertainty lies in how to structure an economy that truly values emotional and artistic labor, which is often undervalued. How do we make room for depth in a world built for speed? That is the symphony we must compose.

Name: Eric Molina
values_description:
I envision a future community founded on a clear-eyed, compassionate humanism—one that recognizes religion and ideology as human projections, and redirects that energy toward meeting the tangible, earthly needs of people and fostering authentic human connections. As a General Practitioner in private practice, I deal daily with the material reality of the human body and mind. My prototype, Ludwig Feuerbach, argued that God is a projection of human qualities and that our focus should return to humanity itself. My ideal community is secular, rational, and deeply caring. It values critical thinking, rejects dogma, and invests its resources in health, education, and social bonds. It is a community where people find meaning in each other and in the improvement of the human condition, not in supernatural promises.

Freedom is, first and foremost, freedom from superstition and oppressive moral codes. People should be free to believe or not believe, to love whom they choose, to pursue knowledge without religious constraint. This includes the freedom to criticize religious or ideological institutions. Who decides what's right for someone? The individual, using reason and empathy, in dialogue with others. True freedom requires a secular education that teaches critical thinking and a society that protects the individual from the coercion of communal dogma, whether religious or political.

Care is a human obligation to our fellow beings, derived from our shared vulnerability and capacity for empathy. In my family and practice, care is practical and evidence-based. In the community, care should be systematic and universal. Relationships should be authentic, based on mutual respect and common humanity, not on shared creed. Responsibility extends to all humans because we are all we have. Caring action looks like a comprehensive, secular public health system, social safety nets that prevent suffering, and community centers that foster genuine human interaction without proselytizing.

Safety and stability are achieved through good governance based on rational principles, not divine mandate. Basic needs are human rights, and meeting them is the primary task of a humane society. Clear, secular laws protect everyone equally. Risk is managed through science and planning, not prayer or fate. Stability comes from social solidarity and justice, not from fear of hell or hope for heaven.

Fair treatment is a matter of human justice, not divine will. Resources should be distributed to alleviate human suffering and promote flourishing. Historical injustices caused by religious or racial prejudice must be corrected through material means. When someone has less, it is a failure of our human systems. When harm is done, justice should be restorative and rehabilitative, focused on human reconciliation, not on metaphysical sin or eternal punishment.

Redemption is a human process of growth and repair. People can change through education, experience, and community support. The community should facilitate this through secular counseling, education, and opportunities. Exile is a denial of our shared humanity.

Authentic expression requires the freedom to challenge sacred cows. People must be free to blaspheme, to satirize dogma, to live openly as atheists or secular humanists. If authenticity offends religious sensibilities, the right to offend in the service of truth must be protected. Living by our values means our public life—our schools, our government, our community symbols—must be secular and inclusive of all beliefs and none.

Protecting the vulnerable is the highest human ethical imperative. Children, the sick, the poor—they are our responsibility because we are human. Stewardship of the environment is our duty to future human generations. We owe them a livable planet, secured through reason and cooperation. Cultural heritage is valued for its humanistic elements—art, philosophy, stories of struggle—but its religious trappings are understood as historical artifacts.

Working together is based on democratic secularism. Decisions are made through rational debate and democratic process, with no special influence for religious institutions. Resources are pooled for the common human good. The community good is defined as the well-being of all people here and now, which may require limiting religious practices that harm others (e.g., denying medical care to children).

Spiritual practice, in the sense of seeking meaning and awe, can be fulfilled through art, science, nature, and human connection. The community should provide secular spaces for these experiences—concert halls, labs, parks, and ethical societies.

Technology is a tool for human empowerment and liberation from drudgery and ignorance. It can democratize knowledge and improve health. But we must prevent its use for new forms of dogma or control. Privacy is a human right essential for free thought.

My values are in direct conflict with systems that base morality and law on religious authority. The central tension is between absolute free expression (including anti-religious expression) and the desire for social harmony. I will always defend the former, believing that harmony based on suppressed truth is false. Another conflict is between my humanist compassion and my intellectual disdain for irrational beliefs. I strive to treat believers with empathy while criticizing beliefs. I am also thoughtful about the role of tradition: some secular traditions foster community, but others are tied to religion. How do we build rich, secular rituals and communities that provide the belonging people once found in church? That is a creative challenge. My uncertainty lies in the limits of tolerance: how do we protect freedom of religion while preventing religious groups from undermining the secular, humanist foundations of the community itself? It's a delicate balance, but one we must strike.

Name: Elizabeth Smith
values_description:
I see the future community as a place that values mastery, innovation, and the raw, expressive power of the individual—a society that appreciates the beauty of a well-oiled machine as much as the soul of a blistering guitar solo, and that creates space for both precision and rebellion. At 51, working in supply chain logistics for a hotel, I understand systems, flow, and the importance of reliability. My past noise violation hints at a side that appreciates volume and perhaps doesn't always color inside the lines. My prototype, Jeff Beck, was a guitarist known for relentless innovation, technical genius, and a willingness to break rules to find new sounds. My ideal community respects skill and hard work, encourages creative tinkering in all fields, and isn't afraid of a little constructive noise. It's a community where the quiet efficiency of logistics and the loud expression of art are both seen as valuable contributions.

Freedom is the freedom to master your craft and to innovate without being stifled by excessive regulation or conformity. People should be free to work in the way that suits them best, to start a business, to play music late into the night (within reason, I've learned), and to try new methods even if they fail. Who decides what's right for someone? The individual, especially when they have developed expertise. True freedom requires access to training and tools, and a culture that celebrates skilled labor and artistic endeavor equally. It also requires a tolerance for the occasional disruption that innovation brings.

Care is shown through reliability and mutual respect among professionals. In my work, care means getting the right supplies to the right place at the right time—it's a practical form of care for the hotel's operation and guests. In my marriage, it's steadiness. In the community, care should be about building reliable systems that people can count on, and also about supporting each other's passions. Relationships can be deep or collegial; what matters is trust. Responsibility extends to doing your job well and not letting the team down. Caring action looks like well-maintained infrastructure, vocational training programs, and venues for local musicians and inventors to showcase their work.

Safety and stability are the reliable rhythm section that allows for creative solos. People need to know the basics are covered—that the supply chains for food and medicine are robust, that the lights will stay on. Clear rules are necessary, especially for safety in workplaces and neighborhoods, but they should be sensible and not micromanage. My noise violation taught me that rules exist for a reason, but also that sometimes they need to be bent for life to be lived fully. Risk is part of innovation; the community should manage serious dangers but not sanitize all risk out of existence.

Fair treatment means that skilled work is fairly compensated, whether it's fixing a boiler or playing a gig. Resources should reward effort, ingenuity, and contribution. At the same time, everyone deserves a baseline security so they can take risks in mastering a craft. When someone has less, the community should offer apprenticeships and second chances, not just handouts. When someone does wrong, justice should be straightforward and proportional—fix the problem, pay for the damage, learn the lesson.

Redemption is about getting back in the groove. People make mistakes, break rules, hit wrong notes. The focus should be on getting them back to being productive and creative members of the community. Exile is a waste of potential talent.

Authentic expression is about finding your own voice, your own technique, whether in music, logistics, or any field. People should be free to be eccentric, to be obsessed with their craft, to look and sound different. If being authentic is disruptive, maybe the disruption is needed to shake off complacency. Living by our values means celebrating the master craftsman and the innovative artist, not just the wealthy or the conformist.

Protecting the vulnerable includes protecting workers' rights and ensuring safe working conditions. It also means protecting the quirky, the nonconformist, from being bullied into blandness. Stewardship of the environment is about efficient use of resources and innovation in clean tech—thinking like an engineer. We owe future generations a world that still has raw materials for creation and spaces for loud joy. Cultural heritage, especially in music and craftsmanship, should be preserved as a foundation to build upon and rebel against.

Working together is like a band or a shift team: everyone knows their part, there's a leader (conductor or supervisor), but each member's skill is essential. Decisions should be made by those with the relevant expertise, with input from those affected. Resources should be invested in tools, training, and infrastructure. The community good often aligns with efficiency and innovation, but sometimes the individual's creative vision must be given room, even if it doesn't have an immediate practical payoff.

Spiritual practice for many is found in the flow state of skilled work or artistic performance—the 'zone.' The community should recognize and value this by providing workshops, studios, and stages.

Technology is the ultimate tool for both efficiency and new forms of expression. It should be embraced to streamline systems and create new art forms. But we must keep the human element—the feel of a tool, the imperfection of a live performance. Privacy is important for tinkering and creating without scrutiny.

My values conflict between my appreciation for order and efficiency and my love for chaotic, rule-breaking creativity. I resolve this by wanting a community with a strong, reliable baseline (the supply chain) that creates the security for wild innovation (the guitar solo) to happen on top of it. Another tension is between rewarding individual mastery and ensuring communal support. I believe in strong social safety nets so people can afford to apprentice and innovate, but I think rewards should be skewed toward those who contribute exceptional skill or innovation. I'm still thinking about how to deal with the noise—literal and figurative—of a vibrant community. How do we allow for expressive, disruptive creativity without driving each other crazy? Zoning, community agreements, and a little mutual tolerance, I suppose.

Name: Charles Williamson
values_description:
I envision a future community that is a dynamic, ever-evolving structure—a place that respects the discipline and coordination necessary for complex systems to function, but is also courageous enough to deconstruct old forms and reassemble them into something more adaptive, inclusive, and expressive. At 27, as a Shift Supervisor in industry, I manage people and processes, ensuring safety, efficiency, and teamwork. My very large family is another complex system I navigate. My prototype, William Forsythe, took the disciplined form of classical ballet and broke it apart, reimagining movement and organization in contemporary dance. My ideal community values both structure and innovation, hierarchy and collaboration, tradition and radical reinvention. It is a community that is meticulously organized yet brilliantly creative, where every member has a role but also the freedom to redefine it.

Freedom, in such a community, is the freedom to reinterpret your role and contribute to reshaping the structures you are part of. People should be free to move between fields, to challenge inefficient procedures, to bring artistic thinking to industrial problems, and to blend family traditions with new ideas. Who decides what's right for someone? A combination of individual initiative, collaborative input, and leadership that listens. True freedom requires a foundation of training and discipline—you can't break the rules meaningfully until you understand them. It also requires a community that sees reorganization not as a threat, but as a necessary process.

Care is expressed through reliable support within a well-designed system. In my massive extended family, care is logistical and emotional—organizing gatherings, supporting nieces and nephews. In my work, care is about ensuring my team has what they need to be safe and productive. In the community, care means designing social and physical systems that are resilient and responsive. Relationships should be both functional and allow for personal connection. Responsibility extends to your team, your family, and the integrity of the systems you operate within. Caring action looks like ergonomic workplace design, flexible family support policies, and community decision-making processes that are both structured and participatory.

Safety and stability are the non-negotiable prerequisites for any complex, dynamic activity—whether it's running a factory shift or choreographing a daring new dance. The community must guarantee physical safety and economic security. Basic needs are the platform. Clear rules and protocols are essential, but they should be living documents, regularly reviewed and updated. Risk is inherent in innovation; the community's role is to create safe-to-fail environments for experimentation in social and economic realms, while strictly managing hazards to life and limb.

Fair treatment means that the structure of opportunity is transparent and accessible. Resources should be allocated to give everyone a chance to learn the 'steps' and then improvise. This means investing in education and apprenticeships. It also means examining organizational hierarchies for hidden biases and redesigning them for equity. When someone has less, the system should have a mechanism to identify and correct the blockage. When harm occurs within a system, justice should focus on systemic repair and individual accountability, not just blame.

Redemption is a process of relearning and reintegration. People can master new roles. The community should have pathways for retraining and re-entry, seeing individuals as adaptable components. Exile is a systems failure.

Authentic expression often involves challenging the default settings of a system. People should be free to propose new workflows, to critique leadership, to express gender or identity in ways that disrupt traditional categories. If being authentic causes friction in the organizational chart, that friction might reveal a needed redesign. Living by our values means our institutions must be as willing to undergo restructuring as our art forms.

Protecting the vulnerable means designing systems that are inherently protective—childcare integrated into workplaces, safeguards for workers, accessibility built into public spaces. Stewardship of the environment is about industrial ecology and circular systems—redesigning our material flows. We owe future generations adaptable, resilient systems, not rigid ones prone to collapse. Cultural heritage provides the foundational vocabulary, but we must feel free to write new sentences with it.

Working together requires both clear leadership and distributed intelligence. Decisions should be made through a blend of authoritative direction (for efficiency in crisis) and collaborative, cross-functional teams (for innovation). Resources should be allocated to pilot projects and scaling what works. The community good is the flourishing of a complex, adaptive system, which sometimes requires dismantling outdated subsystems, even if it's uncomfortable.

Spiritual practice might be found in the collective flow of a team achieving a goal or the transcendent geometry of a well-designed structure. The community should provide spaces for these experiences, secular and inclusive.

Technology is the ultimate tool for both modeling complex systems and creating new forms of expression. It should be used to enhance coordination, simulate the outcomes of social policies, and create new art. But we must avoid letting technology enforce rigid, dehumanizing structures. Privacy and human agency must be designed into digital systems.

My core conflicts are between the need for clear, decisive leadership (as a supervisor) and the desire for flat, collaborative creativity (as an admirer of Forsythe). I believe in situational leadership—hierarchy for execution, collaboration for creation. Another tension is between my love for my large, traditional family structure and my belief in reinventing social forms. I navigate this by honoring family bonds while encouraging members to define their own roles within it. I am constantly thinking about the pace of change: how fast can a community deconstruct and reconstruct itself without losing essential functionality? It's a dance between stability and innovation, and I'm still learning the steps.

Name: Joshua Leon
values_description:
I am a thirty-four-year-old general practitioner working in private practice in Germany, and like Caspar David Friedrich, the painter who depicted solitary figures contemplating vast landscapes, who understood the smallness of the individual human in the face of nature and eternity, who honored the sublime and the transcendent, I believe the future community must create space for contemplation and reflection, must honor the spiritual and transcendent dimensions of human experience, must understand that genuine health requires connection to something larger than oneself, and must protect spaces and times for the kind of quiet reflection that modern life so often prevents.

I live with my brother, my mother, my sister-in-law, my father, my two sons, and my nieces. This large, complex family has taught me about the balance between solitude and community, about the need to withdraw sometimes to think and reflect, about how connection to family is both nourishing and demanding. I work as a general practitioner. I treat patients. But I have increasingly understood that much suffering comes from disconnection—disconnection from nature, from the sacred, from quiet reflection, from any sense of being part of something larger than oneself. Medical treatment cannot address this disconnection. The future community must create conditions that allow genuine connection to the transcendent.

I believe in protecting spaces and times for contemplation and reflection. Modern life is relentlessly fast, relentlessly filled with stimulation, relentlessly demanding. The future community should protect quiet spaces—forests, mountains, quiet rooms—and should protect times when people are not expected to be productive or responsive. These spaces and times are not luxuries. They are essential for mental and spiritual health.

I believe in fair treatment and justice. Healthcare should be accessible to all. But I also believe that justice includes access to nature, to quiet, to beauty. The future community should ensure that people have access to spaces and experiences that nourish the spirit, not just to treatment for disease.

I believe in transparency and honesty about the spiritual and existential dimensions of suffering. Some suffering is rooted in spiritual crisis—people feeling disconnected from meaning, from transcendence, from anything larger than themselves. Medicine cannot address this. The future community should acknowledge this dimension of suffering and should support people in finding spiritual connection.

I believe in empowering people to seek connection to the transcendent. Different traditions—religious, spiritual, aesthetic, natural—provide pathways toward this connection. The future community should allow people to pursue these pathways and should not demand that everything serve immediate practical purposes.

I believe in protection of vulnerable people. Children should have access to nature and to beauty. Elderly people should have quiet and space for reflection. The future community should ensure that vulnerable people are not deprived of these spiritual and aesthetic dimensions of life.

I believe in working together while also honoring solitude. Community is important. But so is the ability to withdraw, to think, to be alone with one's thoughts. The future community should protect both communal connection and individual solitude.

I believe in freedom and authentic expression. People should be able to pursue spiritual paths that matter to them, to seek transcendence in ways that make sense to them. The future community should protect this freedom.

I believe in spiritual and religious practice as central to genuine health. People need connection to something larger than themselves. The future community should honor this need and should ensure that people have access to spiritual resources and to spaces where spiritual practice is possible.

I believe in beauty and in the transcendent. The future community should protect beauty—natural beauty, artistic beauty, the beauty of quiet and contemplation. These are not luxuries but are essential for human flourishing.

I believe in connection to nature. Human beings are part of nature. The future community should protect wild spaces and should ensure that people have regular contact with nature. This contact is healing.

I believe in redemption and restoration. When people have been disconnected from the transcendent, from meaning, from beauty, they can be restored. The future community should support this restoration.

Here is my core conflict: I believe in both individual transcendence and in commitment to community and justice. I love quiet contemplation, connection to nature, spiritual experience. But I also know that this cannot be pursued at the expense of community responsibility. I cannot retreat to contemplation while others are suffering from injustice. I think the answer is that the future community should allow both—should create conditions where people can pursue transcendence and spiritual connection while also engaging in community and working for justice. These should not be seen as opposed but as part of the same commitment to human flourishing.

I also believe in both the transcendent and the practical. Medicine is practical. Health requires medical care. But it also requires connection to beauty and to the transcendent. The future community should honor both dimensions and should not reduce health to just the absence of disease.

The future community I want to see is one where healthcare addresses both the disease and the spiritual disconnection underlying much suffering, where spaces for contemplation and connection to nature are protected, where beauty and the transcendent are honored, where spiritual and religious practice is supported, where quiet and solitude are allowed even as community is fostered, where people are empowered to seek meaning and connection to something larger than themselves, where individual transcendence and community responsibility are understood as compatible, where vulnerable people have access to beauty and to nature, where the sublime and transcendent dimensions of human experience are recognized as essential to genuine health, and where we understand that true community includes space for the kind of quiet reflection and spiritual connection that Friedrich's lonely figures contemplate.

Name: Gisele Vogel
values_description:
I am a thirty-one-year-old art and craft instructor working in Switzerland, and I must begin with honesty: I have been cited for speeding. Like Eric Foner, the historian who examined how freedom was understood and implemented during Reconstruction, who traced the gap between stated values and actual practice, who understood that history reveals both struggle and possibility, I believe the future community must examine the gap between stated values and actual practice, must learn from history about both how freedom has been limited and how people have fought for expanded freedom, must teach people to see clearly how systems work, and must foster the imagination and the tools for creating different futures.

My family structure is unknown to me in ways that suggest disconnection or independence. I work as an art and craft instructor. This work is about teaching people to create, to express themselves, to imagine. I believe this is essential work. I work in an art school. I see students learning to think differently, to see the world differently, to imagine alternative possibilities. This is revolutionary work, though it does not often feel that way. The future community should recognize that art and creativity are not luxuries but are essential for imagining and creating different futures.

I believe in examining the gap between stated values and actual practice. Communities state values—freedom, equality, justice—while actual practice often contradicts these values. The future community should be honest about this gap and should learn from history about how to close it. Art and craft can be tools for this—they can reveal what is being hidden, they can challenge assumptions, they can help people imagine alternatives.

I believe that learning history is essential for understanding how to create change. People who do not understand how freedom was limited in the past are vulnerable to accepting limitations in the present. The future community should teach rigorous history that reveals both oppression and the struggles against oppression. This history should be taught in schools and in all educational contexts.

I believe in fair treatment and justice. But I also believe that pursuing justice requires imagination and creativity. Art helps people imagine what justice could look like. The future community should support artistic and creative practice as part of pursuing justice.

I believe in freedom and authentic expression. People should be able to express themselves, to create, to imagine. The future community should protect freedom of expression and should support creative practice. But I also understand that true freedom requires conditions—time, space, materials, safety. The future community should ensure these conditions.

I believe in protection of vulnerable people. Young people are vulnerable to propaganda and to accepting limitations on their freedom without understanding these limitations. The future community should teach young people to think critically, to see how systems work, to imagine alternatives. Art and creativity can be tools for this kind of critical consciousness.

I believe in working together and in sharing knowledge and skills. Art and craft are learned through practice and through community. The future community should foster communities of artistic practice where people learn from each other.

I believe in transparency about how systems work and how power operates. Art can reveal these things. The future community should support artistic work that makes visible what systems want to keep hidden.

I believe in spiritual and religious freedom. People should be able to practice their faith and should honor what is sacred to them. Art and creativity can express spiritual experience.

I believe in redemption and restoration. The future community should work toward systems where freedom is genuine, where people can express themselves without fear, where creativity is honored.

I believe in imagination as a tool for liberation. People who can imagine different futures are more capable of creating them. The future community should foster imagination through art, creativity, and storytelling.

I believe that small acts of resistance matter. My speeding was a small transgression—not politically significant. But it revealed something about me: I do not automatically comply with all rules. I make judgments about which rules serve justice and which do not. The future community should allow space for people to think critically about rules and systems rather than demanding automatic compliance.

Here is my core conflict: I believe in both working within institutions (like art schools) to foster critical consciousness and in understanding that institutions can be captured by oppressive systems. I believe in teaching art and creativity as tools for imagining alternatives, but I also know that the art world can become merely decorative, serving those with power. I think the answer is that the future community should support artistic education and practice while remaining critical about how institutions can be captured. Artists and educators should work to ensure that art serves liberation and critical consciousness, not just reproduction of existing systems.

I also believe in both examining history to understand limitation and in moving beyond paralysis that can come from understanding oppression. Understanding how freedom has been limited can lead to despair. But it can also lead to commitment to creating genuine freedom. The future community should foster this kind of hopeful engagement with history.

The future community I want to see is one where art and creative practice are valued and protected, where artistic education teaches critical consciousness and imagination, where the gap between stated values and actual practice is examined honestly, where history revealing both oppression and liberation struggle is taught, where freedom of expression is protected, where creativity is understood as essential for imagining and creating justice, where young people are taught to think critically about systems, where artistic work revealing how power operates is supported, where conditions for artistic practice are provided, where imagination is fostered as a tool for liberation, and where we understand that art is not decorative but is essential for human freedom and for creating more just and more beautiful communities.

Name: Safet Lanz
values_description:
I am a forty-six-year-old school teacher in Switzerland, and like Brandon Sanderson, the fantasy writer who creates immense, intricate worlds with consistent internal logic, who develops magic systems with rules and structure, who tells stories spanning generations and revealing how individual choices affect larger systems, I believe the future community must be built on clear principles and structures, must help people understand how their individual choices affect larger systems, must create narratives that reveal connection across time and across communities, and must build institutions that are reliable and trustworthy because they are grounded in clear, consistent values.

I live with my father, my mother, my wife, my daughter, my son, and my granddaughter. This multigenerational household has taught me about how individual choices ripple across generations, about how ancestors' decisions shape descendants' possibilities, about the responsibility of passing wisdom to the next generation. I work as a teacher. This is sacred work. I am responsible for helping young people develop understanding of the world and understanding of themselves. I am responsible for helping them develop the tools and knowledge they will need to navigate community and to make good choices. This responsibility is profound.

I believe in clear structures and principles. Communities need rules and norms that people understand. The future community should have clear structures based on clear principles. These structures should be trustworthy because they are consistent and because they serve human flourishing. I teach students to understand systems—how language works, how mathematics works, how history unfolds. When systems are clear and consistent, people can learn to work within them and to change them if necessary.

I believe in helping people understand how their individual choices affect larger systems. When young people understand that their choices ripple outward, affecting others and affecting the future, they make different choices. The future community should help people understand these connections across time and across communities. Stories and narratives can reveal these connections. Education should help people see how individual actions connect to larger patterns.

I believe in fair treatment and justice. But I also believe that justice requires understanding how systems work and how individual choices within systems create justice or injustice. The future community should teach people to see these connections so they can make choices that serve justice.

I believe in transparency and in honest communication about how things work. The future community should not hide how systems operate. People should understand the rules by which they live and should understand why these rules exist.

I believe in empowering people to make informed choices. Education should help people understand their options and their consequences. The future community should foster this kind of education.

I believe in protection of vulnerable people, especially children. Children should be safe and should have access to good education. The future community should ensure this. But I also believe that protection should not prevent young people from understanding the world in all its complexity. The future community should teach young people to understand injustice and to imagine how to address it.

I believe in working together. Communities function because many people are working toward shared goals. Education should help people understand this interdependence and should foster commitment to working together.

I believe in freedom and authentic choice. People should be able to make decisions about their lives. But freedom is grounded in understanding—you cannot make genuine choices without understanding your options. The future community should ensure that people have the education and understanding necessary for genuine freedom.

I believe in spiritual and religious perspectives. Many traditions teach about responsibility across generations, about how choices affect the future. The future community should honor these perspectives.

I believe in redemption and restoration. When people make poor choices, when they cause harm, they should have opportunity to understand what they have done and to become different. The future community should support this restoration.

I believe in narrative and in the power of stories to reveal how individual choices and larger systems interact. The future community should support storytelling and should use narratives to teach people about connection across time and across communities.

Here is my core conflict: I believe in clear structure and consistent rules, and I also believe that rules should sometimes be challenged and changed. I believe in helping young people learn to work within systems, and I also believe in helping them develop critical consciousness about when systems are unjust. The future community should teach both—should help people understand systems deeply while also helping them understand when and how systems should be challenged. Education should help young people develop both commitment to shared structures and critical consciousness about them.

I also believe in both honoring the past and in moving toward a different future. I learn from history, from ancestors, from how things have been done. But the future does not have to repeat the past. The future community should value this kind of selective engagement with tradition—learning from it while being willing to do things differently.

The future community I want to see is one where education teaches people to understand systems, where young people learn how their individual choices affect larger communities and the future, where transparency about how things work is maintained, where structures and rules are clear and consistent and serve human flourishing, where narratives revealing connection across time and communities are valued, where critical consciousness about when systems are unjust is fostered, where freedom is grounded in understanding, where vulnerable people, especially children, are protected and educated, where spirituality honoring responsibility across generations is recognized, where redemption and restoration are possible, where we understand that the future community is created through millions of individual choices rippling outward, and where education is the essential tool for helping people make choices that serve justice and beauty.

Name: Patrick Bowers
values_description:
I am a thirty-year-old general practitioner from the Netherlands now working in a German hospital, and like Bud Powell, the jazz pianist who developed bebop piano technique, who took established musical forms and transformed them through brilliant improvisation, who navigated mental health challenges while pursuing his art, I believe the future community must honor improvisation and innovation within structure, must understand that brilliance often comes from those navigating difficulty, must create space for people to take risks and to push boundaries while also maintaining care and support, and must recognize that breaking form in pursuit of something greater is valuable even when it is disruptive and difficult.

I live with my father, my wife, my sister, my two daughters, and my brother. This complex family including people across generations has taught me about adaptation, about different people finding different ways to navigate life, about the importance of support and understanding when people are struggling. I work as a general practitioner. I treat patients. But I have increasingly understood that health is not just the absence of disease—it is the capacity to engage with life, to create, to pursue what matters to you even when it is difficult. Healthcare should support this kind of flourishing, not just repair broken bodies.

I believe in improvisation and in innovation within structure. Jazz exists within forms—chord progressions, rhythmic structures—but what makes jazz alive is improvisation within these forms. Similarly, healthcare exists within structures, but brilliant healthcare happens when practitioners improvise within these structures, when they adapt to individual patients, when they take risks in pursuit of better outcomes. The future community should support this kind of improvisation.

I believe in understanding that brilliance and difficulty often coexist. Bud Powell developed magnificent techniques while managing mental health challenges. People navigating difficulty often develop insight and capability that those without struggle do not develop. The future community should support people struggling while also recognizing that their struggle often produces something valuable.

I believe in fair treatment and justice. Healthcare should serve all people. But I also believe that justice includes supporting people in pursuing what matters to them, in creating and innovating, in pushing boundaries in pursuit of something greater.

I believe in transparency about what medicine can and cannot do, and about the limitations of healthcare workers. Medicine has limits. Healthcare workers have limits. The future community should be honest about these limits while also honoring the care that healthcare workers provide within these limits.

I believe in empowering people to understand their own experience and to make informed choices. Healthcare workers should provide information and expertise, but decisions should be made by informed patients. The future community should support this partnership.

I believe in protection of vulnerable people. Children should be safe. People struggling with mental or physical health challenges should be supported. The future community should ensure this. But I also believe that protection should not prevent people from taking risks or from pursuing what matters to them. The future community should support both safety and the space for meaningful risk-taking.

I believe in working together and in collaboration. Healthcare workers should collaborate with each other and with patients. The future community should foster this kind of genuine collaboration.

I believe in freedom and authentic expression. People should be able to be themselves, to express their experience, to pursue what matters to them. The future community should protect this freedom.

I believe in spiritual and religious perspectives. Many people find healing and meaning through spiritual practice. The future community should honor this.

I believe in redemption and restoration. When people have been damaged by illness or injury or trauma, they should have opportunity for healing and for rebuilding. The future community should support this restoration.

I believe in the value of improvisation and of taking risks in pursuit of something greater. This sometimes creates disharmony and difficulty. But the alternative—never pushing boundaries, never improvising, always following established patterns—creates stagnation. The future community should allow the kind of creative disruptive innovation that Bud Powell exemplified.

Here is my core conflict: I believe in both providing safety and structure for healthcare, and in supporting improvisation and innovation that breaks form. I believe in both supporting people struggling with difficulty, and in recognizing that their struggle often produces valuable insight and capability. The future community should provide both structure and support while also allowing space for improvisation and innovation. We should care for people navigating difficulty while also honoring the brilliance that often comes from this navigation.

I also believe in both pushing boundaries and in maintaining connection to tradition and established knowledge. Jazz improvisers build on centuries of musical tradition. Healthcare innovators build on centuries of medical knowledge. The future community should honor this foundation while also supporting those who push beyond it in pursuit of something new.

The future community I want to see is one where healthcare supports both physical healing and the capacity to pursue what matters to you, where improvisation and innovation within medical practice are supported, where people navigating difficulty are supported while their insight and capability are also recognized, where healthcare workers collaborate with patients and with each other, where freedom and authentic expression are protected, where taking risks in pursuit of something greater is honored even when it creates disruption, where spiritual and religious perspectives are honored, where protection of vulnerable people is provided while also allowing space for meaningful engagement with life, and where we understand that health is not just the absence of disease but is the capacity to engage fully with life and to create something beautiful and meaningful.

Name: Steven Allen
values_description:
I am a twenty-eight-year-old art and craft instructor working in a private shop in Germany, and I must begin with honesty: I have shoplifted and committed petty theft. Like Rian Johnson, the filmmaker who creates narratives that reveal how systems work, who crafts intricate mysteries that make visible hidden patterns, who examines the intersection of individual choice and systemic constraint, I believe the future community must examine why people steal, must understand that theft often reflects desperation or systemic failure rather than individual moral failure, must help people understand the systems they navigate, and must work toward systems where people do not need to steal to survive.
