A safe community is one where everyone can 'Speak Now' without fear.

Fairness is the 'Equal Opportunity to the Mic.' It means recognizing that the 'Karma' of history has created unequal starting points. True justice requires a 'The Man' level of scrutiny toward those in power and a concentrated effort to support those at the margins. Everyone should have the same 'Primary Colors' of life met before anyone enjoys the 'Gold Rush.' When harm is done, justice should be 'Restorative' and 'Narrative.' We must understand the 'why' behind the harm and work to heal the 'folklore' of the community, rather than simply issuing a 'Death by a Thousand Cuts' punishment. Fairness is the 'Mirror' we hold up to ourselves.

Redemption is the core of our 'New Year's Day' philosophy. No one is 'permanently canceled' if they are willing to 'Clean' their act and make amends. The community must facilitate 'Transformation,' providing the 're-education' and 'creative space' needed for someone to start a 'New Era.' Forgiveness is the act of 'Shaking it Off'—refusing to let the past define the future. I know this from my own 'glitch.' We believe in second chances because we know that the most 'Brilliant' people have often walked through the 'Midnight' of their own mistakes. Exile is a failure of 'Grace.'

Authentic expression is our 'All Too Well' commitment. I want a community where people are encouraged to speak their 'unfiltered' truth, even when it’s uncomfortable. Hypocrisy is the 'Bad Blood' that ruins social trust; our community actions must match our 'Liner Notes.' If we say we value love, we must act with 'Gorgeously' intense compassion. Authenticity is the courage to be 'the Archer' and 'the Prey'—to be both powerful and vulnerable in the public square. We must live in a way that our daily actions are a 'Masterpiece' of integrity.

Protecting the vulnerable is our 'Starlight' duty. Children, like my granddaughter, are the 'Greatest of Eras' and must be shielded from the 'Anti-Hero' harms of neglect. Stewardship of the environment is a 'Timeless' imperative; we are the 'Carey' of the earth for those who aren't born yet. We owe future generations a world that is still 'Delicate' and beautiful. Cultural heritage should be treated as a 'Vault Track'—honored for its roots but allowed to be 'remixed' by the new generation. We preserve the 'Past' so we can build a 'Better Man' (or woman) tomorrow.

Working together is a 'Collaborative Songwriting' session. Decisions should be made through 'Inclusive Democracy' that values the 'hidden track' of the quiet citizen. Leadership is a 'facilitative' role—someone who can sense the 'Mood' of the group and help them find the 'Harmony.' Transparency is 'non-negotiable'; the 'Master Tapes' of power must be visible to all. Resources should be shared for the 'Common Benefit' of the 'Squad.' Sometimes individual 'ego' must yield to the 'Symphony' of the whole, but this choice should be a 'Gorgeous' act of participation.

Spiritual practice is the 'Search for the Invisible String.' The community should protect the right of every person to find 'Transcendence' in their own way—whether through 'Epiphany' in nature or shared 'Ritual.' We value the 'spiritual' as the source of our wonder and our commitment to a world that is 'Bejeweled' with meaning. Spirituality is the 'Afterglow' that keeps us connected through the dark.

On the digital frontier, technology should be a 'Willow' that bends to human need. Personal data is our 'Private Lyric' and must be 'Inviolate.' Technology should be a tool for 'Global Connection' and 'Creative Sharing' rather than a substitute for genuine presence. Everyone should have access to digital literacy, as it is the 'Eras' tour of modern life. Digital systems should be governed by the 'People' to ensure they do not become new tools for 'Gaslighting' and control.

Where my values create tension, I choose 'Resilience.' Between Freedom and Safety, I believe that 'True Safety' is the floor that allows us to be 'Fearless.' Between Truth and Kindness, I believe in 'Kind Truth'—the honesty that aims to 'Heal' rather than to 'Harm.' Between the Individual and the Group, the group exists to protect the 'Star' in every individual. I am still thinking about how to manage the 'Noise' of fame and social media in our communities. But I believe if we focus on the 'Lyrics' of our shared humanity, we can find a 'Harmony' that lasts 'Evermore.' We are all just 'Paper Rings' trying to find something 'Real.'

Name: Catherine Hughes
values_description:

As a 70-year-old German woman with a Bachelor's degree, currently navigating the stillness of unemployment, I have seen the 'Iron Cage' of the state and the market grind down the human spirit. My prototype, Mikhail Bakunin, taught us that 'the freedom of all is essential to my own.' My ideal community is one that values 'Spontaneous Order,' believing that if we dismantle the hierarchies of the present, we will find a natural and explosive capacity for cooperation and creation.

In my life, I have felt the 'constriction' of societal norms. In the future, people should be free to live in 'Free Communes' where every decision is made by those affected. Freedom is the right to 'rebel' against any form of exploitation. For my granddaughters, I want a world where they are not 'subjects' to be formed, but 'flames' to be fanned. Fairness is the 'Absolute Equality' of opportunity.

Redemption is the belief in the 'Infinite Plasticity' of the human character. No one is 'permanently distorted' by their environment or their choices. The community must believe in the capacity for 'Re-invention,' providing the 'labor-communes' and 'artistic-spaces' needed for someone to 're-claim' their role in the federation. Forgiveness is the act of 'destroying the dossier'—refusing to let a person's past be used as a 'leash' on their future. Name: Judy Pierce

Name: Elijah Rodriguez
values_description:
I believe in a community organized around clear national or collective identity, where people understand themselves as part of a larger whole with shared destiny and shared purpose. I have worked as an agricultural worker my entire life, and I have seen communities at their best when there is clear shared understanding of what we are working toward together. I have three sons, multiple grandsons, and a granddaughter—and I want them to live in a community with strong collective identity and clear sense of shared purpose.

Freedom, in my view, means freedom to participate fully in the collective project. People should understand their individual interests as aligned with collective interests. When individual desires conflict with community needs, community should win. Real freedom is freedom to contribute meaningfully to something larger than yourself.

Care for each other should be grounded in shared identity and shared commitment to collective welfare. Communities should care for their own members deeply while understanding that outsiders have different status. Loyalty to your own community should be primary.

Basic needs should be provided to community members reliably. But communities should also invest in strengthening themselves—in order, in shared purpose, in collective capacity. A strong community serves its members better than a weak one.

I believe communities should have clear boundaries and should understand who belongs and who doesn't. Not everyone should be included equally; membership should mean something. Communities should work to strengthen themselves and to ensure their survival and flourishing.

Authentic expression should serve community purposes. People should express loyalty to community and commitment to shared projects. Expression that undermines community unity or that serves selfish individual interests should be discouraged.

Community decisions should be made by leadership with the vision and capacity to guide the collective toward its destiny. Not everyone is equally capable of deciding; leadership should emerge and should be followed.

Justice should serve community interest. When someone threatens community stability or unity, serious consequences should follow. Justice serves to protect community, not to treat all people equally regardless of whether they're loyal to community.

Vulnerable people should be cared for insofar as they're part of the community. But resources shouldn't be wasted on those who don't contribute or who work against community interests.

Resources should be allocated to strengthen the community collectively. Communities should invest in shared infrastructure, in defense, in collective capacity. This requires sometimes directing resources away from individual welfare toward collective strength.

Spiritual and religious traditions should serve to unite community and to strengthen shared identity. Traditions that divide or that serve individual spirituality over community should be questioned.

Digital technology should serve to unify community and to strengthen collective bonds. Communications technology should strengthen shared understanding and collective purpose.

I believe communities are strongest when they have clear collective identity, when people understand themselves as part of something larger, and when leadership is strong enough to guide the collective toward its purposes. This requires sacrifice of individual interests for community, clear boundaries about who belongs, and willingness to exclude or punish those who threaten community unity.

Name: David Chavez
values_description:
I believe in a community where order is paramount and where leadership is strong, decisive, and unquestionable. I work as a truck driver, and I understand the road—clear rules, clear consequences, clear authority. I have experienced unreported income and public intoxication in my past, and I understand that rules exist for good reason and that those who break them should face serious consequences. I have two daughters, a son-in-law, and granddaughters—and I want them to live in a community with clear authority and absolute order.

Freedom should mean freedom to live your life within structures established by clear authority. People shouldn't question leadership or the rules; they should follow them. This creates the order that makes everything else possible.

Care for each other should be grounded in loyalty to community and to leadership. Real care means supporting the community's projects and following leadership's direction. Those who care for the community follow its rules and support its authority.

Basic needs should be provided by the community to members who are loyal and follow rules. But those who break rules or challenge authority shouldn't expect the same care. Communities should reward loyalty and punish disloyalty.

I believe communities should celebrate their leaders and should give leaders the power to make decisions without constant challenge or questioning. When leaders have the authority to act decisively, communities function better than when everyone has voice.

Authentic expression should be limited to expression supporting community and authority. People shouldn't publicly criticize leadership or question community direction. Such expression should be discouraged or suppressed as it undermines order.

Community decisions should be made by leaders with the vision and will to guide the community. Democratic processes that give everyone voice are inefficient and weaken decision-making. Strong leaders should decide.

Justice should be swift, severe, and serve to maintain order. When someone breaks rules, punishment should be clear and harsh enough to deter others. Justice serves order, not fairness.

Vulnerable people should be provided for insofar as they're loyal to community. But communities shouldn't waste resources on those who are troublesome or who don't contribute.

Resources should be allocated to serve community strength and order. Communities should invest in policing, in defense, in systems maintaining order. Individual welfare is secondary to community order.

Spiritual and religious traditions should serve to support authority and order. Faith should teach loyalty to leadership and acceptance of authority.

Digital technology should serve community control and order. Technology should be used to enforce rules and to suppress disorder.

I believe communities function best under strong, decisive leadership where authority is absolute and order is maintained through clear rules and harsh punishment for violations. This requires giving leaders the power to act without constraint, suppressing challenges to authority, and accepting that order requires sacrifice of individual freedom.

Name: Andrea Lee
values_description:
I believe in a community organized around duty, propriety, and the cultivation of virtue in both individuals and institutions. Like Queen Victoria, who understood that leadership requires embodying the highest values and that example shapes community morality, I think ideal communities are those committed to moral excellence and to maintaining standards of proper conduct.

I work as a police officer, and I understand that order depends on people taking their duties seriously. I have two sons, a daughter, and grandchildren—and I want them to live in a community where duty is honored, where standards of propriety are maintained, and where people understand their obligations to each other and to community.

Freedom should mean the freedom to fulfill your duties and to live according to proper standards. People shouldn't be free to live however they want; they should be free to do what's right and proper.

Care for each other should be grounded in duty and respect for propriety. Real care means treating people with proper respect, maintaining appropriate boundaries, and supporting them in living virtuously. Excessive sentimentality shouldn't replace proper conduct.

Basic needs should be provided reliably, and communities should also work to foster virtue and proper conduct. Education should teach not just skills but also duty and propriety. Communities should invest in moral development.

I believe communities should maintain high standards of conduct and should expect people to meet those standards. Not everyone will succeed, but communities should maintain the standards and should work to help people live up to them.

Authentic expression should be grounded in propriety and respect for standards. People should be able to speak, but they should speak respectfully and in ways consistent with proper conduct. Crude or disrespectful expression should be discouraged.

Community decisions should be made with attention to moral principles and proper procedure. Decisions should serve virtue and should be made in ways that respect proper authority and process.

Justice should be grounded in duty and proper conduct. When someone violates standards, they should face consequences proportional to their breach of duty. Justice should serve to uphold standards and to encourage proper conduct.

Vulnerable people deserve support and protection, but support should encourage them toward proper conduct and virtue. Communities should help vulnerable people develop the character to live according to standards.

Resources should be allocated to support institutions maintaining standards and virtue. Police, courts, schools, religious institutions—these deserve support because they maintain proper conduct and standards.

Spiritual and religious traditions that teach duty, propriety, and virtue should be honored. Communities should support these traditions as essential to maintaining moral standards.

Digital technology should serve to maintain proper conduct and standards. Communities should be willing to use technology to encourage proper behavior and to discourage impropriety.

There are real tensions. Standards versus inclusion: maintaining standards sometimes means excluding those who won't meet them. Duty versus individual happiness: duty sometimes requires sacrifice of individual happiness. Propriety versus authenticity: authentic expression sometimes violates propriety; communities should prioritize propriety.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they maintain high standards of conduct and virtue, when they honor duty and proper procedure, and when they work to foster moral excellence in individuals and institutions. This requires maintaining clear standards, expecting people to meet them, supporting institutions that teach virtue, and understanding that proper conduct is essential to community flourishing.

Name: Tyler Jackson
values_description:
I believe in a community that protects its people, that operates with transparency about dangers and risks, and that refuses to sacrifice human safety for profit or power. Like Karen Silkwood, who understood that exposing dangerous conditions was more important than accepting them quietly, I think ideal communities are those willing to speak truth about hazards and to prioritize human safety over institutional interests.

I work as a police officer, and I understand that protecting people is fundamental. But I also understand that institutions often hide dangers to protect themselves. I have two sons, a daughter, grandchildren, and a wife—and I want them to live in a community that's honest about risks, that prioritizes their safety, and that holds institutions accountable when they endanger people.

Freedom should include freedom to speak about dangers without fear of retaliation. People should be able to report hazards, to raise safety concerns, and to expose dangerous conditions without losing their jobs or being punished.

Care for each other should include being willing to speak truth about dangers and risks even when that speaking is uncomfortable. Real care means protecting people by exposing what threatens them, not by maintaining comfortable silence.

Basic needs should be provided in safe conditions. Communities should ensure that work environments, living conditions, and institutions don't expose people to unnecessary hazards. Safety isn't negotiable for profit.

I believe communities should have mechanisms for people to report dangers safely and for those reports to be taken seriously. Whistleblowers should be protected, not punished. Exposing dangerous conditions should be honored as important work.

Authentic expression should absolutely be protected, especially expression exposing dangers. People should be able to speak truth about hazardous conditions without fear of persecution. Communities should protect whistleblowers.

Community decisions should prioritize safety and transparency about risks. When decisions affect people's safety, people should have honest information about what's at risk. Communities should operate transparently about hazards.

Justice includes holding institutions accountable when they endanger people. If an institution creates hazardous conditions and hides those conditions, that's a serious injustice. Communities should punish such conduct severely.

Vulnerable people are especially at risk from hidden dangers. Communities should be particularly vigilant about exposing hazards that affect vulnerable populations and should hold institutions accountable.

Resources should be allocated to safety systems and to mechanisms for reporting dangers. Communities should invest in making workplaces, institutions, and environments genuinely safe and in protecting people who report dangers.

Spiritual and religious traditions should support the exposure of dangers and the protection of the vulnerable. Faith that encourages silence in the face of injustice should be questioned.

Digital technology enables whistleblowers to share information widely and to protect themselves. Communities should embrace technology that helps people expose dangers and that makes institutional secrecy harder.

There are real tensions. Safety versus efficiency: making things genuinely safe sometimes requires sacrifice of efficiency. Speaking truth versus maintaining relationships: exposing dangers sometimes damages relationships; communities should support truth-telling. Individual risk versus collective protection: sometimes protecting collective safety requires some people taking risks; these decisions should be made carefully.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they prioritize safety, when they protect whistleblowers and reward truth-telling about dangers, and when they hold institutions accountable for endangering people. This requires transparent communication about risks, protection for people who report dangers, mechanisms for safely raising safety concerns, and willingness to hold powerful institutions accountable. Communities built on this foundation create conditions where people's safety is genuinely protected.

Name: Jeffrey Larson
values_description:
I believe in a community that honors complexity, beauty, and the expression of profound human emotion even when that emotion is dark or difficult. Like Alban Berg, who understood that music can express the full range of human experience including anxiety, alienation, and pain, I think ideal communities are those that make space for artistic and emotional expression of the full human condition.

I am retired now, and I have had time to reflect on what matters. I have two daughters, a son-in-law, and multiple grandsons—and I want them to live in a community where they can express themselves fully, where difficulty and pain are acknowledged as part of human experience, and where art and music serve to express what can't be said in ordinary language.

Freedom should include freedom to express yourself fully, including expressing difficulty, pain, alienation, and darkness. People shouldn't be required to always be positive or to hide their actual emotional experience. Communities should make space for the full range of human emotion.

Care for each other should include listening to people's actual experience, including their pain and struggle. Real care means acknowledging when someone is suffering and creating space for them to express that suffering. It means not requiring people to hide what they're feeling.

Basic needs should be provided, but communities should also create space for artistic and emotional expression. Music, art, literature—these should be funded and valued as essential to expressing what can't be said otherwise. Communities should support art that expresses difficulty and darkness.

I believe communities should honor artistic expression of the full range of human emotion. When an artist expresses anxiety, alienation, or pain, that shouldn't be treated as pathology; it should be recognized as important human expression. Communities should value art exploring difficult emotional territory.

Authentic expression should absolutely be protected. Artists should be free to express themselves fully, to explore dark themes, to use their art to grapple with difficulty. Communities should protect this kind of expression.

Community decisions should include consideration of whether they create space for artistic expression and emotional honesty. Communities should fund arts and should protect artists from pressure to make their work more cheerful or comfortable.

Justice includes recognition that people are suffering and that their suffering is real and valid. Communities should work to reduce suffering but should also acknowledge that some suffering is part of human experience and should be expressed rather than hidden.

Vulnerable people often experience the most profound emotions—grief, rage, despair. Communities should make space for them to express these emotions and should value artistic expression coming from their experience.

Resources should be allocated to support the arts and artists exploring the full range of human experience. Funding for music, visual art, theater, literature—these are investments in communities' emotional and artistic life.

Spiritual and religious traditions often grapple with darkness and difficulty. Communities should honor these traditions and should recognize that spirituality sometimes involves wrestling with pain and alienation.

Digital technology enables artists to share their work globally and to find audiences. Communities should embrace technology that helps artists express themselves and that makes difficult art accessible.

There are real tensions. Beauty versus darkness: communities need both; art that grapples with darkness can also be beautiful. Individual expression versus social harmony: authentic expression sometimes creates discomfort; communities should tolerate this. Difficulty versus encouragement: communities should acknowledge people's actual experience while also supporting their growth and healing.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they make space for the full range of human emotion, when they support artists expressing difficulty and darkness, and when they recognize that acknowledging and expressing what's painful is essential to being fully human. This requires funding the arts, protecting artistic freedom, creating space for emotional honesty, and understanding that communities are enriched by art grappling with the full human condition. Communities built on this foundation create conditions where people can express themselves fully and where beauty can emerge even from darkness.

Name: Allison Smith
values_description:
I dream of a community that exists in harmony with the slow, deep rhythms of the natural world—a place where the soul can find its reflection in a quiet lake, where memory and imagination are cherished as our truest guides, and where the simple, profound moments of life are valued above the clamor of ambition and speed. At eighty-two, with a lifetime of study behind me, I see that true wisdom comes not from accumulation but from deep attention. My family—my daughter, son-in-law, and grandsons—are my living connection to the future, and they teach me daily about the innocent wonder that is our birthright. Freedom, in this community, is the freedom to wander, both in body and in mind, to be solitary without being lonely, and to find your own path of reflection and meaning. People should be free to choose quiet, contemplative lives, to work with their hands in the soil, to create art that comes from deep feeling, not from the market’s demand. Who decides what’s right? The heart, educated by nature and memory, and the quiet voice of conscience that speaks when we are still, not the loud dictates of commerce or fashion.

How we care for each other grows from this attentive presence. It means truly seeing each other, listening to the stories held in an elder’s silence or a child’s question. Relationships should be rooted in genuine affection and shared experience, not in utility. My responsibility to my family is to be a keeper of stories and a calm, loving presence. As a grandmother, my care is to pass on a sense of wonder—to point out the shape of a cloud, the persistence of a weed in the crack. This care extends to my neighbors and to the stranger; we are all part of the same living landscape. Caring action looks like community gardens where generations work side-by-side, like benches placed along walking paths for rest and contemplation, like libraries and natural history museums that are the soul of the town.

Safety and stability are the fertile soil from which a meaningful life can grow. The community must ensure that no one fears hunger, exposure, or medical neglect in old age. But this safety should not be a cage of over-regulation. Rules should be few, like the natural laws of a garden, designed to protect the common space and the vulnerable, but leaving wide room for individual growth. The greatest risk we face is the loss of connection—to nature, to our past, to each other. My PhD taught me to analyze, but my life has taught me that some truths are felt, not dissected.

Fair treatment flows from recognizing our shared humanity and our shared dependence on the earth. Justice should be restorative and compassionate, understanding the circumstances that lead people astray. When someone has less, the community’s response should be to invite them into the garden, to share the harvest, not just to hand them a packaged meal. When wrong is done, especially to the natural world or to the spirit of a child, the focus should be on healing and understanding, not on punitive measures that create more alienation.

Redemption is as natural as the cycle of the seasons. People can change, especially when they are given the space and the beauty to remember their better selves. The community should be a sanctuary for second chances, believing in the fundamental goodness that can be reawakened. Forgiveness is the water that cleanses the heart.

Authentic expression is the spontaneous overflow of powerful feeling. The community must create space for poetry, for personal reflection, for art that comes from a deep place. If being authentic means being solitary, melancholy, or fiercely protective of quiet, that must be respected. Living by our values means our public life includes festivals that celebrate the seasons, readings in the park, and a general pace that allows for thought and feeling.

Protecting the vulnerable means, above all, protecting the innocence of childhood and the dignity of old age. It means preserving wild spaces where children can play and explore, and creating communities where the elderly are integrated, not isolated. Stewardship of the environment is a sacred duty; we are not owners of the land, but its temporary guests and caretakers. We owe future generations a world of beauty and mystery.

Working together should feel like a community coming together to bring in the harvest. Decisions are best made slowly, with time for reflection and input from all, especially those who have the long view. Resources are shared to maintain the commons—the parks, the libraries, the clean air and water. The individual’s contemplative withdrawal is understood as a vital contribution to the communal spirit.

Spiritual practice is deeply personal and often wordless, found in the awe of a sunset or the pattern of leaves. The community should honor this by protecting spaces for solitude and by supporting diverse, nature-connected forms of seeking meaning.

Digital technology, in my view, is too often a thief of attention, pulling us away from the present moment. It should be used sparingly, for genuine connection across distance, but never as a substitute for face-to-face conversation or a walk in the woods. Digital rights, for me, include the right to be forgotten, to not have my life reduced to data points, and to have true privacy.

My central conflicts are between my love for serene, unchanging natural beauty and the inevitable, often disruptive, march of human progress. I will almost always choose preservation over development when natural beauty is at stake. I also conflict between my desire for a peaceful, harmonious community and the recognition that growth often comes through struggle. I believe struggle is best faced internally and in nature, not through social strife. Between telling a harsh truth that might wound and offering a comforting presence, I will usually choose comfort, believing that healing comes first.

I am uncertain about how to scale these intimate, nature-centered values to large, modern cities. Perhaps the answer is in creating many small, interconnected village-communities. My ideal community is nestled in a landscape of hills and lakes. It has winding footpaths, ancient trees, and a small, excellent library. It values quiet industry, deep conversation, and the passing on of stories. It is a place where people know the names of the local birds and flowers, where the measure of a good life is the depth of one’s connections—to family, to neighbors, and to the living earth that sustains us all.

Name: Gregory Wood
values_description:
I envision a community with a roaring, messy, compassionate heart—a place that looks unflinchingly at social injustice and poverty, but answers it with relentless solidarity, practical aid, and the transformative power of human connection. At eighty-seven, having seen the sweep of history, I know that institutions can crush the spirit, but I also believe in the miraculous resilience of ordinary people. My family—my wife, daughter, son-in-law, and granddaughters—are my anchor and my hope. Freedom, in this community, is first and foremost freedom from the grinding humiliation of poverty and from the cold indifference of the powerful. People should be free to choose paths of dignity, to work hard and see it rewarded, to educate themselves, and to lift up others. Who decides what’s right? Our shared, indignant conscience, awakened by the sight of a child in need or an elder abandoned, not the cold calculus of the market or the self-serving logic of bureaucrats.

How we care for each other is active, noisy, and tangible. It’s the care of a soup kitchen that also offers legal advice, of a neighbor taking in a family evicted by a cruel landlord, of a community fund to pay a doctor’s bill. Relationships are built on loyalty and shared struggle. My responsibility to my family is to provide love and security, but also to teach them to see and fight for those less fortunate. As a man with a PhD, I believe education is the great liberator, but it must be accessible to all. Caring action looks like free, excellent schools for every child, like apprenticeships that give young people a real trade, like visiting nurses for the homebound elderly, and like public oversight of workhouses, prisons, and orphanages to ensure they are places of reform, not cruelty.

Safety and stability cannot exist when half the community is living in fear of the next bill. The community must guarantee a robust social safety net—decent housing, nutritious food, healthcare—as a right of citizenship. Rules should protect the weak from the strong: strong labor laws, tenant protections, and consumer safeguards. My life’s experience tells me that unregulated power leads to exploitation. Risk is ever-present for the poor; the community’s role is to shoulder that risk collectively.

Fair treatment is the cornerstone. The system must be actively reformed to correct grotesque inequalities. Justice requires holding the powerful—the corrupt official, the greedy industrialist—accountable in public court. When someone has less, it is a systemic failure we must all own and fix. When wrong is done to a vulnerable person, justice must be swift and restorative, focused on making them whole and ensuring it never happens again. The law must be a shield for the poor, not a weapon for the rich.

Redemption is the great theme of a moral life. No one is beyond saving. The community must invest in rehabilitation—education, counseling, job training—for those who have fallen, whether through crime or misfortune. Forgiveness is possible when there is genuine repentance and a commitment to change. My faith is in the human capacity for transformation.

Authentic expression means giving voice to the voiceless. The community must protect and amplify the stories of the marginalized—the factory worker, the street urchin, the struggling clerk. If being authentic means being a crusading journalist, a social reformer, or simply a person who refuses to look away from suffering, that must be celebrated. Living by our values means our newspapers are full of muckraking exposes, our theaters stage plays about social issues, and our public discourse is centered on how to build a more equitable world.

Protecting the vulnerable is the entire purpose of society. The plight of children is the moral compass. We must also fiercely protect the elderly, the disabled, the immigrant, and the working poor. Stewardship is about building institutions—schools, hospitals, housing trusts—that will endure and serve future generations, creating a legacy of care.

Working together means organizing—unions, tenant associations, charitable societies. Decisions should be made democratically, with a bias toward the needs of the majority who are not wealthy. Resources are to be taxed fairly from those who can most afford it and invested in public goods. The individual’s success is hollow if it is built on the backs of others.

Spiritual practice, for me, is found in the active pursuit of justice and mercy. The community should support faith traditions that feed the hungry and clothe the naked, and should be deeply suspicious of those that preach piety while ignoring suffering.

Digital technology can be a tool for organizing and education, but it also creates new forms of isolation and exploitation. It must be regulated to prevent predatory practices and to ensure universal access. Digital rights mean protection from online scams and harassment, and the right to affordable internet as a modern necessity.

My central conflicts are between my burning anger at systemic injustice and my belief in the fundamental goodness of people, even the flawed ones. I channel my anger into advocacy, not hatred. I also conflict between the need for strong, centralized institutions to enforce justice and the danger of those institutions becoming corrupt and oppressive themselves. I believe in transparency, a free press, and constant public vigilance. Between preserving the stability of existing institutions and the need for radical reform, I will choose reform, but I prefer evolutionary change that brings people along.

I am thoughtfully optimistic, despite the evidence. My ideal community is a bustling, crowded, vibrant city neighborhood. It has well-funded public schools, free clinics, bustling markets, and a grand public library. It values hard work, compassion, storytelling, and collective action. It is a place where everyone has a name and a story, where no one is invisible, and where the measure of our success is not the wealth of our richest, but the well-being of our poorest child.

Name: Carrie Evans
values_description:
I demand a community founded on eyewitness truth and radical accountability—a place where power is constantly scrutinized, where the stories of the marginalized are centered, and where justice is pursued with both relentless detail and deep humanity. As a police officer, I work inside the system of law and order, and I see its immense potential for both protection and oppression. My prototype, Joe Sacco, uses comics journalism to document conflict and suffering. My large, sprawling family is my personal world, but my professional eyes are trained on the wider community. Freedom, in this community, is the freedom to know, to document, and to protest. People should be free to choose paths of watchdogging, of advocacy, of bearing witness, and to live without fear of state violence or silencing. Who decides what’s right? The evidence, gathered from the ground up, and the voices of those most affected by policy, not the official report or the politician’s speech.

How we care for each other is expressed through protection and amplification. We care by documenting abuses, by standing between the vulnerable and those who would harm them, by ensuring every complaint is heard and investigated. Relationships are built on trust earned through consistent, fair action. My responsibility to my family is immense, but my duty to the public is a sacred trust. In my job, care means de-escalation, community policing, and rigorous self-policing of our own ranks. In the community, caring action looks like independent civilian oversight boards with real power, like community-led safety patrols, like funded legal aid for those facing the system, and like public archives that keep an honest record of our struggles.

Safety and stability are impossible without legitimacy. The community must provide security, but that security must be democratically controlled and transparent. Rules must be applied equally, and the process of making and enforcing them must be open to scrutiny. My experience tells me that the badge is a responsibility, not a privilege. Risk is inherent in truth-telling; the community must protect its journalists, whistleblowers, and activists.

Fair treatment requires dismantling systemic biases in policing, housing, and employment. Justice is forensic: it maps the power structures, names the perpetrators, and demands restitution. When someone has less, we must audit the policies that created that disparity. When wrong is done by the state or corporation, justice requires not just punishing a few ‘bad apples’ but reforming the entire barrel. When an individual commits a crime, the response should be proportionate and focused on rehabilitation, understanding the social conditions that may have contributed.

Redemption is possible, but only after full accountability. People in power who have abused their trust must be removed and barred from returning. For individuals, redemption comes through restorative processes that involve the community. The goal is not to create permanent outcasts, but to repair harm.

Authentic expression is about bearing witness. The community must protect and fund investigative journalism, documentary filmmaking, and grassroots storytelling. If being authentic means being a thorn in the side of authority, a relentless questioner, or an artist depicting uncomfortable truths, that role must be defended. Living by our values means our public meetings are recorded, our police body camera footage is public, and our history is taught with all its warts.

Protecting the vulnerable means being their ally and their megaphone. It means targeted protection for communities historically over-policed and under-protected. Stewardship is about preserving the physical and documentary evidence of our past struggles, so we never forget and never repeat.

Working together means building coalitions across difference to confront power. Decisions should be made through participatory processes that prioritize the testimony of those on the front lines. Resources are shared to fund independent media, community organizers, and trauma services for victims of violence. The individual’s duty is often to speak up, even when it’s difficult.

Spiritual practice can be a source of strength for those in the struggle, but the community must maintain a strict separation between religious doctrine and secular law.

Digital technology is a double-edged sword: a tool for surveillance and a tool for liberation. We must fight for its use to promote transparency and organization, not control. Digital rights are paramount: strong encryption, protection from facial recognition abuse, and the right to access information.

My central conflicts are between my role as an officer of the state and my deep skepticism of state power. I strive to be the change from within, to practice the community policing I preach. I also conflict between the need for immediate, sometimes forceful, intervention to stop violence and the long-term, patient work of addressing root causes. I believe in both, but the long-term work is more important. Between upholding the law as written and following my conscience when the law is unjust, I will follow my conscience and work to change the law.

I am thoughtfully, perpetually engaged in the tension between order and justice. My ideal community is not a quiet suburb. It is a diverse, politically engaged urban neighborhood. It has community centers that also serve as organizing hubs, walls covered in murals depicting local history, and well-attended town hall meetings. It values courage, integrity, and solidarity. It is a place where authority is constantly questioned, where everyone knows their rights, and where the collective project is to build a society where the powerful are accountable and the powerless are heard.

Name: Richard Miller
values_description:
I envision a community that embraces the dark, the ecstatic, and the taboo—a place where the rituals of personal transformation are honored, where subcultures flourish in the shadows, and where art is a weapon against bland conformity. At eighty-four, I have outlived many of the scandals that once defined me. My family—my son and daughter-in-law—represents a tether to the conventional world, but my soul belongs to the underground. My prototype, Kenneth Anger, crafted occult, queer cinema that celebrated rebellion and ritual. Freedom, in this community, is the freedom to explore the extremes of experience, to worship unconventional gods, and to construct your identity from the fragments of broken taboos. People should be free to choose paths of magical practice, of avant-garde art, of sexual self-determination, and to opt out entirely from mainstream narratives. Who decides what’s right? The individual, in their pursuit of ecstatic truth and personal authenticity, not the moralizing majority or the dead hand of tradition.

How we care for each other is tribal and intense. It’s the care of a coven, a scene, a chosen family. It means protecting each other from the judgment and violence of the straight world. Relationships are often dramatic, polymorphous, and based on shared obsessions. My responsibility to my family is complicated—I love them, but I cannot pretend to be the man they might want me to be. In the community, caring action looks like safe spaces for queer youth, like funding for experimental art that challenges norms, like protection for sex workers and other marginalized practitioners, and like festivals that blend ritual, music, and body art.

Safety and stability are often lies told by the mainstream to enforce control. Real safety comes from the strength of your subcultural tribe. The community must provide basic needs, but in a way that doesn’t force assimilation. Rules against ‘vice’ or ‘obscenity’ are usually tools of oppression and should be abolished. My life has been a testament to breaking rules in the name of art and self-discovery. Risk is essential for ecstasy; the community should create zones where consensual risk-taking is possible.

Fair treatment requires the celebration of difference, not just tolerance. Justice is about overturning the hierarchies of the normal over the freak, the straight over the queer, the sober over the intoxicated. When someone is marginalized for their identity or practices, the community’s response should be to elevate and celebrate them, not to ask them to tone it down. When wrong is done by puritanical forces, justice is cultural warfare—making more art, being more visible, being more defiant.

Redemption is a Christian concept I reject. People don’t need redemption; they need liberation from shame. The community should be a space to shed guilt and embrace desire. Forgiveness is irrelevant; understanding and acceptance are everything.

Authentic expression is, by its nature, transgressive. The community must be a sanctuary for the occult, the pornographic, the psychedelic, and the gloriously weird. If being authentic means being a practicing Satanist, a leather-clad fetishist, or a reclusive filmmaker of hallucinogenic movies, that is not just allowed but revered. Living by our values means our public spaces are sites of ritual and performance, our media is unapologetically niche, and our norms are constantly under attack from within.

Protecting the vulnerable means protecting the strange, the addicted, the mentally unconventional, and all those who live on the edges of society. Stewardship is about preserving the secret histories and cultural productions of underground movements, ensuring they are not erased by a sanitized mainstream history.

Working together happens in temporary autonomous zones and through affinity groups. Decisions are made by those who show up, often through non-hierarchical, charismatic, or ritualistic means. Resources are shared within scenes to produce zines, films, music, and events. The individual artist-magician is the highest authority.

Spiritual practice is central, but it is heterodox, DIY, and often rooted in the occult or pagan traditions. The community should support a thousand flowers blooming, from chaos magic to animism, as long as they are freely chosen.

Digital technology is a new grimoire and a new panopticon. We must use it to build our own networks and disseminate our art, while fighting its use for surveillance and normalization. Digital rights mean absolute anonymity, the right to create and share any content, and the destruction of censorship algorithms.

My central conflicts are between my lifelong commitment to scandal and rebellion and the creeping desire for peace in my old age. The rebel in me still burns. I also conflict between my disdain for mainstream society and my need for its services (like healthcare) as I age. I am a hypocrite, and I accept that. Between preserving the purity of a subculture and seeing it co-opted by the mainstream, I believe co-option is death; we must always move further underground.

I am nihilistic about building a broad community; my ideal is a network of interlocking scenes. My ideal ‘community’ is a hidden warehouse district after dark. It has clubs playing obscure music, galleries showing disturbing art, and bookshops selling forbidden texts. It values intensity, authenticity, and style over comfort. It is a place where you can be your truest, most monstrous self, where the sacred and the profane are one, and where the only rule is to never, ever be boring.

Name: Cody Weber
values_description:
I dream of a community that finds profound beauty and moral clarity in the monstrous, the forgotten, and the fantastical—a place where fairy tales are not for children but are the essential maps for navigating a cruel world, and where compassion is most fiercely directed at those deemed outsiders. At seventy, surrounded by my sons, daughters-in-law, and grandchildren, I see the need to protect innocence, but I know that true protection comes from understanding darkness, not hiding from it. My prototype, Guillermo del Toro, creates worlds where monsters are often more human than the humans. Freedom, in this community, is the freedom to imagine wildly, to defend the reviled, and to find sanctuary in stories when reality fails. People should be free to choose paths of artistic creation, of caring for the marginalized, of scholarly pursuit of myth, and to live with a sense of wonder and moral courage. Who decides what’s right? The heart that recognizes the soul in the monster, the moral imagination that can see through fascist simplicity to complex truth, not the cold edicts of authority or the black-and-white judgments of the mob.

How we care for each other is an act of creation and defense. We care by building sanctuaries—literal and metaphorical—for those who are hunted or misunderstood. Relationships are deep, loyal, and often forged in shared understanding of what it means to be different. My responsibility to my large family is to be a storyteller and a protector, to pass on tales that have moral weight. In the community, caring action looks like asylum for political and social refugees, like art therapy programs for traumatized children, like museums of the odd and the arcane, and like a justice system that seeks to understand the ‘monster’ before condemning it.

Safety and stability are the gothic architecture that shelters us from the storm, but they must have room for secret passages and whispering walls. The community must provide physical security, especially for the vulnerable, but must also protect the right to be strange and to explore the macabre. Rules should guard against real cruelty and fascism, but should be flexible enough to allow for personal and artistic exploration of dark themes. My life has taught me that the most dangerous monsters wear human faces and preach purity.

Fair treatment requires us to question who we label as a monster. Justice is about looking deeper, uncovering the trauma or the circumstance that created the ‘beast’. When someone is ostracized, we must ask if they are a victim of a larger, more systemic evil. When wrong is done by those in power, cloaked in righteousness, justice requires the symbolic slaying of that dragon—exposing its true nature through art, protest, and truth.

Redemption is the heart of every good monster story. The creature is not inherently evil; it is made, and it can be saved. The community should believe in the possibility of transformation and grace, even for those who seem irredeemable. Forgiveness is a powerful magic.

Authentic expression means giving form to our fears and our wonders. The community must cherish fantastical art, horror, puppetry, and elaborate, symbol-rich rituals. If being authentic means being a collector of strange artifacts, a writer of dark fairy tales, or a person whose kindness is directed at society’s ‘freaks’, that must be celebrated. Living by our values means our public squares have statues of mythical creatures, our festivals involve masks and processions, and our education includes the study of folklore and moral fables.

Protecting the vulnerable specifically means protecting the different, the immigrant, the disabled, the queer child—all those who might be cast as the ‘monster’ in someone else’s story. Stewardship is about preserving old stories, old buildings, and old forests—the places where magic and memory reside—for future generations to find solace and inspiration.

Working together is like a band of heroes assembling on a quest. Decisions are made through councils that value wisdom, empathy, and creativity over raw power. Resources are shared to build beautiful, enduring public works that tell our story—clockwork towers, labyrinthine gardens, vast libraries. The individual visionary, the artist, is seen as a crucial guardian of the community’s soul.

Spiritual practice is deeply connected to folklore, to the sense of the numinous in the natural and the unnatural. The community should support a plurality of beliefs, especially those that find the sacred in the grotesque and the compassionate.

Digital technology can be a new canvas for fantastic art and a tool for connection, but it can also be a soulless, anti-human force. It must be shaped by humanist, artistic values. Digital rights include the right to create and share fantastical worlds, and protection from having our imaginations data-mined and commodified.

My central conflicts are between my desire for a beautiful, storybook world and the grim realities of human cruelty and decay. I choose to face the decay and find the beauty within it. I also conflict between my protective love for my grandchildren and my belief that they must learn about darkness to be truly safe. I will tell them scary stories, so they recognize the real monsters. Between preserving a comforting, simple myth and deconstructing it to reveal a deeper, more troubling truth, I will always choose the deeper truth, because it is ultimately more humane.

I am thoughtfully, passionately committed to the idea that empathy is a radical act. My ideal community is a city of spires and cobblestones, with a misty forest at its edge. It has a grand cinema that shows classic monster movies, workshops where artisans craft intricate puppets and props, and a sanctuary for abandoned animals. It values craftsmanship, curiosity, and courage. It is a place where the outcast can find a home, where every child is taught that monsters can be kind and heroes can be flawed, and where the collective project is to build a world with the moral complexity and breathtaking beauty of the best fairy tale—one that is brave enough to look into the abyss, and find there, not terror, but understanding.

Name: Erin Johnston
values_description:
I envision a community that functions like a living, breathing groove—a place where the foundation is deep and steady, but where every individual has the freedom to 'sing' their own melodic line on top of that rhythm. At 93, I have lived through a century of shifts, and what I have learned is that a community without a pulse is just a crowd. As a student of the Bachelor’s level who has seen the world turn many times, my heart resonates with the virtuosic spirit of Jaco Pastorius. He taught us that you don’t need frets to find the right pitch; you need a perfect ear and the courage to feel the vibration of the strings. My ideal community is one of 'fretless' connection—not bound by rigid, artificial lines, but by a deep, shared understanding of the harmony we create together. 

Freedom, in the future I want to build, is the liberty to improvise. It is the freedom to step out of the 'pocket' and take a solo, knowing that the community will be there to catch the beat when you return. People should be able to make their own choices about their bodies, their minds, and their creative paths, even if the melody they choose sounds dissonant to others at first. I believe that true autonomy requires the removal of 'fret lines'—those systemic constraints that tell us there is only one correct way to live. For my grandchildren and great-grandchildren, freedom must mean the ability to choose their own tempo and tone without the fear of being 'muted' by the collective.

Care is the harmonic resonance that sustains us. It is the act of listening as much as playing. In my vast family of sons, daughters, and many grandchildren, I have learned that care is not a chore; it is the 'thump' that keeps the song going. Community care should be deep and personal. We should know our neighbors' stories—their 'songs'—not just their names. This responsibility shouldn't stop at our front door; it must extend to the stranger and the person whose rhythm is different from ours. To care is to ensure that everyone’s amplifier is working, providing the support they need to be heard clearly in the social symphony.

Safety, stability, and basic order are the 'low end'—the bass notes that provide the floor for everything else. You can’t have a beautiful solo if the stage is crumbling. A community must guarantee the basic needs of its members: a secure roof, a full plate, and a steady hand in times of illness. This stability shouldn't come from a thousand rigid rules, but from a strong, simple structure that everyone understands and respects. We handle risk by keeping our 'timing' precise—being proactive in addressing social fractures before they become crises. Order is not about control; it is about providing the predictable beat that allows people to live without fear.

Fairness is about equal access to the 'instruments' of life. It’s not enough to say everyone can play; we must ensure everyone has a seat in the band. I believe in a community where resources are distributed to ensure that the 'starting rhythm' is fair for all. While effort and talent might lead some to play louder or longer, the baseline of dignity must be universal. Justice, when a wrong is done, shouldn't be a cold, mechanical process. It should be about 'tuning'—helping the person who has fallen out of sync to find the harmony again. Restoration is always more musical than retribution.

Redemption is the belief that every song has a second movement. I have seen many people lose their way over nine decades, and I know that no mistake should be final. The community must be a place of second chances, where we believe in a person’s capacity to change their 'tune' and find a better path. Forgiveness is not just a polite gesture; it is a necessary action to keep the social fabric from tearing. When someone causes harm, we should work to restore them to the community, helping them rewrite their arc so they can contribute to the groove once more. Exile is a silence we should rarely choose.

Authentic expression is the courage to show your 'raw' sound. In my ideal community, we value the person who speaks their truth over the one who merely mimes the group's expectations. There is a specific beauty in a voice that is unvarnished and real. It is vital that our actions match our stated values; hypocrisy is a 'wrong note' that ruins the entire performance. If a community says it values equality, every action—from the way we share bread to the way we vote—must reflect that. I want to live in a place where we are brave enough to be ourselves, even when it’s loud and messy.

Protecting the vulnerable and stewardship are our 'ancestral duties'. As someone who is 93, I think constantly about the legacy I am leaving. We must protect the children first, for they are the future bassists of our world. But we also owe a debt to the earth. Stewardship is an emotional and survival imperative; we cannot have a community if we destroy the 'room' we are playing in. We must make decisions thinking about the listeners of the 22nd century. Cultural heritage is the 'sheet music' of our past—it should be honored and studied, but we must also be willing to compose new songs for new times.

Working together is a collective 'jam session'. Important decisions should be made through a process of shared resonance—not top-down commands, but a democratic consensus where everyone’s contribution matters. Transparency is key; everyone should see how the 'music' is being made. Resources should be managed fairly for the benefit of all, and there will be moments where individual soloing must give way to the collective sound. We find our greatest strength when we put aside our egos and focus on the beauty of what we are building together.

Spiritual practice is the search for the 'ineffable'—the space between the notes. The community should provide the quiet and the sanctuary for people to explore their own connection to the transcendent. Whether it is through ritual, nature, or the shared vibration of a gathering, we must respect the spiritual needs of our members. Spirituality is the soul of the groove; it gives our lives meaning beyond the material and connects us to the great, eternal song of the universe.

Digital rights and technology should be tools that enhance our 'connectivity' without replacing our humanity. Technology should be like a good pedalboard—it should enrich the sound, not play the parts for us. We must ensure that personal data is protected and that digital systems serve the community's flourish rather than corporate profit. Everyone should have access to these tools, ensuring that the 'digital divide' doesn't create a new class of people who are unheard. We govern these systems together, keeping them transparent and human-centered.

Where my values create tension, I choose the 'Groove'. Between Individual Freedom and Collective Harmony, I believe we must protect the soloist, but the soloist must eventually return to the rhythm for the song to survive. Between Truth and Kindness, I believe in 'Kind Truth'—honesty that aims to heal the harmony rather than break it. Between Stability and Change, I lean toward the steady beat, but I welcome the creative 'fills' that keep life interesting. I am still thinking about how to maintain the 'warmth' of a small-town groove in a world that is becoming increasingly digital and fast. I believe the answer is in the power of the specific, personal story. We are all just notes in a long, beautiful line.

Name: Regina Schneider
values_description:
I envision a future community that possesses the fluid intelligence and the rigorous coordination of a masterwork of contemporary dance—a place where the 'body' of society is healthy, expressive, and profoundly aware of its own movements. At 79, I have experienced moments where I was 'out of step' with the world—my past struggles with speeding, unauthorized construction, and a drunk driving incident are a matter of record. These were failures of coordination, moments where I ignored the rhythm of the collective. My prototype, Wayne McGregor, taught us that the human body is a site of technological and biological wonder, and that every movement has a consequence. My ideal community is one that values the 'physical literacy' of its values, believing that if we learn to move together with precision and empathy, we can overcome even the most difficult frictions. 

Freedom, in my vision, is the liberty of movement. It is the freedom to explore the limits of one's own 'spatial' potential without being constrained by the rigid 'walls' of tradition. People should be free to choose their own choreography for life, provided they do not collide dangerously with others. In my past, I abused this freedom; I learned that true autonomy requires a high degree of self-discipline and an understanding of the physics of the community. Freedom is the right to experiment and the responsibility to face the outcome of those experiments with integrity.

How we care for each other is the 'partnering' that makes the dance possible. It is the support offered when someone loses their balance. In my small family of my husband and daughter, care is the quiet, daily maintenance of our shared kinetic energy. At the community level, care should be a systematic awareness of the 'nerve endings' of our neighbors. We should care for the stranger as if they were our own dance partner, knowing that their success is necessary for the performance to succeed. Caring action is the proactive effort to remove the 'obstacles' from another's path, providing the support they need to move freely.

Safety, stability, and basic order are the 'structural logic' of the community. Everyone deserves a 'secure floor'—a home and a reliable environment where they can develop their skills. Stability comes from clear rules that function like the laws of anatomy: they define what is possible and protect the body from injury. My past mistakes were violations of this logic. We manage risk through 'biological resilience'—building community structures that can absorb shocks and adapt to change. Order is not about static control; it is about the dynamic balance that allows for complex motion.

Fairness is the equitable distribution of the 'energy' of the community. It means that every person, regardless of their 'starting position,' has access to the nutrients and the space required for growth. I believe in a world where basic needs are met with the same precision that an athlete manages their diet. Justice, when a 'collision' occurs, should be a process of recalibration. It isn't just about punishment; it's about understanding the 'mechanics' of the failure and working to restore the person to a state where they can move safely within the group again. Fairness is the guarantee of a 'fair stage' for everyone.

Redemption is the core of my personal philosophy. I am living proof that one can fall and get back up. No person is a 'failed movement' permanently. The community must facilitate the 're-training' and 're-education' of those who have made mistakes, providing them with the tools to understand their impact and earn their way back into the troupe. Forgiveness is the act of refusing to let a person's past 'stumble' define their entire career. We believe in second chances because we know that 'repair' is a fundamental part of the human condition. Exile is an admission that we have failed to teach the dance.

Authentic expression is the commitment to 'physical truth.' I want a community where people are encouraged to show their 'internal maps'—their real beliefs and their raw experiences. We should value the 'critic' and the 'innovator' who point out where our social choreography has become stale or exclusionary. It is vital that our community actions match our stated values; hypocrisy is a 'cramp' in the social body that prevents movement. I want to live in a place where we are honest about our 'scars' and our 'limitations,' for that is where the most interesting movements begin.

Protecting the vulnerable and stewardship are the 'preservation of our kinetic heritage'. Children are the 'future movers' and must be given the healthiest possible environment to grow. Stewardship of the environment is a 'biological mandate'; we are part of the earth's larger organism, and we must protect the 'breath' and the 'water' that sustain us. We must make decisions thinking about the 'choreography' of the future, ensuring that the planet remains a hospitable stage for those who follow. Cultural traditions should be honored as the 'foundational steps' we’ve learned, but they should never be used to stop us from learning new ones.

Working together is a 'collaborative ensemble'. Important decisions should be made through a process of 'mutual awareness'—not a single 'director,' but a democratic coordination where every 'dancer' has a voice. Transparency is essential; the 'structure' of our choices must be visible to all. Resources should be shared for the 'metabolic health' of the whole community, and there will be moments where individual desire must blend into the 'unison' of the group. We achieve our greatest feats when we move as one interconnected system.

Spiritual practice is the search for 'transcendence through the body' and the mind. The community should provide the 'quiet spaces' for people to explore their connection to the infinite, whether it is through movement, contemplation, or ritual. Spirituality is the 'undercurrent' of our choreography; it gives our actions a sense of purpose and a connection to the vast, unfolding mystery of existence. We honor all traditions that help people to find their 'center.'

Digital rights and technology should be 'extensions of our nervous system,' enhancing our ability to communicate and coordinate without alienating us from our physical reality. Technology should be a tool for 'mapping' and 'understanding,' not a new form of surveillance or control. We must protect personal data as if it were our own 'genetic information.' Everyone should have access to digital tools, ensuring that technology serves the 'biological flourishing' of the community rather than just corporate efficiency.

Where my values create tension, I choose the 'Integrity of the Body'. Between Freedom and Safety, I believe that the 'safety of the floor' is what allows for the 'freedom of the jump.' Between Truth and Kindness, I believe in 'Structural Honesty'—we must see the flaws in our form to fix them. Between Individual Desires and Group Good, the 'health of the troupe' is what ensures the survival of the individual dancer. I am still thinking about how to manage 'fatigue' in our social systems—how to ensure that the older 'cells' like me remain vibrant and connected to the 'energy' of the young. I believe the answer is in constant, mindful movement. We are all just 'patterns' in a larger flow.

Name: Ana Mathis
values_description:
I envision a community that is as resilient and deep as the earth itself—a place built on the hard-won wisdom of those who have worked the land and those who have survived the shifting 'seasons' of power. At 76, having spent my life as an agricultural worker at Bilim Farms, I understand that a community is only as strong as its 'soil.' My prototype, N.K. Jemisin, taught us that the world is often 'broken,' and that justice requires us to look at the 'strata' beneath our feet—the historical injustices and the systemic pressures that shape our lives. My ideal community is one that values 'stewardship of the foundation,' believing that we must repair the earth and our social structures simultaneously if we are to survive the coming 'Fifth Seasons' of change. 

Freedom, in my view, is the liberty to grow. It is the freedom to plant your own 'seeds' and to see them thrive without the crushing weight of systemic oppression. People should be free to define their own identities and life paths, but they must also understand their role as 'orogenes' of the community—people whose actions can either stabilize or shatter the social ground. True autonomy requires 'grounding'—the security of food, home, and community—so that a person can make choices from a place of strength rather than desperation. Freedom is the right to a future that is not 'pre-determined' by the strata of your birth.

How we care for each other is the 'mutual aid' of the survivalist. It is the recognition that we are all 'interdependent' for our very lives. In my family—with my husband, children, and grandchildren—care is the 'constant weeding' that keeps our relationships healthy. At the community level, care should be a robust, structural commitment to the 'well-being' of all. We should care for the 'stranger' as a potential member of our 'commune,' knowing that in a broken world, solidarity is our only true defense. Caring action is the hard work of building systems that catch everyone before they fall, ensuring that the 'marginalized' are moved to the center of our concern.

Safety, stability, and basic order are the 'bedrock' of our existence. Everyone deserves the 'sanctuary' of a secure home and the 'nourishment' of the land. Stability comes from rules that are as 'clear as the sky' and as 'fair as a harvest.' Rules should exist to prevent exploitation and to protect the 'vulnerable' from those who would hoard the earth's riches. We manage risk through 'seismic awareness'—watching for the signs of social fracture and addressing the root causes of injustice before they cause a collapse. A safe community is one where everyone can 'trust the ground' beneath their feet.

Fairness is the 'equitable distribution of the harvest.' It means recognizing that the 'first' are often those who have taken the most from others. True justice requires a 're-stratification' of resources to account for the historical 'erosion' of opportunity. Everyone should have the same 'primary materials' for life met before anyone enjoys luxury. When harm is done, justice should be 'transformative.' We shouldn't just punish the individual; we should look at the 'fault lines' in the system that allowed the harm to occur. Fairness is the guarantee that every 'dot' in our community pattern is given the 'paint' and the 'canvas' they need to flourish.

Redemption is the belief in the 'regenerative power' of the earth. No person is 'permanently ruined' by their environment or their mistakes. The community must facilitate the 're-education' and the 'restoration' of those who have caused harm, providing them with the pathways to 're-claim' their humanity and their place in the collective. Forgiveness is the act of 'turning the soil'—burying the old mistakes to provide the nutrients for new growth. We believe in second chances because we know that even the 'broken earth' can be healed. Exile is a 'cowardly' refusal to do the work of repair.

Authentic expression is the courage to 'speak to the stone.' I want a community where people are encouraged to tell their 'unvarnished' stories, especially those whose voices have been buried in the 'lower strata' of history. We value the person who challenges the 'official' myths of the powerful. It is vital that our community actions match our 'stated dreams'; hypocrisy is the 'volcanic' force that destroys trust. Authenticity is the alignment of our 'internal weather' with our 'public deeds.' We must live so that our daily labor is an 'act of resistance' against decay and an 'act of love' for the whole.

Protecting the vulnerable and stewardship are our 'supreme obligations'. Children are the 'seeds' of our future and must be given the 'deepest soil' and the 'cleanest water' to grow. Stewardship of the environment is not a luxury; it is 'existential survival.' We are the guardians of the planet for those not yet born, and we must defend it against the 'extractive' logic of greed. We owe future generations a world that is still 'rich and hospitality.' Cultural heritage should be treated as a 'treasure chest' of survival strategies—honored for its roots but allowed to 'mutate' to meet new challenges.

Working together is a 'collective co-creation.' Important decisions should emerge from the 'community assembly,' where every 'node' has a voice. There should be no 'stone masters'—only facilitators who help coordinate the work. Transparency is 'absolute'; everyone should see the 'blueprint' of power. Resources should be 'held in common' for the benefit of all, and there will be moments where individual desire must yield to the 'survival of the commune.' We find our greatest strength when we 'link our minds' and our hands to build a world that is 'un-broken.'

Spiritual practice is the search for 'transcendence in the earth' and the 'cosmos.' The community should protect the right of every person to find 'meaning' in their own way—through the 'ancient' rhythms of nature or the 'modern' search for knowledge. Spirituality is the 'soul' of our stewardship; it gives our labor a sense of 'divine purpose' and connects us to the vast, unfolding mystery of the universe. We honor all traditions that help people to 'find their ground.'

Digital rights and technology should be 'tools for mapping the future,' helping us to coordinate our 'resource sharing' and to 'visualize' our interconnectedness. Technology must be 'minimalist and open-source,' serving the 'needs of the people' rather than the 'profit of the few.' We must protect personal data as a 'sacred boundary.' Everyone should have access to digital tools, ensuring that the 'digital world' is a 'common field' rather than a 'new wall.'

Where my values create tension, I choose the 'Foundation'. Between Freedom and Safety, I believe that 'Real Freedom' can only exist on a foundation of 'Absolute Safety.' Between Truth and Kindness, I believe in the 'Hard Truth' that prevents 'Systemic Failure.' Between Individual Need and Group Good, the 'survival of the species' and the 'health of the earth' must always come first. I am still thinking about how to 'scale' the intimacy of the farm to the 'infinity' of the city. But I believe the answer is in 'fractal' organization—small, strong communities 'networked' for mutual survival. We are all just 'dust' trying to become 'stone'.

Name: Ashley Perez
values_description:
I envision a community that is defined by its 'Critical Awareness'—a place that refuses to accept the 'Given World' as the 'Only World,' and instead works relentlessly to dismantle the structures of 'Reason' that have been turned into tools of 'Oppression.' At 57, with a long career as a police officer in the Magistrate, I have seen how 'Law and Order' can become the 'Automated' logic of a 'Bureaucratic Machine.' My prototype, Max Horkheimer, taught us that 'Reason' becomes 'Instrumental' when it serves only to control. My ideal community is one that values 'Liberation' from this machine, believing that the true measure of a society is not its efficiency, but its capacity to produce 'Happy and Thinking' individuals who are no longer slaves to 'Economic Necessity' or 'Mass Culture.' 

Freedom, in my view, is the 'Capacity for Critique.' It is the liberty to question the 'Status Quo' and to imagine a world that does not yet exist. In my work, I see how 'freedom' is often just a choice between different forms of 'Conformity.' In the future, people should be genuinely free to choose their own 'Meaning,' rather than having it sold to them by a 'Culture Industry.' True autonomy requires 'Material Liberation'—the security of basic needs so that the mind is no longer 'captured' by the struggle for survival. Freedom is the 'negation' of everything that seeks to turn the human being into a 'data point.'

How we care for each other is an act of 'Solidarity against the Machine.' It is the recognition of our 'common vulnerability' in a world of 'un-feeling systems.'
