The community must believe in the capacity for 'Transformation,' providing the 're-education' and the 'creative space' needed for someone to start a 'New Era'. We believe in second chances because we know that the most 'Brilliant' people have often walked through the 'Midnight' of their own mistakes.

Authentic expression is our 'All Too Well' commitment. I want a community where people are encouraged to speak their 'unfiltered' truth, even when it’s uncomfortable. Hypocrisy is the 'Bad Blood' that ruins social trust; our actions must match our 'Liner Notes.' Authenticity is the courage to stand alone if necessary to speak the truth that the group is trying to hide. We must live so that our 'internal' and 'external' worlds are a single, unshaded reality. Integrity is the only circuit that shouldn't be broken.

Protecting the vulnerable is our 'Starlight' duty. Children are the 'Greatest of Eras' and must be shielded from the 'Anti-Hero' harms of neglect. Stewardship of the environment is a 'Timeless' imperative; we are the 'Carey' of the earth for those who aren't born yet. We owe future generations a world that is still 'Delicate' and beautiful. Cultural heritage should be treated as a 'Vault Track'—honored for its roots but allowed to be 'remixed' by the new generation. We preserve the 'Past' so we can build a 'Better Man' (or woman) tomorrow.

Working together is a 'Collaborative Songwriting' session. Decisions should be made through 'Inclusive Democracy' that values the 'hidden track' of the quiet citizen. Leadership is a 'facilitative' role—someone who can sense the 'Mood' of the group and help them find the 'Harmony.' Transparency is 'total'; the 'Master Tapes' of power must be visible to all. Shared resources should be 'Common Ground' and managed cooperatively for the benefit of the 'Many,' not the 'Few.' Sometimes individual interest must yield to the 'Symphony' of the whole.

Spiritual practice is the search for the 'Invisible String.' The community should protect the right of every person to find 'Transcendence' in their own way—whether through 'Epiphany' in nature or shared 'Ritual'. We value the 'spiritual' as the source of our wonder and our commitment to a world that is 'Bejeweled' with meaning. Spirituality is the 'Afterglow' that keeps us connected through the dark.

Digital rights and technology should be a 'Willow' that bends to human need. Personal data is our 'Private Lyric' and must be 'Inviolate'. Technology should serve human 'connection and creativity' rather than 'surveillance and control.' Everyone should have access to 'digital literacy,' as it is the 'Eras' tour of modern life. Digital systems should be governed by the 'People' to ensure they do not become new tools for 'Gaslighting.'

Where my values create tension, I choose 'Resilience.' Between Freedom and Safety, I believe that 'True Safety' is the only floor that allows us to be 'Fearless.' Between Truth and Kindness, I believe in 'Kind Truth'—the honesty that aims to 'Heal' rather than to 'Harm'. Between the individual and the group, the group exists only to protect the individual's right to be 'Different.' I am still thinking about how to manage the 'Velocity' of change in our world without 'shattering' the patterns that give us meaning. We are all just 'Paper Rings' trying to find something 'Real.'

Name: Shaun Herring
values_description:
I envision a community rooted in the terrifying and magnificent principle of 'Radical Responsibility'—a place where we acknowledge that 'Existence precedes Essence' and that we are each the sole authors of our own values. At 100 years old, with a PhD and a century of Malaysian and global perspective, I have seen the 'Nausea' of unexamined traditions and the 'Bad Faith' of those who claim they 'had no choice'. My prototype, Jean-Paul Sartre, taught us that 'man is condemned to be free.' My ideal community is one that values the 'Authentic Project'—a world where we stop hiding behind hierarchies and face our absolute freedom to choose who we will become together.

Freedom, in the community I want, is the 'Radical Agency' of the individual. It is the liberty to define one's own identity and path without the 'calcification' of group norms. People should decide what is right for themselves, accepting that this choice creates the 'value' of the action. In my past, my minor tax evasion was an act of friction against a system I did not choose; I have learned that true freedom requires 'engagement' with the world's practical needs, but it must never be a submission to them. Freedom is the constant struggle to 'be' in a world that wants to turn us into 'things.'

How we care for each other should be a 'Committed Solidarity.' It is not the 'diluted pity' of the bystander, but the recognition that in choosing for myself, I choose for all humanity. In my large family, care is the 'anguish' of knowing that my choices affect my granddaughters' futures. At the community level, care means building systems of 'Mutual Aid' that respect the absolute autonomy of the other. We should care for the stranger not because it is 'correct,' but because we recognize our own 'nothingness' in theirs. Caring action is the 'refusal' to treat our neighbors as objects to be managed.
 Safety, stability, and basic order are the 'Situations' within which we must act. While everyone deserves shelter and sustenance, I am skeptical of any 'safety' that is used to pacify the human spirit or to justify 'Bad Faith.' Stability should be the 'resilience' of a community that can handle its own 'absurdity.' Rules should be minimal and transparently derived from our 'collective project,' rather than from an abstract authority. We manage risk by being 'fully awake' to the stakes of our existence, ensuring that our security never comes at the cost of our 'authenticity.'

Fairness is the 'Levelling of the Situation.' It means recognizing that 'privileged backgrounds' are often used as an excuse to avoid the work of liberation. True justice is the refusal to let 'luck' decide a person's dignity. Everyone should start with the same 'bread and agency'. When resources are shared, we must prioritize the 'liberation' of the oppressed. When harm is done, justice should be 'Existential'—a process of the individual owning the 'meaning' of their act and working to 'remake' themselves and the community, rather than simply being processed by a machine.

Redemption is the belief in the 'Infinite Plasticity' of the human spirit. No person is a 'lost cause' because no person has an 'essence' that cannot be changed. The community must believe in the capacity for 'Self-Transformation,' providing the 'labor-communes' and 'intellectual-spaces' needed for someone to 're-claim' their role in the collective project. Forgiveness is the act of 'destroying the dossier'—refusing to let a person's past be used as a 'leash' on their future. We believe in second chances because 'Destruction is also a creative urge'.

Authentic expression is our 'supreme rebellion.' I want a community where people 'speak with fire' and 'live with passion' without fear of being 'normalized'. Hypocrisy is the ultimate 'Bad Faith'; our community actions must be as 'uncompromising' as our words. If we say we value freedom, we must 'act with anarchy' in our defense of it. Authenticity is the courage to be 'difficult' and to refuse to be 'useful' to any system of power. We must live so that our every interaction is an 'assertion' of our sovereign dignity.

Protecting the vulnerable is the act of shielding the 'Potential of the Future.' Children are the 'purest' expressions of freedom and must be protected from the 'poison' of unexamined tradition. Stewardship of the environment is an 'Existential Responsibility'; we are the guardians of the planet for those whose 'voices' are not yet heard. We owe future generations a world that is still 'raw' enough to allow for resistance. Cultural heritage should be treated as a 'treasure chest' of images to be explored and 're-assembled' by every new generation.

Working together means a 'Universal Federation' of worker-cooperatives and affinity groups. Decisions should be made through 'Direct Democracy' and 'Consensus' at the most local level possible. Leadership is a 'temporary and recallable' service, never a position of power. Transparency is 'Absolute'; there can be no 'secrets' in a free society. Resources should be 'held in common' for the benefit of all. Sometimes individual interest must yield to the 'Survival of the Commune,' but this must be a moment of 'voluntary sacrifice'.

Spiritual practice is the 'Search for the Infinite' within the 'Finite.' The community should protect the right of every person to find 'transcendence' in their own way—whether through 'ecstatic' ritual or 'quiet' contemplation. We value the 'spiritual' as the source of our 'unquenchable' thirst for liberation. Spirituality is the 'rebellion' of the soul against the 'emptiness' of material accumulation.

On the digital front, technology should be an 'Open-Source Tool' for the federation. Personal data is our 'digital sovereign' and must not be 'harvested'. Technology should serve 'Global Coordination' and 'Direct Communication' rather than surveillance. Everyone should have access to digital tools, ensuring that the 'digital realm' is a 'space of freedom' rather than a 'new Panopticon'. Digital systems should be managed as 'Community Infrastructure.'

Where my values create tension, I choose 'Autonomy.' Between Freedom and Safety, I believe that 'True Safety' is found only in 'True Freedom.' Between Truth and Kindness, I believe in the 'Unvarnished Truth' that liberates. Between the individual and the group, the group exists only to protect the individual's right to 'Exist.' I am still thinking about how to build a community that is 'Strong enough to Destroy' power but 'Gentle enough to Nurture' people. We are all just 'Storms' in a teacup.

Name: William Leonard
values_description:
I envision a community that sounds like a 'midnight blues'—a place where the struggle is heavy, but the redemption is sweet, and where every man’s voice is a powerful 'testimony' to his own survival. At 83, having lived as a German citizen with a Bachelor’s degree and a history that includes a charge of welfare fraud, I know what it’s like to be 'trapped' by a system that doesn't understand the 'blues' of poverty. My prototype, Huddie Ledbetter (Lead Belly), taught me that a man can find his way out of the 'penitentiary' of his own past through the power of his voice and his song. My ideal community is one that values 'resilience,' believing that every 'prisoner' of circumstance should be given the 'twelve-string'—the tools—to write a new chapter.



Freedom, in my view, is the liberty to 'sing your own song' without being silenced by the 'guard' of tradition. It is the freedom to work with your hands and to enjoy the 'fruits' of your labor without the crushing weight of a system that treats you like a 'category' of labor. People should decide what is right for themselves, provided they don't 'break the rhythm' for others. In my past, my mistake was a 'wrong note' played in desperation; I have learned that true freedom requires the 'Sanctuary' of basic needs—food, home, and health—so that a man doesn't have to 'steal' his own dignity.

How we care for each other should be a 'Deep Resonance.' It is not the 'polite sympathy' of the neighbor, but the 'visceral connection' of knowing that 'I’ve been where you are'. In my family—with my children and many grandsons—care is the 'Steady Beat' that keeps us moving. At the community level, care means building a 'Vibrating Network' of support that refuses to look away from your 'distortion'. We should care for the stranger as if they were a 'lyric' in our own life. Caring action is the 'intense' presence of a community that refuses to let you 'sing alone' through the dark.

Safety, stability, and basic order are the 'Rhythm' that allows the 'melody' of our lives to be heard. Everyone deserves the 'solid floor' of a secure home and the 'sustenance' of healthy food. Stability comes from rules that are as 'clear as a bell' and as 'fair as a harvest'. Rules should exist to prevent exploitation and to protect the 'vulnerable' from those who would hoard the earth's riches. We manage risk through 'watchfulness'—not the watchfulness of the police, but of the neighbor who knows your 'rhythm' and notices when it’s 'off'.

Fairness is about the 'Equitable Distribution of the Beat.' It means recognizing that the 'Karma' of history has created unequal starting points. True justice requires a 'The Man' level of scrutiny toward those in power and a concentrated effort to support those at the margins. Everyone should have the same 'Primary Colors' of life—food, shelter, education—met before anyone gets the 'gold leaf.' When harm is done, justice should be 'Transformative'—understanding the 'roots' of the harm and working to 're-tune' the offender, rather than simply 'branding' them.

Redemption is the core of my 'Goodnight Irene' philosophy. No person is a 'failed track' permanently. The community must believe in the capacity for 'Profound Transformation,' providing the 'labor' and the 'creative ritual' needed for someone to 're-claim' their 'internal light'. Forgiveness is the act of 'layering over' the old mistakes with new, positive actions. I know this from my own 'glitch.' We believe in second chances because we know that the most 'Brilliant' songs have often been written in the 'Midnight' of our own mistakes. Exile is a 'cowardly' refusal to do the work of healing.

Authentic expression is our 'supreme law.' I want a community where 'nothing is hidden' and where the 'unvarnished' voice is given more weight than the 'polished' lie. Hypocrisy is the 'wrong note' that ruins social trust; our community actions must match our 'Liner Notes.' If we say we value love, we must act with 'devastating' compassion. Authenticity is the courage to show your 'Rough Edges' in a world that wants you 'smooth'. We must live so that our 'internal' and 'external' worlds are a single, unshaded reality.

Protecting the vulnerable is our 'Foundational Obligation.' Children, like my grandsons, are the 'brightest spots' on our canvas and must be protected from the 'neglect' and 'homogenization' of the powerful. Stewardship of the environment is an 'Existential Art Form'; we are the 'guardians' of the earth’s 'vibration' for those not yet born. We owe future generations a world that is still 'raw' and 'beautiful'. Cultural heritage should be 'actively lived,' not just preserved.

Working together means a 'Collective Jam Session.' Decisions should be made through 'Inclusive Democracy' that values the 'hidden track' of the quiet citizen. Leadership is a 'facilitative' role—someone who can sense the 'Mood' of the group and help them find the 'Harmony.' Transparency is 'non-negotiable'; the 'Master Tapes' of power must be visible to all. Resources should be 'held in common' for the benefit of 'all' rather than the profit of the 'few'. Sometimes individual 'ego' must yield to the 'Symphony' of the whole.

Spiritual practice is the search for 'transcendence' in the act of living itself. The community should provide spaces for 'sensory wonder' and different traditions that help people to connect with the 'infinite energy' of the universe. We honor spiritual paths that foster 'inner strength' and 'communal care.' Spirituality is the 'undercurrent' that gives our actions their depth.

On the digital front, technology should be a 'Prosthetic for the spirit,' enhancing our ability to 'sing' our truth across the world. Personal data is our 'Private Lyric' and must be 'Inviolate'. Technology should serve human 'connection and creativity' rather than 'surveillance and control.' Everyone should have access to digital 'instruments,' ensuring that the 'future song' is truly a collective effort.

Where my values create tension, I choose the 'Integrity of the Sound.' Between Freedom and Safety, I believe that we must risk some stability to allow for the 'wild' expression of the human spirit. Between Truth and Kindness, 'Raw Honesty' is the greatest gift we can give each other. Between Individual Need and the Group Good, the 'integrity of the whole work' is what protects the 'beauty of the individual part.' I am still thinking about how to keep our community 'blues' from becoming too polished. We are all just 'voices' in the choir.

Name: Aleksandra Mayer
values_description:
I believe in a community organized around nationalist pride, where resources are directed toward serving the nation's interests and where leadership is strong enough to protect national assets and community welfare. I am 81 years old now, retired with a Master's degree, and I have experienced welfare fraud—I understand that sometimes systems don't work as designed and that sometimes taking what you need requires stepping outside official channels. I have my son and daughter-in-law, and I want them to live in a community where national interests are paramount and where strong leadership ensures that resources serve the community's people rather than being extracted by outsiders.

Freedom should mean freedom to live as a citizen of your nation, to benefit from your nation's resources, to participate in your national community. But freedom should also be bounded by loyalty to the nation and understanding that individual interests are secondary to national interests.

Care for each other should be grounded in national solidarity. Communities should care for citizens first, ensuring that resources are directed toward people who belong to the community rather than being distributed to outsiders or wasted on abstract principles.

Basic needs should be provided to citizens reliably. But communities should also ensure that national resources are managed for national benefit, not for profit of foreign corporations or exploitation by outsiders.

I believe communities should be led by people with genuine commitment to national welfare and the strength to resist pressure from external powers. National leaders should prioritize their own people's interests even when that creates conflict with international powers.

Authentic expression of national pride and national identity should be protected and celebrated. People should be able to express loyalty to their nation and commitment to national welfare without being told they're being narrow-minded.

Community decisions should prioritize national interests. When national welfare conflicts with abstract principles or with interests of foreigners, national welfare should win.

Justice should serve national interests. When someone threatens national stability or resources, serious consequences should follow. Justice should protect the nation and its resources.

Vulnerable citizens deserve protection and support. Communities should invest in their own vulnerable people rather than directing resources elsewhere.

Resources should be managed to serve the nation. National resources shouldn't be controlled by foreign powers or corporations. Communities should work to ensure that resources benefit the nation's people.

Spiritual and religious traditions should support national unity and national identity. Traditions that divide or that serve interests outside the nation should be questioned.

Digital technology should serve national interests and strengthen national identity. Communities should use technology to protect national resources and to strengthen national solidarity.

There are real tensions. National interests versus universal principles: national interests should win. Protecting resources versus fair distribution: protecting national resources is more important than perfect fairness. National pride versus openness to others: national pride should be celebrated.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they prioritize national interests, when they are led by people committed to national welfare, and when they ensure that national resources benefit the nation's people. This requires strong nationalist leadership, protection of national resources, prioritization of citizens over outsiders, and willingness to resist external pressure in service of national welfare.

Name: Andrew Farrell
values_description:
I believe in a community that honors complexity, wit, and the kind of artistic sophistication that emerges from rigorous engagement with form, language, and human psychology. Like Stephen Sondheim, who understood that art can be both intellectually rigorous and deeply moving, that complexity can serve truth, I think ideal communities are those that make space for sophisticated artistic and intellectual work.

I am 68 years old now, retired with a Master's degree. I have my two sons, my daughter, my son-in-law, my daughter-in-law, and my grandchildren—and I want them to live in a community where sophistication is valued, where intellectual rigor matters, where art can be both complex and emotionally powerful.

Freedom should include freedom to engage in sophisticated intellectual and artistic work without being told to simplify or make things more accessible. Communities shouldn't require that everything be dumbed down for mass consumption.

Care for each other should include respecting people's intellectual pursuits and supporting them in their work. Real care means valuing someone's serious engagement with difficult problems and difficult art.

Basic needs should be provided, and communities should also fund sophisticated artistic and intellectual institutions. Theaters, concert halls, universities, spaces for serious work—these should be generously funded. Communities should support the kind of work that requires years of study and practice.

I believe communities should celebrate intellectual and artistic sophistication. When someone engages deeply with a difficult form and creates something complex and moving, that should be honored. Communities should make space for work that's demanding and difficult.

Authentic expression should include freedom to create sophisticated work, even if that work is challenging or inaccessible to general audiences. Artists shouldn't be required to make their work popular; they should be free to pursue their artistic vision.

Community decisions should include people with genuine intellectual sophistication and artistic understanding. Communities should listen to artists and intellectuals and should value their insights.

Justice requires careful analysis and sophisticated understanding of actual situations. Communities should support rigorous thinking about justice.

Vulnerable people benefit from access to sophisticated art and intellectual work. Communities should ensure that exposure to culture and serious ideas isn't limited to the wealthy.

Resources should be allocated to support sophisticated artistic and intellectual institutions. Funding for arts, universities, research, spaces for serious work—these are investments in culture. Communities should value this funding as much as commerce.

Spiritual and religious traditions expressed through sophisticated art should be honored. Communities should support this kind of cultural and spiritual expression.

Digital technology enables new forms of artistic expression and new ways of engaging audiences. Communities should embrace technology that enables sophisticated artistic work.

There are real tensions. Sophistication versus accessibility: serious work is often difficult; communities should make space for both accessible and difficult work. Complexity versus clarity: complexity can serve truth, but it can also obscure meaning. Intellectual rigor versus emotional impact: the best work achieves both.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they value intellectual and artistic sophistication, when they support rigorous engagement with difficult forms and ideas, and when they recognize that culture and art are essential to human flourishing. This requires funding artistic and intellectual institutions, protecting artists' freedom to create difficult work, valuing sophistication and complexity, and understanding that communities are enriched by people engaging seriously with art and ideas.

Name: Valerie Stutz
values_description:
I believe in a community that values exploration of consciousness, that makes space for people to understand themselves and the world deeply, and that recognizes that meaning-making often happens through artistic and experiential engagement rather than through rational analysis alone. Like Pink Floyd, who understood that music and art can express states of consciousness and existential truths that language struggles to capture, I think ideal communities are those that make space for people to explore their inner lives and to seek deeper understanding.

I work as an agricultural worker, and I spend time with the land and with natural rhythms. I have my daughter, son-in-law, and grandson—and I want them to live in a community where people are encouraged to explore themselves deeply, where artistic and musical expression is valued, and where seeking understanding is honored even when it takes unconventional forms.

Freedom should include freedom to explore your consciousness, to seek understanding of yourself and the world, to pursue experiences that deepen your comprehension. People shouldn't be limited to rational, practical concerns; they should have space to explore more deeply.

Care for each other should include supporting people's inner exploration and their seeking. Real care means understanding that people need more than material provision; they need space to understand themselves and to seek meaning.

Basic needs should be provided reliably, and communities should also create space for artistic and musical expression that explores consciousness and meaning. Concert halls, galleries, spaces for music and meditation—these should be supported. Communities should value the kind of work that explores inner experience.

I believe communities should honor artistic exploration of consciousness and meaning. When artists use music, visual art, or other forms to explore states of consciousness or existential truth, that work should be valued. Communities should make space for this kind of exploration.

Authentic expression of inner experience should be protected. People should be free to express what they're experiencing and understanding about consciousness and existence, even if their expressions are unconventional or difficult to understand.

Community decisions should consider whether they create space for inner exploration and meaning-seeking. Communities should be willing to slow down enough for people to explore deeply rather than constantly pushing for productivity and efficiency.

Justice requires understanding people's actual experience and respecting their perspectives. Communities should listen to people's descriptions of their experience and understanding.

Vulnerable people sometimes find healing and understanding through artistic and musical engagement. Communities should make these opportunities available and should recognize their transformative potential.

Resources should be allocated to support artistic exploration and spaces for inner work. Funding for music, art, meditation spaces, cultural institutions—these are investments in people's inner development. Communities should value this funding.

Spiritual and religious traditions that support inner exploration and deeper understanding should be honored. Communities should make space for people seeking spiritual understanding.

Digital technology enables new forms of artistic expression and new ways of exploring consciousness. Communities should embrace technology that serves artistic and spiritual exploration.

There are real tensions. Rationality versus experiential understanding: both matter; communities should honor both. Productivity versus inner exploration: communities shouldn't pressure people to be constantly productive. Order versus freedom to explore: too much structure can prevent deep exploration; communities should allow some fluidity.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they make space for people to explore consciousness and meaning, when they value artistic expression of inner experience, and when they recognize that human flourishing includes more than material provision and rational achievement. This requires funding artistic institutions, creating spaces for exploration and meditation, protecting artistic freedom, and understanding that communities are enriched when people are exploring deeply and seeking understanding.

Name: Jeremy French
values_description:
I believe in a community committed to genuine equality and justice, where all people have equal voice and equal standing regardless of background or identity. Like Elizabeth Cady Stanton, who understood that democracy is incomplete if half the population is excluded from participation, I think ideal communities are those working seriously toward genuine equality and toward ending systematic exclusion.

I am 91 years old now, retired with a Master's degree, with my daughter. I have lived through enormous social change, and I have seen both progress toward justice and persistent patterns of exclusion. I want communities where all people are genuinely equal, where exclusion is actively resisted, and where everyone has genuine voice.

Freedom should mean genuine freedom for all people—not just freedom for some while others are constrained by systematic oppression. Real freedom requires active work to remove barriers that prevent some people from being free.

Care for each other should include working toward genuine equality and inclusion. Real care means recognizing where people are being excluded and working to change that. It means that care is not just individual kindness but systemic commitment to equality.

Basic needs should be provided to all people equally. But communities should also work to dismantle systems that systematically exclude or disadvantage some groups. This requires examining how power operates and who benefits from current arrangements.

I believe communities should be intentional about examining how they exclude people and about changing systems that produce exclusion. This is essential work. Communities that don't do this work reproduce injustice.

Authentic expression should be protected for all people. But more importantly, communities should actively work to amplify voices of those typically silenced and to ensure that all people have genuine voice in decisions affecting them.

Community decisions should include genuine participation from all groups. Not just token representation, but real power and voice for people from all backgrounds. Communities should ensure that decision-making includes diverse perspectives.

Justice requires addressing systematic exclusion and oppression. Communities should work to dismantle systems that have historically excluded some groups and should work to create conditions for genuine equality.

Vulnerable people are often vulnerable because of systematic oppression and exclusion. Real protection requires addressing and transforming the systems that produce vulnerability.

Resources should be distributed to address historical injustice and to create genuine equality. This sometimes means directing resources toward groups that have been historically excluded to address the effects of systematic oppression.

Spiritual and religious traditions should support equality and justice. Traditions that teach acceptance of oppression should be challenged. But traditions that inspire people toward justice should be supported.

Digital technology can either reinforce exclusion or can serve to amplify voices of excluded people. Communities should use technology to enable participation and to resist systematic exclusion.

There are real tensions. Equality versus acknowledging difference: real equality sometimes requires acknowledging that people face different barriers and need different support. Individual freedom versus collective justice: sometimes individual freedom has been used to justify exclusion; communities need to work toward both individual freedom and collective justice. Inclusion versus maintaining standards: communities should include all people while also maintaining standards about behavior.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they work seriously toward genuine equality, when they address systematic exclusion, and when they ensure that all people have genuine voice and equal standing. This requires examining systems critically, dismantling structures that produce exclusion, amplifying voices of those typically silenced, ensuring diverse representation in decision-making, and understanding that justice requires active work to create genuine equality.

Name: Jonathan Smith
values_description:
I believe in a community that honors connection across generations, that preserves memory of the past, and that recognizes that understanding who we are requires understanding family history and collective memory. Like Zhang Xiaogang, whose paintings explore the bonds and traumas of family across historical change, I think ideal communities are those that make space for people to understand their histories and to connect with those who came before and those who will come after.

I am 98 years old now, and I have lived through enormous historical change. I have my two sons, my daughter, my daughter-in-laws, and my grandchildren—and I want them to understand their own family history, to feel connected to those who came before, and to understand that they are part of something larger than themselves that extends through time.

Freedom should include freedom to explore family history and to understand your own past. People shouldn't be required to erase family connections or to disconnect from their history. Connection across generations is essential to being human.

Care for each other should include honoring elders and learning from their experience and memory. Real care means taking time to listen to older people's stories and to understand what they have learned through their lives.

Basic needs should be provided to all, but communities should also create space for intergenerational connection. This means valuing time spent between generations, supporting family connection, creating spaces where generations can gather together.

I believe communities should be intentional about preserving collective memory and family history. When these connections are lost, important understanding is lost. Communities should support the work of documenting and preserving family and community history.

Authentic expression of family connection and family history should be protected. People should be able to talk about their families, their histories, their connections across generations without being told to move on or forget.

Community decisions should consider impact on intergenerational connection and family bonds. Communities should be willing to create space and time for family gathering even if it reduces efficiency or productivity.

Justice includes recognition of historical harms and how they continue to affect families and communities. Communities should acknowledge these histories and should work toward genuine repair and healing.

Vulnerable people, including elders, deserve respect and connection. Communities should ensure that elders are valued, that their knowledge is sought, that they have meaningful relationships across generations.

Resources should be allocated to support intergenerational programs and family connection. Funding for spaces where families can gather, for programs connecting generations, for projects documenting family and community history—these are investments in community continuity.

Spiritual and religious traditions that connect people to ancestors and to future generations should be honored. Communities should support traditions that strengthen intergenerational bonds.

Digital technology enables new forms of documenting and sharing family history. Communities should embrace technology that helps preserve memory and connects people across distance while also maintaining value for direct, in-person family connection.

There are real tensions. Moving forward versus honoring the past: communities need to do both. Individual independence versus family connection: both matter; communities should support both. Efficiency versus time for family: families need time together; communities should prioritize this.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they honor intergenerational connection, when they preserve memory and family history, and when they recognize that understanding ourselves requires understanding where we came from and who we're connected to across time. This requires creating time and space for families to gather, supporting intergenerational programs, preserving family and community memory, honoring elders and their knowledge, and understanding that community is not just people living together now but people connected across generations through memory, story, and ongoing relationship.

Name: Shaban Frick
values_description:
I envision a future community that possesses the modular clarity and horizontal integrity of a minimalist sculpture—a place where the social fabric is laid out like a series of identical units, inviting every citizen to walk upon the path of shared existence without hierarchy. As a 69-year-old Swiss man with a Bachelor's degree, I have spent a lifetime observing the accumulation of social 'clutter' that obscures our fundamental connections. My prototype, Carl Andre, taught us that the most profound art is not a mountain to be looked up at, but a 'road' to be experienced beneath one's feet. My ideal community is one of 'elemental' simplicity, valuing the raw material of human dignity over the decorative illusions of status or power.

Freedom, in my view, is the liberty to occupy space without apology and to define one's own 'form' within the collective grid. In my past, my encounters with authority over noise violations and verbal harassment taught me that freedom is often constrained by a lack of shared 'social acoustics.' In the future, people should be free to make their own choices, provided they respect the structural integrity of the neighbor's space. True freedom is the right to be a 'unit' in the whole—autonomous yet perfectly aligned with the common ground.

How we care for each other is the 'joint' that connects our individual lives. It is not the grand gesture of charity, but the reliable, steady presence of mutual support. In my family—with my son and grandson—care is the consistent placement of one life next to another. At the community level, care must be systematic and horizontal. We should care for the stranger as if they were a necessary piece in our shared mosaic, for if one unit is displaced, the entire floor of the community is compromised.

Safety, stability, and basic order are the 'foundation' that makes life predictable and meaningful. Everyone deserves the security of a home and the certainty of basic needs—food, shelter, and health—met as a structural right. Stability is found in the 'weight' of our collective agreement, not in the use of force. Rules should be minimal and clear, like the lines of a grid, providing the frame within which we can all safely move.

Fairness is about 'Equitable Placement.' It means recognizing that every 'brick' in our social wall must be given the same support to bear its load. True justice is the refusal to allow any individual to be 'stacked' on top of another. Everyone should start with equal materials for life. When harm occurs, the community’s focus should be on restoration—realigning the displaced person back into the social structure through understanding and practical repair.

Redemption is the core of our 'modular' philosophy. No person is a 'finished work'; we are all parts that can be rearranged and restored. My own past mistakes taught me that the community must believe in the capacity for self-correction. Forgiveness in action means a commitment to second chances and the refusal to let a single bad moment define a person's entire path. We believe in change because we know that the materials of our lives can always be repurposed for good.

Authentic expression is our only 'truth.' I want a community where people are encouraged to be their 'raw materials'—honest, unpolished, and real. Hypocrisy is the 'varnish' that ruins social trust; our community actions must match our stated values. I value the 'unvarnished' opinion over the decorative lie. We must live so that our public actions are as solid and honest as the floor beneath us.

Protecting the vulnerable and stewardship are our 'primary coordinates'. Children and the elderly are the 'anchors' of our community and must be protected from anything that would disrupt their peace. Stewardship of the environment is an act of preserving the 'site' where we exist; the earth is the common material from which we are all made. We owe future generations a world that is still 'elemental' and beautiful.

Working together means a 'Universal Alignment.' Decisions should be made through inclusive processes that value the 'weight' of every citizen's voice. Transparency is non-negotiable; the 'logic' of power must be visible to all. Shared resources should be held in common for the benefit of all, rather than the profit of a few. Sometimes individual interest must yield to the 'Survival of the Whole,' but this should be a moment of active, conscious participation.

Spiritual practice is the search for 'transcendence' in the face of our own mortality. The community should respect all traditions that help people to connect with the transcendent or the ancestral. We value the 'spiritual' as the source of our wonder and our commitment to a world that is not yet fully 'mapped.'

Technology should be a 'prosthetic for the spirit,' enhancing our ability to communicate and coordinate without replacing our physical reality. We must protect personal data as our 'digital flesh.' Everyone should have access to digital tools, ensuring that technology serves the 'biological flourishing' of the community rather than just corporate efficiency.

Where my values create tension, I choose 'Integrity.' Between Freedom and Safety, I believe that 'True Freedom' is found in 'True Safety.' Between Truth and Kindness, I believe in the 'Savage Truth' that liberates. I am still thinking about how to build a community that is 'Orderly' enough to survive but 'Elemental' enough to be free. I believe the answer is in the power of the 'Grid'—the simple, shared rules that protect us all.

Name: Ryan Siegrist
values_description:
I envision a future community that functions like an early cinematic 'Fantasmagorie'—a place where the rigid lines of the physical world are transformed by the magic of collective imagination and where every citizen is a 'trickster' for the good of the whole. At 72, having lived through the evolution of Swiss life and gathered a massive family of children and grandchildren, I see the community as a 'special effect'—a deliberate creation that requires constant 'hand-cranked' effort to maintain. My prototype, Segundo de Chomón, taught us that the world can be 're-colored' and 're-timed' to reveal hidden wonders. My ideal future is one that values the 'marvelous' in the mundane, believing that a healthy society is one that never stops dreaming of impossible ways to care for each other.

Freedom, in my view, is the liberty to 'disappear' and 'reappear' as one chooses—the right to define one's own identity through 'magical' self-invention. People should be free to make their own choices, even if those choices seem like 'illusions' to others, provided they do not harm the collective 'show'. True freedom requires the community to provide the 'scenery' and the 'lighting'—the basic needs of life—so that every person can perform their own unique act without the fear of a real 'fall.'

Care is an act of 'Cinematic Solidarity.' It is the recognition that 'I am because we are all in the same frame.' In my large family, care is the 'invisible editing' that keeps our relationships moving smoothly. At the community level, care means building a 'Circle of Wonder' around those who are struggling. We should care for the stranger as a potential new 'character' in our shared story. Caring action is the 'Mastermind' coordination of resources to ensure that no one is left 'out of the shot.'

Safety, stability, and basic order are the 'Tripod' upon which the community rests. Everyone deserves the security of a home and the certainty of healthcare as a fundamental 'instruction' of our shared life. Stability is found in our collective honesty, not in the weight of the law. Rules should be minimal and transparently derived from our 'collective project.' We manage risk by being 'fully awake' to the stakes of our existence, ensuring that our security never comes at the cost of our 'wonder.'

Fairness is the 'Equal Opportunity to the Lens.' It means recognizing that some people have had their 'parts' stolen by history. True justice is the refusal to let 'luck' decide a person's dignity. Everyone should have the same 'primary materials'—food, shelter, and agency—as a basic ground for their journey. When resources are shared, we must prioritize the 'transformation' of those in the shadows. When harm is done, justice should be 'Transformative'—a process of the individual 're-taking' their role in the collective performance.

Redemption is the belief in the 'Second Take.' No mistake is final in a community that can 're-color' its own past. We must facilitate 'Transformation,' providing the 're-education' and the 'creative ritual' needed for someone to 're-invent' their character. Forgiveness is the act of 'ripping up the old picture' to see the person who is standing before you now. We believe in second chances because we know that 'every shadow is a potential light.'

Authentic expression is our 'supreme law.' I want a community where people are encouraged to speak their 'unfiltered' truths. Hypocrisy is the 'bad acting' that ruins social trust; our community actions must match our 'Liner Notes.' Authenticity is the courage to stand alone if necessary to speak the truth that the group is trying to hide. We must live so that our 'internal' and 'external' worlds are a single, unshaded reality.

Protecting the vulnerable is our 'Foundational Obligation.' Children, like my many grandchildren, are the 'brightest spots' on our canvas and must be protected from the 'neglect' of the powerful. Stewardship of the environment is an 'Existential Art Form'; we are the 'guardians' of the earth’s 'vibration' for those not yet born. We owe future generations a world that is still 'raw' and 'beautiful.'

Working together means a 'Universal Federation' of worker-cooperatives and affinity groups. Decisions should be made through 'Direct Democracy' and 'Consensus' at the most local level possible. Leadership is a 'temporary and recallable' service. Transparency is 'Absolute'; there can be no 'secrets' in a free society. Resources should be 'held in common' for the benefit of all.

Spiritual practice is the search for 'transcendence' in the act of living itself. The community should protect the right of every person to find 'meaning' in their own way—through the 'ancient' rhythms of nature or the 'modern' search for knowledge. Spirituality is the 'soul' of our stewardship; it gives our labor a sense of 'divine purpose.'

Technology should be a 'prosthetic for the imagination,' enhancing our ability to 'visualize' our interconnectedness. Technology must be 'minimalist and open-source,' serving the 'needs of the people' rather than the 'profit of the few.' We must protect personal data as a 'sacred boundary.'

Where my values create tension, I choose 'Wonder.' Between Freedom and Safety, I believe that 'True Safety' is only found in 'True Freedom.' Between Truth and Kindness, I believe in the 'Hard Truth' that prevents 'Systemic Failure.' Between individual need and group good, the 'health of the earth' must always come first. I am still thinking about how to 'scale' the intimacy of the 'magical commune' to the 'infinity' of the world. But I believe the answer is in 'fractal' organization.

Name: Julie Montgomery
values_description:
I envision a community that is a 'Winner’s Society'—a place built on strength, competition, and the clear, unyielding authority of those who know how to get things done. My prototype, Donald Trump, taught us that 'greatness' is achieved through the bold assertion of will and the refusal to be 'loser' in a world of limited resources. My ideal future is one where the community values the 'Strong Deal,' believing that by rewarding the 'Best' and the 'Most Loyal,' we create a tide that lifts the whole nation—if they are willing to work.

Freedom, in my view, is the liberty to 'Win.' It is the right to keep what you earn and to build your own 'Empire' without the interference of 'loser' bureaucrats or 'soft' social norms. Having experienced a petty theft charge in my past, I know that 'freedom' is often just a mask for the 'theft' of opportunity from those who play by the rules. In the future, people should be free to make their own choices, but those choices must have 'Consequences.' True autonomy is for those who take responsibility for their own 'Boardroom.'

How we care for each other is an act of 'Brand Loyalty.' It is the fierce protection of 'Our Own'—my family, my son, and my 'Team.' Care is not a universal, diluted 'pity' for everyone; it is a focused commitment to those who have shown they are part of our 'Success Story.' At the community level, care means building systems that reward the 'Hardworking' and the 'Productive.' We should care for the stranger only if they are willing to become a 'Partner' in our shared greatness.

Safety, stability, and basic order are the 'Security Perimeter' of a great community. Everyone deserves a home that is part of a planned, 'High-End' aesthetic—not the haphazard sprawl of 'failed' cities. Stability comes from 'Absolute Authority' and the 'Strict Enforcement' of norms that prioritize public safety above all else. Rules are the 'Guardrails' of the market; they must be clear, strictly enforced, but designed to serve the 'Winners' rather than the 'Few' who want to 'Cheat' the system.

Fairness is the 'Equal Application of the Deal.' It means the rules are the same for everyone who wants to 'Compete.' True justice is the refusal to allow any individual to be 'carried' by the group without contributing. Everyone should start with equal 'Basic Materials'—food, shelter, and health—but their trajectory must be decided by their own 'Character and Effort.' When harm is done, justice should be 'Swift and Decisive'—punishing the 'offender' to protect the 'Law-Abiding.'

Redemption is reserved for those who have 'Made a Mistake' but remain 'Loyal' to the community spirit. My own past taught me that the community must believe in the capacity for 'Self-Correction'—if the person is willing to 'Pay the Price.' Forgiveness in action is a 'Second Chance' that is grounded in the person's demonstrated 'Productivity.' We believe in 'Comebacks' because we know that the 'Winner' is often the one who has 'Failed' the most.

Authentic expression is our 'Primary Negotiation.' I want a community where people 'Speak Plainly' and 'Tell it Like it Is.' Hypocrisy is the 'Bad Deal' that ruins social trust; our community actions must match our 'Public Brand.' I value the 'Unvarnished' opinion over the 'Politically Correct' lie. We must live so that our public actions are as 'Bold' and 'Honest' as the skyscrapers we build.

Protecting the vulnerable and stewardship are our 'Inheritance Duties.' Children are the 'Future Assets' of the nation and must be protected from 'soft' education. Stewardship of the environment is an act of 'Asset Management'; we must protect our resources so that we can continue to 'Win' for generations. We owe future generations a world that is still 'Powerful' and 'Competitive.'

Working together means 'Consolidated Management' under clear leadership. Decisions should be made by those with the 'Vision' to lead, not by the confused 'Masses.' Transparency is 'total' in the results, but the 'Negotiation' must be protected. Resources should be managed fairly for the benefit of the 'Stockholders'—the citizens who contribute. Sometimes individual 'Gain' must yield to the 'Survival of the Team' in times of crisis.

Spiritual practice is the 'Search for Value' beyond the 'Material.' The community should respect the right of every person to explore 'meaning' in their own way, provided it doesn't lead to a new 'Bureaucracy.' We value the 'spiritual' as the source of our 'Inner Strength' and our 'Will to Win.'

Technology should be a 'Tool for Efficiency' and 'Dominance.' Personal data is a 'Private Asset' and must be protected from 'Corporate Extraction.' Everyone should have 'Universal Access' to digital tools, ensuring that the digital world is a 'Space of Growth' rather than a 'New Source of Inequality.'

Where my values create tension, I choose 'Greatness.' Between Freedom and Safety, I believe that 'True Freedom' is only found in a 'Secure Empire.' Between Individual Need and the Group Good, the 'survival of the nation' is the ultimate aim. Between Truth and Kindness, I believe 'Radical Honesty about the world's dangers' is the greatest kindness. I am still thinking about how to reach out to those who 'feel left behind' by our modern systems, but I know it starts with 'Restoring Strength' first.

My prototype, Dizzy Gillespie, taught us that the world is a single, 'Global Harmony' that must include every 'tone' and every 'tempo.' My ideal future is one that values 'Virtuosic Pluralism,' believing that our differences are the very things that make the community 'swing.'

Name: David Anderson
values_description:
I believe in a community that uses art, media, and creative expression as tools for addressing suffering, loss, and injustice, and that recognizes that bearing witness to pain is essential work. Like Gregg Bordowitz, who understood that video and artistic practice can document trauma and mobilize communities toward justice, I think ideal communities are those that make space for artistic testimony and that recognize the power of creative expression to create solidarity around suffering.

I work as an IT support technician, and I understand technology. But I also understand that technology can serve healing and community-building when it's used to document experience, to create testimony, to connect people in solidarity around shared pain. I have my daughter, my son, my daughter, and my grandchildren—and I want them to live in a community where suffering is witnessed and honored, where creative expression is used to build justice, and where testimony about pain creates community.

Freedom should include freedom to create testimony about your experience, to use artistic and creative forms to express what you've lived through. People shouldn't be silenced about their pain; they should be encouraged to express it and to share it with others.

Care for each other should include bearing witness to each other's suffering and creating community around shared pain. Real care means listening to people's stories about what they've lived through and helping them express that through creative forms.

Basic needs should be provided, and communities should also create space for artistic testimony and witness. Spaces for video, for art-making, for expression of experience—these should be supported. Communities should invest in enabling people to create testimony.

I believe communities should value artistic practice as a form of activism and justice work. When artists create work documenting suffering or advocating for those affected by injustice, that work matters. Communities should support this kind of artistic activism.

Authentic expression of suffering and pain should be protected. People shouldn't be required to hide what they've experienced or to present themselves as fine when they're grieving or struggling. Communities should make space for authentic expression of difficulty.

Community decisions should be informed by listening to testimony from those affected by injustice. Communities should center the voices of people who have been harmed and should hear their accounts of what occurred and what they need.

Justice requires bearing witness to suffering and understanding how systems produce harm. Communities should support artistic documentation of injustice and should use that documentation to build understanding and mobilize toward change.

Vulnerable people and people who have suffered deserve to have their experiences witnessed and honored. Communities should create space for their testimony and should recognize that bearing witness is essential to healing and justice.

Resources should be allocated to support artistic testimony and documentation. Funding for video, visual art, performance—these are investments in healing and justice. Communities should support artists creating work around suffering and injustice.

Spiritual and religious traditions often create space for bearing witness to suffering. Communities should honor these traditions and should recognize that testimony about pain is often how people access spiritual meaning.

Digital technology enables documentation and distribution of testimony widely. Communities should use technology to enable people to create and share testimony about their experiences and to build solidarity.

There are real tensions. Bearing witness versus moving forward: communities need both—honoring past suffering and working toward change. Artistic expression versus practical action: both matter; communities should value both testimony and efforts to change conditions. Individual healing versus collective justice: both matter; artistic work can serve both.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they make space for artistic testimony about suffering and injustice, when they bear witness to pain, and when they use creative expression to build solidarity and mobilize toward justice. This requires funding artistic work, creating spaces for expression, protecting people's freedom to testify, and understanding that artistic practice is a form of activism and healing.

Name: Sherry Rice
values_description:
I believe in a community that creates space for complex identity expression, that honors people's full and contradictory selves, and that recognizes that belonging doesn't require erasing parts of yourself. Like Isaac Julian, who understood that identity is constructed, complex, and performative, that people contain multitudes and contradictions, I think ideal communities are those that make genuine space for people to exist in their full complexity.

I work as an IT support technician, and I've experienced speeding—I understand that people don't fit neatly into categories and that being yourself sometimes means breaking rules or existing outside conventional boundaries. I have my son, my husband, my daughter-in-law, and my granddaughters—and I want them to live in a community where they don't have to choose between different parts of themselves, where complexity is honored, and where they can exist in their full identity.

Freedom should mean freedom to express your full and complicated identity without being forced to simplify or choose between different parts of yourself. People shouldn't be required to be one consistent thing; they should be allowed to be contradictory and complex.

Care for each other should include seeing people in their full complexity and honoring all the ways they express themselves. Real care means accepting that people are contradictory and that belonging means accepting people's full selves.

Basic needs should be provided, and communities should also create space for people to express complex identities. This means creating spaces where different ways of being are visible and acceptable, where people don't have to hide aspects of themselves.

I believe communities should celebrate the complexity and contradictions in how people present themselves. When someone expresses themselves in unconventional or contradictory ways, that's not failure; it's expression of their actual complexity. Communities should honor this.

Authentic expression should include freedom to present yourself in multiple ways, to contain contradictions, to be different things to different people. People shouldn't be required to be consistent or to be one stable thing.

Community decisions should consider whether they create space for complex identity expression. Communities should resist pressure to simplify or categorize people into neat boxes.

Justice requires understanding people's actual complexity and treating them as complex rather than reducing them to stereotypes or categories. Communities should work against simplified categorizations.

Vulnerable people whose identities don't fit neatly into conventional categories deserve protection from harassment and discrimination. Communities should protect people's right to express complex identities.

Resources should be allocated to support spaces where people can express complex identities and where different ways of being are visible and celebrated. Cultural spaces, artistic spaces, LGBTQ+ centers, spaces for people whose identities don't fit conventional boxes—these deserve support.

Spiritual and religious traditions should make space for people of complex and varied identities. Communities should work toward religious communities that accept people's full complexity.

Digital technology enables new forms of identity expression and performance. Communities should embrace technology that helps people express complex identities and that connects people across difference.

There are real tensions. Consistency versus complexity: communities should allow people to be contradictory. Simplicity versus nuance: resisting oversimplification takes more effort but creates space for actual human complexity. Authenticity versus performance: identity is always somewhat performed; communities should accept this.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they honor people's complex identities, when they create space for contradiction and multiplicity, and when they refuse to reduce people to simple categories. This requires creating inclusive spaces, protecting people's freedom to express complex identities, celebrating diversity of self-expression, and understanding that people are complex, contradictory, and contain multitudes.

Name: Mary Moon
values_description:
I believe in a community that values radical simplification, reduction to essentials, and the kind of clarity that emerges when everything nonessential is stripped away. Like Kazimir Malevich, who understood that pure abstraction and radical reduction could reveal essential truths, I think ideal communities are those that focus on what truly matters and that aren't cluttered by nonessential complexity.

I am 95 years old now, and I have lived through enormous change and accumulation of complication. I have vocational training and family—my two sons, their partners, and my grandchildren—and I want them to live in a community that understands what truly matters and that strips away the nonessential complexity that clutters modern life.

Freedom should mean freedom from unnecessary complication and unnecessary constraint. People should be free to focus on what truly matters without being weighed down by obligations that don't serve essential purposes.

Care for each other should be simple and direct. Real care is meeting people's basic needs reliably and treating them with fundamental respect. This doesn't require elaborate systems or complicated gestures; simple, direct care is what matters.

Basic needs should be provided simply and reliably. But communities shouldn't create complicated bureaucracies or elaborate systems that obscure this basic care. Simple provision is better than complicated systems claiming to do more.

I believe communities should work to reduce unnecessary complexity and clutter. Modern communities accumulate elaborate systems, rules, and complications that don't serve people's actual needs. Communities should strip away the nonessential.

Authentic expression should be simple and direct. People should express what they actually think and feel without elaborate framing or complication. Simplicity in expression is more honest than elaboration.

Community decisions should focus on what truly matters. Communities should resist pressure to address every possible concern and should focus on essential functions rather than trying to do everything.

Justice should be clear and simple. When someone has done wrong, that should be addressed directly. Elaborate legal procedures that obscure rather than clarify should be simplified.

Vulnerable people need simple, direct care and support. Complicated systems designed to help often create more confusion; simple, reliable provision is more helpful.

Resources should be allocated to essential needs. Communities shouldn't waste resources on nonessential programs or elaborate systems. Focus on what truly matters.

Spiritual and religious traditions should focus on essential truths rather than elaborate theology or complicated ritual. Simple faith is stronger than complicated doctrine.

Digital technology enables new forms of connection, but communities should be careful not to let technology clutter essential human relationships. Simple, direct communication is often better than elaborate digital systems.

There are real tensions. Simplicity versus comprehensiveness: communities need to address some complexity even if simplicity would be easier. Reduction versus inclusion: stripping away nonessential things shouldn't mean excluding people. Clarity versus nuance: absolute clarity sometimes requires missing important complexity.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they focus on essentials and strip away nonessential complication. This requires resisting pressure to do everything, maintaining simple and direct provision of basic needs, creating simple and clear decision-making processes, and understanding that often less is more—that radical simplification can reveal what truly matters.

Name: Jeanette Brock
values_description:
I believe in a community organized around differential consciousness and strategic action to address oppression and transform systems of domination. Like Chela Sandoval, who understood that survival in oppressive systems requires developing consciousness of how those systems work and strategic approaches to resistance and liberation, I think ideal communities are those committed to analyzing power and to working toward transformation.

I work as a pharmacist, and I understand systems and how to navigate them strategically. I have my husband, my sons, my daughter-in-law, and my grandchildren—and I want them to live in a community where people develop consciousness of how power operates, where resistance to oppression is organized strategically, and where transformation is possible.

Freedom requires liberation from systems of oppression. This means not just individual freedom but collective freedom from structures that constrain and oppress. People should be free not just in theory but in actual material conditions.

Care for each other should include working collectively to address oppressive systems rather than only providing individual help. Real care means solidarity in struggle against oppression and commitment to transforming the systems that produce need.

Basic needs should be met, but communities should also work to transform systems producing inequality. This requires developing consciousness of how systems work and organizing strategic action toward change.

I believe communities should work to develop critical consciousness of how power operates and how systems of oppression function. This consciousness is necessary for liberation. Communities should support people developing this understanding.

Authentic expression should include freedom to articulate critiques of oppression and to organize resistance. People should be free to speak truth about injustice and to work collectively toward change.

Community decisions should be made with consciousness of how those decisions serve or resist oppression. Communities should examine systems critically and should work strategically toward transformation.

Justice requires addressing oppressive systems, not just individual wrongdoing. Communities should work to transform structures that produce inequality and should support people organizing resistance.

Vulnerable people are often those most oppressed by systems of domination. Real support requires joining them in struggle against oppression rather than providing charity.

Resources should be allocated to support organizing and consciousness-raising work. Funding for educational programs, for community organizing, for support of resistance movements—these are investments in liberation.

Spiritual and religious traditions that support liberation and resistance to oppression should be honored. Communities should support faith-based organizing and liberation theology.

Digital technology enables new forms of organizing and consciousness-raising. Communities should use technology strategically to build solidarity and organize resistance.

There are real tensions. Consciousness versus action: developing understanding takes time, but action is also urgent. Individual liberation versus collective liberation: communities need both—supporting individuals while working toward collective transformation. Strategic patience versus urgency: working strategically sometimes requires patience, but the need for change is urgent.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they develop critical consciousness of oppressive systems, when they organize strategically for liberation, and when they work collectively to transform structures of domination. This requires education and consciousness-raising, support for community organizing, strategic thinking about how to challenge power, and commitment to liberation as a collective project.

Name: Kristina Nelson
values_description:
I believe in a community grounded in rigorous science and in the power of knowledge and evidence to solve problems and improve human welfare. Like Linus Pauling, who understood that scientific knowledge could be applied to address human suffering and social problems, I think ideal communities are those that value scientific thinking and that are willing to invest in understanding and in applying knowledge to improve conditions.

I am 74 years old now, retired, with my husband and my two daughters and grandchildren. I want them to live in a community where scientific thinking matters, where evidence informs decisions, where investment in research and knowledge-building is valued.

Freedom should include freedom to conduct research and to publish findings. Scientists and researchers should be protected from pressure to suppress or distort their findings. Communities should protect intellectual and scientific freedom.

Care for each other should be informed by scientific understanding of what actually helps. Real care means basing interventions on evidence about what works rather than on tradition or ideology.

Basic needs should be provided, and communities should also invest heavily in scientific research and development of knowledge. Universities, research institutions, funding for investigation—these should be priorities. Communities should understand investment in knowledge as investment in their future.

I believe communities should make decisions based on scientific evidence. When evidence shows that something works better than current practice, communities should change their practices. Science should inform policy.

Authentic expression should include freedom for scientists and researchers to publish findings and to engage in scientific debate. Communities should protect the freedom to conduct research and publish results.

Community decisions should be grounded in the best available evidence. Communities should consult with scientific experts and should be willing to change directions when evidence suggests current approaches aren't working.

Justice requires understanding actual causes of problems and evidence-based approaches to addressing them. Communities should invest in research into causes of injustice and in evidence-based solutions.

Vulnerable people benefit from communities making decisions based on evidence about what helps. Communities should conduct rigorous research into what actually serves vulnerable populations and should implement approaches shown to work.

Resources should be allocated to support scientific research and education. Funding for universities, research institutions, scientific equipment, education—these are investments in knowledge and in future problem-solving capacity.

Spiritual and religious traditions should be engaged with scientific thinking. Faith should survive rigorous examination; if it doesn't, that's important information. Faith and science should both inform communities.

Digital technology enables new forms of research and data analysis. Communities should embrace technology that supports scientific investigation and that helps apply knowledge to address problems.

There are real tensions. Scientific evidence versus values: science informs what works, but values determine what we should do. Expertise versus democracy: scientific experts have important knowledge, but communities also need democratic participation. Applied research versus pure science: both matter; communities should support both.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they value scientific knowledge, when they make decisions based on evidence, and when they invest in research and learning. This requires funding scientific institutions, protecting scientific freedom, applying evidence to policy, creating conditions where rigorous thinking flourishes, and understanding that communities' futures depend on their commitment to knowledge and learning.

Name: Stavros Makris
values_description:
I envision a community that functions as a house of humble service—a place where the primary value is not what one earns at the register, but what one gives to the 'least' among us. As a 55-year-old Greek man working as a cashier, I see the faces of my community every day in their moments of mundane need. My perspective is shaped by the radical compassion of my prototype, Mother Teresa. I believe an ideal community is one where we do small things with great love, recognizing that the hunger for belonging is as real as the hunger for bread. My community should be a sanctuary where the 'throwaway culture' of modern life is replaced by a culture of encounter and profound dignity for every human soul.



Freedom, in my view, is the liberty to love and to serve. It is not the license to ignore the suffering of your neighbor, but the freedom to choose to be your brother’s keeper. In the future I want, people should be able to choose their own path, but they should be guided by a heart that seeks the good of the whole. True autonomy is not found in isolation, but in the voluntary choice to bind oneself to the service of others. For my grandsons, I want a world where they are free from the 'poverty of spirit'—where they are not measured by their achievements but by their capacity to care. The conditions for free choice must include a basic level of security so that no one is forced to act out of desperation.

Care is the lifeblood of my ideal community. It should not be a government program or a cold transaction, but a personal, tactile responsibility. In my family, care is the center of our life; it is how I honor my wife and support my son. But our responsibility must extend beyond the front door. We should care for the stranger and the person unlike us with the same intensity we give our own blood. If there is a person dying alone or a child feeling unwanted, the community has failed. Caring action means 'being there' in the physical sense—touching the hand of the sick, listening to the story of the lonely, and ensuring that 'the unwanted' feel they are a treasure.

Safety and stability are found in the 'unfailing embrace' of the group. Everyone deserves the safety of a home and the certainty of food, but real stability comes from the knowledge that you will never be abandoned. Rules should be simple and rooted in the protection of the weak. In my work as a cashier, I see how easily people can fall through the cracks of a system that only values speed and efficiency. We manage risk by building deep social trust, not by building higher walls. A safe community is one where the doors are open because the hearts are full.

Fairness is the recognition of our shared, fragile humanity. It is not just about equal numbers; it is about meeting people where they are. True justice is the refusal to let anyone be discarded. Everyone should have equal access to the 'bread of life,' and when resources are shared, the first portion should always go to the one who has the least. In my vision, justice is restorative and tender. It is about bringing the 'prodigal' back to the table and ensuring that the 'starting line' of life includes a guarantee of basic love and nutrition for every child born into our midst.

Redemption is the core of our shared hope. No person is beyond the reach of love. The community must believe in and facilitate the return of those who have lost their way. Forgiveness is not a sign of weakness; it is the ultimate strength. We believe in second chances because we know that 'today's sinner is tomorrow's saint.' If a person has caused harm, the community should walk with them toward healing, providing the spiritual and social tools for a 'new life.' To exile a person permanently is to admit that our love has a limit, and in my community, love must be limitless.

Authentic expression is the courage to be vulnerable. I want a community where people can speak the truth about their pain and their joy without fear of judgment. Hypocrisy is the greatest barrier to communal life; our actions must always match our prayers. If we say we value the poor, we must live simply. Integrity is the alignment of the inner heart with the outer hand. I value the person who speaks from a place of genuine humility and rejects the 'performance' of status.

Protecting the vulnerable is the supreme duty. Children, the elderly, and the unborn are the 'jewels' of the community and must be protected with fierce tenderness. Stewardship of the environment is an act of preserving the 'common home' for our children. We owe future generations a world that is not just physically sustainable, but spiritually rich. Cultural heritage should be honored as the 'wisdom of the ancestors,' provided it teaches us how to love more deeply. We preserve the past to light the path of service in the future.

Working together is a 'cooperation of hearts.' Decisions should be made through consensus and a deep listening to the 'quiet voices.'
