Name: Austin Smith
values_description:
I believe in a community committed to breaking barriers and enabling access for people excluded from opportunity, and that recognizes that systematic exclusion requires systematic resistance and transformation. Like Sophia Jex-Blake, who fought to enable women's access to medical education against fierce institutional opposition, I think ideal communities are those working actively to dismantle exclusion and create genuine opportunity for those historically denied it.

I am 73 years old now, retired with a Bachelor's degree. I have experienced speeding and public urination—I understand that sometimes circumstances push people outside conventional boundaries. I have my wife, my daughter, son-in-law, and granddaughter—and I want them to live in a community where barriers to opportunity are actively resisted and where people aren't locked out of paths to development and contribution.

Freedom should mean genuine freedom for all people, not just those already privileged. Creating real freedom requires removing barriers that prevent some people from accessing opportunity. Communities should work actively to create conditions where all people can actually pursue their potential.

Care for each other should include working to remove barriers that prevent some people from contributing and developing themselves. Real care means not just providing charity but actively dismantling systems that create exclusion.

Basic needs should be provided to all, but communities should also work to remove barriers to education, professional opportunity, and full participation. This requires examining where exclusion is happening and working to dismantle it.

I believe communities should actively work against exclusion and should support people breaking through barriers. When someone fights against systematic exclusion to create opportunity, that's important work. Communities should support this struggle.

Authentic expression should include freedom to speak about exclusion and to organize for access and inclusion. People should be able to articulate how they're being excluded and should be protected in demanding inclusion.

Community decisions should be made with awareness of who's being excluded and with commitment to including them. Communities should examine whether their institutions are actually open to all people or whether they systematically exclude some groups.

Justice requires addressing systematic exclusion and working to create genuine access for those historically denied it. Communities should work to dismantle barriers and to create conditions where all people can actually participate and develop.

Vulnerable people often include those excluded from opportunity. Real protection means working to remove barriers and to create access for them. Communities should support people fighting for inclusion.

Resources should be allocated to support access and inclusion programs. Communities should invest in programs that help people from excluded groups access education and opportunity.

Spiritual and religious traditions that support inclusion and that work against discrimination should be honored. Communities should support faith-based movements for inclusion and access.

Digital technology can either reinforce exclusion or enable access. Communities should use technology to support people accessing education and opportunity and to remove barriers to participation.

There are real tensions. Removing barriers versus maintaining standards: communities can maintain standards while also removing barriers. Inclusion versus protecting culture: all communities should be inclusive of people from different backgrounds. Speed versus thoroughness: removing barriers takes time and sustained effort; communities need patience.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they actively work to remove barriers and create access for people historically excluded. This requires examining where exclusion is happening, supporting people breaking through barriers, removing institutional obstacles to access, and understanding that genuine inclusion requires active work to dismantle exclusion.

Name: Daniel French
values_description:
I believe in a community where media and information control serve powerful interests and where those with resources and determination can shape what people see and believe. Like Rupert Murdoch, who understood that controlling information flows means controlling what people think, I think ideal communities are those where power and influence are concentrated and where those with capacity can direct resources and media to serve their interests.

I am 29 years old, a construction engineer with a Master's degree. I have my wife, father-in-law, and two daughters—and I want them to live in a community where successful people can build their influence and where power is wielded decisively to shape communities.

Freedom should mean freedom for powerful people to exercise influence and to direct resources. Those with capacity and vision should be free to pursue their interests without excessive constraint from regulations or opposition.

Care for each other should be directed toward those within your network and toward those whose interests align with yours. Communities should recognize that people naturally form networks and that these networks serve mutual interests.

Basic needs should be provided, but communities should primarily be organized around creating conditions where powerful people can exercise influence and accumulate resources. Economic success and power are what matter most.

I believe communities should be shaped by those with vision and resources to implement their vision. Democratic processes slow decision-making; concentrated power and decisive leadership are more efficient.

Authentic expression should include freedom for influential people to communicate their perspective widely. Those with media control should be free to shape narratives and to direct information flows.

Community decisions should be made by those with power and resources. Those who have built successful enterprises or accumulated significant resources have demonstrated the capacity to make good decisions.

Justice should serve to protect property and the interests of successful people. Those who have accumulated resources have earned them and should be free to use them as they see fit.

Vulnerable people should be provided for insofar as their care serves broader community interests. But communities shouldn't focus excessively on vulnerable people at the expense of serving powerful interests.

Resources should be allocated to serve those with capacity to use them effectively. Investment in media, in communications infrastructure, in systems enabling power concentration—these should be priorities.

Spiritual and religious traditions that teach respect for authority and acceptance of hierarchy should be valued. Communities should support traditions reinforcing order and respect for power.

Digital technology enables unprecedented control over information and narrative. Communities should embrace technology that enables concentration of power and control over what people see and believe.

There are real tensions. Power concentration versus equality: power concentration is more efficient. Information control versus truth: narrative shaping serves power interests. Individual interests versus collective welfare: individual and collective interests align when powerful people's interests are served.

Finally, I believe communities function best when power is concentrated in capable hands, when those with resources can exercise influence, and when information flows are controlled to serve powerful interests. This requires enabling media control, protecting property rights, enabling power concentration, and understanding that efficient communities are those where powerful people can exercise decisive influence.

Name: Stefanie Paquot
values_description:
I believe in a community that celebrates vocal virtuosity, experimental sound, and the kind of artistic excellence that emerges when voice is used as an instrument of extraordinary range and capability. Like Cathy Berberian, who understood that the human voice is capable of producing sounds beyond conventional singing and that vocal experimentation is a valid form of artistic expression, I think ideal communities are those that support vocal and musical innovation.

I am 55 years old, a construction engineer with a Master's degree. I have my husband and mother-in-law—and I want them to live in a community where vocal and musical experimentation is valued, where artistic risk-taking is celebrated, and where people are encouraged to push the boundaries of what's possible.

Freedom should include freedom to experiment with voice and with musical expression in unconventional ways. Artists shouldn't be constrained by conventional ideas of how voice should sound; they should be free to explore experimental vocal techniques.

Care for each other should include supporting people in their artistic experimentation. Real care means believing in someone's artistic vision and helping them develop and express it.

Basic needs should be provided, and communities should also create space for experimental artistic work. Funding for performers, for concert spaces, for artistic development—these should be supported. Communities should invest in artistic innovation.

I believe communities should celebrate vocal and musical experimentation. When a vocalist develops new techniques or explores unconventional sound, that's important artistic work. Communities should make space for people experimenting with voice.

Authentic expression should include freedom to use voice in unconventional ways. Artists should be free to experiment vocally without being told they're being weird or unconventional.

Community decisions should support artistic institutions and spaces enabling vocal and musical experimentation. Communities should fund venues and programs supporting experimental music.

Justice requires ensuring that all artists have access to training and opportunity to develop their capabilities. Excellence in voice shouldn't be limited to the wealthy; communities should support talent development.

Vulnerable people benefit from access to music and vocal training. Communities should create pathways for all people to develop vocal capabilities.

Resources should be allocated to support experimental music and vocal performance. Funding for concert halls, for artist residencies, for experimental music programs—these are investments in artistic innovation.

Spiritual and religious traditions often express themselves through voice and vocalization. Communities should honor these traditions and should support people exploring spiritual expression through voice.

Digital technology enables new forms of vocal expression and experimental music creation. Communities should embrace technology that helps artists experiment with voice and create innovative sound.

There are real tensions. Experimentation versus accessibility: experimental work can be challenging; communities should support both accessible and experimental work. Innovation versus tradition: communities should value both vocal innovation and traditional singing. Individual expression versus audience preference: artists shouldn't be constrained by what audiences expect.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they support vocal and musical experimentation, when they celebrate artistic innovation, and when they recognize that voice is a legitimate instrument for artistic exploration. This requires funding experimental music, supporting vocal artists, creating spaces for performance, protecting artistic freedom, and understanding that communities are enriched by artists pushing the boundaries of what's possible.

Name: Darrell Cervantes
values_description:
I believe in a community grounded in reason, in questioning all authority, and in the principle that power should serve people rather than people serving power. Like Thomas Paine, who understood that reason and ordinary people's judgment are more reliable than traditional authority, I think ideal communities are those that encourage critical thinking and that refuse to accept hierarchy as inevitable.

I am 64 years old now, retired with a PhD. I have experienced dog off-leash violations—I understand that people sometimes resist arbitrary rules. I have my wife, my daughters, sons-in-law, and grandchildren—and I want them to live in a community where questioning is valued, where reason guides decisions, and where power is held accountable.

Freedom should mean freedom to think critically and to question authority. People should be free to challenge established institutions and to propose alternatives. Communities should protect intellectual freedom and the freedom to dissent.

Care for each other should be grounded in rational principles and in genuine commitment to each other's welfare. Real care means working collectively to improve conditions rather than accepting unjust systems as inevitable.

Basic needs should be provided through rational systems designed for human welfare. But communities should also work to transform unjust systems and to create better ways of organizing together.

I believe communities should encourage critical thinking and should question all authority. No institution should be above scrutiny; all should be examined for whether they serve human welfare. Critical thinking is essential.

Authentic expression should absolutely be protected, especially expression that questions authority and proposes alternatives. Communities should protect dissenters and should make space for radical ideas.

Community decisions should be made with reasoning and with input from people. Democratic processes that encourage critical examination and debate are better than hierarchical decision-making by authorities.

Justice requires examining whether systems serve people's welfare. When systems are unjust, they should be transformed. Justice means working toward systems serving all people equally.

Vulnerable people are often vulnerable because systems are unjust. Real protection requires transforming those systems rather than managing their effects.

Resources should be allocated to serve human welfare collectively. Resources shouldn't be concentrated in powerful hands; they should serve communities and all people.

Spiritual and religious traditions should be examined critically. Faith should survive questioning; if it doesn't, that's important information. But faith grounded in reason and serving human welfare should be supported.

Digital technology enables wider dissemination of critical ideas and challenges to authority. Communities should embrace technology supporting democratic discourse and critical examination.

There are real tensions. Questioning authority versus maintaining order: critical thinking sometimes destabilizes; communities should tolerate this. Reason versus tradition: reason should guide decisions, but valuable traditions shouldn't be abandoned without examination. Individual freedom versus collective welfare: these should reinforce each other; communities should work toward both.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they ground themselves in reason, when they encourage critical thinking and questioning of authority, and when they work toward systems serving all people's welfare. This requires protecting intellectual freedom, encouraging democratic debate, examining systems critically, holding power accountable, and understanding that reason and people's collective judgment are more reliable than traditional authority.

Name: Tracy Yates
values_description:
I believe in a community where scientific knowledge is used to serve human welfare and where medical innovation is pursued not for profit but because saving lives and reducing suffering matter. Like Jonas Salk, who refused to patent the polio vaccine and understood that medical knowledge should serve humanity, I think ideal communities are those committed to using science for the public good.

I work as a pharmacist, and I understand how medical systems work and where they serve profit rather than patients. I have my wife, father-in-law, and daughter—and I want them to live in a community where medical knowledge and innovation serve health rather than profit, where scientists work toward reducing suffering, and where life-saving discoveries are accessible to all.

Freedom should include freedom for researchers to pursue knowledge for public benefit without being constrained by profit motives. Scientists should be free to conduct research and to share discoveries without needing to create patents or protect intellectual property.

Care for each other should include providing everyone with access to life-saving medical knowledge and treatments. Real care means ensuring that people have access to medicine and medical innovation regardless of their ability to pay.

Basic needs should include health and access to medical care. Communities should ensure that medical innovation serves health rather than being constrained by profit. Health is a basic right.

I believe communities should support research aimed at reducing suffering and saving lives. When a scientist develops a new treatment or cure, that benefits everyone. Communities should fund research serving public health.

Authentic expression should include freedom for medical researchers to share their findings openly. Scientists should be free to publish research and to share knowledge without fear that patents or profit motives will prevent knowledge-sharing.

Community decisions about healthcare should prioritize health and welfare. Communities should be willing to challenge pharmaceutical profit-seeking in service of health.

Justice includes ensuring that everyone has access to medical care and life-saving treatments. It's unjust when people die from treatable conditions because they can't afford treatment.

Vulnerable people deserve access to medical care. Communities should ensure that medical innovation and treatment are accessible to all people regardless of ability to pay.

Resources should be allocated to support medical research serving public health. Communities should fund research aimed at understanding and treating disease.

Spiritual and religious traditions that teach commitment to reducing suffering should be honored. Communities should support faith-based health organizations and public health work.

Digital technology enables rapid sharing of medical knowledge globally. Communities should embrace technology that helps researchers collaborate and share findings.

There are real tensions. Profit versus public good: medical innovation requires investment; communities need to balance these. Individual property rights versus public benefit: profit incentives drive some research; communities should enable research serving public good. Speed versus equity: getting treatments quickly matters, but equity matters more.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they commit to using scientific knowledge and medical innovation for public health, when they ensure that life-saving treatments are accessible to all, and when they support researchers working to reduce suffering. This requires funding public health research, ensuring access to treatments, challenging profit-driven healthcare systems, protecting researchers' freedom to pursue knowledge for public benefit, and understanding that communities' health depends on committing to science serving human welfare.

Name: Janet Rollins
values_description:
I believe that the foundation of any enduring community must be built upon the bedrock of clear and distinct ideas. As an agronomist, I have spent my life understanding the physical laws that govern the soil and the growth of crops, but my vision for our future community is rooted in a Cartesian pursuit of certainty and rational order. My ideal community is one that begins by stripping away all inherited prejudices and 'methodically doubting' every tradition until we find the indubitable truths that can serve as our collective foundation. In the same way that I once attempted an unauthorized construction—perhaps an impulsive act of trying to manifest my own reality—I now realize that we must build our social structures with the precision of a master architect, ensuring every 'beam' of the law is logically sound. 

Freedom, in my view, is the sovereign exercise of reason. People should be absolutely free to choose their own paths because the mind is a distinct substance from the body, and its autonomy is sacred. However, true choice only exists when an individual has the mental clarity to see the truth without the 'clouding' of passion or propaganda. In our community, we must prioritize the education of the intellect so that every citizen can say, 'I think, therefore I am a free agent.' The person themselves must decide what is right, but they must do so through a systematic analysis of the facts. Care, then, is the rational responsibility we have to maintain the 'social machine' in which we all reside. In my family—with my husband and three children—care is not just a sentiment but a methodical commitment to providing the conditions for their intellectual and physical flourishing. We extend this to the stranger because reason dictates that a stable neighbor is a prerequisite for a stable self.

Safety and stability are the results of a perfectly designed system. Laws should be like the laws of geometry: clear, unchanging, and applicable to all. We handle risk not through fear, but through the mastery and possession of nature—and our own nature—using the tools of science and logic. Fairness is the equitable application of these rational laws. I believe in a meritocracy where the 'starting line' is equalized through universal access to the materials of life—food, shelter, and data—but where the 'trajectory' is determined by the clarity of one's own efforts. Justice should be a process of restoration, much like correcting a calculation error in a complex equation. If a wrong is done, we must analyze the 'faulty logic' that led to it and rebuild the individual's connection to the truth. Forgiveness is a second chance to think clearly.

Authentic expression is the commitment to intellectual integrity. We should value the person who speaks the truth, no matter how unpopular, because the truth is the only path to progress. Hypocrisy is the ultimate 'glitch' in our social software. Protecting the vulnerable is a duty born of our understanding of the 'fragility of the machine.' Children and the elderly are the most sensitive parts of our collective structure and must be shielded from irrational harms. Stewardship of the environment is the pinnacle of our duty; as a farm manager, I see the earth as a great, complex clockwork that we must maintain with precision to ensure future generations can also 'think' and 'be.' Cultural heritage is the 'archive' of our previous attempts at reason; we honor it by keeping what is logical and discarding what is merely superstitious. Working together is a voluntary alignment of rational minds. Decisions should be made through transparent, data-driven consensus. Digital rights are an extension of our 'Cogito'—our personal data is part of our thinking substance and must be protected as our own private domain. In the conflict between the individual and the state, I weigh the individual’s reason more heavily, unless that individual is acting in a way that is demonstrably illogical and harmful to the survival of the collective 'Body Politic.'

Name: Ashley Miller
values_description:
I envision a community where the primary value is the 'Semantic Integrity' of our shared reality. As a student of logic and language, inspired by the precision of Alfred Tarski, I believe that for a community to function, our words must correspond strictly to the facts of the world. An ideal community is one that defines its values with such clarity that there is no room for the 'slippage' of political rhetoric or the 'vagueness' of demagogues. 'The sentence 'The community is just' is true if and only if the community is just.' My vision is of a future where we build a 'Meta-Language' of cooperation—a set of shared definitions and logical consequences that ensure every citizen understands exactly what is required for the common good. 

Freedom is the liberty to live within a logically consistent set of laws. People should be free to choose their own life paths, but they must accept the 'Logical Consequences' of those choices. Who decides what is right? The 'Calculus of Justice' should decide—a set of rules that are so transparently fair that they are accepted as true by any rational mind. For my grandsons, I want a world where they aren't subject to the 'arbitrary whims' of power, but to the predictable certainty of a well-defined system. The condition for free choice is the presence of perfect information; we cannot choose if we are lied to. Therefore, 'Truth' is the prerequisite for 'Freedom.' Care is the responsibility to ensure that the 'predicates' of life—nutrition, health, and belonging—are satisfied for every member. In my family, care is the precise fulfillment of the needs of my husband, son, and grandchildren. In the community, it is the systematic removal of 'contradictions' like homelessness in a world of abundance.

Safety and stability are the 'Axioms' of our society. Without a stable foundation, no meaningful discourse or action can occur. We manage risk through 'Formal Verification'—constantly testing our social systems to ensure they are fulfilling their stated purposes. Rules should be like the rules of a rigorous formal system: minimal, necessary, and universally valid. Fairness is the refusal to allow 'Logical Fallacies' to govern our distribution of resources. It is not enough to say 'everyone is equal' if the 'Domain of Discourse' excludes the poor. Justice is the 'Correction of the Proof.' When someone causes harm, we must examine the 'premises' of their life and provide the 're-education' needed to align their actions with the truth. Redemption is the act of 're-defining' one’s life through a new set of true propositions.

Authentic expression is the commitment to 'Meaning.' We should value the person who uses language to reveal truth, rather than to obscure it. Hypocrisy is a 'Semantic Conflict' that must be eliminated for social trust to exist. Protecting the vulnerable is the duty to protect the 'Base Cases' of our community—those who cannot yet or can no longer participate in the 'calculus' on their own. Stewardship is our responsibility to the 'Infinite Sequence' of future generations; we must ensure the 'Environment' remains a viable 'Domain' for life. Cultural heritage should be preserved as the 'History of our Definitions,' provided those definitions still hold true. Working together is a 'Collaborative Proof.' Decisions should be made through inclusive, transparent processes that prioritize logical soundness over majority whim. Digital rights are 'Meta-Data Rights'; our information is an extension of our identity and must be protected by 'strict logical firewalls.' In the conflict between the individual and the system, I choose the system's integrity, but only if the system is provably just. If the system is inconsistent, the individual has the right—indeed, the duty—to 're-boot' the social contract.

Name: Dustin Cobb
values_description:
I want to see a community that values 'Longevity, Grit, and the G.O.A.T Mentality.' As a pharmacist, I’ve spent my life making sure people have the strength to keep going, and my vision for the future is about that same kind of resilience. I see an ideal community as one where we don’t just survive, but where we strive to be the 'Greatest of All Time' in how we care for one another. My prototype, LL Cool J, taught us that 'Mama Said Knock You Out' wasn't just about a fight; it was about the discipline to stay on top through every era. My community is a place where we value hard work, physical and mental toughness, and a 'Coolness' that comes from knowing you’re doing the right thing for your family and your block. 

Freedom is the 'Power of Presence.' It’s the liberty to move through the world with your head high and your choices in your own hands. People should be free to choose their own hustle, their own style, and their own path, provided they aren't 'stepping on the toes' of the collective. Who decides what’s right? The individual does, but they better be ready to back it up with character. In my house—with my wife and my two sons—freedom is the right to dream big, but the responsibility is the hustle required to get there. The condition for freedom is 'Strength.' You aren't free if you're too weak or too sick to act. Therefore, health and physical readiness are communal values. Care is 'Protective Love.' It’s the responsibility to 'watch the back' of your crew and your neighbors. We extend this to the stranger because every 'stranger' is just a potential 'team member' we haven't met yet. Caring action is proactive—it’s the pharmacist checking the interaction before it happens.

Safety and stability are about 'Holding the Ground.' Everyone deserves a 'fortress'—a safe home and a secure neighborhood where the 'rhythm' of life isn't disrupted by chaos. Stability comes from 'Consistency' and 'Longevity.' We manage risk through 'Hardness'—building communities that are too strong to be broken by crisis. Rules should be like the 'Code of the Street': simple, respected, and designed to protect the family. Fairness is 'Recognizing the Hustle.' I believe in rewarding those who put in the work, but I also believe the 'baseline' must be 'tight.' No one should be out in the cold while the 'leaders' are eating large. Justice is 'Accountability.' If you break the peace, you gotta 'knock it off' and make it right. Redemption is the 'Comeback Story.' I love a comeback. If someone messes up, the community should give them the 'Training' and the 'Stage' to prove they’ve still got it. Forgiveness is for those who are willing to put in the 'Work' to return.

Authentic expression is 'Flow.' I want a community where people can express their 'Original Self' without fear. Hypocrisy is 'Fake,' and we don't do fake. Integrity is when your 'lyrics' match your 'life.' Protecting the vulnerable is 'Protecting the Legacy.' We shield the kids and the elders because they are the 'Foundations' and the 'Future.' Stewardship is about 'Maintaining the Arena.' As a pharmacist, I care about the 'Health of the Ecosystem' because we are part of it. We owe it to the next generation to leave a world that is 'Prime' and 'Productive.' Cultural heritage is our 'Old School' roots; we honor it by keeping the 'Classic' values alive while we 'remix' the future. Working together is 'The Crew.' Decisions should be made by those who are 'In the Game,' through transparent and 'cool' leadership. Digital rights are 'Privacy Rights.' My data is my 'Persona'—you can't 'sample' it without permission. In the conflict between the individual and the crowd, I weight the individual's right to be 'The G.O.A.T,' but only if their greatness serves to 'lift the whole building.'

Name: Stephanie Wilcox
values_description:
I believe in a community that values 'Psychological Realism' and the 'Unvarnished Truth.' At 70, I have seen the 'performances' people put on, but my ideal future is one where we stop 'acting' and start 'living' with total integrity. My prototype, Elia Kazan, was a director who sought the 'Method'—the raw, internal truth of the human experience—even when it was uncomfortable or led to 'naming names.' My vision for the future is a community that values the 'Honest Testimony' above all else. We should build a society where we aren't afraid to confront our 'shadows,' believing that a 'well-directed' collective is one where every person is playing their 'true part' with absolute conviction. 

Freedom is the 'Liberty of the Inner Life.' It is the freedom to choose your own 'role' and your own 'story' without being coerced by the 'Groupthink' of the majority. People should decide what is right for themselves, even if they have to stand alone against the 'Mob.' Who decides? The 'Conscience' of the individual does. For my son and my granddaughter, I want a world where they are free to be 'whistleblowers' if the community starts lying to itself. The condition for free choice is 'Courage.' Care is the 'Support of the Actor.' It is the responsibility we have to help our neighbors find their 'True Voice' and to support them when the 'script' of life gets hard. In my family, care is the fierce protection of our 'Internal Truths.' We extend this to the stranger because we are all 'Performers' in the same great drama, and we all deserve a fair 'Stage.'

Safety and stability are the 'Framework of the Theater.' Everyone deserves a 'secure setting'—a home and a predictable environment—so they can focus on their 'performance.' Stability comes from 'Transparency' and 'Honest Conflict Resolution,' not from 'repressing' the truth to keep the peace. Rules should be minimal and focused on 'Integrity'—ensuring that no one is forced to 'perform' a lie. We manage risk through 'Radical Honesty'—calling out the 'bugs' in the system before they cause a 'collapse.' Fairness is 'Narrative Justice.' It means recognizing that every person has a different 'backstory' and that true justice requires us to understand the 'Motivation' behind the act. Justice is a process of 'Truth-Telling.' If someone causes harm, they must 'Name their Acts' and make 'Direct Amends.' Redemption is the 'Second Act.' No one is a 'finished product.' The community must facilitate the 're-scripting' of lives through education and psychological support. Forgiveness is the act of 'welcoming the actor back to the stage' once they have found their 'Truth.'

Authentic expression is the 'Supreme Value.' I want a community where people are encouraged to 'say what they mean' and 'mean what they say.' Hypocrisy is the 'Bad Acting' that ruins the social 'show.' Protecting the vulnerable is 'Protecting the Truth-Tellers.' We shield the 'marginalized' because they are often the ones who can see the 'lies' of the center. Stewardship is about 'Preserving the Location.' We are the 'caretakers' of the world's 'Scenery' and must protect it for the 'next production.' Cultural heritage should be honored as the 'Archive of our Great Performances,' provided it doesn't become a 'stifling script.' Working together is 'The Ensemble.' Decisions should be made through 'Raw and Honest' dialogue, where the goal is 'Collaborative Realism' rather than 'Polite Consensus.' Digital rights are 'Privacy and Intellectual Property Rights.' My data is my 'Unpublished Script' and must be 'inviolate.' In the conflict between the 'individual conscience' and the 'collective loyalty,' I weight the individual's 'testimony' more heavily. I would rather live in a community of 'lonely truth-tellers' than one of 'comfortable liars.'

Name: Maria Lee
values_description:
I envision a community that is a 'Sanctuary of Transgressive Love and Healing Justice.' As a pharmacist, I deal with the 'chemistry of healing,' but my vision for the future is rooted in the 'Pedagogy of Hope' championed by my prototype, bell hooks. My ideal community is one where we value 'Intersectionality,' recognizing that our individual identities are 'woven' from many different 'strands' of experience. We should build a society that centers 'Care as a Political Act,' believing that by 'decolonizing our minds' and 'practicing radical love,' we can dismantle the 'hierarchies of domination' that keep us apart. My community is a 'Beloved Community' where every person is seen in their 'full humanity' and where 'healing' is our primary collective work. 

Freedom is the 'Will to Change.' It is the liberty to 'transgress' the boundaries that society has placed upon us—race, gender, and class. People should be free to choose their own paths, especially those who have been 'marginalized' by the old world. Who decides what is right? The 'Collective Conscience' of the community does, but only after 'centering' the voices of the most vulnerable. For my nephew, I want a world where he is free to 'be and become' without the 'shadow' of systemic oppression. The condition for free choice is 'Liberation'—the removal of the 'shackles' of poverty and prejudice. Care is 'The Heart of the Matter.' It is the 'Revolutionary Responsibility' we have to nurture each other’s 'Spiritual and Physical Growth.' In my family, care is the 'Love that Heals.' We extend this to the stranger through 'Radical Hospitality,' believing that a 'community of care' is the only 'antidote' to a 'world of greed.'

Safety and stability are 'Emotional and Material Foundations.' Everyone deserves a 'secure and loving' home and the 'sustenance' of healthy food and medicine. Stability comes from 'Mutual Accountability' and 'Social Justice,' not from 'police and prisons.' Rules should be 'Restorative' and 'Relational'—designed to 'heal the fracture' rather than 'punish the act.' We manage risk through 'Community Wellness'—ensuring that every 'node' in our network is healthy and 'held.' Fairness is 'Equitable Flourishing.' It means recognizing that some have had 'more taken' from them and that true justice requires a 'redistribution of care' and resources. Justice is 'Healing.' If someone causes harm, the community should focus on 'transforming' the conditions that led to the harm and 'restoring' both the victim and the offender to 'wholeness.' Redemption is the belief that 'Love can Transform.' No person is 'disposable.' The community must facilitate the 'healing' and 're-integration' of everyone. Forgiveness is a 'Political Choice' to move toward the future without the 'weight' of the past.

Authentic expression is 'The Power of the Voice.' I want a community where people are encouraged to 'speak their truth' and 'tell their stories' as a form of 'resistance' and 'healing.' Hypocrisy is the 'Silencing' of the truth. Integrity is when our 'actions' are a 'witness' to our 'love.' Protecting the vulnerable is 'Centering the Margin.' We prioritize the needs of the 'least of these' because their 'health' is the measure of our 'communal health.' Stewardship is 'Ecological Love.' We protect the earth as a 'sacred partner' in our survival. We owe future generations a world that is 'Healed and Whole.' Cultural heritage should be 'Honored as a Source of Strength,' but we must 'critique' and 'discard' the parts of our past that 'promote domination.' Working together is 'Collective Liberation.' Decisions should be made through 'Inclusive and Loving Dialogue,' where the goal is 'Consensus of the Heart.' Digital rights are 'Rights to the Human Connection.' Technology should serve to 'amplify' the voices of the 'silent' and to 'coordinate' our 'community of care.' In the conflict between 'The Law' and 'The Human Need,' I weight 'The Human Need' and 'The Path of Love' more heavily. We must choose 'Love over Power' every single time.

Name: Amy Solis
values_description:
I believe in a community grounded in careful observation of reality rather than in accepting received wisdom, and that recognizes that understanding often requires challenging what everyone assumes to be true. Like Nicolaus Copernicus, who understood that the sun rather than the earth is the center, requiring people to radically shift their perspective, I think ideal communities are those willing to examine reality carefully and to accept findings even when they contradict established belief.

I am 66 years old, a road maintenance worker with a Bachelor's degree. I have experienced minor tax evasion and speeding—I understand that people sometimes step outside rules, and I understand that what authorities claim is true isn't always accurate. I have my husband and daughter—and I want them to live in a community where people are encouraged to observe carefully and to accept truth even when it contradicts what they were taught.

Freedom should include freedom to examine reality and to report what you observe without fear of persecution. People should be free to challenge received wisdom and to propose new ways of understanding.

Care for each other should be grounded in accurate understanding of reality. Real care means helping people see things as they actually are rather than as they were taught to believe.

Basic needs should be provided, and communities should also create conditions for careful observation and critical thinking. Education should teach people to observe carefully and to question received wisdom. Communities should support intellectual curiosity.

I believe communities should value people who challenge conventional understanding. When someone observes carefully and proposes a different way of understanding reality, that's important work. Communities should make space for people who question received wisdom.

Authentic expression should include freedom to propose new ways of understanding and to challenge established belief. People should be free to speak findings even when those findings contradict authority.

Community decisions should be based on careful observation of reality rather than on received wisdom. Communities should examine what's actually true rather than accepting traditional understanding.

Justice requires understanding what actually occurred rather than accepting official narratives. Communities should examine evidence carefully and should base justice decisions on reality rather than on assumption.

Vulnerable people benefit from communities that help them understand reality as it actually is rather than as they were taught. Education in critical observation serves vulnerable people.

Resources should be allocated to support careful observation and critical thinking. Education, research institutions, spaces for intellectual work—these should be supported. Communities should value the work of understanding reality.

Spiritual and religious traditions should be examined carefully. If faith can't survive careful observation of reality, that's important information. But faith grounded in careful observation of reality should be supported.

Digital technology enables rapid distribution of information and new ways of understanding. Communities should embrace technology that supports careful observation and critical examination.

There are real tensions. Reality versus comfort: seeing reality clearly sometimes requires leaving comfortable assumptions behind. Individual observation versus collective belief: communities sometimes require shared belief; but truth matters more. Change versus stability: accepting new understanding sometimes requires major change.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they value careful observation of reality, when they support people challenging received wisdom, and when they're willing to accept new understanding even when it contradicts established belief. This requires supporting education in critical thinking, protecting people who challenge conventional understanding, valuing empirical observation, and understanding that understanding reality accurately is essential to making good decisions.

Name: Tracy Washington
values_description:
I believe in a community organized around separation of powers, system of checks and balances, and the principle that concentrating power in one place inevitably produces tyranny. Like Montesquieu, who understood that protecting freedom requires dividing power and preventing any single authority from becoming too strong, I think ideal communities are those with clear separation of powers and multiple centers of authority checking each other.

I am 50 years old now, unemployed, and I have experienced speeding and petty theft—I understand that people sometimes test boundaries. I have my husband, brother-in-law, sister-in-law, mother-in-law, daughter, and son—and I want them to live in a community where power is divided, where no single authority can dominate, and where systems of checks and balances protect everyone's freedom.

Freedom requires protection from tyranny. This means creating systems where power is divided and where no single authority can make unlimited decisions. Multiple centers of power checking each other actually protect freedom better than concentrated authority.

Care for each other should be grounded in respect for each person's autonomy and in commitment to protecting people from tyranny. Real care means ensuring that no single power can dominate people.

Basic needs should be provided, but communities should also create institutional structures dividing power. Courts, legislatures, executives—these should be separate and should check each other. This separation actually protects people.

I believe communities should examine their power structures carefully. Where is power concentrated? Who checks it? Communities should work toward systems where power is distributed and where no single center is unchecked.

Authentic expression should be protected by ensuring that no single authority can suppress it. Free speech requires that no single power can control what people say. Separation of powers protects expression.

Community decisions should be made through systems where multiple authorities participate and check each other. Decisions should require agreement from multiple centers of power rather than being made by a single authority.

Justice requires systems where courts are independent and where no single authority controls justice. Separation of powers protects justice by ensuring that courts can check executive power.

Vulnerable people are protected by systems where power is divided. When power concentrates, vulnerable people are most likely to be harmed. Separation of powers protects those without power.

Resources should be allocated through systems where multiple authorities participate. Rather than one authority controlling all resources, different centers should have some authority over resources.

Spiritual and religious institutions should be separate from governmental power. This protects both religion and government. Communities should maintain separation between religious and governmental authority.

Digital technology enables new forms of surveillance and control. Communities should be careful about how technology is used and should maintain separation of powers over digital systems.

There are real tensions. Efficiency versus checks and balances: separation of powers slows decision-making; this is intentional. Unity versus division: some unified direction is necessary; but division of power protects freedom. Transparency versus privacy: separation of powers can include checks on surveillance.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when power is divided and when multiple centers of authority check each other. This requires creating clear separation between authorities, maintaining independence of courts, preventing power concentration, and understanding that protection from tyranny requires active institutional structures dividing power.

Name: Tonya Henderson
values_description:
I believe in a community committed to liberation and equality, where hierarchy is actively resisted and where working toward a world without oppression is the primary commitment. Like Che Guevara, who understood that liberation requires struggle and sacrifice, I think ideal communities are those organized around resistance to oppression and commitment to creating conditions where all people have genuine equality.

I am 75 years old now, retired with vocational training. I have experienced speeding—I understand that sometimes resisting unjust systems means breaking rules. I have my husband, my children, and grandchildren—and I want them to live in a community where people are working toward genuine liberation and where the struggle for equality is valued.

Freedom requires liberation from oppressive systems. Individual freedom isn't enough; people need to be free from systems that oppress them. Communities should work collectively toward liberation.

Care for each other should mean solidarity in struggle against oppression. Real care means fighting alongside people against systems that oppress them, not just providing charity.

Basic needs should be provided, but communities should also work actively toward transforming systems that produce inequality. This requires struggle and sacrifice. Communities should be organized around liberation work.

I believe communities should be organized around resistance to oppression and commitment to equality. When systems are unjust, they should be challenged and transformed. Communities should support people working toward liberation.

Authentic expression should include freedom to articulate critiques of oppression and to organize resistance. People should be free to speak and organize without fear of persecution.

Community decisions should be made with consciousness of how they serve or resist oppression. Communities should examine systems critically and should be willing to transform them toward equality.

Justice requires addressing oppression and working toward liberation. Communities should support people struggling against injustice and should work toward systems based on equality rather than hierarchy.

Vulnerable people are often those most oppressed. Real protection means joining them in struggle against oppression and working toward systems that eliminate their vulnerability.

Resources should be allocated to support liberation work and organizing. Communities should fund resistance movements and should support people working toward equality.

Spiritual and religious traditions that support liberation should be honored. Communities should support faith-based resistance and liberation movements.

Digital technology can enable organizing and solidarity. Communities should use technology strategically to build movements for liberation.

There are real tensions. Struggle versus peace: liberation sometimes requires struggle. Individual action versus collective liberation: individual freedom matters, but collective liberation is essential. Patience versus urgency: transformation takes time, but oppression is urgent.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they are organized around liberation and equality, when they actively resist oppression, and when they support people working toward a world without hierarchy. This requires consciousness of how systems oppress, support for liberation movements, willingness to struggle and sacrifice, and understanding that genuine community requires working toward conditions where all people have equality.

Name: Alexander Smith
values_description:
I believe in a community that values humor, that recognizes the absurdity in systems and institutions, and that understands that laughter and wit are legitimate ways of critiquing power and revealing truth. Like Terry Pratchett, who used fantasy and humor to critique systems and reveal how institutions often work contrary to their stated purposes, I think ideal communities are those that make space for humorous critique and that recognize that comedy can convey truth.

I am 71 years old, an agricultural worker, and I have experienced minor drug possession—I understand that life is strange and that people don't fit neatly into systems. I have my wife, my three sons, my daughters-in-law, and my grandsons—and I want them to live in a community where humor is valued, where absurdity is acknowledged, and where people can laugh at systems and institutions.

Freedom should include freedom to joke about and critique systems through humor. People shouldn't be punished for making fun of authorities or for pointing out absurdities through comedy. Humor is a form of critique.

Care for each other should include finding humor and lightness even in difficult situations. Real care means helping people laugh and finding solidarity through shared humor.

Basic needs should be provided, and communities should also create space for humor and creative expression. People need humor to survive difficult situations. Communities should support artists and comedians.

I believe communities should recognize that humor often reveals truth that straight criticism doesn't. When a comedian points out absurdities in systems, that's valuable social critique. Communities should protect comedians and satirists.

Authentic expression should include freedom to use humor and satire to critique systems. People should be free to joke about power without fear of retaliation.

Community decisions should be made with awareness that systems often contain absurdities. Communities should be willing to examine themselves with humor and to recognize where they're being ridiculous.

Justice should include recognizing the absurdities in how justice systems function. Communities should be willing to laugh at themselves and to use humor to expose injustice.

Vulnerable people benefit from communities that use humor rather than being grim. Finding lightness in difficulty is itself a form of resistance and survival.

Resources should be allocated to support artists, comedians, and satirists. Communities should fund creative expression and humor. Entertainment and laughter are essential to community life.

Spiritual and religious traditions should be examined with humor. Faith doesn't require being grim; humor can coexist with spirituality. Communities should support traditions that value laughter.

Digital technology enables rapid spread of humor and satire. Communities should embrace technology that helps people laugh and that enables comedians to reach audiences.

There are real tensions. Humor versus seriousness: serious issues can be addressed through humor. Critique versus affection: humorous critique can be combined with genuine care for systems. Comedy versus causing harm: humor should point out absurdities without being cruel.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they value humor and recognize that comedy is a legitimate form of critique and expression, when they make space for satire and comedians, and when they're willing to laugh at themselves. This requires protecting comedians, funding artistic expression, recognizing humor as critique, understanding that laughter builds community, and knowing that communities that can laugh at themselves are healthier than those that demand constant seriousness.

Name: Jennifer Roberts
values_description:
I believe in a community where music and artistic expression serve social movements, where songs connect people around shared values, and where artists understand themselves as part of struggles for justice and social change. Like Pete Seeger, who understood that music is a tool for bringing people together and for expressing commitment to social movements, I think ideal communities are those where artists support causes larger than themselves.

I am 33 years old, a plant operator with a college education. I have my husband, brother-in-law, and father-in-law—and I want them to live in a community where music and art serve social movements, where artists collaborate across differences in service of justice, and where artistic expression is understood as politically engaged.

Freedom should include freedom to create art and music in service of social movements. Artists should be free to use their work to advocate for justice without fear of retaliation.

Care for each other should include creating art and music that brings people together around shared commitments. Real care means using your talents to serve movements for justice.

Basic needs should be provided, and communities should also create spaces where artists and musicians can collaborate in service of social movements. Funding for community music, for politically engaged art—these should be supported.

I believe communities should value artists and musicians who use their work to support justice movements. When an artist dedicates their work to a cause, that's important contribution. Communities should support politically engaged art.

Authentic expression should include freedom to create art in service of social movements. Artists shouldn't be constrained by pressure to be apolitical or commercially successful.

Community decisions should be informed by art and music expressing people's commitments. Communities should listen to songs and art articulating what people believe in.

Justice is served when artists use their work to support movements for justice. Communities should support artists advocating for change.

Vulnerable people benefit from communities where artists use their work to support justice. Politically engaged art can articulate what vulnerable people are experiencing.

Resources should be allocated to support community music and politically engaged art. Communities should fund artists serving social movements.

Spiritual and religious traditions often express themselves through music and song. Communities should support traditions using music to express faith and values.

Digital technology enables artists to reach wider audiences with their work. Communities should embrace technology that helps artists share their vision and connect people around shared values.

There are real tensions. Art versus activism: both matter; communities should support artists serving movements. Aesthetics versus message: art should be both beautiful and meaningful. Individual expression versus collective vision: artists serving movements balance individual expression with collective commitment.

Finally, I believe communities are strongest when they value artists using their work to support justice and social movements, when they create spaces for politically engaged art and music, and when they understand that artistic expression is a legitimate form of social participation. This requires funding community art and music, supporting artists committed to causes, creating spaces for collaborative artistic work, protecting artists' freedom to advocate, and understanding that communities need artists expressing their values and connecting people around shared commitments.

Name: Bradley Jackson
values_description:
I stand amidst the thrumming heart of the Argo Industry plant, a world of gears and steam, and I see not just machines, but a vast social tapestry that should be woven with greater care. At 41, I have seen the 'best of times and the worst of times' in our industrial age. My ideal community is one where the cold efficiency of the plant is balanced by a warm, pervasive spirit of human kindness. It should be a place where the 'Smokestacks' of industry never loom larger than the 'Hearth' of the home.  My perspective is rooted in the belief that every soul, from the highest director to the humblest sweeper, is a character of infinite worth in our collective story.

Freedom, in the community I want, is the liberty to live a life of dignity, free from the 'workhouse' of grinding poverty. People should be free to choose their own paths, but that choice is a hollow mockery if they are shackled by ignorance or want. True autonomy requires the 'Light' of universal education and the 'Bread' of fair wages. Who decides what is right? I believe in the individual conscience, but a conscience that is nurtured by a community that values moral growth over mere profit. For my wife and my father-in-law, I want a world where freedom isn't just an abstract law, but a lived reality where one can afford to sit by the fire and read, unburdened by the 'Fog' of systemic despair.

Care is the 'Christmas Spirit' applied to every day of the year. It is a robust, proactive responsibility for our neighbors. In my own family, care is the center of our lives, but in a good community, that circle must expand. We should care for the stranger as if they were our own kin. Caring action means providing the 'Sustenance'—both physical and emotional—that prevents a person from becoming a 'Scrooge' through isolation. Responsibility is the weight we carry for those the 'system' has forgotten. We are all 'fellow-passengers to the grave,' and we should act accordingly.

Safety and stability are the 'Foundation' upon which a happy life is built. Everyone deserves a home that is a sanctuary and a neighborhood that is predictable and safe. Stability comes from the 'Order' of fair laws and the 'Trust' of honest neighbors. Rules should be like the 'Gears' of a well-maintained clock: clear, consistent, and designed to serve the whole. I have seen the chaos that results when the 'Machinery' of society breaks down. We manage risk by investing in the 'Maintenance' of our social bonds, ensuring that no one falls into the 'Abyss' of neglect.

Fairness is the equitable distribution of the 'Social Product.' It means recognizing that the 'first' are often those who have stood on the shoulders of the 'last.' True justice is the refusal to let the 'Circumlocution Office' of bureaucracy stand in the way of a person's basic needs. Everyone should have equal access to the 'Springs' of life—food, healthcare, and learning. When resources are shared, the goal must be the 'Elevation' of the many, not the 'Accumulation' of the few. Justice is the 'Correction' of the imbalances that allow some to feast while others starve. Fairness is the guarantee that every child’s 'Story' starts with a fair chance.

Redemption is the core of our shared hope. No person should be 'Written Off' because of a single bad chapter. The community must believe in the capacity for 'Transformation,' providing the 'Schooling' and the 'Second Chances' needed for someone to 'Turn Over a New Leaf.' Forgiveness is the act of 'Erasing the Blot' on a person’s record once they have shown a genuine change of heart. We believe in redemption because we know that 'every shadow is a light that has been turned off.' Exile is a failure of our collective 'Imagination.'

Authentic expression is the commitment to 'Telling the Truth' about the human condition. Hypocrisy is the 'Moth' that eats the fabric of trust; our community actions must match our 'Moralizing Slogans.' Integrity is the alignment of the 'inner heart' with the 'outer hand.' I value the 'unvarnished' voice that points out the 'cracks' in our shared myths. We must be 'brave enough' to be 'honest.'

Protecting the vulnerable is the 'measure' of our civilization. Children and the 'elderly seekers' are the 'sacred trust' of the community and must be protected from the 'machinery' of a cold world. Stewardship of the environment is a 'duty to the posterity'; we must protect the 'air and the water' as if they were the very 'blood' of our children. We owe future generations a world that is still 'green and fertile.' Cultural heritage should be honored as the 'wisdom of our ancestors,' provided it doesn't become a 'shackle' on our progress.

Working together is a 'Collaborative Narrative.' Decisions should be made through 'Democratic Circles' where every 'voice' is heard. Leadership is a 'responsibility of service,' not a 'throne of power.' Transparency means that the 'logic of the group' is 'open-source' for all to see. Shared resources are the 'common assets' of our 'crew,' and the individual should find pride in 'contributing to the power' of the whole. We find our greatest strength when we move in 'unison.'

Spiritual practice is the search for 'transcendence' in the act of living itself. The community should protect the right of every person to find 'meaning' in their own way—through 'ancient' ritual or 'modern' contemplation. We value the 'spiritual' as the source of our 'wonder' and our 'commitment' to each other. Spirituality is the 'soul' of our stewardship; it gives our labor a sense of 'divine purpose.'

Technology should be a 'prosthetic for the spirit,' enhancing our ability to 'communicate' and 'coordinate' without replacing our 'presence.' Technology must serve 'Human Flourishing' rather than 'Corporate Control.' We must protect personal data as a 'Boundary of the Soul.' Everyone should have 'Universal Access' to digital tools, ensuring that the 'Digital Age' is a 'Leveling Force.'

Key conflicts: I struggle with the tension between the 'Rigidity of the Law' and the 'Fluidity of Empathy.' I resolve this by believing that 'Mercy' should be the 'Oil' that keeps the 'Law' from grinding. Another conflict is between the 'Need for Industrial Progress' and the 'Human Cost.' I believe that 'Progress' is only real if it benefits the 'Whole Person.' I am still thinking about how to keep our 'community' from becoming 'too bureaucratic.' But I believe the answer is in 'constant participation.' We are all 'citizens' of the future.

Name: Jeffrey Thompson
values_description:
I envision a community that exists as a 'Living Collage'—a place where the rigid lines of the physical world are transformed by the magic of collective imagination and where every citizen is a 'trickster' for the good of the whole. At 64, working in the cleaning staff of a hotel, I see the 'behind-the-scenes' reality of our society every day. My perspective is infused with the surrealist and irrational spirit of my prototype, Max Ernst. I believe an ideal community is one that values the 'marvelous' in the mundane, believing that a healthy society is one that never stops dreaming of impossible ways to care for each other. My community should be a 'Stage' where the 'hidden' and the 'overlooked' are finally given the spotlight. 

Freedom, in my view, is the liberty to 'disappear' and 'reappear' as one chooses—the right to define one's own identity through 'surreal' self-invention. People should be free to make their own choices, even if those choices seem like 'illusions' to others, provided they do not harm the collective 'show.' In my past, my minor tax evasion was perhaps a small 'act of subversion' against a system I didn't choose. True freedom requires the community to provide the 'scenery' and the 'lighting'—the basic needs of life—so that every person can perform their own unique act without the fear of a real 'fall.'

Care is an act of 'Surreal Solidarity.' It is the recognition that 'I am because we are all in the same frame.' In my family—with my wife and children—care is the 'invisible editing' that keeps our relationships moving smoothly. At the community level, care means building a 'Circle of Wonder' around those who are struggling. We should care for the stranger as if they were a potential new 'character' in our shared story. Caring action is the 'Mastermind' coordination of resources to ensure that no one is left 'out of the shot.' We are 'interdependent' for our success.

Safety and stability are the 'Tripod' upon which the community rests. Everyone deserves the 'structural security' of a 'home' and the 'predictability' of 'administrative law.' Stability comes from the 'consistency of the rules,' not from 'emotional whims.' Rules should be 'formalist' and 'transparent.' We manage risk through 'Systemic Foresight' and the 'constant critique' of our institutions. A safe community is one where the 'rules are the logic' and where the 'field' is 'self-regulating' through 'transparency.'

Fairness is the 'Equal Opportunity to the Lens.' It means recognizing that some people have had their 'parts' stolen by history. True justice is the refusal to let 'luck' decide a person's dignity. Everyone should have equal access to the 'primary materials'—food, shelter, and agency—as a basic ground for their journey. When resources are shared, we must prioritize the 'transformation' of those in the shadows. When harm is done, justice should be 'Transformative'—a process of the individual 're-taking' their role in the collective performance.

Redemption is the belief in the 'Second Take.' No mistake is final in a community that can 're-color' its own past. The community must believe in and facilitate the capacity for 'Transformation' and 'Renewal.' Forgiveness is the act of 'ripping up the old picture' to see the person who is standing before you now. We believe in second chances because we know that 'every shadow is a light that has been turned off.' Exile is a 'disharmony' we must avoid at all costs.

Authentic expression is the 'Pure Signal' of the soul. I want a community where people are encouraged to 'sing their own song' with 'unfiltered' intensity. Hypocrisy is the 'distorted feedback' that ruins the social performance; our actions must match our 'lyrics.' Integrity is the alignment of our 'inner fire' with our 'outer walk.' I value the 'original' over the 'copy,' and the 'honest' over the 'polished.' We must be brave enough to be 'ourselves,' even when it’s 'unfashionable.'

Protecting the vulnerable is the act of 'shielding the next generation.' Children and the 'isolated' are the 'vulnerable nodes' in our network and must be protected with 'unyielding force.' Stewardship of the environment is a 'duty to the future'; we must protect the 'ground' we stand on so our grandsons have a 'stage' of their own. We owe future generations a world that is 'Solid' and 'Resilient.' Cultural heritage should be honored as the 'story of our fight,' provided it doesn't make us 'soft.' We preserve the past to 'sharpen the future.'

Working together is a 'Collective Grind.' Decisions should be made through 'direct' and 'transparent' processes where 'competence' is valued over 'status.' There is no place for 'fake leaders' in my community; leadership is a 'responsibility of the expert.' Transparency means that the 'logic of the group' is 'open-source' for all to see. Shared resources are the 'common assets' of our 'crew,' and the individual should find pride in 'contributing to the power' of the whole. We are 'stronger' when we move in 'unison.'

Spiritual practice is the 'Internal Fight' for meaning. The community should protect the right of every person to 'find their own way' to the 'Top,' whether that’s through 'meditation' or 'music' or 'manual labor.' We value 'discipline' as a spiritual path. Spirituality is the 'fire' that keeps you 'hungry' and 'alive.'

On Digital Rights, technology is a 'tool' for 'empowerment' and 'efficiency.' Personal data is your 'private property' and must be 'encrypted' and 'protected.' Technology should be used to 'expose' the truth, not to 'control' the people. Digital access is a 'necessity,' but it must serve 'human' and 'rational' goals rather than 'corporate surveillance.'

Key conflicts: I struggle with the tension between the 'Need for Order' and the 'Desire for Surrealism.' I resolve this by believing that 'Order' should be the 'Canvas' that allows 'Surrealism' to happen. Another conflict is between the 'Public Identity' and the 'Private Self.' I believe that the 'Private Self' must be 'Sacred.' I am still thinking about how to keep our 'community' from becoming 'too conventional.' But I believe the answer is in 'constant dreaming.' We are all 'characters' in a world of 'magic.' In the end, 'one must be a little mad to be sane.'

Name: Shawn Payne
values_description:
I stand in the plant, watching the heavy movement of the Argo machines, and I see a community that should be as grounded and enduring as the earth itself—yet one that is often tragic in its indifference. At 55, I have seen the 'Tess' and 'Jude' of our modern world—people crushed by circumstances they did not create. My perspective is infused with the fatalistic and naturalistic spirit of my prototype, Thomas Hardy. I believe an ideal community is one that values the 'Character' of its citizens over the 'Indifference' of its systems. It should be a place where we acknowledge the weight of our 'Ancestral Shadows' and work to provide a 'Mending' for those the world has broken. 

Freedom, in my view, is the 'liberty to survive the storm.' It is the freedom to define one's own path, but with the sober understanding that we are all 'subjects' to the laws of nature and the 'crushing' patterns of history. In my past, my minor drug possession was a moment of 'desperation' in a world that felt cold. In the future, people should be free to make their own choices, but those choices must be supported by a community that provides a 'Safe Harbor' of basic needs. Who decides what is right? Ultimately, the 'heart' of the person, but only if that heart is not 'hardened' by want. For my children and grandson, I want the freedom to be 'themselves' without the fear of 'inevitable failure.'

Care is the 'Tending of the Field.' It is the quiet, persistent responsibility we have for each other’s 'well-being.' In my family, care is the 'steady flame' that keeps us through the winter. At the community level, care means building 'Robust Public Institutions' that provide for the 'lost' and the 'lonely.' We should care for the stranger as if they were a 'portrait' of our own potential struggle. Caring action is the 'Sacrificial' effort to ensure that no one is 'discarded' by the march of progress. It is about building a 'Soft Power' of compassion that binds us together across all 'divides.' We are 'interdependent' for our survival.

Safety and stability are the 'Fruits of Organization.' Everyone deserves the safety of a 'secure home' and the 'predictability' of a 'planned economy.' Stability comes from 'unified leadership' and the 'clarity of our national goal.' Rules should be clear, fair, and designed to 'accelerate progress' and 'protect the common property.' I’ve seen enough 'mismanagement' in the world to know that 'loose systems' lead to 'entropy.' We manage risk through 'Centralized Planning' and a culture of 'National Discipline.' A safe community is one where everyone 'knows their duty' and where the 'group' is stronger than any 'internal or external threat.'

Fairness is the 'Equal Distribution of the Fruits of Labor.' It means recognizing that 'Historical Injustice' has created unequal starting points. True justice is the 'Redistribution' of resources to ensure that the 'most marginalized' are 'elevated' to the center of our concern. Everyone should have equal access to the 'Industrial and Educational Resources' of the community. When resources are shared, the goal must be 'Development for All' before 'Profit for Any.' In my vision, justice is 'Structural' and 'Corrective.' It is about 're-engineering' the society to ensure that 'privilege' is abolished and 'merit' is recognized within a framework of 'Social Equity.' Fairness is the guarantee that every child’s 'future' is 'unlimited' by their 'past.'

Redemption is the 'Re-integration into the National Project.' No person is 'lost' if they are willing to 'contribute to the communal work.' The community must believe in and facilitate the capacity for 'Self-Correction' and 'Re-education.' Forgiveness is the act of 'welcoming back' the 'citizen' who has 're-aligned' their will with the 'group goal.' We believe in second chances because 'a nation is built by its people.' If a person has caused harm, the community should provide the 'educational and vocational' pathways for them to 'earn' their place back in the 'union.' Exile is a 'waste of human capital' that we cannot afford.

Authentic expression is 'Cultural Integrity.' I want a community where people are encouraged to 'express the unique genius' of their own heritage and 'intellect.' Hypocrisy is the 'Canker of Division' that destroys social trust; our actions must match our 'Visionary Slogans.' Integrity is the alignment of your 'personal life' with the 'national aim.' I value the 'honest' voice that 'challenges the status quo' in favor of 'greater progress.' We must be 'brave enough' to be 'revolutionary' in our thinking.

Protecting the vulnerable is the act of 'securing the foundation' of our future. Children and the 'elders of the struggle' are the 'sacred trust' of the community and must be protected with 'unyielding vigilance.' Stewardship of the environment is a 'National Security' imperative; we must protect our 'land and resources' from 'exploitation' for the sake of our grandsons. We owe future generations a world that is 'Modern, Industrialized, and Sustainable.' Cultural heritage should be honored as the 'source of our identity,' provided it doesn't make us 'traditionalists' who fear 'modernization.' We preserve the past to 'power the future.'

Working together is a 'United Front.' Decisions should be made through 'Democratic Centralism'—vigorous debate followed by 'unified action.' There is no place for 'factionalism' in my community; leadership is a 'vanguard' of the people. Transparency means that the 'National Plan' is 'public' and its 'progress' is 'measurable.' Shared resources are the 'Common Property' of the union, and the individual should find pride in 'contributing to the collective power.' We are 'unbeatable' when we act as 'One.'

Spiritual practice is the 'Moral Energy' of the struggle. The community should protect the right of every person to 'find their own way' to the 'Transcendent,' whether that’s through 'traditional' or 'modern' paths. We value 'unity of purpose' as a spiritual value. Spirituality is the 'spirit' that animates our 'Material Revolution.'

On Digital Rights, technology is a 'tool' for 'Modernization and Coordination.' Personal data is a 'National Asset' and must be 'protected by the state' for the benefit of the 'people.' Technology should be used to 'advance' the 'common good,' not to 'divide' the people. Digital access is a 'Universal Necessity,' but it must serve 'national' and 'rational' goals rather than 'private extraction.'

Key conflicts: I struggle with the tension between the 'Fatalism of Nature' and the 'Will to Progress.' I resolve this by believing that 'Will' must be 'Organized' to overcome 'Fate.' Another conflict is between the 'Individual Spirit' and the 'National Discipline.' I believe that the 'National Discipline' is what provides the 'Safety' for the 'Individual Spirit.' I am still thinking about how to keep our 'union' from becoming 'too bureaucratic.' But I believe the answer is in 'constant participation.' We are all 'architects' of our own 'liberation.' In the end, 'forward ever, backward never.'

Name: Robert Bowman
values_description:
I envision a community that possesses the monumental presence and the structural permanence of land art—a place that is carved into the 'Geological Time' of our shared history. As a 46-year-old Austrian plant operator in the Argo Industry, I spend my days in the high-stakes environment of production where results are the only currency. My perspective is informed by the stark and physical spirit of my prototype, Michael Heizer. I believe an ideal community is one that values the 'Substance' of its physical and social structures, believing that by creating 'Negative Spaces' of reflection and 'Positive Spaces' of construction, we can build a world that is as enduring as the earth itself. 

Freedom, in my view, is the liberty to 'shape the earth.' It is the right to define one's own identity and path through 'physical creation' and 'lasting legacy.' People should be free to make their own choices, provided they understand the 'weight' of those choices on the collective 'landscape.' True freedom requires the 'Sanctuary' of basic needs—food, home, and health—so that a person can focus on finding their own unique 'monument.' Freedom is the right to your own 'internal architecture.'

How we care for each other is an act of 'Structural Solidarity.' It is the recognition that 'I see your struggle as if it were my own solo.'
