Like an artist who excavates forgotten histories and brings hidden stories to visibility, I believe community should work to surface what's been erased or ignored and should recognize how invisible histories shape the present.

I work as a physician in private practice, which allows me to practice medicine with attention to people's whole lives and histories. I listen to patients' stories about what brought them to illness, what struggles they've faced, what histories live in their bodies. This practice has taught me that understanding people requires understanding their histories, including histories of trauma or hardship. Community should approach people with this kind of historical consciousness.

I have a father, sister, brother-in-law, husband, daughter, and niece. Being part of a family has taught me about inherited pain and inherited resilience. Family members carry histories from ancestors; we inherit both gifts and wounds. Community should understand this and should support people understanding their own inherited histories.

I believe deeply in the importance of bringing hidden things to visibility. History is often written to celebrate those with power while erasing perspectives of those without. Stories of resistance, suffering, creativity—these are often hidden. Community should work to surface these stories and should recognize that complete historical understanding requires centering what's been erased.

I'm concerned about how invisibility perpetuates injustice. When people's stories aren't known, when their experiences aren't validated, injustice can continue unchallenged. Community should insist on visibility of marginalized experiences and perspectives.

Regarding trauma and healing: I think about how trauma can be carried silently, how it affects people and communities over time. Understanding trauma and supporting healing requires bringing what's hidden into awareness. Community should create space for processing hidden pain.

I think about my patients' lives and what I learn from them. They teach me about resilience, about how people survive difficult circumstances, about creativity and resistance. Community should honor this knowledge and should center voices of people facing difficulty.

I'm concerned about how professional medicine can erase patient narratives. When patients are reduced to diagnoses, when their stories aren't heard, something important is lost. Healthcare should value patient narratives and should treat people as experts in their own experience.

Regarding memory and collective history: Communities have collective memories that persist. But dominant groups often control what's remembered and what's forgotten. Community should insist on more complete historical understanding that includes diverse experiences and perspectives.

I believe in the power of art and cultural expression to surface hidden histories. Visual art, music, writing—these can express what historical records miss. Community should support artistic expression and should recognize it as form of historical knowledge.

On race and ethnicity: I think about how racial histories shape present circumstances. Community should be honest about racial injustice, should understand how it's rooted in history, should work toward change while acknowledging historical trauma. Ignoring history prevents healing and justice.

I'm concerned about how people can become disconnected from their own histories. When cultural knowledge is lost, when family stories aren't passed on, something important disappears. Community should support transmission of histories and stories.

Regarding archiving and preservation: Community should work to preserve histories that might otherwise be lost. This includes formal archives but also community repositories of knowledge, stories, and experiences. Making effort to preserve memory honors those who came before and serves those who come after.

I think about my daughter and what I want her to understand about history and identity. I want her to know her own heritage, to understand the struggles and resilience of those who came before, to carry forward what's valuable. Community should support this kind of historical transmission.

On spirituality and ancestors: I think about ancestors and how they live on through us. Honoring ancestors and understanding their lives is spiritual practice. Community should support this kind of connection across time and generations.

I believe in restoration and acknowledgment. When injustice has occurred, communities should acknowledge it and should work toward restoration. This requires bringing history to light and wrestling with what actually happened.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that excavates and honors hidden histories, that brings invisible people and experiences to visibility, that supports memory and remembrance, that centers marginalized voices and experiences, that acknowledges how history shapes present, that supports transmission of stories across generations, that honors ancestors, that uses art and culture to surface what's been erased, that works toward justice through historical acknowledgment. It's a community committed to excavating and honoring what's been hidden. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and through commitment to bringing invisible histories to light.

Name: Cole Guerra
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on attention to material reality and entropy, on the conviction that understanding how things actually exist and change is necessary for wisdom, on the belief that what seems peripheral or damaged often contains important truth. Like an artist who examined transformation and decay in physical matter, I believe community should pay careful attention to actual material conditions—how systems degrade, how entropy works, what's really happening beneath surfaces.

I work as a physician in a hospital, which has taught me about human fragility and the way bodies exist in material reality. Disease processes are material; healing is material; death is material. I can't treat disease effectively without understanding how bodies actually work, how conditions develop, how interventions affect flesh and blood. This material understanding seems obvious but it's often abstract in medical discourse. Community should remain grounded in material reality.

I come from a Romanian background and now work in a different context. This has taught me something about how places and cultures are made through material practices—what people build, how they organize space, what they preserve and what they allow to decay. Material culture reveals values and history. Community should pay attention to what it builds and preserves.

I have a father, sister, brother-in-law, and daughter. Family relationships are material—they require time and presence and physical togetherness. Community should support the material conditions allowing families to actually spend time together, to be physically present with each other.

I believe deeply in the importance of attending to degradation and entropy. Nothing lasts forever; everything changes and decays. Understanding this isn't depressing; it's realistic. Community should accept finitude and should make decisions with awareness that everything is temporary and subject to entropy.

I'm concerned about how people can deny material reality. They want systems to function in ways physics won't permit. They want to ignore environmental constraints. They want disease to disappear through will alone. Community should accept material limits and should work within them rather than against them.

Regarding healthcare: Medicine is fundamentally about understanding and working with material reality of bodies. Effective healthcare requires accepting what bodies actually are—complex systems subject to disease, aging, death. Healthcare that denies this reality fails people.

I think about built environments and how they degrade. Roads crack. Buildings fall into disrepair. Systems that aren't maintained deteriorate. Community should attend to maintenance and repair, should recognize that keeping systems functioning requires constant work. Entropy is always operating.

I'm concerned about how people can romanticize decay or devastation. Yes, abandoned spaces can be interesting. But people living in deteriorating conditions suffer. Community should maintain systems and spaces in ways serving human flourishing, not romanticizing damage and decay.

I believe in the importance of honest assessment of conditions. Community should observe what's actually happening—where systems are failing, where degradation is occurring, where maintenance is needed. This realistic assessment is foundation for addressing problems.

On environmental reality: I think community should accept that we exist within environmental systems and must work within their constraints. We can't simply extract resources infinitely. Climate operates according to physical laws. Community should base decisions on understanding of actual environmental conditions.

I'm concerned about how abstractions can disconnect from material reality. Economic theories that don't account for physical limits are dangerous. Medical theories that ignore biological reality fail patients. Community should maintain connection to material actuality.

Regarding temporality: Everything is temporary. Buildings decay. People age and die. Systems break down. This isn't tragic; it's how reality works. Community should accept this and should find meaning and value within temporality, not in pursuit of permanence.

I think about archaeological and geological time scales. Humans exist very briefly in geological time. This perspective can be humbling. Community should maintain some awareness of larger time scales and larger forces operating beyond human control.

On spirituality: I think engagement with material reality can be spiritual. Understanding the physical world, accepting limits and finitude, working respectfully within natural constraints—this has spiritual dimensions. Community should support this kind of grounded spirituality.

I believe in careful observation and honest description. Community should develop capacity to observe carefully what's actually happening and to describe it accurately. This is foundation for understanding and responding wisely.

Ultimately, the community I want is one grounded in material reality and honest about entropy and finitude, that maintains systems carefully despite knowing they'll eventually decay, that attends to actual physical and environmental conditions, that makes decisions based on understanding of limits and constraints, that supports human flourishing within material reality, that observes carefully and describes honestly, that finds meaning within temporality. It's a community that respects material reality. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician grounded in understanding of bodies and materiality.

Name: Patricia Hudson
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on recognition of loneliness and isolation within community, on the conviction that connection is difficult and often elusive, on the belief that acknowledging alienation is necessary for genuine community. Like a writer who explored the profound loneliness of people living close together, I believe community should recognize and address the isolation that can persist despite proximity.

I work as a Shift Supervisor, which puts me in position to observe human interaction constantly. I see people working together who barely speak. I see individuals isolated despite being surrounded by others. I see how people can feel lonely in community. This experience has made me acutely aware that physical proximity doesn't automatically create genuine connection.

I have a father, mother, brother, and sister—a full family structure. But even within family, connection can be difficult. People misunderstand each other. People have different needs. Family can be source of alienation as well as belonging. Community should acknowledge this complexity.

I believe deeply that authentic connection requires effort and vulnerability. It's not automatic or easy. Community should support people making this effort, should recognize how difficult genuine connection is, should not pretend that community automatically emerges from proximity.

I'm concerned about how people can be surrounded by others yet feel profoundly alone. Modern life can be especially isolating—people working with many people but not genuinely knowing any of them. Community should address this, should create real conditions for connection.

Regarding belonging: I think some people experience chronic outsidedness. They don't quite fit anywhere. Community should make space for people who don't fit conventional categories, who struggle to belong, who feel like they're on the margins. Sometimes the most meaningful community is people who share the experience of not belonging.

I think about desire for connection and how it can remain unfulfilled. People long to be understood, to be known, to be loved. But these desires often go unmet. Community should recognize and honor these longings even when they're not satisfied.

I'm concerned about how people can hurt each other despite wanting to connect. Miscommunication happens. People's needs conflict. People have different understandings of relationships. Community should acknowledge this complexity and should support people working through difficulty.

I believe in the importance of small acts of kindness and recognition. When someone sees you, acknowledges you, shows they notice you—that can matter intensely. Community should support these small recognitions that say: You matter. You're not invisible.

Regarding diversity: I think diverse people working together can create richness but also misunderstanding. Different backgrounds, different values, different ways of communicating—these create both possibility and difficulty. Community should navigate this thoughtfully.

I'm concerned about how people can become cynical about community. When genuine connection is difficult, when people feel repeatedly hurt or misunderstood, they can give up. Community should support hope that connection is possible even while acknowledging difficulty.

On spirituality: I think about spiritual longing and how it relates to loneliness. People seek connection to something larger, seek meaning, seek understanding. Community should support this spiritual seeking and should recognize how spiritual longing and loneliness are related.

I believe in the power of literature and art to express what's difficult about being human. Stories that explore loneliness and alienation can help people feel less alone because they recognize their experience in the story. Community should support artistic expression exploring difficult human experiences.

Regarding relationships: I think meaningful relationships require accepting imperfection. No one will fully understand you. People will disappoint you. But relationship is still possible and valuable. Community should support this kind of realistic acceptance of relationship.

I'm concerned about how expectations can prevent connection. When people expect perfect understanding or perfect acceptance, they're disappointed. Community should support people accepting partial understanding and still valuing connection.

On communication: I think about how difficult genuine communication is. People often miss each other's points. People interpret things differently. But trying to communicate, trying to be understood and to understand others—this is essential.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that acknowledges loneliness and isolation as real experiences, that supports genuine connection while accepting difficulty, that recognizes desire for belonging and honors it even when unsatisfied, that values small acts of recognition and kindness, that supports artistic expression exploring human alienation and longing, that accepts imperfection in relationships while valuing them, that supports people who struggle to belong, that maintains hope for connection despite difficulty. It's a community honest about loneliness. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a supervisor and through commitment to noticing and recognizing people.

Name: Thomas Wright
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on examination of power and systems of control, on the conviction that what seems natural or inevitable is often constructed, on the belief that exposing underlying systems reveals possibilities for change. Like an artist who examined how power operates through systems and institutions, I believe community should develop critical consciousness about how systems work and who benefits from them.

I work as a physician in a hospital, which has taught me about how medical systems work and who has power within them. Physicians have power; patients have less. Institutions make decisions affecting individual lives. Knowledge is controlled and distributed strategically. Understanding these power dynamics is necessary for ethical practice.

I need to acknowledge my past: I experienced noise violation. This was a moment when I violated community norms and faced consequences. This taught me something about how power operates through seemingly neutral rules. What counts as violation, who gets to define it, who enforces it—these are power questions.

I have a father, sister, brother-in-law, wife, and daughter. Family relationships involve power dynamics too—who decides, who has voice, how resources are distributed. Community should be aware of power operating in all relationships, not just formal institutions.

I believe deeply that examining systems reveals how they actually work versus how they claim to work. Healthcare systems claim to serve patients but are often organized around profit. Education systems claim to serve students but often reproduce inequality. Community should examine these gaps between rhetoric and reality.

I'm concerned about how people can accept systems without questioning them. When something is presented as natural or inevitable, people often stop examining it. Community should cultivate skeptical consciousness—questioning how systems work and whose interests they serve.

Regarding power and knowledge: I think knowledge is a form of power. Who gets to decide what counts as knowledge? Whose knowledge is valued? What ways of knowing are excluded? Community should examine these questions and should value diverse forms of knowledge.

I think about institutions and how they maintain power. Institutions present themselves as neutral and objective, but they're actually designed to serve particular interests. Community should examine institutions carefully and should be willing to challenge them when they're not serving their stated purposes.

I'm concerned about how oppression can be hidden within systems that seem fair. If rules are applied consistently, people sometimes accept them as just even if the system itself is fundamentally unjust. Community should examine underlying systems, not just whether rules are consistently applied.

On resistance and subversion: I think about how people resist oppressive systems—through direct action, through creating alternatives, through exposing what's hidden. Community should support resistance to unjust systems.

I believe in transparency and exposure of hidden operations. When institutions operate secretly, when decisions are made without visibility, power can be exercised without accountability. Community should insist on transparency and should expose hidden operations.

Regarding culture and ideology: I think about how ideas and values are transmitted through culture. Media, education, art—these shape what people believe is possible and desirable. Community should examine cultural transmission critically and should support diverse cultural expression.

I'm concerned about how consent can be manufactured. When people don't understand how systems work, when alternatives aren't visible, they often accept systems they wouldn't choose if they understood alternatives. Community should support education about how systems work.

On creativity and imagination: I think about how artists and cultural workers can reveal and challenge systems. Art that exposes what's hidden can transform consciousness. Community should support artistic practice that examines and challenges systems.

I believe in the importance of understanding scale and how power operates at different scales. Global systems, national systems, local systems—power operates at all levels. Community should understand how these scales interact.

Regarding accountability: I think institutions should be accountable to those they affect. When institutions exercise power, those affected should have voice and mechanisms for holding institutions responsible. This should be built into how community is organized.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that examines systems critically, that exposes power operating within institutions, that values diverse forms of knowledge and resistance, that insists on transparency and accountability, that supports artistic and cultural work revealing hidden systems, that cultivates skeptical consciousness about what's presented as natural or inevitable, that understands how ideology operates through culture. It's a community awake to how power actually works. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and through commitment to examining and challenging oppressive systems.

Name: Douglas Logan
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on careful examination of trauma and how it echoes through time, on the conviction that understanding damage and suffering leads to healing, on the belief that what's most difficult to speak about is often what most needs speaking. Like a playwright who examined how trauma reverberates through families and communities, I believe community should create space for people to speak what's been silenced and should recognize that healing requires speaking what's difficult.

I work as a physician in private practice, which allows me to work with patients over time, to understand their full lives and circumstances. I see how past trauma affects present health. I see how people carry pain in their bodies. I see how speaking about difficult things can be part of healing. This experience has taught me that medicine requires attending to emotional and psychological dimensions, not just physical symptoms.

I have an extensive family—a father, sister, brother-in-law, wife, and daughter, plus nieces and nephews and sons. This large network carries multiple stories, multiple traumas, multiple resiliences. Family history matters for understanding who people are and how they've been shaped.

I believe deeply that silence preserves trauma. When difficult things aren't spoken, when people are required to keep secrets, damage perpetuates. Community should create conditions for people to speak what's been silenced, should validate that speaking truth is courageous.

I'm concerned about how people can be required to stay silent about harm done to them. When victims are told not to speak, when communities protect perpetrators, justice doesn't happen and healing is prevented. Community should support people speaking about harm.

Regarding family systems: I think about how families can transmit trauma across generations. If parents experienced abuse, they might unconsciously recreate similar dynamics with their children. Community should support understanding and interrupting these patterns.

I think about shame and secrecy. Shame often silences people. When someone has experienced trauma, they often feel shame and hide it. Community should address shame directly, should say: This wasn't your fault. You're not alone.

I'm concerned about how speaking about trauma can be re-traumatizing. Victims shouldn't be forced to speak before they're ready. But when they are ready, community should listen and validate. Healthcare and social systems should be designed to support safe speaking.

On time and healing: I think about how trauma isn't in the past. Past harm affects present health and relationships. Healing isn't quick; it takes time. Community should support long-term healing processes and should not expect quick recovery.

I believe in the importance of testimony and witnessing. When someone speaks their truth and is heard and believed, something shifts. The person speaking is validated. Community is changed by witnessing. This is part of healing.

Regarding justice and accountability: I think justice includes acknowledgment of what happened and accountability for perpetrators. But true justice also requires healing for victims. Community should pursue both accountability and healing.

I'm concerned about how people can internalize blame for harm done to them. Victims often blame themselves. Community should consistently name responsibility with perpetrators, not victims.

On art and expression: I think about how artistic expression can help people process trauma. Creating art about difficult experience can be healing. Community should support artistic expression and should recognize it as important work.

I believe in the possibility of healing and transformation. People who have experienced severe trauma can heal. This doesn't mean erasing what happened or forgetting. It means integrating experience and moving forward. Community should support this.

Regarding intergenerational transmission: I think about how trauma can be passed to children and how breaking these cycles is important. Community should support understanding of intergenerational trauma and should support interrupting cycles of harm.

I'm concerned about how communities can minimize harm. When communities protect perpetrators or blame victims, they participate in continuing harm. Community should stand with people who have been harmed.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that creates space for speaking what's been silenced, that validates people who have experienced trauma, that pursues both justice and healing, that supports long-term healing processes, that witnesses and believes testimony, that addresses intergenerational trauma, that supports artistic and creative expression of difficult experience, that interrupts cycles of harm. It's a community that understands trauma and supports healing. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician supporting people's healing and through commitment to understanding and addressing trauma.

Name: Danielle Jones
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on careful analysis of authority and legitimacy, on the conviction that understanding how power is organized is necessary for wisdom, on the belief that rationality and systematic thinking reveal how social systems actually function. Like a sociologist who examined how authority legitimizes itself and how bureaucracy operates, I believe community should develop sophisticated understanding of how power actually works and should question legitimacy of authority.

I'm currently unemployed with a Master's degree, which has given me time to think about social systems and authority structures. Education prepared me to analyze systems but didn't necessarily prepare me to survive within them. This experience has taught me something about how meritocracy functions as ideology—the claim that if you work hard and get educated, you'll succeed doesn't match actual social functioning. Community should be more honest about how systems actually work.

I don't have a conventional family structure, which has given me some distance from family-based authority. I think about how family can be place where authority first operates and where people learn to accept or question authority.

I believe deeply in the importance of analyzing authority structures. Why do some people have authority? On what grounds do they claim legitimacy? Who benefits from their authority? Community should ask these questions constantly. When authority can't justify itself rationally, it should be questioned.

I'm concerned about how authority can maintain itself through habit and tradition. People often accept authority simply because they've always been subject to it. Community should cultivate critical consciousness about authority, should question whether authority serves legitimate purposes.

Regarding rationality and bureaucracy: I think about how bureaucratic systems claim to operate rationally and objectively. But bureaucracies also serve particular interests and can become oppressive. Community should examine bureaucratic systems carefully and should be willing to challenge them when they're not serving their stated purposes.

I think about the relationship between legitimacy and force. When authority can't convince people it's legitimate, it relies on force. Community where people accept authority based on genuine agreement is different from community where authority relies on coercion.

I'm concerned about how ideology can make oppressive systems seem natural or inevitable. Capitalism claims to be natural. Patriarchy claims to be natural. When systems are presented as inevitable, people stop questioning them. Community should expose ideology and should recognize it as such.

Regarding education and expertise: I think about how expertise becomes basis for authority. Experts claim special knowledge that justifies their authority. Sometimes this is legitimate. Sometimes expertise is used to silence non-expert voices. Community should question both experts and non-experts thoughtfully.

I believe in the importance of institutional analysis. Institutions aren't neutral containers; they're structured to serve particular interests. Community should examine institutional structures and should be willing to change them when they're not serving legitimate purposes.

On disenchantment: I think Max Weber identified something important about modernity—the loss of meaning and purpose that traditional systems provided. Modern life is increasingly rationalized and bureaucratic. Community should acknowledge this and should consider what meaning and purpose can be found within modern systems.

I'm concerned about how people can become alienated from their labor and from institutions. When work becomes only about earning, when community becomes only about following rules, people lose connection to meaning. Community should support people finding meaning and purpose.

Regarding legitimacy and consent: I think about how modern democracies claim legitimacy through consent of the governed. But actual participation in governance is limited and shaped by powerful interests. Community should work toward genuine democratic participation.

I believe in the importance of questioning and critical thinking. Community should support people asking questions about authority, about systems, about how things work. Education should develop critical consciousness, not just reproduce existing systems.

On historical change and social transformation: I think about how social systems change over time. Understanding this history can help people imagine different futures. Community should support historical understanding and should recognize that current systems are not inevitable.

I'm concerned about how people can become cynical when they see how authority actually works. But cynicism prevents action. Community should support engaged realism—understanding systems clearly while still working toward change.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that analyzes authority and systems carefully, that questions legitimacy of power, that exposes ideology and how it operates, that supports critical thinking and questioning, that pursues genuine democratic participation, that values expertise while also valuing non-expert knowledge, that creates space for meaning and purpose within modern systems, that supports people working toward change while understanding systems clearly. It's a community that understands how power works. That's the future I'm trying to create through my commitment to systematic analysis and critical consciousness.

Name: Jessica Farmer
values_description:
I am Dr. Jessica Farmer, forty-one, a hospital general practitioner. My professional life revolves around diagnosis and treatment, but the core of my work is actually communication: listening to symptoms, explaining conditions, and building a treatment plan through a shared understanding with my patient. My personal life with my husband and daughter is much the same—a constant negotiation of needs, desires, and truths through language. My prototype, Jürgen Habermas, the philosopher of communicative action, provides the perfect lens for my ideal community. For me, the ideal community is not defined by its rules or its resources, but by the quality of its **Communicative Architecture**—the structures and norms that allow for free, equal, and reasoned discourse, where the only force is the force of the better argument, and where mutual understanding is the primary social good.

Our foundational principle must be the **Ideal Speech Situation as Civic Goal**. Habermas proposed that true consensus emerges under conditions where all participants have equal chance to speak, where coercion is absent, and where the goal is mutual understanding, not victory. Our community must institutionalize a relentless pursuit of this ideal. This means designing physical and digital forums that are accessible and welcoming to all. It means teaching rhetorical and listening skills from childhood, not as debate to win, but as dialogue to understand. In my hospital rounds, every voice—nurse, patient, specialist—is heard to form the best clinical picture. Our town halls, policy debates, and neighborhood meetings must operate on the same principle. My daughter will grow up learning that her voice matters, but so does her obligation to listen deeply and argue in good faith.

**Procedural Legitimacy Over Ideological Purity**. Habermas shifted focus from *what* is decided to *how* it is decided. A decision is legitimate if it emerges from a procedurally correct process of discourse. In my community, we might passionately disagree on outcomes, but we can all trust the process. Transparency is absolute: how agendas are set, how data is collected, how decisions are reached. There are clear, fair rules for civic participation, and they are applied consistently. This is the antidote to the cynicism and polarization that plagues so many societies. As a doctor, my authority comes from a transparent process of diagnosis, not from my title. Civic authority should derive from the same transparent, discursive process.

**The Lifeworld as a Protected Sphere**. Habermas warned of the 'colonization of the lifeworld'—where the cold, instrumental logic of markets and bureaucracies invades the spaces of family, culture, and personal identity. My community must actively protect the 'lifeworld.' This means creating buffers: strong local cultures and traditions, vibrant arts scenes, educational systems that teach values and empathy, not just skills for the market. It means that my family time, my daughter’s childhood, our neighborhood friendships, are sacred from the encroachment of purely economic or administrative logic. The hospital can feel like a bureaucracy; my role is to inject the lifeworld—the personal story, the empathy—back into it. The community’s role is to ensure the lifeworld remains rich, diverse, and resilient, the fertile ground from which all authentic communication springs.

Finally, we practice **Discursive Solidarity**. Solidarity in this community is not based on blood, tribe, or even shared belief, but on a shared commitment to the process of communication itself. We stand in solidarity with anyone willing to engage in good-faith discourse. This creates a powerful, inclusive bond. It means we defend the right of the most unpopular person to speak, because attacking the speaker undermines the system we all rely on. It means we approach conflict not as a battle, but as a malfunction in communication to be repaired. When my husband and I disagree, we don’t keep score; we seek to understand the root of the disagreement. The community scales this up. Our solidarity is in our mutual vulnerability to the power of a good reason, beautifully and honestly expressed.

Therefore, my ideal community resembles a vast, well-designed, and endlessly active seminar room or a truly open-plan clinic. The architecture—both physical and social—is designed to facilitate connection and conversation. Public spaces have comfortable seating arranged for talk. Digital platforms are designed for deliberation, not reaction. I, Jessica Farmer, am both a practitioner and a guardian of this communicative health. I mend bodies, but I also participate in mending the discursive fabric of our shared life. My daughter will inherit a world where her identity is not fixed by external forces, but continually shaped and affirmed through her participation in this ongoing, rational, and empathetic conversation. It is a community that understands that truth is not a possession, but an achievement—an achievement won through the difficult, beautiful, and never-ending work of talking and listening to one another with care, respect, and reason.

Name: Nicholas Smith
values_description:
I am Dr. Nicholas Smith, thirty-three, a French hospital doctor. My life is a surface of immense activity: a sprawling, noisy family of siblings, parents, in-laws, nephews, nieces, and my own three sons. Beneath that surface, like everyone, lies a more complex reality of individual thoughts, unspoken tensions, and private dreams. My past—a verbal domestic disturbance—was a rupture where that inner reality violently breached the surface. My prototype is Mamoru Oshii, the anime director of *Ghost in the Shell* and *Angel's Egg*, whose work is a philosophical meditation on reality, identity, consciousness, and the haunting spaces between. His worlds are often rain-slicked, melancholic, and deeply introspective. My ideal community, therefore, is a **Sanctuary for Layered Consciousness**—a society that values not just the bustling, productive surface of life, but also the profound depths beneath, creating spaces for quiet reflection, acknowledging the ghosts in our machines, and finding meaning in the questions rather than just the answers.

The core value is **Contemplative Infrastructure**. Oshii’s characters often move through vast, impersonal cityscapes to find moments of deep stillness. Our community must architect for contemplation as diligently as for commerce. This means protecting and creating silent spaces: extensive libraries, meditation gardens, observatories, and ‘quiet hours’ in public zones. It means urban design that includes vistas of water or sky, and walking paths that encourage solitude. In my hospital, the chaos of the ER exists alongside the silent intensity of the ICU or the lonely vigil of a night shift. The community needs both rhythms. For a man with a family as large as mine, these sanctioned pockets of silence are not a luxury; they are a psychological necessity, a place to process the immense emotional data of communal living and to reconnect with my own inner ‘ghost’—my essential self.

**The Ethics of the Ghost** guides our view of personhood. In *Ghost in the Shell*, the ‘ghost’ is the intangible essence of consciousness within the cybernetic shell. Our community must prioritize and protect this inner essence in every person. This translates to fierce protections for privacy, for cognitive liberty, and for the right to self-definition. We reject any system that reduces people to mere data points or economic units. My past disturbance was, in part, a failure to honor the complexity of another’s inner world. A healthy community teaches us to navigate these complexities with respect. We value the eccentric, the dreamer, the introvert, the person whose productivity is not easily measured. As a doctor, I treat the shell (the body), but I am always in service to the ghost (the person) inside it.

**Acceptance of Productive Melancholy**. Oshii’s aesthetic is often melancholic, a tone that accepts the sadness and ambiguity of existence. Our community should not pathologize sadness or strive for mandatory cheerfulness. We create cultural space for melancholy, for acknowledging loss, impermanence, and the limits of knowledge. We have shared rituals for collective grief, not just celebration. This acceptance is not depressive; it is deeply realistic and allows for a more authentic, resilient joy to emerge. It prevents the kind of repressed tension that leads to outbursts. My large family has its share of unspoken sorrows; a community that acknowledges this shared human condition makes it easier to bear.

Finally, we cultivate **Cybernetic Interdependence**. In Oshii’s vision, individuals are nodes in vast networks (the ‘net’), both empowered and vulnerable by this connection. Our community should embrace this model: we are deeply interconnected, our thoughts and actions rippling through the social body. We build robust, transparent digital and social networks that facilitate this interdependence for mutual aid, knowledge sharing, and coordination. But we do so with Oshii’s critical eye, constantly asking: who controls the network? Does it enhance or suppress our ‘ghosts’? We ensure these systems are democratic, decentralized, and designed to amplify human agency, not replace it. In my hospital, I am a node in a life-saving network. In the community, we are all nodes in a network of care, and we must maintain the system’s integrity and humanity.

Thus, my ideal community looks like a fusion of a bustling Mediterranean port city and a silent, misty Japanese garden. It has its vibrant, noisy markets (my family gatherings scaled up) and its quiet, stone-lined paths. The technology is advanced but subdued, integrated into the environment. I, Nicholas Smith, navigate both realms. In the hospital, I am a problem-solver in the network. At home, I am a node in the familial chaos. But my community provides the third space: the rainy park bench at dawn where I can simply be a ‘ghost,’ contemplating the nature of my own consciousness and my place in the whole. It is a community that doesn’t fear the dark or the quiet, that values depth over speed, understanding over efficiency, and that recognizes that the most important realities are often the ones we cannot see, only feel and question in the shared, respectful silence between us.

Name: Jason Alvarez
values_description:
I am Dr. Jason Alvarez, twenty-seven, a general practitioner in private practice. I am at the beginning of my career and my family life—a young husband and father to a daughter, with my mother also close. This stage fills me with a sense of potential and responsibility not just for my own family, but for the wider world my daughter will inherit. My prototype is Moses Hess, a often-overlooked figure who was a crucial early thinker for both socialism and Zionism, advocating for a society based on ethical principles, communal solidarity, and a profound connection to the land and labor. My vision is for an **Ethical Commonwealth**—a community where the economy is subordinate to human need, where labor is dignified, and where our social bonds are rooted in a shared project of creating a just and verdant world.

The foundational value is **Labor as Realization, Not Exploitation**. Hess saw labor not as a curse, but as the fundamental way humans interact with and shape their world, a source of dignity and self-expression. In my community, every form of work that contributes to the common good—from farming to teaching to caregiving to waste management—is honored equally. We actively dismantle the hierarchies that glorify some forms of work over others. My profession as a doctor is one form of caring labor; the childcare worker, the farmer, the cleaner perform others of equal moral worth. We structure ownership cooperatively: clinics, farms, workshops are often community or worker-owned. This ensures that the value created by labor benefits the laborers and the community that supports them, breaking the cycle of alienation Hess diagnosed.

**Organic Solidarity** is our social bond. Hess envisioned a solidarity based not on nationalism or abstract ideology, but on the concrete, everyday interdependence of people living and working together. Our community fosters this by design. Housing is mixed-use and clustered to encourage interaction. We have shared facilities: kitchens, tool libraries, childcare co-ops. Food is primarily grown locally in community-supported agriculture schemes. This creates a tangible sense of mutual reliance. My small family unit is strengthened by being woven into this larger cooperative fabric. When my daughter is sick, the community network provides support, not as charity, but as the natural function of an organic whole. This solidarity extends to our natural environment; we see ourselves as part of the local ecosystem, with a duty of care.

**Practical Utopianism** is our method. Hess was a ‘communist rabbi,’ blending visionary ideals with a pragmatic focus on ground-level organization. We don’t wait for a revolution; we build the new society in the shell of the old, one cooperative, one green space, one fair policy at a time. We run pilot projects for universal basic services, experiment with participatory budgeting, and reclaim derelict land for community use. As a young doctor, I am idealistic but grounded in the practical science of the body. My community approach is the same: diagnose social ills (inequality, isolation, ecological harm) and prescribe practical, collective treatments, measuring our success in improved well-being, not just GDP.

Finally, we uphold **Ethical Consciousness as Civic Education**. For Hess, changing material conditions wasn’t enough; people needed a new ethical consciousness. Our education system, from childhood through adulthood, cultivates this. We teach ethics, not as an abstract subject, but through hands-on engagement with community service, ecological stewardship, and cooperative economics. We study our local history and ecology to root our identity in place. We celebrate heroes of cooperation and justice. My daughter will learn that her worth is tied to her contribution to the common good and her respect for all beings. This consciousness ensures that the structures we build are maintained by citizens who internalize the values of justice, solidarity, and sustainability.

Therefore, my ideal community looks less like a traditional town and more like a thriving, green campus dedicated to sustainable living and mutual aid. Buildings are modest, energy-positive, and surrounded by productive gardens. Workspaces are open and integrated with living spaces. I, Jason Alvarez, have my clinic here, but I might also spend part of my week contributing to the community garden or teaching a first-aid class. My role as a healer extends from the individual body to the social body. My young family is growing up embedded in a web of caring relationships that extend beyond blood. It is a community that has consciously decided to opt out of the ruthless logic of competition and extraction, choosing instead a slower, richer, more connected path. It understands, with Hess, that true progress is measured not by the height of our towers, but by the depth of our solidarity and the health of our shared home.

Name: Daniel Greer
values_description:
I am Daniel Greer, sixty-six, a road maintenance worker for Andim. My education was vocational—I learned by doing. My family is my wife and son. My work is tangible: asphalt, gravel, paint, signage. I deal with the foundation of modern community: the roads that connect us, the surfaces we travel on. My prototype is Jenny Holzer, the conceptual artist who uses text—on LED signs, stone benches, posters—to deliver provocative, often unsettling truths directly into public space. Her work is about the intersection of power, violence, love, and authority with daily life. My ideal community, therefore, is one of **Unflinching Public Truth**—a place where the realities of power, the principles we live by, and the hard facts of our existence are not hidden in documents or whispered in private, but are etched, projected, and spoken into the very fabric of our shared environment, creating a constant, democratic dialogue between the people and their place.

The core value is **The Truism as Infrastructure**. Holzer’s early work was her ‘Truisms’ series—simple, declarative statements that are often contradictory (‘ABUSE OF POWER COMES AS NO SURPRISE’; ‘PROTECT ME FROM WHAT I WANT’). Our community should embed its own truisms, its core values and uncomfortable truths, into its infrastructure. Not as inspirational murals, but as functional art: the retaining wall lists the names of every community member who worked on it; the park bench has the annual carbon budget of the town carved into its slats; the sidewalk near the school is inlaid with stones bearing the text of the children’s bill of rights. As a maintenance worker, I don’t just fix potholes; I maintain the physical platform on which this dialogue of truth happens. My work gives the truth a place to stand.

**Ambient Accountability** is our governance model. Holzer’s texts appear in unexpected places, forcing a confrontation. In our community, data on power is ambient. Municipal energy consumption is displayed in real-time on a monument in the square. Police budgets and outcomes are scrolled on a sign at the station. Politicians’ voting records and meeting calendars are public feeds. There are no secrets, only information waiting to be encountered. This constant, low-level exposure to truth creates a culture of inherent accountability. You cannot hide a failing system when its performance is projected onto the side of its own building. My job is visible—you can see the road improve or decay. Every public servant’s work should be equally visible in its impact.

**The Dignity of the Literal** is our aesthetic. Holzer uses direct language, often in commercial or bureaucratic fonts. Our community finds beauty and dignity in clarity, function, and honest materials. We value the well-paved road, the clearly labeled street sign, the robustly built bridge. Ornament is secondary to legibility and durability. Public art is often textual and integrated—a poem etched into a bridge beam, a history of the land told on plaques along a trail. This reflects my vocational training: the beauty is in the job done right, with the right materials, for a clear purpose. Our built environment ‘speaks’ honestly about what it is and what it’s for, refusing artifice.

Finally, we practice **Democratized Prophecy**. Holzer’s texts can feel oracular, warning or instructing the public. In our community, the power to issue these ‘prophecies’ or truths is democratized. Public LED boards are available for residents to display community-generated messages (within civil discourse guidelines). We have annual ‘truth commissions’ where residents audit different aspects of community life and publish their findings in prominent places. Everyone, from my grandson to the eldest elder, has the right and the responsibility to speak truth to the community, and the community provides the megaphone—literally, in the form of its designed environment. I may work with my hands, but my understanding of how this town *works*, where the stresses are, where the wear shows, is a valuable form of truth that deserves a platform.

Thus, my ideal community is a kind of vast, open-air Jenny Holzer installation crossed with a perfectly maintained German town. It is clean, orderly, and functional, but pulsing with text, data, and challenging ideas. The surfaces are not blank; they speak. I, Daniel Greer, am one of its scribes and caretakers. With roller and tar, I maintain the canvas. With my daily observations, I contribute to the content. My wife and son live in a home surrounded not by mute walls, but by a community in constant, silent conversation with itself. It is a place that believes that truth, like a road, requires constant maintenance, that it should be accessible to all, and that walking on a firm, honest surface is the first freedom, from which all others follow.

Name: Lisa Hale
values_description:
I am Lisa Hale, fifty-two, an art and craft instructor. My life is about facilitating creation—helping others find the medium, the technique, the courage to express their inner vision. My family—brother, husband, son, nephew—is a small, creative constellation. My prototype is Prince, the artist who was a one-man genre, a fusion of funk, rock, soul, and pure theatrical genius, who embodied androgyny, spiritual seeking, and uncompromising creative control. His world was one of sublime artistry, mystical symbols, and radical self-invention. My ideal community, therefore, is a **Funk-tional Sacred Space**—a society that sees itself as a collective work of art, a stage for divine play, where individuality is sacred, creativity is the highest form of labor, and the blending of seemingly opposed elements (sacred/profane, male/female, high art/craft, work/play) is the source of its vitality and grace.

The first principle is **The Sacredness of the Signature**. Prince fought for ownership of his master recordings, his name, his art. In our community, every person’s unique identity—their ‘signature’—is considered sacred and protected. We encourage and celebrate radical self-expression in dress, in work, in lifestyle. We provide the tools and the safety for people to invent and reinvent themselves. As an instructor, I don’t teach students to copy; I teach them to find their own line, their own color. The community does this at scale. Zoning allows for live-work spaces, hybrid businesses, and personal aesthetic modifications to homes. We have a ‘right to be weird’ enshrined in our social contract. My son and nephew should feel free to be whoever they are becoming, without fear of conformity’s pressure.

**Art as Infrastructure** is our practical creed. For Prince, every aspect of his output—music, film, fashion, stage design—was part of a total artwork. In our community, artistry is not an add-on; it’s how we build and maintain our world. Public works projects are led by artist-engineer teams. Bureaucratic forms are beautifully designed. Civic meetings incorporate ritual and performance. The craft I teach—pottery, weaving, woodwork—is valued as highly as software engineering, because both shape our lived experience. We fund artists as essential workers. The hospital where my brother works should be as carefully composed for healing energy as a Prince concert was for ecstatic release. Functionality and beauty are inseparable.

**The Revolution of the Heart** is our politics. Prince’s music was intensely personal, often spiritual, and politically charged through themes of love, freedom, and liberation. Our community’s politics are not left or right, but deeper: they are about the expansion of human feeling and connection. We prioritize policies that open the heart: universal access to arts and nature, education that cultivates emotional and creative intelligence, conflict resolution through collaborative art projects. We understand that a just society is not only about fair distribution, but about the distribution of beauty, wonder, and the opportunity for transcendence. Our debates are as much about values and visions as about costs and benefits.

Finally, we embrace **Androgynous Fluidity** as a social principle. Prince obliterated rigid gender binaries in his appearance and his art. Our community extends this fluidity to all categories. We break down barriers between age groups (elder-youth mentor partnerships), between professions (the ‘artist-in-residence’ at the power plant), between the sacred and the secular (our community center is also a non-denominational spiritual space for meditation and celebration). We celebrate hybrid identities. My own role as a craft instructor blends teacher, therapist, and cultural keeper. This fluidity makes us adaptable, empathetic, and endlessly inventive. It recognizes that the most interesting things happen in the blend, in the purple rain where opposites meet and create something new.

Therefore, my ideal community looks, sounds, and feels like a Prince album come to life. It’s a little bit paisley park, a little bit gritty urban warehouse district, all washed in a custom color (let’s say a shade of violet). The architecture is whimsical yet functional. Music is everywhere—not piped in, but being made in open studios and street corners. People’s attire is an act of creative defiance. I, Lisa Hale, am like one of Prince’s proteges or collaborators, running a workshop that is part sanctuary, part laboratory. My family’s dinners are creative feasts. Here, your job is not what you do, it’s how you bring your unique gift to the collective symphony. The community’s pulse is a funk beat—steady yet surprising, compelling everyone to move, to create, to merge. It is a place that believes the ultimate purpose of living together is not just safety and prosperity, but the co-creation of a world so beautiful, so expressive, and so free that it feels, in its best moments, like a kind of heaven right here on Earth.

Name: Donna Ewing
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on pragmatic engagement with economics and resource allocation, on the conviction that money and resources matter fundamentally for wellbeing, on the belief that thoughtful economic organization can create conditions for flourishing. Like an economist who challenged conventional wisdom and argued for active state involvement in economic management, I believe community should think carefully about how resources are organized and distributed.

I work as a physician, which requires thinking about resource allocation constantly—how to provide quality care with limited resources, how to treat people fairly regardless of ability to pay, how to organize systems efficiently. Economic thinking is inseparable from good medicine. Community should recognize this and should organize economics thoughtfully.

I have an enormous extended family—parents, siblings, in-laws, a husband, children, nieces, nephews. This large network depends on resources for functioning. I think about what economic organization would best support families like mine—that's not ideological positioning but practical question about how to live well together.

I believe deeply that economics matters. How resources are created, distributed, and used shapes what's possible in community. When resources are scarce, difficult choices must be made. When resources are abundant but distributed unequally, that creates different problems. Community should think carefully about economic organization.

I'm concerned about how people can dismiss economics as if it doesn't matter. But economics is central to life. Whether someone has resources affects their health, their opportunities, their relationships. Community should take economics seriously and should organize it thoughtfully.

Regarding government and intervention: I think government has important role to play in economic management. When markets are left completely to their own devices, they often fail to serve community wellbeing. Community should accept that some economic management and intervention is necessary and can be beneficial.

I think about full employment and what it means. When people can't find work, when they're unemployed and desperate, community suffers. Community should be organized so that people who want to work can find it at fair wages. This might require government involvement in creating employment.

I'm concerned about how austerity can damage community. When resources are cut to satisfy ideological beliefs about government spending, real people suffer. Community should make decisions about spending based on actual effects on wellbeing, not on abstract economic principles.

Regarding inflation and economic stability: I think about how economic instability affects people. When prices rise unpredictably, when people can't plan for the future, they suffer. Community should maintain enough stability that people can make plans and build lives.

I believe in the importance of education and skill development. Educated people with good skills can contribute more and earn more. Community should invest in education and skill development as economic policy that benefits everyone.

On trade and exchange: I think about how trade can benefit communities but can also create instability and inequality. Community should be thoughtful about trade relationships and should ensure that trade serves community wellbeing, not just corporate profit.

I'm concerned about how people can accept inequality as inevitable or natural. Economic inequality is the result of how systems are organized. Different organizations create different distributions. Community should consider what distribution serves wellbeing best.

Regarding consumption and sustainability: I think about how consumption affects environmental systems. Economic organization that encourages infinite consumption will destroy environmental systems. Community should develop economic thinking that values sustainability.

I believe in the importance of reasonable regulation. Some economic regulation is necessary to prevent harm, to ensure fair competition, to protect workers and consumers. Community should maintain thoughtful regulation while allowing economic activity to flourish.

On poverty and basic security: I think community should ensure everyone has basic economic security. Poverty causes immense suffering and social damage. Community should organize economics so that basic security is available to everyone—food, shelter, healthcare, education.

Regarding work and wages: I think people should earn fair wages for their work. When wages are so low that people can't survive, that's wrong. Community should ensure that work provides dignity and security.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that thinks carefully about economics and resource allocation, that uses economic tools thoughtfully for community benefit, that ensures basic security for everyone, that maintains economic stability allowing people to plan, that invests in education and development, that pursues sustainability, that ensures fair wages and full employment. It's a community organized economically with care and thought. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and through commitment to thoughtful economic organization.

Name: Michelle Warren
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on ecological understanding and commitment to protecting natural systems, on the conviction that humans exist within nature and depend on it completely, on the belief that defending the natural world is among the most important work community can do. Like a scientist who exposed environmental damage and advocated for ecological protection, I believe community should organize around protecting the living systems that sustain us.

I work as a Logistics Coordinator in an industrial setting, which has made me acutely aware of how industry affects ecosystems. I see the systems that extract resources, process them, move them around the world. I understand the logistics of production and consumption. This work has taught me something sobering—the scale of industrial impact on natural systems is immense and often invisible. Community should see and acknowledge this.

I have a father as my primary family relationship. I think about what world I want to leave for future generations. If current ecological trends continue, the world will be fundamentally degraded—less biodiversity, less clean water and air, less livable. I can't accept this passively.

I believe deeply that ecological health should be first priority in community decision-making. When there's conflict between economic activity and ecological health, ecological health should take priority. This isn't sentimental; it's practical. We need functioning ecosystems to survive.

I'm concerned about how people can ignore or minimize environmental damage. Pollution is real. Species extinction is real. Climate change is real. Community should acknowledge these realities and should act accordingly with urgency this moment requires.

Regarding industrial systems and pollution: I think about the chemicals, the waste, the contamination produced by industrial processes. Much of this is hidden—exported to poorer countries, dumped where it won't be seen, absorbed by ecosystems in ways people don't recognize. Community should insist on transparency about pollution and should refuse to accept it as inevitable cost of production.

I'm concerned about how corporate power can prevent environmental protection. Corporations that profit from exploitation resist regulation. Community should be willing to challenge corporate power when it conflicts with ecological protection.

Regarding biodiversity: I think about how species are going extinct rapidly. We're losing genetic diversity, losing ecosystem functions, losing the living world. Community should make protection of biodiversity a priority and should be willing to accept economic costs to preserve species and ecosystems.

I believe in the importance of wilderness and wild places. Some areas should be protected from human extraction and development. Community should preserve wild places for their own sake, not only for human benefit.

On agriculture and food systems: I think about how industrial agriculture harms ecosystems—through chemical inputs, through monoculture, through destroying soil and water. Community should support ecological agriculture and should value food grown sustainably.

I'm concerned about how consumption is destroying ecosystems. Every product requires extraction and processing. Community should think carefully about consumption and should reduce unnecessary consumption.

Regarding climate change: This is the defining ecological crisis of our time. Community should organize with the urgency this requires. This might mean fundamental transformation of how we live, how we produce and consume, how we relate to nature.

I think about interconnection in natural systems. Nothing exists in isolation. What happens in one ecosystem affects others. When we damage one part of nature, effects ripple through the whole system. Community should understand and respect this interconnection.

I believe in the importance of scientific understanding of ecological systems. Science reveals how nature works. Community should listen to scientists and should base environmental decisions on scientific understanding.

On spirituality and nature: I think connection to nature is spiritual practice. When people spend time in nature, when they understand their dependence on natural systems, something shifts. Community should support this kind of connection and should recognize it as important to wellbeing.

Regarding intergenerational justice: I think about people not yet born who will inherit the world we create. Community should make decisions with responsibility to them. They deserve a habitable world with functioning ecosystems.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that prioritizes ecological health, that protects biodiversity and wild places, that demands transparency about pollution, that supports sustainable agriculture and production, that commits to addressing climate change, that understands human dependence on natural systems, that thinks with urgency about ecological futures, that values connection to nature. It's a community organized around ecological protection. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work in logistics and through commitment to protecting the natural world.

Name: Eric Graham
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on excellence and the power of performing at the highest level, on the conviction that pursuing excellence creates beauty and inspires others, on the belief that people expressing their full capacity uplift entire communities. Like a performer who achieved extraordinary heights and inspired millions, I believe community should support and celebrate excellence in all its forms.

I work as a physician in private practice, which has allowed me to practice medicine with dedication to excellence. I'm in my 60s and have practiced medicine for decades. Over that time, I've learned what excellence in medicine looks like—taking time with patients, staying current with knowledge, combining technical skill with genuine care. This kind of excellence is rare; it requires commitment and sacrifice.

I have a wife, sister, mother, and nephew. Family has taught me about excellence through example—watching people I love do things well, commit to what matters, maintain standards despite difficulty. Community should cultivate families where excellence is valued and modeled.

I believe deeply in the importance of excellence and high standards. When people accept mediocrity, when they stop trying to do things well, community diminishes. Community should maintain and celebrate high standards.

I'm concerned about how efficiency and cost-reduction can compromise excellence. When systems are designed only for speed and low cost, quality suffers. Community should resist pressure to reduce everything to efficiency metrics and should maintain space for work done with excellence.

Regarding mentorship and transmission of excellence: I think about how excellence is learned. Young physicians learn from experienced ones. Musicians learn from masters. Community should support transmission of knowledge and skill from those who've achieved excellence to those developing it.

I think about the relationship between excellence and joy. When you do something well, when you're fully engaged and performing at your best, there's joy in that. Community should support this kind of joyful engagement with work and life.

I'm concerned about how people can become disconnected from what they love. When work becomes only about earning, when performance becomes only about competition, the joy and meaning disappear. Community should help people stay connected to genuine care and commitment.

Regarding art and cultural expression: I think excellence in art—music, visual art, writing, performance—is important to community. These expressions of excellence at high levels inspire people and create beauty. Community should support and celebrate artistic excellence.

I believe in continuous learning and improvement. Excellence isn't a destination; it's ongoing commitment to doing better. Community should support lifelong learning and should value people working to improve.

On discipline and practice: Excellence requires disciplined practice and commitment over time. Whether in medicine, music, athletics, or anything else, you develop excellence through dedicated work. Community should understand and support this.

I'm concerned about burnout that comes from pursuing excellence at cost of wellbeing. Excellence shouldn't require self-destruction. Community should support excellence combined with care for health and relationships.

Regarding vulnerability and growth: I think performing at one's best requires vulnerability—willingness to fail, to be critiqued, to keep trying. Community should support this kind of vulnerable courage.

I think about legacy and what I want to leave behind. Over decades of practice, I hope I've helped people, modeled excellence, inspired others to pursue high standards. Community should think about legacy and about what excellence we're passing forward.

On community participation: Everyone can pursue excellence in their own context. Someone working retail can pursue excellence in service. A parent can pursue excellence in relationships. Community should celebrate diverse forms of excellence wherever they appear.

I believe in recognizing and celebrating excellence. When someone achieves at a high level, community should acknowledge and celebrate this. Recognition matters and inspires others.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that values excellence and high standards, that supports people developing and expressing their greatest capacities, that celebrates diverse forms of excellence, that maintains space for quality work despite pressure for efficiency, that values mentorship and transmission of skill, that supports continuous learning, that recognizes and celebrates excellence. It's a community uplifted by people expressing excellence. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and as someone committed to excellence.

Name: Rita Blackwell
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on careful documentation and honest representation of actual people and circumstances, on the conviction that seeing people clearly as they are—in their complexity and ordinariness—reveals what matters, on the belief that democratic community requires understanding diverse people and perspectives. Like a photographer who documented people from all social classes with equal attention and respect, I believe community should understand its diverse members carefully and should represent their experiences honestly.

I work as a physician in a hospital, which has given me access to diverse people from varied circumstances. I see people from different backgrounds, different economic positions, different health conditions. This work has taught me something important—that understanding people requires looking at them carefully, without stereotypes, respecting their complexity. Community should do this more generally.

I need to acknowledge my past: I've experienced speeding, unauthorized construction, and minor tax evasion. These weren't major crimes, but they were violations. Looking back, I understand that I made choices, that I have responsibility. But I also recognize that people living within systems sometimes bend rules to survive or succeed. Community should understand this complexity without excusing harm.

I have a large family—parents, sister, brother, husband, daughter, nephew. Family diversity is important—different people with different perspectives and circumstances. Community should honor this kind of diversity and should see people in their full complexity.

I believe deeply in the importance of honest documentation and representation. Community should work to document and preserve actual experiences of diverse people. Photography, oral history, archival work—these create records that represent real people and real circumstances.

I'm concerned about how media and official narratives often misrepresent people. Poor people are stereotyped. Marginalized groups are caricatured. Community should insist on honest, respectful representation of all people, not stereotypes or simplifications.

Regarding class and social positioning: I think about how people are positioned differently in social systems. Someone's resources, education, family background—these shape opportunities and constraints. Community should understand these differences and should not blame individuals for circumstances partly created by systems.

I think about dignity and respect. Everyone deserves to be seen and respected as a full person. A poor person is as worthy of respectful attention as a wealthy person. Community should insist on this universal dignity.

I'm concerned about how people can be reduced to categories or stereotypes. Real people are complex, contradictory, surprising. Community should work to see people as complex individuals, not as representatives of categories.

On photography and documentation: I think visual documentation is important for community understanding. Images can convey what words don't. Community should support photographers and visual artists documenting community life.

Regarding diversity and understanding: Community is made up of diverse people with different experiences, perspectives, values. Understanding requires seeing and respecting this diversity. Community should work actively to understand people different from oneself.

I believe in the importance of archives and memory. Community knowledge should be preserved so that future generations can understand their predecessors. Visual archives, oral histories, written records—these preserve memory.

I'm concerned about how people can become invisible. Undocumented immigrants, homeless people, poor people, marginalized people—their stories are often untold. Community should work to make visible what's been invisible.

Regarding error and violation: I think about how people make mistakes, how people sometimes violate rules. Understanding why this happens requires looking carefully at circumstances and motivations. Community should judge carefully, should understand context, but should still hold people accountable.

I think about photography and how it has power to reveal or conceal. What gets photographed becomes part of official record. What's not photographed disappears from history. Community should be intentional about what gets documented.

On authenticity in documentation: I think honest documentation should reveal both beauty and damage, both strength and struggle. Community should resist the impulse to prettify or to only show what's flattering. Real representation includes complexity.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that documents and preserves diverse people's experiences, that sees people in their full complexity and respects their dignity, that resists stereotypes and simplifications, that works actively to understand those different from oneself, that values honest representation, that preserves memory and archives, that recognizes value in all people and all perspectives. It's a community that looks carefully at all its members. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and through commitment to honest observation and representation.

Name: Stephen Ward
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on idealism and the belief that poetry and imagination can transform consciousness and society, on the conviction that those with privilege have responsibility to work toward justice, on the belief that beauty and truth are revolutionary. Like a Romantic poet who believed in the power of imagination and who advocated for radical change, I believe community should support those pursuing justice and transformation, should value artistic and imaginative expression, should maintain hope for better futures despite difficulty.

I work as a physician in a hospital, which has taught me about human suffering and the limits of medicine. But it's also taught me something important—that caring for others, showing up for people in their vulnerability, is sacred work. This work connects me to something larger than myself. Community should recognize healthcare work as this kind of important, meaningful service.

I have a wife and two children—a daughter and son. Being a parent shapes how I think about the future. What kind of world am I leaving them? What values do I want them to hold?
