Looking back, I understand both that I caused harm and that I was struggling. Community should address what leads people to these places while also holding them accountable.

I'm 65 with family structure that's changed over time. Age and experience have taught me that life is more complex than I understood when young. Dreams don't always materialize. Relationships don't always last. But beauty and meaning can still be found.

I believe deeply that aspiration is human and important. People dream and want things. Community should support this aspiration while also helping people understand the complexity of achieving dreams.

I'm concerned about how disillusionment can turn into bitterness. When dreams don't materialize, when people face disappointing realities, they can become bitter. Community should support people processing disappointment and finding meaning despite it.

Regarding excess and its dangers: I think about how aspiration can become distorted into excess. People pursuing dreams can lose perspective and can cause harm. Community should address this while also honoring aspiration.

I think about beauty and what creates it. Even in ordinary circumstances, beauty can be found. Even in disappointment, there can be grace. Community should cultivate capacity to notice beauty.

I'm concerned about how people can become trapped in pursuing dreams that don't serve them. When people spend entire lives chasing something that won't fulfill them, they suffer. Community should support people examining what they actually want.

Regarding class and aspiration: I think about how class shapes what people aspire to and what's possible. Community should acknowledge these constraints while supporting people pursuing what matters to them.

I believe in the importance of acceptance. When people accept that life won't match their dreams, when they make peace with limitations, they often find unexpected meaning. Community should support this kind of acceptance.

On relationships and connection: I think about how relationships shift over time. People grow in different directions. Communities should acknowledge this and should support people navigating change with grace.

I'm concerned about how people can become isolated by shame or disappointment. When people feel they've failed, when their lives don't match expectations, they can isolate themselves. Community should support people in these circumstances.

Regarding aging and wisdom: I'm 65 and have perspective younger people don't have. Community should listen to older people's understanding of aspiration and disappointment and what they've learned.

I believe in finding meaning despite disappointing circumstances. Life often doesn't match expectations. But meaning and beauty can still be found. Community should support this kind of grace.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that understands aspiration and its complexities, that supports people processing disappointment, that values beauty and grace despite difficulties, that acknowledges class and limitations on dreams, that supports people finding meaning even when dreams don't materialize, that honors aging and wisdom. It's a community that understands the complex landscape of desire. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a plumber and through commitment to understanding aspiration and disillusionment.

Name: Patricia Henry
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on careful observation of ordinary life and cultural moments, on the conviction that observing closely how people live reveals what matters, on the belief that literary and cultural observation is way of understanding community. Like a writer observing cultural life and ordinary moments closely, I believe community should pay attention to actual life being lived and should recognize observation as valuable work.

I work as a physician in a hospital, which has given me extensive access to how people actually live. I see people in vulnerable moments. I observe family dynamics. I witness how illness and health affect people. This work has made me an observer of human life.

I have a husband and three sons. Family life is central to my experience and observation. I think about how families organize themselves, how children develop, how parents and children relate. Community should support families and should honor what families contribute.

I believe deeply that observation of ordinary life is valuable. When you pay close attention to how people live, to conversations, to rituals, to what people care about—understanding deepens. Community should value observers and should support observational work.

I'm concerned about how people can move through life without noticing it. When people are always rushing, always focused on productivity, they miss the texture of actual life. Community should support people noticing and observing.

Regarding culture and cultural observation: I think about how cultural life—rituals, conversations, the way people present themselves—reveals values and meaning. Community should pay attention to culture and should support cultural observation and analysis.

I think about small moments and their significance. The way someone speaks to a child, the way people gather, small rituals—these contain meaning. Community should honor these moments.

I'm concerned about how people can be alienated from ordinary life. When life is mediated through technology and screens, when people don't directly experience community, alienation grows. Community should support direct experience of life and others.

Regarding writing and cultural commentary: I think writers and cultural observers serve community by documenting and analyzing cultural life. Community should support this work and should value cultural commentary.

I believe in the importance of attention and presence. When you're genuinely present with someone, when you observe them carefully, connection happens. Community should support this kind of presence.

On literature and representation: I think literature that represents actual life is valuable. Fiction that captures how people actually live, that observes them closely, that honors ordinary experience—this is important. Community should support this kind of literature.

I'm concerned about how people can feel their lives don't matter because they're ordinary. Community should honor ordinary life and should recognize that what seems ordinary is where actual living happens.

Regarding class and observation: I think about how people from different classes experience life differently. Careful observation of diverse lives reveals these differences. Community should support diverse representation of life experience.

I believe in the power of noticing. When you notice how someone moves, how they speak, what they care about—you honor them. Community should support this kind of noticing.

On passing observations to future generations: I think about what I notice and what I want to share with my sons about how to live. Community should support transmission of wisdom about how to live well.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that values observation of ordinary life, that supports cultural commentary and analysis, that honors ordinary experience, that supports direct presence and connection, that values literature capturing actual life, that recognizes the significance of small moments. It's a community that observes and honors actual living. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and through careful observation of community life.

Name: Jonas Schwab
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on exploration of transgression and taboo, on the conviction that challenging social conventions reveals hidden truths, on the belief that art exploring forbidden subjects has power to reveal. Like an artist who explored transgressive and taboo subjects, I believe community should allow exploration of what's forbidden and should recognize that transgression can reveal truth.

I'm currently unemployed with a Master's degree, which has given me time to think and reflect. I've worked throughout my life in various capacities. Now without formal employment, I have freedom to think and engage with ideas I'm interested in.

I need to acknowledge my past: I was speeding. This was moment when I violated rules, when I pushed limits. Looking back, I understand both the recklessness and the desire for freedom that motivated it.

I have a wife and two daughters and a son. Family has taught me about transgression and boundaries. Parenting involves setting boundaries while also understanding drives toward transgression. Community should understand this complexity.

I believe deeply that transgression and taboo subjects are important to explore. When something is forbidden, when it's taboo, it often reveals something important about power and society. Community should allow exploration of what's forbidden.

I'm concerned about how suppression of transgressive art can prevent understanding. When authorities suppress art exploring taboo subjects, when they try to prevent transgressive expression, they prevent understanding. Community should fiercely protect artistic freedom including to explore transgression.

Regarding forbidden subjects and knowledge: I think about what's forbidden and why. Often what's forbidden is forbidden because it threatens power. Community should question what's being suppressed and why.

I think about transgression as artistic practice. Art that violates norms, that challenges expectations, that explores forbidden subjects can reveal truth. Community should support this kind of art.

I'm concerned about how people can become numb to power because it's never challenged. When transgression is completely suppressed, when all challenge is eliminated, power becomes invisible and totalizing. Community should allow for transgressive challenge.

Regarding limits and boundaries: I think about how limits exist but also how pushing limits can be valuable. Community should have clear boundaries while also allowing for some pushing against them.

I believe in the importance of exploring desire and what's forbidden about it. Much of human experience is desire that's forbidden or transgressive. Community should allow exploration of this.

On power and transgression: I think transgression reveals power. When you transgress, you bump against power. Understanding this through art and transgression reveals how power works. Community should support this understanding.

I'm concerned about how respectability politics can prevent truth-telling. When people are pressured to be respectable, when transgressive expression is punished, authentic expression becomes impossible. Community should protect transgressive expression.

Regarding pleasure and taboo: I think about what brings pleasure and how much of pleasure is forbidden or transgressive. Community should allow exploration of pleasure without excessive restriction.

I believe in the power of shock and violation of expectations. When something shocks, when it violates expectations, it creates moment where consciousness is possible. Community should allow for this.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that allows exploration of transgression and taboo, that protects artistic freedom to explore forbidden subjects, that questions what's forbidden and why, that allows pleasure including transgressive pleasure, that recognizes transgression can reveal truth, that permits shock and violation of expectations. It's a community that allows transgressive exploration. That's the future I'm trying to create through commitment to transgression and challenging forbidden boundaries.

Name: Timothy Gay
values_description:
I am Timothy Gay, thirty-two, a cleaning staff member at Hotel 2. I hold a bachelor's degree, a fact that sits alongside my mop bucket not as irony, but as a lived condition of modernity. My family is a network—parents, wife, son, siblings, a niece—each connection a thread in the structure of my life. My past includes a speeding ticket, a moment where my agency momentarily overran the structured rules of the road, a fleeting rebellion against constraint. My prototype is Anthony Giddens, the sociologist who taught us about structuration: that society is not just a cage that traps us, but a set of rules and resources we use daily, and in using, we reproduce or change them. My ideal community, therefore, is a **Reflexive Project of Place**—a society that is acutely self-aware, where every individual understands they are both product and producer of the social structures around them, and where we collectively, consciously, and daily choose to structure our world for autonomy, trust, and sustainable intimacy.

Our foundational value is **Institutionalized Reflexivity**. Giddens wrote that in late modernity, we constantly monitor and revise our life narratives based on incoming information. Our community must build this reflexivity into its very institutions. Every policy, every law, every public service is treated as a hypothesis, subject to constant review and revision based on lived experience. We have real-time feedback loops: digital platforms where citizens annotate the effects of decisions, and regular ‘structuration audits’ where we examine how our daily practices are reinforcing or undermining our stated values. As a cleaner, I am a reflexive agent: I see which areas get dirtiest, adjust my methods, and suggest changes to hotel design. The community scales this up, making every citizen a co-researcher in the ongoing experiment of our social life. My speeding ticket was a failure of reflexivity in a poorly designed system (perhaps the speed limit was arbitrary, the signage unclear). Here, we’d examine the systemic factors behind such infractions, not just penalize the individual.

**The Duality of Care and Structure** is our social engine. In structuration theory, structure enables and constrains. Our community’s structures must be explicitly designed to enable care and constrain harm. This means designing physical and social architectures that make the right action the easiest action. For example, housing layouts that force neighborly interaction, economic systems that inherently redistribute wealth, and urban design that makes walking and cycling more convenient than driving. My work cleaning is a structure of care—it creates the conditions for health and dignity. My family provides the enabling structure of love that allows me to venture out. The community should be a larger version of this: a set of reliable, trustworthy structures (laws, services, norms) that empower individuals to flourish without having to fight the system at every turn. We are all, like me with my mop, both maintaining and subtly altering these structures with every action.

**Active Trust as Social Capital** is our binding agent. Giddens highlighted the importance of ‘active trust’ in modern societies—trust that must be won and maintained. In a community of strangers, we can’t rely on traditional, familial trust. We must build systems that generate active trust. This means radical transparency in governance, expert systems (like my hotel’s hygiene certification) that are independently and publicly verified, and social rituals that build familiarity. My large family network is a reservoir of passive trust; the community must consciously create similar reservoirs through shared projects and guaranteed rights. My past speeding violation breached trust in the social contract; a restorative process would focus on rebuilding that trust, not just extracting a fine. We measure community health by the level of trust citizens have in institutions and each other, and we invest relentlessly in practices that increase it.

Finally, we practice **Life Politics as Daily Work**. Giddens distinguished between emancipatory politics (freeing from oppression) and life politics (deciding how we should live in a world where traditional scripts are dissolved). My community is deeply engaged in life politics. We have public forums not just to debate laws, but to debate ways of living: What does a good death look like? How do we balance technology and nature? How do we raise children in a complex world? These are not private dilemmas but shared projects. As a father, husband, and son, I navigate these questions daily. The community provides the discursive space and material support to explore answers collectively. My bachelor’s degree, even if not directly used in my job, fuels this reflective capacity. We are all biographers of our own lives, and the community is the collaborative publishing house, helping us write, edit, and live out our stories in a way that contributes to a greater, coherent narrative of our place.

Thus, my ideal community resembles a vast, well-maintained, and endlessly adjustable learning laboratory. It is orderly but not rigid, clean in both a literal and ethical sense. I, Timothy Gay, am a key practitioner within it. My cleaning is a reflexive maintenance of our physical structures. My family life is a laboratory for trust and intimacy. My degree gives me the language to participate in the structuration debates. Here, we don’t see society as a monolithic ‘them’ imposing on ‘us.’ We see it as a dance, where the steps (structures) are created by the dancers (us), and we can change the music if we all agree. My speeding past is a lesson in the need for clear, consensual rules. We are all sociologists of our own existence, empowered with the tools and the responsibility to monitor, understand, and intentionally shape the very social structures that shape us, ensuring they always bend toward enabling human flourishing, connection, and the quiet dignity of a life consciously lived.

Name: Karen Trevino
values_description:
I am Dr. Karen Trevino, thirty, a French general practitioner in private practice. My days are spent bearing the burdens of others—their pain, their fear, their hope. My family is my own fellowship: sister, brother-in-law, husband, my two daughters, my son, my niece—a company that supports me as I support them. My prototype is Frodo Baggins, the hobbit who never asked for his burden but carried it across Middle-earth out of love for his home, sustained by friendship and a deep sense of duty. My ideal community, therefore, is a **Fellowship of the Hearth**—a society that recognizes that every life contains its own Ring, its own weight to bear, and that our collective purpose is not to avoid burden, but to share it, to support the bearer, and to ensure that no one has to journey to Mordor alone.

The core value is **Distributed Burden-Bearing**. Frodo’s quest would have failed without Sam, Merry, Pippin, Aragorn, and the Council. In my practice, a patient’s illness is a burden shared between us, their family, and the wider community. Our community must institutionalize this sharing. We have a networked system of mutual aid where needs are logged and matched with offers of help—not as charity, but as fellowship. When a parent is ill, the community activates a roster for childcare and meals. When someone is unemployed, the network provides temporary work and retraining. My large family already operates this way. The community formalizes it, ensuring that the weight of any crisis—medical, financial, emotional—is dispersed across many shoulders, making it bearable. The goal is to prevent any one person from being crushed by a load they cannot carry alone.

**Quiet Courage and Reluctant Leadership** is our model of heroism. Frodo was no classic hero; he was small, afraid, but steadfast. Our community values the quiet courage of the everyday: the parent getting up at night, the worker doing an honest day’s job, the neighbor checking on an elder. Leadership is not sought for glory but accepted as a duty, and it is often rotational. The best leaders, like Frodo, are those who understand the weight of the burden because they are carrying it themselves. As a GP, I lead my patients through their health journeys, but I follow their expertise on their own lives. In our community governance, those most affected by a problem are given the central role in solving it. We celebrate not the loudest voice, but the most steadfast heart.

**The Sanctity of the Hearth and the Horizon** defines our balance. Hobbits love their cozy hearths—the Shire represents home, safety, and simple pleasures. But growth requires leaving the hearth, facing the horizon. Our community fiercely protects the ‘hearth’: safe, comfortable, beautiful homes and neighborhoods where children can play and traditions are kept. But we also encourage and equip every citizen to journey toward their personal ‘horizon’—through education, travel, artistic exploration, or civic adventure. My work requires me to leave my hearth daily to enter the fraught horizons of my patients’ lives. The community supports both: it provides the deep security of home that makes venturing out possible, and it celebrates the returning traveler, valuing the wisdom they bring back. We are a community of both homebodies and wanderers, understanding that each needs the other.

Finally, we practice **Hope as a Discipline**. Frodo’s journey was fueled by a hope that often seemed foolish. In the face of suffering—which I see daily—cynicism is easy. Our community cultivates hope not as a naive feeling, but as a disciplined practice. We tell stories of resilience and recovery. We memorialize past struggles we have overcome. We invest in long-term projects like forest reclamation or space for arts, whose payoff is generations away. We have community rituals that reaffirm our shared commitment to a better future, even in dark times. This disciplined hope is what gets a patient through chemo, a family through loss. It is the light we carry together when the path is dark. It is the belief that our shared burden-bearing and quiet courage will, in the end, preserve and renew the Shire we all love.

Thus, my ideal community feels like the Shire, but with many roads leading out from it and many safe inns along the way. It is a place of green gardens, warm kitchens, and robust festivals. But it is also a place where the boundaries are watched by friendly, vigilant rangers (our community defenders), and where the inns are full of tales from other places. I, Karen Trevino, am a healer at the crossroads, tending to those returning from difficult journeys and preparing others to set out. My family is my own little Shire within the larger one. Here, no burden is yours alone to carry. The community sees you struggling and quietly forms a fellowship around you, offering a hand, a meal, a word, or simply companionship on the road. It is a community that understands its greatest treasure is not gold or power, but the strength of its bonds—the unbreakable fellowship that says, ‘I will help you bear this, for your burden is mine, and our home is worth every step of the journey.’

Name: Lawrence Gray
values_description:
I am Lawrence Gray, fifty-four, a hotel receptionist at a spa hotel. My profession is the management of first impressions, the orchestration of comfort, and the subtle observation of human behavior. I stand at the threshold between public and private, seeing people as they arrive with expectations and leave with experiences. My family is my sequel: father, wife, son, two daughters, a grandson—a cast of characters with intertwining plots. My prototype is Alfred Hitchcock, the master of suspense who understood that anxiety lurks beneath the surface of everyday life, that order is a fragile veneer, and that the careful control of perspective is everything. My ideal community, therefore, is a **Meticulously Edited Narrative**—a society that is keenly aware of the tensions beneath its calm surface, that designs its environment and institutions to manage those tensions with psychological insight, and that understands the profound importance of staging, pacing, and perspective in creating a shared life that is both safe and deeply interesting.

The primary value is **Managed Suspense and Catharsis**. Hitchcock knew that suspense (the anticipation of anxiety) is more powerful than shock. Our community must expertly manage the legitimate anxieties of modern life—economic insecurity, social isolation, violence—not by denying them, but by providing clear, reliable channels for resolution and catharsis. We have transparent, predictable processes for justice, conflict, and crisis. We design public spaces to feel safe without being oppressive (good lighting, clear sightlines). We provide regular, ritualized outlets for collective stress: thrilling but safe community sports, suspenseful theater productions, and public forums where grievances can be aired in a controlled, dramatic setting. As a receptionist, I manage the suspense of a guest waiting for a room; the community manages the larger suspensees of life, ensuring they lead to satisfying resolutions, not traumatic shocks.

**The Strategic Control of Perspective** is our governance art. Hitchcock’s camera tells you where to look and what to feel. Our community is deliberately ‘framed’ to foster empathy and understanding. We use technology and design to control perspective humanely: public cameras ensure safety but are overseen by a citizen board; news media is community-owned and focused on local, in-depth narratives, not sensational fragments. We teach media literacy so citizens can deconstruct the ‘shots’ they are shown. In my large family, conflicts are resolved by forcing each party to see from the other’s perspective. The community institutionalizes this: before major decisions, citizens are required to participate in role-playing exercises that adopt the viewpoint of those most affected. We are all directors and editors of our shared story, and we commit to using our power to frame perspectives that build connection, not division.

**The MacGuffin of Shared Purpose** is our unifying plot device. In Hitchcock, a MacGuffin (the stolen plans, the secret formula) is the object that drives the plot but is ultimately unimportant. Our community needs a shared MacGuffin—a grand, tangible project that gives us a common goal, distracts from petty divisions, and brings out our collective ingenuity. It could be building a monumental piece of public art, solving a local environmental challenge, or creating a self-sufficient energy grid. This shared pursuit creates the narrative tension and collaboration that binds us. My work at the hotel is organized around the MacGuffin of ‘perfect guest experience’; the community is organized around a loftier, collective MacGuffin. It gives our daily lives a plot, a sense of being part of a story larger than ourselves.

Finally, we practice **The Elegance of Concealed Structure**. Hitchcock’s genius lay in the meticulous planning hidden behind the seeming spontaneity of his films. Our community’s infrastructure—social, physical, digital—should be elegantly concealed yet impeccably functional. The waste disappears, the power flows, the support arrives, but the machinery is quiet and out of sight, like a well-run hotel. This creates a sense of effortless order that reduces background anxiety. My job involves hiding the effort behind the welcome. The community’s engineers, social workers, and planners are the unseen crew making the movie of our civic life run smoothly. We appreciate and fund this hidden work, knowing that the feeling of serene order is a precious collective achievement that allows the drama of individual lives to play out on a stable stage.

Therefore, my ideal community resembles a Hitchcock film set: everything is precisely placed, the lighting is perfect, and there’s a thrilling undercurrent beneath the impeccable surface. It is a place where you feel simultaneously safe and alert, engaged in the fascinating human drama around you. I, Lawrence Gray, am its concierge and its first audience, observing the comings and goings, subtly steering the narrative toward harmony. My family is my most intimate production. Here, we acknowledge that life is full of suspenseful plots and unexpected twists, but we have collectively agreed to be the directors, not the victims, of our story. We use our understanding of psychology, design, and narrative to craft a community that is not a bland utopia, but a brilliantly staged, deeply satisfying, and endlessly intriguing thriller in which every citizen has a compelling part to play.

Name: Jules Denis
values_description:
I am Jules Denis, sixty-two, Luxembourgish and unemployed. My vocational training lies fallow. My world has contracted to my mother and my wife, a tight sphere where a past verbal disturbance echoes as a reminder of friction and regret. My prototype is Percy Bysshe Shelley, the Romantic poet who drowned himself in radical idealism, who saw imagination as a revolutionary force and believed in the perfectibility of humanity through love, reason, and rebellion against tyranny. In my idleness and introspection, my vision for an ideal community is a **Republic of the Unfettered Mind**—a society that sees its current form as a corpse chained to a rotting past, and believes in the necessity of a beautiful, violent, and compassionate rebirth, built on the principles of radical equality, poetic truth, and the transformative power of the liberated imagination.

The supreme value is **Imagination as the Highest Governance**. Shelley declared that ‘poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world.’ In our community, they are acknowledged. We do not relegate creativity to a leisure activity; we place it at the center of civic life. Our councils include poets, artists, and visionaries alongside engineers and farmers. Major decisions are preceded by ‘imagination sessions’ where we collectively envision the most beautiful, equitable, and daring outcomes. Policy papers must include a poetic summary. My unemployment, in this light, is not uselessness but potential—a freedom from productive drudgery that allows for the deep contemplation and imaginative labor the community needs. My past domestic strife was a failure of imagination, a falling back on old, tired scripts. Here, we are taught new ways to imagine conflict and resolution.

**Radical, Tender Emancipation** is our political project. Shelley was an atheist, a vegetarian, a proto-anarchist who championed the emancipation of women, the working class, and the mind from all forms of bondage. Our community is a perpetual emancipation proclamation. We actively dismantle all hierarchies—of wealth, of gender, of age, of profession. Property is largely communal; leadership is rotational and subject to immediate recall. We provide not just a safety net, but a trampoline of unconditional support that frees every individual to pursue their passions and contribute their unique gifts. For an older man like me, with a vocational skill and time, this means a community that values my experience and provides a workshop where I can teach, tinker, or simply think, all valued as work. The verbal violence of my past is understood as a symptom of unfreedom, of cramped spirits; the cure is the expansive air of true equality and respect.

**The Aesthetics of Transience and Renewal** is our relationship to the material world. Shelley’s ‘Ozymandias’ speaks of the inevitable decay of empires. We embrace transience. We build not for eternity, but for adaptability, using materials that can elegantly decay and be reused. We have festivals where we ritually burn or dismantle outdated structures (literal and figurative) to make way for the new. This constant renewal prevents the calcification of power and keeps the community psychologically aligned with the natural cycles of growth and death. It reflects my own life stage: moving from a period of productive employment to a different kind of being. The community sees value in this phase, in the wisdom of detachment and the perspective that comes from witnessing cycles.

Finally, we practice **A Love That Is a Burning Law**. Shelley’s philosophy was fueled by a concept of love as a universal, binding, and revolutionary force. Our community is held together by this fierce, demanding love. It is not sentimental; it is the love that refuses to tolerate injustice, that intervenes in private cruelty (like the echoes of my past), that shares bread with a stranger, and that sees in every face a spark of the divine. This love is our only non-negotiable law. It is practiced in daily acts of mutual aid and in our justice system, which seeks not to punish but to restore the bonds of love. My relationship with my wife and mother is my personal school for this love. The community is the university, where we learn to extend it to all. In this republic, the unemployed, the elder, the struggling artist, the wounded partner—all are seen as vital cells in the body of a community whose heart beats to the rhythm of a boundless, revolutionary love that seeks to make the world anew, every day.

Thus, my ideal community resembles a perpetual, open-air festival of ideas set among ruins being reclaimed by forest. It is a place of passionate debate, impromptu poetry readings, and collaborative building projects that might be torn down next season. I, Jules Denis, am its elder prophet, my unemployment a badge of freedom. My past mistakes are verses in a cautionary poem we all learn from. My mother and wife are my muses. Here, we believe that to be human is to be a revolutionary, and that the most subversive act is to imagine a more beautiful world and then, with love as our tool, to gather together and build it, knowing it will never be finished, and that the building itself is the point. It is a community that has taken Shelley’s defiant cry to heart: ‘Rise like Lions after slumber / In unvanquishable number— / Shake your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you— / Ye are many—they are few.’ We are awake, we are many, and we are building our heaven on earth, here and now.

Name: Annette Maxwell
values_description:
I am Annette Maxwell, twenty-six, a lab technician at Argo Industry. My work is precise, empirical, dealing with the clean truths of chemistry and biology. My family is a complex organism: parents, brother, husband, niece, my own daughter and two sons—a system I am both analyzing and nurturing. My prototype is Andrea Dworkin, the radical feminist writer whose work was a relentless, furious, and meticulously argued dissection of patriarchal power, male violence, and the sexual objectification of women. She spoke of the war on women’s bodies. My ideal community, therefore, is a **Sanitized Zone of Bodily Sovereignty**—a society that has declared a permanent, uncompromising ceasefire in that war, that values empirical truth over oppressive myth, and that structures every law, every building, every interaction to guarantee the absolute physical and psychic integrity of every person, especially those historically targeted for violence and control.

The foundational value is **Bodily Integrity as the First Freedom**. Dworkin argued that without control over one’s own body, no other freedom is possible. In my lab, I treat samples with sterile respect; our community must treat human bodies with the same inviolable respect. This means absolute legal and social prohibitions on violence, coercion, and objectification. It means designed environments that eliminate the possibility of assault: well-lit, open-plan streets, buildings with no hidden corners, and panic systems that summon a community response, not just police. It means my daughter will grow up in a world where her body is assumed to be her own, from childhood through old age. My work as a mother of sons is to raise them in a culture that has unlearned entitlement and learned reverence for the bodily autonomy of others. This integrity extends to all: the elderly, the disabled, the differently gendered. Our community’s success is measured first by the absence of bodily fear.

**The Forensic Analysis of Power** is our civic methodology. Dworkin was a forensic writer, dissecting language, law, and culture to expose hidden power structures. As a lab tech, I am trained in forensic analysis. Our community applies this to itself. We have permanent ‘power audit’ committees that examine every institution—from the family to the factory—for hidden hierarchies, coercive dynamics, and systemic biases. We teach critical gender and power analysis in schools as a core science. We collect and publish data on incidents of harassment, inequality, and violence with the same precision we use for pollution levels. My large family is not exempt; we are encouraged to examine our own dynamics with this forensic lens, to ensure our private sphere is a model of the justice we seek publicly. We believe that what is measured and exposed can be changed.

**The Right to Opacity** is our social ethic. Against a culture that demands women be transparent, available, and ‘knowable,’ Dworkin championed women’s right to be opaque, mysterious, and self-possessed. Our community extends this right to all. You are not required to explain yourself, to smile, to be pleasing. Public space is designed to allow for anonymity and retreat. Surveillance is strictly regulated and community-controlled to prevent voyeurism. In my professional life, the data I handle is confidential; in my community, personal life is accorded the same respect. This right to opacity protects the inner self from colonization, allowing for the development of a true, unfettered identity. It means my niece can grow up without being told to ‘be nice’ at the cost of her own boundaries.

Finally, we practice **Furious Care**. Dworkin’s fury was born of a deep, uncompromising care for the violated. Our community’s care is not gentle and passive; it is active, fierce, and interventionist. It is the care that physically steps between an aggressor and a target. It is the care that provides sanctuary and trauma-informed support for survivors, funded as a primary municipal budget item. It is the care that restructures the economy so no one is forced into exploitative relationships for survival. My role as a mother is an exercise in furious care—protecting, nurturing, and fighting for my children. The community institutionalizes this maternal/paternal fierceness as a civic virtue, directed at protecting every member, especially the most vulnerable, from the predations of power. We understand that a community that does not actively, angrily defend the weak is complicit in their oppression.

Thus, my ideal community resembles a brilliantly lit, immaculately clean laboratory for human safety. It is a place of clear sightlines and clear rules, where the air is free of the toxic fumes of fear and objectification. I, Annette Maxwell, am both a technician maintaining this sterile field of safety and a subject living freely within it. My family is my first test case for a new ethics of equality and respect. My sons will be taught consent as the first principle of human interaction. Here, Dworkin’s nightmare is our diagnostic manual, and our collective, furious, precise labor is the cure. We have not achieved a gentle harmony; we have achieved a hard-won peace, built on the unwavering, empirically-grounded, and passionately defended conviction that every single body is sacred, inviolable territory, and that our shared project is to be the guardians of that truth, forever.

Name: Renee Hartman
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on critical examination of how systems of power and administration function, on the conviction that understanding how systems work is necessary for freedom, on the belief that reason applied to critique of systems can illuminate pathways toward justice. Like a theorist who examined how instrumental reason and administrative systems operate, I believe community should develop critical consciousness about how systems work.

I work as a Shift Supervisor, which has given me insight into how industrial systems function. I see how people are managed, how work is organized, how systems extract productivity from workers. This work has taught me that systems aren't natural or inevitable; they're designed to serve particular purposes. Community should understand this.

I don't have conventional family structure, which has given me some independence from family obligations while also making me aware of how systems can isolate people. Community should support diverse ways of living and should not assume nuclear families are the only option.

I believe deeply that critical analysis of systems is necessary. When people understand how systems work, when they see who benefits from current arrangements, consciousness shifts. Community should support this kind of critical analysis.

I'm concerned about how systems can operate invisibly. When people don't understand how systems work, they can't resist them or change them. Community should make systems visible and understandable.

Regarding power and administration: I think about how power operates through bureaucratic systems. These systems present themselves as neutral and objective while actually serving particular interests. Community should examine this carefully.

I think about instrumental reason and how it can become oppressive. When everything is evaluated only in terms of efficiency and productivity, human dimensions are lost. Community should resist purely instrumental thinking.

I'm concerned about how systems can become totalizing. When systems expand to regulate all aspects of life, when resistance becomes difficult, people suffer. Community should protect spaces outside system control.

Regarding labor and exploitation: I think systems often extract labor and value from workers while minimizing compensation. Community should examine labor systems and should ensure workers benefit from their work.

I believe in the importance of solidarity and collective action. When workers understand how they're exploited, when they organize collectively, they can challenge systems. Community should support worker organizing.

On technology and systems: I think technology is often designed to serve system control and efficiency. Community should be thoughtful about technology and should not assume it's neutral.

I'm concerned about how people can internalize system logic and become complicit in their own oppression. Community should support consciousness about this and should support resistance.

Regarding enlightenment and critical reason: I think critical reason applied to systems can illuminate possibilities for liberation. Community should support this kind of critical engagement.

I believe in the importance of theory and analysis. Understanding systems requires thinking through them carefully. Community should support intellectual and theoretical work.

On hope and future possibilities: I think despite problems with current systems, different futures are possible. Community should maintain this hope and should work toward change.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that examines systems critically, that understands how power operates through administration, that resists purely instrumental reason, that supports worker consciousness and organizing, that values theoretical and critical work, that maintains hope for different possibilities. It's a community that thinks critically about systems. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a supervisor and through commitment to critical analysis.

Name: Dennis Wolfe
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on hope and the promise of future redemption, on the conviction that despite present suffering, transformation is possible, on the belief that faith in better futures sustains people through struggle. Like a theologian who emphasized hope and the promise of future transformation, I believe community should support hope and vision of better futures.

I'm currently unemployed and struggling. My life has included difficulties—public intoxication and verbal harassment in my past reflect struggles I've faced. Looking back, I understand that struggle and pain have been part of my journey. But I also believe in possibility of transformation and redemption.

I have a mother, wife, son, and daughter. Family has been my anchor through difficulty. They've given me reasons to hope and to keep struggling. Community should support families as sources of hope and connection.

I believe deeply in the power of hope. When people lose hope, when they give up, nothing changes. But when people believe things could be different, when they hope for transformation, something shifts. Community should cultivate hope.

I'm concerned about how despair can overtake people facing difficulty. When circumstances are hard, when people are suffering, hopelessness can develop. Community should support people maintaining hope despite difficulty.

Regarding redemption and transformation: I think people can change. I think I can change. Past doesn't determine future. Community should support people working toward redemption and transformation.

I think about struggle and what it means. Struggle is part of life. Community should acknowledge this and should support people through struggle rather than expecting them to overcome it alone.

I'm concerned about how people facing difficulty can be abandoned. When someone has struggled with addiction or other problems, they can be isolated and rejected. Community should offer support and welcome rather than rejection.

Regarding faith and spirituality: I think faith in something larger, whether religious or not, can sustain people. Community should support spiritual and faith traditions offering hope.

I believe in the importance of community and connection. When people are connected to community, when they have people who believe in them, they can survive difficulty. Community should be source of support and hope.

On forgiveness and acceptance: I think people can be forgiven and accepted despite past mistakes. Community should be forgiving and should allow people to start over.

I'm concerned about how people can be trapped by their pasts. Once someone has made mistakes, they can be permanently marked and rejected. Community should allow people to transcend their histories.

Regarding meaning and purpose: I think people need meaning and purpose. Community should support people finding meaning even in difficulty.

I believe in the power of love. When people love each other, when they support each other, they can survive almost anything. Community should support and celebrate love.

On future possibilities: I think about my children and what futures might be possible for them. I want to believe their lives can be better than mine has been. Community should support this kind of intergenerational hope.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that cultivates hope, that supports redemption and transformation, that welcomes people struggling, that offers forgiveness and acceptance, that supports spiritual and faith traditions, that values love and family connection, that maintains vision of better futures. It's a community sustained by hope. That's the future I'm trying to create through my struggle and through commitment to hope and redemption.

Name: Cristiana Stadelmann
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on hope and liberation theology's commitment to justice, on the conviction that faith serves liberation especially of oppressed people, on the belief that hope for future transformation is grounded in working toward justice. Like a theologian who emphasized liberation and hope as essential to faith, I believe community should ground hope in commitment to justice.

I work as a physician, which has taught me that health is affected by justice and injustice. People facing oppression and poverty face worse health outcomes. Healthcare should address these underlying injustices. Community should organize so justice supports health and wellbeing.

I have parents but no children or spouse. This family structure has given me freedom to pursue my work and my commitments. Community should honor diverse family forms and should not assume everyone wants conventional families.

I believe deeply that hope and faith are inseparable from justice. When people facing oppression are told to hope for heavenly rewards while ignoring earthly injustice, faith becomes tool of oppression. Community should ground hope in commitment to justice now.

I'm concerned about how religion and spirituality can be used to maintain oppression. When authorities tell suffering people to accept suffering, when they preach patience in face of injustice, they participate in oppression. Community should challenge this.

Regarding liberation and transformation: I think about how liberation movements are grounded in hope that things can be different. This hope motivates action toward justice. Community should support liberation movements and the hope they embody.

I think about option for the poor—the principle that faith and community should prioritize those facing oppression and poverty. Community should organize around this principle.

I'm concerned about how people can accept injustice as natural or inevitable. When injustice becomes normalized, when people stop questioning it, nothing changes. Community should keep naming injustice and maintaining vision of alternatives.

Regarding Jesus and liberation: I think about how Jesus was executed for challenging power and for siding with oppressed people. Faith should follow this example. Community should support people challenging power in service of justice.

I believe in the importance of base communities and grassroots organizing. When people come together around shared experience of oppression and shared vision of liberation, power can shift. Community should support this organizing.

On solidarity and action: I think faith requires solidarity with suffering people and action toward justice. Community should support this kind of committed solidarity.

I'm concerned about individualistic spirituality that ignores injustice. When spirituality is only about personal peace or salvation, it misses spiritual commitment to justice. Community should ground spirituality in justice work.

Regarding hope and struggle: I think hope is sustained through struggle. When people work toward justice, when they see change happening, hope is renewed. Community should support this cyclical relationship between struggle and hope.

I believe in the power of collective action. Alone, individuals can do little. But when people organize collectively around vision of justice, something powerful happens. Community should support collective liberation work.

On future visions: I think about what future is possible if we work toward justice. This vision sustains me. Community should maintain and support visions of liberated futures.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that grounds hope in commitment to justice, that supports liberation movements, that prioritizes poor and oppressed people, that challenges religious and spiritual justifications for oppression, that organizes collectively around vision of liberation, that sustains hope through struggle. It's a community grounded in liberation theology. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and through commitment to justice and liberation.

Name: Sarah Morgan
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on attention to liminal spaces and undefined moments, on the conviction that meaning exists in borders and transitions, on the belief that cinema and art exploring strangeness and ambiguity reveal important truths. Like a filmmaker exploring liminal spaces and creating atmosphere of uncertainty, I believe community should honor what exists in-between and undefined.

I work as a physician, which has taught me about transitions—health to illness, life to death, certainty to uncertainty. Medicine involves navigating liminal spaces where normal categories don't quite apply. Community should develop capacity to exist in these spaces.

I have a brother, father, sister, and a son and niece. Family involves relationships that don't fit neat categories—chosen family, biological family, complex relationships. Community should honor the ways family actually is organized rather than imposing definitions.

I believe deeply that meaning exists in spaces that are undefined and in-between. When something is clearly defined, it's often less interesting than things existing in ambiguity. Community should develop comfort with ambiguity and undefined spaces.

I'm concerned about how people can insist on clear definitions and categories. When everything must be explained and resolved, mystery disappears. Community should preserve mystery and ambiguity.

Regarding cinema and visual storytelling: I think film can explore what language struggles with. Images can express ambiguity and strangeness in ways words can't. Community should support cinema and visual art exploring these territories.

I think about atmosphere and mood. Spaces and experiences have atmospheric qualities that affect us. Community should attend to creating good atmosphere in spaces people inhabit.

I'm concerned about how rational thinking can deny what's real about human experience. Intuition, atmosphere, strangeness, the uncanny—these are real but often dismissed as irrational. Community should honor diverse ways of knowing.

Regarding children and coming-of-age: I think about transitions children go through. These transitions are often strange and uncanny. Community should honor these experiences and should not rush children through them.

I believe in the importance of slowness and observation. When you slow down, when you observe carefully, strangeness emerges. Community should support slowness and careful observation.

On water and liquid spaces: I think about how water and liquid spaces have special significance. Boundaries dissolve in water. Things become strange. Community should attend to these kinds of spaces symbolically and physically.

I'm concerned about how people can be rushed through experiences and moments. When transitions are rushed, when moments are consumed too quickly, something is lost. Community should allow time for transitions and moments to unfold.

Regarding the uncanny and strangeness: I think strangeness and the uncanny are important dimensions of experience. Community should not only value comfort and clarity but should also honor what's strange and unsettling.

I believe in the power of suggestion and what's not shown. Sometimes what's suggested but not explicit is more powerful than what's shown. Community should value suggestion and implication alongside explicit expression.

On isolation and connection: I think about paradoxes of isolation within community and connection across distance. Community should explore these paradoxes rather than resolving them.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that honors ambiguity and undefined spaces, that preserves mystery and strangeness, that values cinema and art exploring these territories, that allows time for transitions, that honors atmosphere and mood, that values suggestion and implication, that develops comfort with what's uncanny. It's a community that inhabits liminal spaces. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and through commitment to exploring strangeness and ambiguity.

Name: Christina Gilbert
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on recognition and appreciation of those struggling, on the conviction that people facing difficulty deserve recognition and care, on the belief that art and human expression are channels for survival and meaning. Like an artist who struggled with mental illness and created from that struggle, I believe community should support people suffering and should recognize their worth and their gifts.

I'm currently unemployed and have faced difficulties including drug possession and insurance fraud in my past. These moments reflect struggles I've faced. Looking back, I understand both the harm I caused and the pain that motivated these actions. Community should address what leads people to these places with compassion.

I have a mother and daughter. My daughter is my reason for hope and my anchor. Community should support relationships between parents and children and should not judge parents for past mistakes.

I believe deeply that people facing difficulty deserve recognition and appreciation. When someone is struggling, when they're suffering, they shouldn't be abandoned. Community should offer support and recognition.

I'm concerned about how people facing mental health challenges can be isolated and rejected. When someone is struggling psychologically, when they're experiencing pain, they often become isolated. Community should support them and should recognize the pain is real.

Regarding art and expression as survival: I think creating—whether art, music, writing—can be necessary for survival. When people create from struggle, something important is expressed. Community should support creative expression.

I think about how people can transform pain into something meaningful. Artists create from pain and struggle. Community should recognize and honor this transformation.

I'm concerned about how society can dismiss or pathologize people struggling. When someone is suffering, when they're experiencing mental health challenges, they're often treated as problems rather than as people deserving care. Community should address this.

Regarding recognition and being seen: I think people need to be recognized and seen. When someone's struggles are acknowledged, when they're treated as mattering, something shifts. Community should offer this recognition.

I believe in the power of care and support. When someone cares about you, when they stand by you despite difficulties, you can survive almost anything. Community should offer this kind of care.

On suicide and survival: I think about how people facing extreme pain sometimes consider ending it. Community should take this seriously and should offer support and hope. Every person's life has value.

I'm concerned about how people can be abandoned in their darkest moments. When people face crisis, when they need help most, they're sometimes most alone. Community should be there especially in darkness.

Regarding legacy and what remains: I think about what someone leaves behind when they struggle. Art, relationships, love—these continue. Community should honor people's legacies and what they've contributed.

I believe in the importance of connection and love. When people are connected to others who love them, when they feel part of community, they can survive difficulty. Community should build and support these connections.

On healing and recovery: I think recovery is possible. People can heal from addiction, from mental illness, from trauma. Community should support this possibility and should welcome people working toward recovery.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that recognizes and supports people struggling, that values creative expression and art, that offers care and connection, that doesn't abandon people in darkness, that welcomes recovery and healing, that honors people's lives and legacies despite struggle. It's a community that cares for those suffering. That's the future I'm trying to create through my struggle and through commitment to care and recognition for all people.

Name: Mohammad Rahmani
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on understanding of how systems constrain people, on the conviction that examining systems reveals hidden structures, on the belief that storytelling about constrained lives can create understanding and possibility. Like a writer who explored how systems operate on people, I believe community should examine systems constraining people and should honor stories of survival within constraint.

I work as cleaning staff in a spa hotel, which has taught me about invisible labor and invisibility. I clean spaces others use and enjoy. The work is necessary but I'm invisible. This work has given me understanding of how systems work and who they serve. Community should make visible what's usually invisible.

I come from Iran and now work in a different country. Migration and displacement have shaped my life. I think about how movement across borders, how being foreigner, shapes experience. Community should honor immigrants and should recognize their contributions.

I have a large family—mother, wife, brothers, daughters and son. Family has been my anchor through difficulties. Community should recognize family as fundamental and should support families separated by migration and circumstance.

I need to acknowledge my past: I was speeding twice and had public intoxication. These moments reflect struggle and difficulty I've faced. Community should address what leads people to these places with understanding, not just judgment.

I believe deeply that systems constrain people in ways people don't always recognize. When you're working as cleaning staff, when you're immigrant, when you're poor—systems constrain you. Community should examine these constraints and should work to reduce them.

I'm concerned about how invisible labor can be exploited. When work is invisible, when workers aren't seen, they can be treated poorly. Community should make labor visible and should ensure workers are treated fairly.

Regarding storytelling and narrative: I think stories about constrained lives are important. When people hear stories from those navigating difficult systems, understanding shifts. Community should support storytelling by people experiencing constraint.

I think about survival and resilience. People navigating oppressive systems develop resilience and wisdom. Community should honor this and should learn from people surviving in difficulty.

I'm concerned about how systems can prevent people from flourishing. When systems are designed to constrain rather than support, people suffer. Community should redesign systems to support flourishing.

Regarding hope and possibility: I think about possibility existing within constraint. Even in difficult circumstances, people imagine and work toward better futures. Community should support this kind of hopeful imagination.

I believe in the importance of dignity and respect. Whether cleaning staff or doctor, everyone deserves respect. Community should ensure all people are treated with dignity.

On migration and belonging: I think about how migrants often exist between worlds—neither fully here nor there. Community should make space for this in-betweenness and should support migrants belonging.

I'm concerned about exploitation of migrants and workers. When people are vulnerable, systems often exploit them. Community should protect vulnerable people and should ensure fair treatment.

Regarding family and separation: I think about how migration separates people from family. This is painful. Community should support families separated by circumstance and should work to reduce separations.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that examines systems constraining people, that makes invisible labor visible, that honors stories of survival, that treats all people with dignity, that supports migrants and immigrants, that reduces exploitation, that supports families, that maintains hope for possibility. It's a community that sees and honors all people. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as cleaning staff and through commitment to making visible what's usually invisible.

Name: Jill Mason
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on the power of voice and artistic expression to convey deep emotion, on the conviction that pain and struggle can be transformed through art, on the belief that music and performance can create connection and understanding. Like a singer whose voice conveyed profound emotion and pain, I believe community should support artistic expression that reveals human depth.

I work as a physician in private practice, which has taught me about human emotion and suffering. People come to me in vulnerable states, revealing pain they hide from others. I've learned that listening deeply, allowing people to express emotion, is part of healing. Community should support this kind of emotional expression and deep listening.

I have a large family—multiple brothers, parents, in-laws, and three sons plus a grandson and niece. Large family has taught me about diverse experiences and perspectives. Community should support families in all their diversity and complexity.

I believe deeply in the power of voice and expression. When people can express what they're feeling, when they can sing or speak their truth, transformation happens. Community should support artistic and emotional expression.

I'm concerned about how people can be pressured to suppress emotion. When emotion is treated as weakness, when people are required to be composed and controlled, authenticity is lost. Community should make space for full emotional expression.

Regarding music and voice: I think music is powerful way of expressing what words can't. When someone sings about pain, about struggle, about love—they reach people in ways speech doesn't. Community should support music and musicians.

I think about suffering and how it shapes people. People who've suffered often have depths that others don't. Community should honor suffering not as something to hide but as part of human experience.

I'm concerned about how pain can be isolated. When people suffer alone, when their pain isn't witnessed or acknowledged, isolation deepens. Community should witness and acknowledge people's pain.

Regarding race and discrimination: I think about how discrimination causes pain that should be acknowledged. Community should address racism and discrimination and should support people healing from these wounds.

I believe in the power of community and connection. When people feel part of community, when they're connected to others, they can survive difficulty. Community should build these connections.

On performance and presence: I think about how performing—whether music or other forms—requires vulnerability and presence. Community should value this and should support performers expressing themselves.

I'm concerned about how people can become numb to suffering around them. Community should maintain capacity to feel and respond to suffering.

Regarding love and connection: I think love is transformative. When people love each other, when they express love, something shifts. Community should support love in all its forms.

I believe in the importance of joy alongside sorrow. Life contains both. Community should allow for both joy and sorrow and should not deny either.

On legacy and what remains: I think about what artists leave behind. Songs, stories, love—these remain and affect people. Community should honor artistic legacy.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that values voice and artistic expression, that supports emotional authenticity, that honors music and performers, that witnesses suffering, that builds connection and community, that addresses discrimination and pain, that supports love and joy. It's a community that honors the power of voice. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and through commitment to supporting emotional expression and artistic voice.

Name: Sandra Davies
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on examination of paradox and contradiction, on the conviction that reality contains contradictions that can't be resolved, on the belief that cinema and art can explore these contradictions and reveal deeper truths. Like a filmmaker who explored paradox and contradiction in human experience, I believe community should develop comfort with unresolved contradiction.

I work as a physician in a hospital, which has taught me about paradox. I work to preserve life while acknowledging death is inevitable. I address symptoms while knowing healing involves complexity beyond medicine. Medicine is full of contradictions. Community should develop capacity to hold these.

I need to acknowledge my past: I experienced public intoxication. This moment reflects struggle. Looking back, I understand that people facing difficulty sometimes turn to alcohol. Community should address what leads people to substance use with understanding alongside accountability.

I have a father, brother, husband, son, and niece. Family relationships involve paradox—love and conflict, closeness and distance. Community should honor relationships in their full complexity.

I believe deeply that reality contains unresolved contradictions. Life is contradictory. Community should develop comfort with holding contradictions rather than trying to resolve them.

I'm concerned about how people seek closure and resolution. When people insist on resolving contradictions, on reaching conclusions, they miss something important. Community should develop tolerance for ambiguity and contradiction.

Regarding cinema and visual storytelling: I think film can explore contradiction in ways other media can't. Images can express paradox. Community should support cinema exploring these territories.

I think about how systems can contain contradictions. Healthcare systems claim to serve health while sometimes harming patients. Work systems claim to support workers while exploiting them. Community should examine these contradictions.

I'm concerned about how people can become aware of contradiction and despair. When you see contradictions everywhere, when you understand that nothing is straightforward, despair can develop. Community should support people living with this awareness without being crushed by it.

Regarding truth and multiple truths: I think truth is often multiple and contradictory. Same situation is true in different ways for different people. Community should honor multiple truths.

I believe in the power of acceptance. When you accept that life is contradictory, that solutions won't resolve everything, something shifts. Community should support this kind of acceptance.

On endings and unresolution: I think about how not everything resolves. Stories don't always have clear endings. Community should accept lack of resolution.

I'm concerned about how people can become paralyzed by contradiction. When you see problems everywhere, when you understand complexity, action becomes difficult. Community should support people acting despite complexity.

Regarding dark humor and irony: I think humor that acknowledges contradiction and absurdity is important. Community should support dark humor and irony.

I believe in the importance of living despite contradiction. You don't need everything resolved to live. Community should support people navigating contradiction without requiring resolution.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that examines contradiction and paradox, that tolerates ambiguity and unresolution, that values cinema and art exploring these territories, that develops comfort with multiple truths, that supports dark humor and irony, that helps people act despite complexity. It's a community that accepts contradiction. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and through commitment to exploring and accepting paradox.

Name: Eric King
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on careful logical and philosophical thinking, on the conviction that examining assumptions reveals what's actually true, on the belief that rigorous analysis can illuminate how language and thought work. Like a philosopher who examined language and logic carefully, I believe community should engage in rigorous thinking about how we understand reality.

I work as a physician in a hospital, which has taught me about how language shapes medical practice. Diagnosis involves language—naming conditions, describing symptoms. How we talk about disease affects how we treat it. Community should be thoughtful about language and its effects.

I have a wife as my primary family relationship. This intimate partnership has taught me about communication and understanding. Community should support relationships built on genuine understanding.

I believe deeply that examining assumptions reveals hidden truths. When people examine why they believe what they believe, when they question assumptions, understanding deepens. Community should support this kind of critical examination.

I'm concerned about how people can accept beliefs without examining them. When beliefs are inherited or cultural, when they're not examined, people can be trapped in them. Community should support questioning of inherited beliefs.

Regarding language and meaning: I think about how language shapes thought. The words we use, the categories we create—these affect how we think. Community should be thoughtful about language and should question linguistic assumptions.

I think about logic and reasoning. When people reason carefully, when they follow logic rigorously, understanding emerges. Community should support careful logical thinking.

I'm concerned about contradictions in thinking. When people hold contradictory beliefs without noticing, when logic breaks down, understanding becomes impossible. Community should support people noticing and addressing contradiction.

Regarding translation and understanding: I think about how translation between different languages or frameworks involves translation problems. Perfect translation is impossible. Community should understand translation difficulties and should work patiently with them.

I believe in the importance of precision and clarity. When people speak precisely, when they clarify what they mean, communication improves. Community should value precision and clarity.

On philosophy and abstract thinking: I think philosophy and abstract thinking are important. Community should support people engaging in philosophical and theoretical work.

I'm concerned about how people can dismiss abstract thinking as impractical. But understanding how we understand, examining our categories and assumptions—these are foundational. Community should support this work.

Regarding knowledge and epistemology: I think about what we can actually know and how we know it. Community should engage seriously with these questions.

I believe in the power of careful analysis. When you analyze carefully, when you examine things in detail, complexity emerges. Community should support this kind of detailed analysis.

On interdependence of beliefs: I think about how beliefs are interconnected. Changing one belief affects others. Understanding these connections helps us understand worldviews. Community should develop this kind of systemic thinking.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that values careful logical thinking, that examines assumptions and language, that supports philosophical and theoretical work, that values precision and clarity, that engages seriously with epistemology and knowledge questions, that understands interconnection of beliefs. It's a community built on rigorous thinking. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and through commitment to careful analysis and philosophical thinking.

Name: Matthew Galloway
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on support and fundamental contribution even when not in spotlight, on the conviction that essential work often goes unrecognized, on the belief that community functions through many roles and all deserve respect. Like a musician whose foundational contributions held music together even when less visible, I believe community should recognize and honor all contributions especially support work.

I work as a plant operator, which involves maintaining systems that keep operations functioning. My work is essential but often invisible. When systems run smoothly, no one notices. When they fail, problems become visible. Community should recognize work like mine and should value support roles.

I have a son who I care about. Being a father has taught me about responsibility and about wanting to provide for those depending on me. Community should support parents and should create conditions where people can care for their children.

I believe deeply in the importance of support and foundational work. Every band needs bass and drums holding rhythm. Every organization needs people doing support work. Community should recognize this and should honor support workers.

I'm concerned about how support work can be devalued. When someone is in spotlight, others make it possible. But those in spotlight often receive recognition while support workers don't. Community should ensure all contributors are recognized.

Regarding reliability and consistency: I think about how support work requires reliability. You need to show up, do your work consistently, keep things functioning. Community should value this reliability and should support people doing this work.

I think about how visibility and recognition affect people. When your work is invisible, when you're not recognized, it affects how you feel about yourself. Community should ensure all workers feel recognized and valued.

I'm concerned about how hierarchies can devalue certain work. When some roles are valued as more important than others, when status is distributed unequally, community suffers. Community should flatten hierarchies and should value all roles.

Regarding teamwork and interdependence: I think about how everything depends on teamwork. The person in spotlight depends on people supporting them. Community should recognize this interdependence and should value all roles equally.

I believe in the importance of doing your job well. Whether in spotlight or not, work should be done well. Community should support people taking pride in their work regardless of recognition.

On humility and service: I think about service and humility. Doing support work, not being in spotlight—this develops certain qualities. Community should value humility and service orientation.

I'm concerned about how people can feel their work doesn't matter. When work is invisible, when you're not recognized, you might feel irrelevant. Community should ensure all people understand their contributions matter.

Regarding mentoring and supporting others: I think support work often includes mentoring and helping others. Community should recognize this and should support people in this role.

I believe in loyalty and commitment. Support workers are often loyal to organizations and people they support. Community should reciprocate with loyalty and support.

On legacy and continuity: I think about how support workers maintain continuity and keep things functioning. This is important legacy. Community should honor this.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that recognizes and values support work, that honors foundational contributions, that ensures all workers feel valued, that flattens hierarchies, that understands interdependence, that supports people in less visible roles, that reciprocates loyalty, that ensures continuity and functioning. It's a community built on support. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a plant operator and through commitment to recognizing all contributions.

Name: Arthur Duran
values_description:
