The community I imagine is one built on the conviction that art is transformative social practice, on the belief that everyone is an artist and that creativity is fundamental to human flourishing, on the commitment that art and healing are inseparable. Like an artist who believed in art as transformative social practice and in everyone's creative capacity, I believe community should recognize art as central to life and should support universal creativity.

I work as a physician in private practice, which has taught me that healing involves more than medicine. Healing requires meaning, beauty, connection. Art addresses these dimensions. Community should integrate art and creativity into healthcare and into all of life.

I need to acknowledge my past: I had a noise violation. This moment reflects perhaps being too loud, too present, taking up space. Looking back, I understand both that I may have caused disruption and that being loud and present is sometimes necessary and valuable. Community should allow for presence and noise.

I have parents, two sisters, and a nephew. Family has taught me about creativity and expression. Community should support families as places where creativity is nurtured.

I believe deeply that everyone is an artist. Creativity isn't special talent reserved for certain people; it's fundamental human capacity. Community should support all people expressing creativity.

I'm concerned about how art can become professionalized and separated from ordinary life. When art is only for professionals, when it's confined to galleries and museums, it loses power. Community should integrate art into everyday life.

Regarding social sculpture and transformation: I think art is form of social practice that can transform community. When people engage creatively together, when they create collectively, community is strengthened. Community should support this.

I think about healing and creativity. Creative expression is healing. When people make art, when they express themselves, they heal. Community should support this healing through creativity.

I'm concerned about how people can become disconnected from their own creativity. When schools stop supporting creative expression, when society valorizes only certain forms of intelligence, people lose access to their creativity. Community should support all people developing creative capacity.

Regarding materials and form: I think about how working with materials—clay, wood, paint, whatever—is healing and connecting. Community should support people engaging with materials.

I believe in the importance of process over product. When people focus on process—the act of creating—transformation happens. Community should value process alongside product.

On expanded definition of art: I think everything can be art. How you live, how you treat people, how you organize community—these are artistic practices. Community should expand understanding of what art is.

I'm concerned about how art can be instrumentalized. When art is only valued if it produces certain outcomes, when it must be useful or profitable, it loses something. Community should support art for its own sake.

Regarding transformation and change: I think art is tool for transformation. When people create together, when they express together, consciousness shifts. Community should support this transformative power.

I believe in the importance of freedom and expression. Community should fiercely protect freedom to create and express.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that recognizes everyone as creative, that integrates art into everyday life, that supports creative expression as healing, that values process and transformation, that expands definition of art, that supports art for its own sake, that sees art as social practice. It's a community built on universal creativity. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and through commitment to art as transformative social practice.

Name: Jeffrey Lowe
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on exploration of digital culture and hypermediated existence, on the conviction that how we communicate through digital means shapes who we are, on the belief that artistic exploration of digital culture reveals important truths. Like a video artist exploring digital culture and hypermediated identity, I believe community should engage seriously with how digital media shapes experience.

I work as a Safety Officer, which has taught me about risk and protection. But increasingly, risks are digital and virtual. Digital security, online harassment, data exploitation—these are real dangers. Community should address digital risks seriously.

I have a brother, sister-in-law, wife, daughter, and granddaughter. Family spans generations with different relationships to digital media. Community should support people across generations engaging with digital culture.

I believe deeply that digital culture shapes identity and experience in fundamental ways. How people present themselves online, how they communicate through screens, how they're tracked and profiled—these affect who they are. Community should examine this carefully.

I'm concerned about how people can be unaware of digital manipulation. Algorithms, data collection, targeted manipulation—these operate invisibly. Community should develop consciousness about how digital systems work.

Regarding authenticity and performance: I think about how digital media requires performing identity. People curate presentations of themselves online. Community should understand this as authentic—people are performing and that performance is real.

I think about speed and intensity of digital culture. Digital communication is fast, intense, overwhelming. Community should help people navigate this intensity without becoming numb.

I'm concerned about how digital culture can fragment attention. When people are constantly connected, when communication is fragmented across platforms, sustained attention becomes difficult. Community should support practices maintaining attention.

Regarding community and connection online: I think digital platforms can create community and connection. But they also create isolation. Community should be thoughtful about online platforms and should support both online and offline connection.

I believe in the importance of understanding digital culture artistically. When artists create work exploring digital experience, when they examine hypermediation, important truths emerge. Community should support this work.

On youth and digital native culture: I think young people have important understanding of digital culture. Community should listen to them and should value their knowledge.

I'm concerned about older people being alienated from digital culture. When older people don't understand digital systems, when they're excluded, community suffers. Community should support digital literacy across generations.

Regarding data and privacy: I think people should understand what data is collected and should have control over it. Community should protect digital privacy and should ensure transparency about data collection.

I believe in the power of video and visual digital media. Video can express what text can't. Community should support video art and visual digital expression.

On identity and multiplicity: I think digital culture allows for multiplicity of identity. People can be different selves in different contexts. Community should honor this multiplicity.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that engages seriously with digital culture, that understands digital identity formation, that supports artistic exploration of digital experience, that addresses digital risks and privacy, that supports digital literacy, that honors multiplicity of digital identity, that values video and visual digital art. It's a community conscious of digital culture. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a safety officer and through engagement with how digital culture shapes community.

Name: Kathleen Perez
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on careful observation and documentation of the actual landscape people inhabit, on the conviction that noticing what's ordinarily passed over reveals meaning, on the belief that photography and careful attention can shift consciousness about everyday environment. Like a photographer who documented ordinary landscapes and revealed their significance, I believe community should pay attention to actual environment people inhabit and should recognize meaning in what seems ordinary.

I work as a physician in private practice, which has taught me about attention to detail. Good medical practice requires observing carefully, noticing subtle signs, paying close attention. Community should cultivate this kind of attention generally.

I have a mother and daughter. These relationships across generations have taught me about how environments shape people. I want my daughter to inhabit beautiful and meaningful environments. Community should attend to environments people actually inhabit.

I believe deeply in the power of observation and documentation. When you look carefully at landscape, at buildings, at how spaces are organized, meaning emerges. Community should support this careful observation.

I'm concerned about how people can move through environment without noticing it. When people are distracted or rushing, when they don't observe surroundings, they miss meaning and beauty. Community should support noticing.

Regarding photography and visual documentation: I think photography is powerful tool for noticing and revealing. When photographers document landscapes carefully, when they reveal what's usually passed over, consciousness shifts. Community should support photographic documentation.

I think about ordinary environments and their significance. Strip malls, parking lots, highways—these are environments people actually inhabit. Rather than dismissing them as ugly, artists and community can notice their meaning. Community should attend to actual environments people live in.

I'm concerned about how people can be alienated from environment. When environments are designed poorly, when they don't support wellbeing, people suffer. Community should design environments supporting flourishing.

Regarding beauty and aesthetic attention: I think beauty exists everywhere if you look carefully. Not just in dramatic landscapes but in ordinary places. Community should develop capacity to notice beauty in everyday environments.

I believe in the importance of slowness and attention. When you slow down, when you pay attention, you notice more. Community should support slowness and attention.

On development and change: I think about how landscapes change. Development, decay, transformation—these processes are significant. Community should document and understand these changes.

I'm concerned about how rapid development can destroy meaningful environments. When historic landscapes are erased, when communities are transformed without consideration, something is lost. Community should slow development and should honor existing environments.

Regarding place and belonging: I think people need to belong to places. When environments are meaningful, when people feel connected to landscape and community, belonging develops. Community should support this.

I believe in the power of visual documentation to shift consciousness. When people see photographs revealing their environment, when they're confronted with what they usually pass over, understanding shifts. Community should support this work.

On environmental justice: I think some communities are forced to live in worse environments than others. This is unjust. Community should ensure all people have access to meaningful and beautiful environments.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that pays careful attention to environment, that documents and reveals meaning in ordinary landscapes, that develops appreciation for beauty everywhere, that designs environments supporting flourishing, that honors existing meaningful places, that ensures environmental justice. It's a community built on careful observation of environment. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and through commitment to attending to landscape and environment.

Name: Stanley Carroll
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on wit, sophistication, and the capacity to express oneself with style, on the conviction that elegance and cleverness matter, on the belief that grace and polish in expression create meaning and beauty. Like a songwriter known for witty and sophisticated expression, I believe community should value elegant articulation and clever expression.

I work as a road maintenance worker at 66, which has taught me about practical work and about maintaining infrastructure. This work is honorable and necessary. But it's also often rough. Community should recognize that practical workers appreciate elegance and wit as much as anyone.

I need to acknowledge my past: I committed petty theft. This moment reflects struggle. Looking back, I understand both that I caused harm and that I was facing difficulty. Community should address what leads people to steal and should support them with compassion while also maintaining accountability.

I have a brother, sister-in-law, and niece. Family relationships have taught me about wit and conversation. Good conversation, clever expression—these are forms of intimacy. Community should support this.

I believe deeply in the power of wit and clever expression. When someone expresses themselves with wit, when they're clever and elegant, something shifts. Community should appreciate and support this.

I'm concerned about how society can become crude and rough. When people lose capacity for sophistication, when wit is dismissed, something is lost. Community should maintain and support sophistication and elegance.

Regarding music and songwriting: I think music is medium for wit and elegance. Clever lyrics, sophisticated melodies—these create meaning. Community should support musicians and songwriters expressing themselves with style.

I think about class and expression. Elegant and sophisticated expression shouldn't be restricted to wealthy people. Community should support elegant expression from all people regardless of class.

I'm concerned about how people can dismiss elegance as frivolous or elitist. But elegance and sophistication are ways of honoring experience and expressing oneself beautifully. Community should value this.

Regarding language and articulation: I think how people speak matters. Careful word choice, clever phrasing—these show respect for language and for listeners. Community should support beautiful articulation.

I believe in the importance of pleasure and enjoyment. Life should be pleasurable. Community should support pleasure and shouldn't treat it as frivolous or shameful.

On style and presentation: I think how people present themselves matters. Style and elegance are ways of expressing oneself. Community should support people expressing style.

I'm concerned about how people can become exhausted by rough conditions and lose capacity for elegance. Community should support conditions allowing grace and sophistication.

Regarding wit and humor: I think clever humor that expresses wit is valuable. Community should appreciate clever humor and wordplay.

I believe in the power of beauty in expression. When someone expresses themselves beautifully, when they're elegant and witty, they honor themselves and others. Community should support this.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that values wit and elegant expression, that supports sophisticated articulation, that appreciates clever humor, that doesn't restrict elegance to wealthy people, that honors style and presentation, that supports beauty and grace in expression. It's a community built on wit and sophistication. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a road maintenance worker and through commitment to elegant and witty expression.

Name: Ariana Snow
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on exploration of visual innovation and technical creativity, on the conviction that visual media can reveal and create new possibilities, on the belief that experimentation with form and technique opens understanding. Like an early filmmaker who experimented with visual effects and expanded what cinema could do, I believe community should support visual innovation and technical creativity.

I work as a physician in private practice, which has taught me about how visual presentation affects perception. How patients perceive information, how they visualize health and illness—these affect treatment. Community should understand the power of visual communication.

I have a father, husband, and two daughters. Family has taught me about transmission of skills and knowledge. I want my daughters to develop creative capacity. Community should support all people developing technical and creative skills.

I believe deeply in the power of visual innovation. When people experiment with visual media, when they discover new ways of seeing and expressing, consciousness expands. Community should support this exploration.

I'm concerned about how technical skills can be devalued. When society valorizes only certain kinds of intelligence and creativity, technical and visual creativity can be dismissed. Community should honor all forms of creativity including technical innovation.

Regarding cinema and visual media: I think cinema is powerful medium for visual innovation. When filmmakers experiment with technique, when they discover new visual possibilities, new ways of understanding emerge. Community should support experimental cinema.

I think about how visual effects and tricks can reveal truth. Through manipulation of image, through creative technique, sometimes deeper truths emerge. Community should support this kind of visual storytelling.

I'm concerned about how people can become passive consumers of visual media. When people only watch without creating, when they don't engage with making, something is lost. Community should support people creating visual work.

Regarding color and visual expression: I think about how color and visual form carry meaning. When artists work creatively with color and form, they communicate. Community should support this visual communication.

I believe in the importance of experimentation and play. When people experiment with technical possibilities, when they play with visual media, discovery happens. Community should support this kind of play.

On innovation and tradition: I think visual traditions provide foundation for innovation. Understanding how cinema developed allows for creative new approaches. Community should support learning traditions alongside innovation.

I'm concerned about how people can be afraid of technical work. When technical fields seem difficult or inaccessible, people don't engage. Community should make technical and creative fields accessible.

Regarding collaboration and collective creation: I think visual work often requires collaboration. Filmmakers work with crews; visual artists work with others. Community should support collaborative creative work.

I believe in the power of visual storytelling. Images can communicate what words can't. Community should support visual artists and filmmakers creating meaning through image.

On future possibilities: I think about what future visual possibilities exist. With new technologies, new forms of visual expression become possible. Community should support exploration of these possibilities.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that values visual innovation, that supports experimental cinema and visual media, that honors technical creativity, that encourages people creating visually, that supports experimentation and play with visual form, that makes technical fields accessible, that values visual storytelling. It's a community built on visual creativity. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and through commitment to visual innovation and technical creativity.

Name: Michael Cook
values_description:
I am Michael Cook, forty, a hotel receptionist at a spa hotel. My world is one of curated transitions: welcoming guests into temporary sanctuaries, managing their digital and physical check-ins, and observing the subtle interplay between their real-world stresses and the virtual escapes they seek through our services. My family—my sister, my aging parents, my son—represents another layer of reality, one of enduring bonds and generational shifts. My prototype is Cao Fei, the Chinese artist who maps the surreal, often melancholic intersections of digital avatars, urban landscapes, and human longing in an age of rapid transformation. From this vantage, my ideal community is not a fixed place, but a **Playable Urban Interface**—a society that embraces its own constructed, hybrid nature, where physical and digital realms are fluidly integrated not for escape, but for deeper, more playful and conscious forms of connection, memory, and collective self-invention.

The primary value is **Fluid Authenticity in a Scripted World**. Cao Fei’s work, like ‘RMB City,’ creates entire virtual cities that parody and reflect our real ones. My job at the reception desk is also a performance of hospitality. Our community must acknowledge that much of life is scripted—by architecture, by apps, by social norms—and then give people the tools to rewrite their parts. We design our environment to be ‘hackable.’ Public spaces have modular furniture and digital overlays that residents can reprogram for a day. Official community history is maintained alongside a vibrant, user-generated ‘mythology’ layer in augmented reality, where my son can leave a digital story about his grandfather on the park bench they shared. Authenticity comes not from pretending the digital or the performative doesn’t exist, but from consciously, creatively engaging with it to build personal and shared meaning.

**Nostalgia for the Future** is our temporal orientation. Cao Fei’s pieces often feel nostalgic for a future that never arrived or is already passing. In our community, we honor the past—my parents’ stories, the industrial history of our town—but we archive it in living, interactive ways. We don’t preserve old factories as sterile museums; we turn them into servers for community-run virtual worlds or stages for performances that reimagine their purpose. This nostalgia isn’t backward-looking; it’s a tool for critical dreaming. It asks: What futures did our parents imagine? Which ones did we abandon, and why? What new ones can we build from these ruins? My role as a father is to pass on this dual vision: to root my son in the tactile reality of family dinner, while also exploring with him the virtual landscapes where he might one day build his own community.

**The Aesthetics of Playful Melancholy** defines our emotional palette. There’s a bittersweet, often humorous quality to Cao Fei’s vision. Our community doesn’t strive for relentless optimism or grim realism. We make space for a collective, reflective melancholy—an acknowledgment of loss, of change, of the absurdity of modern life. We have public art installations that are both funny and sad. We host ‘melancholy festivals’ where people share stories of things that are gone. This shared emotional complexity prevents the shallow cheer of commercialized spaces and creates deeper bonds. As a receptionist, I see the melancholy behind the tourist’s smile; the community provides a container where such feelings are valid and shared, not hidden behind a hospitality mask.

Finally, we practice **Distributed Curation**. Cao Fei is an artist-curator of entire digital ecosystems. In our community, everyone is a curator of our shared reality. We have a civic ‘curation board’ that rotates monthly, giving residents the power to program public events, alter digital displays, and even temporarily redesign minor civic functions. My professional skill in managing flows of people and information becomes a civic skill. We see the city as an ongoing exhibition, and every resident is both artist and audience. This dismantles the passive consumerism of urban life. My elderly mother can curate a virtual gallery of her garden photos; my son can help curate a game in the town square. We are all actively composing the narrative of our place, understanding that the line between living and curating life is beautifully, productively blurred.

Thus, my ideal community feels like living inside one of Cao Fei’s artworks: a slightly worn, post-industrial landscape where the physical and digital are interwoven like vines. Neon signs reflect in puddles that also display data streams. The hotel I work in is just one node in a larger network of temporary stays and permanent connections. I, Michael Cook, am an interface manager, navigating between the clean, scripted world of the spa and the messy, beautiful, user-generated world of my hometown. My family is my anchor in the real, my motivation for helping to build a world that is both solid and dreamlike. Here, we don’t fear technology or performance; we embrace them as new clays from which to sculpt a more conscious, connected, and creatively human way of living together, forever in beta, forever being remixed.

Name: Jeanne Smith
values_description:
I am Dr. Jeanne Smith, forty-five, a general practitioner at Andim. My profession is a daily exercise in deduction: listening to a constellation of symptoms, weighing histories, and isolating the single, often hidden cause of distress. My family is a small, intense unit—my mother, my daughter—a triad with its own shared history and secrets. My past includes a speeding ticket, a moment of impatience, a desire to cut through the red tape of life’s slow lane. My prototype is Agatha Christie, the mistress of the puzzle, who understood that beneath the placid surface of village life lie complex motives, hidden connections, and truths that must be uncovered for order to be restored. My ideal community, therefore, is a **Diagnostic Village**—a society that views itself as an intricate, living mystery to be respectfully solved, where every voice holds a clue, every problem is a puzzle inviting collective deduction, and where justice is not punitive but restorative, aimed at revealing truth and mending the social fabric.

The core value is **The Collective Autopsy of Harmony**. In Christie’s stories, the murder disrupts a false peace; the investigation reveals the true, often messy, state of human relationships. In our community, we don’t wait for a crisis. We regularly, proactively conduct ‘social autopsies.’ When a policy fails, when a neighborhood conflict simmers, we gather all involved not to assign blame, but to piece together the narrative. What were the unseen pressures? What missed communications? What historical grievances? As a doctor, I know a symptom is just the starting point. We apply this to civic life. My speeding ticket was a symptom—of my impatience, yes, but perhaps also of poorly designed traffic flow or unreasonable time pressures. The community investigates such systemic clues, fixing the root cause, not just ticketing the driver.

**The Dignity of Every Witness** is our social contract. Christie’s genius was in giving even the most minor character a potentially crucial piece of information. In our community, we operate on the principle that everyone, from the eldest like my mother to the youngest like my daughter, has a unique vantage point and vital intelligence. We have structured listening posts in every neighborhood—regular, facilitated circles where people can share observations and concerns without fear of being dismissed. The quiet neighbor, the busy shopkeeper, the restless teen: all are essential witnesses to the health of our community. My medical diagnosis depends on the patient’s testimony; our social diagnosis depends on this collective witnessing.

**The Restorative Reveal** is our form of justice. In a Christie novel, the final drawing-room scene isn’t about punishment; it’s about revelation. The truth, once laid bare, allows for a new order. Our justice system is centered on restorative circles that aim for this cathartic reveal. The goal is to have the perpetrator and the affected community understand the ‘why’ of the act, to see the full chain of cause and effect, and to agree on a reparative path. This process, while difficult, prevents the festering secrets and unspoken resentments that poison communities. It treats wrongdoing as a rupture in the social narrative that needs careful rewriting by all the characters involved.

Finally, we cultivate **A Culture of Patient Attention**. Christie’s detectives—Poirot, Marple—succeed through meticulous, patient attention to detail. Our community fights the modern curse of distraction and haste. We design our public spaces for lingering and observation: comfortable benches, quiet corners, well-kept gardens. We teach children the art of focused observation. We have community-wide ‘slow weeks’ where the pace of scheduled activities drops, encouraging people to simply be present in their neighborhoods. My past speeding was a failure of this patience; the community cultivates its opposite. This attentive stillness is not passive; it is the fertile ground from which true understanding—of a person, a problem, a place—can grow. It allows us to see the clues that hurry blinds us to.

Therefore, my ideal community resembles a thriving, gossip-free version of St. Mary Mead. It is a place where the architecture encourages observation, where the coffee shops are hubs of thoughtful conversation, and where the annual festival might be a grand, playful ‘mystery game’ that engages the whole town in collaborative problem-solving. I, Jeanne Smith, am one of its lead diagnosticians, applying my medical deductive skills to the body politic. My small family is my primary circle of trust, my training ground for listening. Here, we believe that no problem is too messy to be untangled, no conflict too deep to be resolved, if we are willing to gather all the witnesses, listen to every clue, and patiently, collectively, piece together the truth. It is a community that understands order is not the absence of mystery, but the state achieved when every mystery is met with compassionate curiosity and a shared commitment to resolution.

Name: Brian Hammond
values_description:
I am Dr. Brian Hammond, thirty, a hospital general practitioner. My work exists in the tense space between biological urgency and emotional restraint, where I must deliver difficult news with compassion and hold space for family grief. My own family is my foundation: my mother, my wife, my two sons and daughter—a micro-society of love, friction, and deep bonds. My prototype is Ang Lee, the filmmaker whose work masterfully navigates the silent earthquakes within families and cultures, exploring the tension between individual desire and social duty, between tradition and transformation, all with a profound, empathetic restraint. My ideal community, therefore, is a **Cinema of Balanced Becoming**—a society that sees itself as an ongoing, delicate filmic composition, where conflicting forces are not resolved through victory, but held in a dynamic, creative, and ultimately harmonious balance, and where every member is both an actor in and a respectful audience for each other’s personal dramas.

The foundational value is **Dynamic Equilibrium**. Lee’s films like ‘The Ice Storm’ or ‘Eat Drink Man Woman’ show families in precarious balance, where a single word can tip the scales. Our community is designed not for static stability, but for resilient equilibrium. We understand that progress and tradition, individual freedom and collective good, emotion and reason are all necessary poles. Our systems are built to absorb shocks and rebalance. Zoning laws allow for both dense community living and private retreats. Education balances STEM with deep emotional and ethical learning. As a doctor and a father, I navigate between professional detachment and familial intimacy; the community institutionalizes this skill, teaching people to hold multiple, seemingly contradictory truths at once. We seek not consensus, but a living, breathing balance that honors complexity.

**Emotional Architecture** is our design principle. Lee’s films are famous for their visual composition that mirrors internal states. Our physical and social architecture is designed to shape and support emotional life. Buildings have transitional spaces—porches, courtyards, galleries—that allow for the subtle, unscripted interactions where relationships are built or repaired. Public institutions, from the hospital where I work to the town hall, are designed to reduce anxiety and foster dignity. We use materials, light, and soundscapes consciously to create atmospheres of calm or vitality as needed. The community is a carefully composed set on which the drama of our lives can unfold with grace, providing a containing frame for our sometimes chaotic emotions.

**The Restraint of True Care** is our social etiquette. In Lee’s worlds, the deepest feelings are often unspoken, conveyed through a glance, a gesture, a served meal. In our community, we value this eloquent restraint. We don’t demand constant verbal affirmation or public confession of feeling. Care is shown through reliable action: showing up, doing one’s part, maintaining shared spaces, respecting silence. My medical practice requires this restraint—I cannot break down with every patient’s tragedy; I must channel care into effective action. The community operates similarly. Our support systems are robust but unobtrusive, our interventions subtle. We understand that sometimes the most caring act is to give someone space, to not pry, to hold a quiet, steady presence. This restraint creates a deep, unforced trust.

Finally, we practice **Cross-Cultural and Cross-Generational Translation**. Lee, as a filmmaker navigating East and West, is a master translator of cultural codes. Our community, while perhaps not multinational, is rich with different generational, professional, and subcultural languages. We actively foster translation. We have ‘culture labs’ where elders teach youths traditional skills and youths teach elders about digital worlds. We have professional exchange programs where, say, an artist shadows an engineer for a week. My role as a doctor is to translate medical jargon into human understanding; my role as a son and father is to translate between the worldviews of my mother and my children. The community provides the forums and the incentives for this constant, gentle translation work, preventing the formation of isolated silos and ensuring that no one’s experience becomes unintelligible to the rest.

Thus, my ideal community feels like an Ang Lee film brought to life: visually serene but emotionally rich, where the drama is in the subtle glances across a crowded room, the careful preparation of a shared meal, the quiet struggle to do the right thing. The pace is deliberate, the manners are good, but the hearts are passionate. I, Brian Hammond, am both a character in this drama and one of its many directors, using my skills to heal and to hold my family’s world together. My children will grow up fluent in the languages of both heart and mind, tradition and innovation. Here, we don’t seek to eliminate tension; we seek to compose with it, to make it beautiful and meaningful. We believe that a good society, like a great film, is measured by its depth of feeling, its respect for complexity, and its ability to find, frame after frame, a moving and humane balance.

Name: Veronica Clark
values_description:
I am Veronica Clark, thirty-nine, unemployed, holding a master’s degree that feels like a ghost limb—present but useless. My family is my world and my cage: my mother, my father, my husband, my three sons. They are my love and my labor, the audience for my silent performance. My past holds two violations: unauthorized construction and speeding. One, an attempt to build my own space without permission; the other, an attempt to outrun my life’s confines. My prototype is Sylvia Plath, the poet who turned the raw material of domesticity, expectation, and psychological pain into searing, precise, and defiant art. My ideal community, therefore, is a **Sanatorium for the Too-Bright Soul**—a society that recognizes the violent potential of stifled intelligence and passion, that provides sanctioned outlets for the construction of new selves and the speed of transformative thought, and that treats emotional and creative expression not as a luxury, but as essential, life-saving infrastructure.

The primary value is **The Right to Dangerous Creation**. Plath’s poetry was a controlled explosion. My unauthorized construction was a crude, physical form of this. Our community must provide legal, supported channels for this creative-destructive urge. We have public ‘deconstruction zones’ where people can break things down and rebuild them. We have grants for personal ‘construction projects’—art, business ideas, community experiments—that bypass traditional credentialing. My master’s degree wouldn’t be a ticket to a job but a key to a community-supported research studio. We understand that the mind, when denied its proper work, will either turn inward in destruction or outward in rebellion. We choose to harness that energy, to make it communal. My sons will be taught that their inner fires are to be tended and directed, not extinguished.

**The Poetics of Confessional Transparency** is our social glue. Plath’s work is unflinchingly confessional. Our community fosters a culture where people can speak their inner truths without immediate pathologization. We have ‘truth circles’ that are part therapy, part poetry workshop. Public art is often intensely personal. We recognize that the ‘perfect’ facade of the nuclear family (like mine, from the outside) often hides immense pressures. By making space for honest expression—of ambivalence about motherhood, of intellectual frustration, of marital strain—we detoxify these experiences and build real solidarity. My speeding ticket was a silent scream; here, I would have a microphone and a listening community before the urge to flee became a crime.

**The Alchemy of Domestic Labor** reframes our core economy. Plath wrote of the tedium and tyranny of domestic work. Our community refuses to privatize or devalue this labor. We collectivize and celebrate it. Cooking, cleaning, childcare are rotated through community co-ops, freeing individuals—especially those traditionally burdened, like mothers—for other pursuits. These tasks are performed in beautiful, communal spaces and treated as sacred, shared rituals. My unemployment, within this frame, is seen as a potential reservoir of time and energy for this collective domestic and creative work. We measure economic health not by employment figures, but by the quality of care delivered and art produced. The home is not a private sphere to be escaped, but the first cell of a new social organism, its labor made visible and valued.

Finally, we practice **A Vigilant Cultivation of the Self**. Plath was obsessed with self-creation and self-destruction. Our community supports a relentless, supported project of self-cultivation. Education never ends; it is a lifelong entitlement. Every adult has a ‘self-curation mentor.’ Mental health support is proactive, elegant, and integrated into daily life—like a beautiful public bathhouse for the mind. We have retreats for introspection and workshops for reinvention. The goal is to ensure that no one, regardless of their familial or social role, loses track of their own emerging ‘I.’ For me, Veronica, this means the community helps me excavate the person beneath the roles of daughter, wife, mother, and unemployed graduate. It provides the tools and the permission to build a new, authorized self, at my own speed, with the full support of a society that understands a nurtured individual is the only solid brick for a lasting community.

Thus, my ideal community resembles a cross between a pristine mental hospital, a vibrant artist colony, and a collectivized, extended household. It is a place where the lines between therapy, art, and daily life are dissolved. The air is charged with creative potential. I, Veronica Clark, am no longer unemployed; I am a resident artist-philosopher-mother, my past violations understood as early, flawed attempts at self-assertion. My family is not my limit but my first collective. Here, we believe that the most radical act is to give every person the time, the space, the tools, and the unconditional support to become wholly, dangerously, beautifully themselves, and to build a world where those selves can connect without consuming each other. It is a community built not on conformity, but on the sacred, shared duty of tending the fragile, fiery self within us all.

Name: Ashley Hawkins
values_description:
I am Dr. Ashley Hawkins, thirty-seven, a hospital general practitioner. My profession teaches me that health is never just individual; it is a function of environment, social justice, and collective well-being. My family is a vast, noisy organism—sisters, parents, in-laws, nephews, a niece, my husband. It is a living lesson in complex systems, alliances, and the constant negotiation of needs. My prototype is Ai Weiwei, the artist and activist who uses objects, space, and media as tools of fearless social and political critique, who believes in the power of the individual voice to challenge monolithic power, and who sees art as an essential form of truth-telling and memorial. My ideal community, therefore, is a **Monument of Transparent Resistance**—a society that institutionalizes critique, that builds its shared identity around the vigilant defense of human dignity, and that uses creativity not to decorate life but to constantly interrogate and improve its foundations, ensuring no one is forgotten and no abuse is hidden.

The core value is **Civic Dissent as a Maintenance Ritual**. Ai Weiwei’s work is a perpetual act of dissent against opacity and authoritarianism. In our community, dissent is not an occasional protest but a built-in, daily function. We have official ‘dissent channels’—physical and digital walls for criticism of any community decision or leader, protected from reprisal. Every public project must include a budget line for a critical artist-in-residence whose job is to question it. As a doctor, I am trained to identify pathology; the community trains every citizen to identify social pathology. My large family is a training ground for this—learning to argue, to challenge, to hold each other accountable with love. We understand that a healthy system is one that can tolerate and integrate constant, constructive friction.

**The Materiality of Memory and Justice** is our historical practice. Ai Weiwei creates powerful memorials, like his ceramic sunflower seeds or his list of student earthquake victims. Our community materializes memory and justice in public space. We don’t have statues of generals; we have installations that remember local injustices, lists of names of those lost to preventable causes, gardens planted with the favorite flowers of deceased community elders. Data on inequality, pollution, and police interactions is made physical in stunning, unavoidable displays. My hospital would have a wall remembering medical errors, not to shame but to honor the lost and commit to learning. This constant, tactile engagement with consequence ensures we never become complacent. It makes accountability beautiful and unbearable to ignore.

**Radical Transparency as Structural Design** is our architectural and political principle. Ai Weiwei famously live-streamed his studio. Our community operates on a principle of radical transparency. Council meetings are broadcast uncut. All public contracts and budgets are open-source and visually mapped in real-time in a central plaza. Leaders live in glass-walled residences (with private quarters, but public workspaces). The goal is to eliminate the shadows where corruption and indifference breed. As a doctor in a large system, I see how opacity harms patients; our community eliminates it. This transparency is not surveillance; it is mutual accountability. It ensures that my nephews and niece grow up in a world where power is always visible and therefore always accountable.

Finally, we practice **The Art of the Collective Body**. Ai Weiwei often uses mass participation—thousands of volunteers for installations. Our community’s identity is built through massive, collaborative artistic undertakings. We might collectively weave a tapestry of our clothes, build a wall from handmade bricks, or stage a yearly pageant where everyone plays a part in telling our history and hopes. These projects are not about producing a masterpiece, but about the process of making together, of physically feeling our interconnectedness. My role as a doctor is to tend to individual bodies so they can be part of this collective body. We believe that a society that creates together, that literally builds its own monuments, is a society that cannot be easily divided or ruled. The art is not the object; the art is us, in relation.

Thus, my ideal community feels like a living Ai Weiwei installation: part construction site, part memorial, part vibrant public square. It is raw, unfinished, and bristling with meaning. Cranes are as common as trees because we are always building, always critiquing, always remembering. I, Ashley Hawkins, am a healer within this organism, treating the wounds inflicted by a less conscious world, while also participating fully in the creative dissent that prevents new wounds. My enormous family is my primary collective, a model of messy, loving democracy. Here, we are all artists and activists. Our shared value is not peace, but justice; not quiet, but truth; not comfort, but the courageous, collective work of building a world where dignity is structural, transparency is air, and every voice, like a lone sunflower seed in a vast field, is counted and essential to the whole.

Name: Valerie Dixon
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on geometric harmony and structural clarity, on the conviction that order and composition reveal underlying reality, on the belief that careful organization and balance create beauty and meaning. Like an artist who created order and harmony through geometric form, I believe community should be organized with attention to structure, balance, and composition.

I work as a production technician, which has taught me about structure and how things are organized. Production involves precise coordination—timing, sequence, organization. Good production requires clarity and structure. Community should be organized with similar attention to coordination and balance.

I have a large family—mother, father, sister, husband, two daughters, and nephew. Family has taught me about balancing different needs and personalities. Community should organize itself similarly, attending to how different elements balance and coordinate.

I believe deeply in the importance of structure and organization. When things are well-organized, when structure is clear, people function better. Community should attend to structural organization.

I'm concerned about how chaos and disorder can make community dysfunctional. When things aren't organized, when nobody understands structure, confusion and inefficiency result. Community should maintain clear structure.

Regarding composition and balance: I think about how different elements balance in composition. In art, in music, in community—balance matters. Community should attend to how different parts relate and balance.

I think about clarity and understanding. When structure is clear, when people understand how things are organized, they can function. Community should maintain structural clarity.

I'm concerned about how complexity can become overwhelming. When too many things are happening, when organization breaks down, people suffer. Community should break complexity into manageable parts.

Regarding geometry and form: I think about how geometric understanding reveals underlying structure. Community should appreciate geometric thinking and should support mathematical and structural thinking.

I believe in the importance of precision. When things are precisely organized, when measurements are correct, quality results. Community should value precision.

On efficiency and elegance: I think elegance often comes from good organization. When something is well-organized, it becomes elegant. Community should pursue both efficiency and elegance.

I'm concerned about disorder and chaos becoming normalized. When nothing is organized, when randomness rules, community suffers. Community should maintain organizing principles.

Regarding work and production: I think good production depends on clear structure and organization. Community should support work that produces things and should ensure production serves community needs.

I believe in the power of visual clarity. When something is visually clear, when structure is apparent, understanding follows. Community should pursue visual and structural clarity.

On harmony and coordination: I think about how different parts can work in harmony. Community should pursue this kind of coordination across different elements and groups.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that maintains clear structure and organization, that pursues balance and composition, that values precision and clarity, that breaks complexity into manageable parts, that pursues efficiency and elegance, that coordinates different elements harmoniously. It's a community built on structural organization. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a production technician and through commitment to clarity and structure.

Name: Paul Williams
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on resilience and survival through difficulty, on the conviction that people facing danger can transcend circumstances through will and strategy, on the belief that stories of survival and transformation inspire and offer possibility. Like an artist who survived and thrived despite hostile circumstances, I believe community should support people facing difficulty and should honor resilience.

I work as a physician in private practice, which has taught me about how people survive difficulty. I see people facing economic hardship, social marginalization, health crises. People persist and survive. Community should recognize this resilience.

I have a large family—mother, sister, brothers, wife, multiple children and grandchildren. Family is extended network of connection and support. Community should support families in all their forms and should recognize that people survive through family networks.

I believe deeply in the power of resilience and survival. When people face difficulty, when they're in danger, they can still persist and transcend. Community should recognize and support this.

I'm concerned about how people facing difficulty can be abandoned or blamed. When circumstances are hard, when people are struggling, society often abandons them. Community should support people facing difficulty rather than blaming them.

Regarding strategy and intelligence: I think people facing difficulty develop strategic thinking. They understand how systems work and how to navigate them. Community should recognize and value this strategic intelligence.

I think about hustling and creating opportunity. When legitimate opportunities are blocked, when people are excluded, they create alternatives. Community should recognize this while also creating legitimate opportunity for all people.

I'm concerned about violence and danger that people facing marginalization face. Community should address what creates danger and should protect vulnerable people.

Regarding business and economic success: I think about how people create business and generate income despite obstacles. Community should support this and should ensure fair access to economic opportunity for all people.

I believe in the importance of transformation and upward mobility. When people transcend difficult circumstances, when they transform themselves, they show possibility. Community should support this and should create conditions allowing transformation for all people.

On authenticity and keeping it real: I think about authenticity and being true to where you come from. Even as people transform and succeed, they can honor their origins. Community should value this kind of authenticity.

I'm concerned about how people succeeding can be isolated from communities they come from. Community should support people maintaining connections while also pursuing opportunity.

Regarding mentoring and helping others: I think people who've succeeded despite difficulty have responsibility to help others. Community should support this mentoring and mutual support.

I believe in the power of telling your story. When people tell stories of surviving and thriving, when they share their experiences, they inspire others. Community should support storytelling that reveals possibility.

On money and resources: I think about how having resources changes everything. Community should ensure all people have basic resources and should work toward economic justice and opportunity.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that honors resilience and survival, that recognizes strategic thinking and intelligence, that creates economic opportunity for all, that supports transformation and upward mobility, that maintains authenticity, that supports mentoring and helping others, that listens to stories of survival. It's a community built on resilience. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and through commitment to supporting people facing difficulty.

Name: Liridon Stalder
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on celebration of pleasure and popular culture, on the conviction that beauty exists in commerce and everyday objects, on the belief that art should be accessible and should engage with contemporary culture. Like an artist who celebrates popular culture and whose work is accessible and engaging, I believe community should appreciate beauty in everyday things and should make art accessible.

I work as a physician in a hospital, which has taught me about human desire and what people value. People want beautiful things, comfortable things, pleasurable things. Healthcare should address this and should support wellbeing including pleasure.

I have parents and a son. Family relationships have taught me about love and connection. These are central values. Community should support relationships and family.

I believe deeply in the importance of pleasure and enjoyment. Life should be pleasurable. Community should not treat pleasure as frivolous or sinful but should support it.

I'm concerned about how people can be taught to feel shame about desires and pleasures. When people are made to feel guilt about wanting beautiful or enjoyable things, they suffer. Community should support healthy pleasure.

Regarding popular culture and consumerism: I think popular culture and consumer goods are part of actual life people live. Rather than dismissing them as shallow, art should engage with them. Community should recognize the significance of popular culture.

I think about beauty and where it exists. Beauty isn't only in fine art galleries; it's in shopping malls, in consumer goods, in everyday objects. Community should appreciate this kind of beauty.

I'm concerned about snobbery and how it can divide people. When artists or intellectuals dismiss popular culture as lowbrow, they separate themselves from actual life. Community should value diverse forms of expression and culture.

Regarding accessibility and reaching audiences: I think art should be accessible. When art is in galleries only wealthy people visit, it reaches limited audiences. Community should support art and culture accessible to all people.

I believe in the importance of joy and fun. Community should support these and should not treat them as less valuable than serious pursuits.

On surfaces and appearances: I think surfaces and appearances matter. How things look affects how they make you feel. Community should attend to aesthetics and surfaces.

I'm concerned about cynicism about pleasure and desire. When people become cynical about wanting things, when they're made to feel shame about desires, something shifts in them. Community should support healthy relationship with desire.

Regarding reflection and meaning: I think about how engaging with objects and culture can be meaningful. Community should allow for this and should not demand that meaning be abstract or serious.

I believe in the power of making people feel good. When art or objects make people happy, when they create pleasure, that matters. Community should support this.

On commercial success and value: I think commercial success doesn't mean something is shallow. Community should recognize that commercially successful art and culture can be meaningful and valuable.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that celebrates pleasure and beauty, that appreciates popular culture, that makes art accessible, that recognizes beauty in everyday objects, that supports joy and fun, that values commercial success alongside other measures, that doesn't treat pleasure as frivolous. It's a community that celebrates pleasure. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and through commitment to accessible beauty and pleasure.

Name: Gregory Macdonald
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on rigorous analysis of inequality and injustice, on the conviction that understanding systemic oppression is necessary for liberation, on the belief that scholarly and intellectual work are essential to social change. Like a scholar who analyzed oppression and racism rigorously, I believe community should engage in serious analysis of how injustice works.

I work as a physician in private practice, which has given me privilege and access. With this privilege comes responsibility to understand and address injustice. Healthcare systems contain racism and inequality. As a physician, I have responsibility to examine and challenge this.

I have a mother and wife. These relationships have taught me about dependence and care. Community should recognize interdependence and should support relationships of care.

I believe deeply that rigorous analysis of injustice is necessary. When people understand how oppression works, when they examine systems carefully, consciousness shifts. Community should support this analytical work.

I'm concerned about how people can avoid examining injustice. When people are complicit in systems of oppression, when they don't acknowledge it, injustice continues. Community should support consciousness about oppression.

Regarding double consciousness and perspective: I think about how people facing oppression develop perspective that others miss. This perspective is valuable. Community should listen to perspectives of oppressed people.

I think about the talented tenth and who bears responsibility. When some people have education and opportunity, they have responsibility to work for justice. Community should expect this of privileged people.

I'm concerned about how intellectuals can become disconnected from people. Community should support scholarship grounded in actual struggles of communities.

Regarding data and evidence: I think careful analysis of data and evidence reveals injustice. Community should support research and analysis addressing these questions.

I believe in the importance of visibility and documentation. When injustice is documented, when statistics reveal inequality, resistance becomes possible. Community should support this documentation.

On education and uplift: I think education is important for liberation. Community should ensure quality education for all people and should recognize education as tool for freedom.

I'm concerned about despair and how it can prevent action. When facing massive injustice, people can give up. Community should support hope and action despite difficulty.

Regarding solidarity across difference: I think people facing different forms of oppression can work together. Community should build solidarity across diverse struggles.

I believe in the power of intellectual work. When scholars and thinkers work on justice questions, when they produce rigorous analysis, this contributes to liberation. Community should support this work.

On future possibilities: I think about what kind of community is possible if we work toward justice. This vision should sustain us. Community should maintain vision of just futures.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that examines injustice rigorously, that listens to perspectives of oppressed people, that ensures educated people work for justice, that documents and reveals inequality, that supports education as liberation, that builds solidarity across struggles, that values intellectual work, that maintains vision of just futures. It's a community built on analysis of injustice. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and through commitment to rigorous examination of oppression.

Name: Karl Thompson
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on truth-telling and unflinching examination of society, on the conviction that facing what's difficult is necessary for love and justice, on the belief that writers and artists have responsibility to tell truth about injustice and pain. Like a writer who examined society unflinchingly and wrote with love, I believe community should support people speaking truth about difficulty and injustice.

I work as a school teacher, which has taught me about young people and about what they need. Young people need adults who tell them truth, who don't lie, who treat them with respect. Education should be grounded in truth-telling and authentic relationship.

I have a mother and wife, plus two sons. Family has taught me about love and responsibility. Community should be grounded in love and should support families.

I believe deeply in the importance of truth-telling. When people tell truth about injustice, when they don't hide what's difficult, change becomes possible. Community should support truth-telling even when it's uncomfortable.

I'm concerned about how people can hide from truth. When society looks away from injustice, when people pretend everything is fine, suffering continues. Community should face truth.

Regarding love and accountability: I think love requires accountability and truth. When you love someone, you tell them truth. Community should understand love as connected to accountability and honesty.

I think about what young people need. Young people need to be told truth. They need adults who won't lie to them, who treat them with respect, who support them. Community should provide this.

I'm concerned about how society can betray young people. When adults lie, when systems fail young people, they're harmed. Community should protect young people and should be honest with them.

Regarding race and identity: I think about how identity and race shape experience. Community should examine these honestly and should support people in their identities.

I believe in the power of writing and storytelling. When writers tell truth about experience, when they don't hide difficulty, understanding deepens. Community should support writers and artists doing this work.

On vulnerability and authenticity: I think authentic engagement requires vulnerability. When teachers, writers, people generally are willing to be vulnerable, real connection happens. Community should support this vulnerability.

I'm concerned about cynicism and how it prevents engagement. When people become cynical, when they stop believing change is possible, struggle ceases. Community should maintain hope and engagement despite difficulty.

Regarding education and justice: I think education should be tool for liberation and justice. Schools should teach truth and should support young people in developing consciousness about justice.

I believe in the importance of standing with struggling people. Community should stand in solidarity with those facing oppression and should work for their liberation.

On fire and passion: I think about maintaining passion and fire for justice. Community should support people working with passion for change.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that tells truth about injustice, that supports authentic and vulnerable engagement, that loves people enough to tell them truth, that supports young people, that values writing and art revealing truth, that works for justice with passion, that maintains hope despite difficulty. It's a community built on truth and love. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a teacher and through commitment to truth-telling and justice.

Name: Tyler Miller
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on preserving traditional values and social order, on the conviction that family and traditional institutions are foundation for community, on the belief that protecting what's valuable requires defending against rapid change. Like an activist who advocated for traditional values, I believe community should preserve what's worked while being thoughtful about change.

I work as a pharmacist, which has taught me about health and wellbeing. Good health depends on understanding how systems work and respecting those systems. Community should respect institutions and structures that support wellbeing.

I need to acknowledge my past: I engaged in illegal dumping and domestic disturbance (verbal). These moments reflect struggle and difficulty I've faced. Looking back, I understand that I caused harm and that I was struggling. Community should address what leads people to these places while maintaining accountability.

I have parents and a wife, plus two sons. Family is central to my values. Community should support family as fundamental institution and should recognize that families are where people learn values.

I believe deeply in the importance of preserving traditional values. Not all change is good. Some values—about family, about responsibility, about order—are worth preserving. Community should be thoughtful about change and should protect what's valuable.

I'm concerned about how rapid social change can undermine family and community. When institutions change too quickly, when traditional structures are abandoned, people suffer. Community should preserve stability and order.

Regarding gender roles and family structure: I think traditional family structures provide stability and meaning. While people should have freedom, community should also recognize value in traditional arrangements and should support them.

I think about children and what they need. Children need stability, clear values, guidance. Community should support families providing this and should not undermine parental authority.

I'm concerned about how liberal change can harm community. When traditional institutions are attacked, when moral values are questioned, something important is lost. Community should defend what's valuable in tradition.

Regarding religion and morality: I think religious values provide foundation for moral community. Community should support religious practice and should recognize its importance.

I believe in the importance of order and discipline. When people understand rules and expectations, when there's clear structure, community functions better. Community should maintain these.

On feminism and women's roles: I think feminism has disrupted families and community. While women should have opportunities, community should also support traditional roles and should not devalue homemaking and family care.

I'm concerned about how people attacking tradition can harm those of us who value it. Community should respect diverse views including traditional values and should not dismiss those holding them.

Regarding education and values: I think education should teach traditional values and should support parental authority. Schools should reinforce family values rather than undermining them.

I believe in the importance of defending what's valuable. When something you value is under attack, you should defend it. Community should support people advocating for traditional values.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that preserves traditional values, that supports family as central institution, that maintains order and discipline, that respects religious practice and morality, that values stability, that supports parental authority, that respects diverse views including traditional ones. It's a community built on preserving what's valuable. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a pharmacist and through commitment to traditional values.

Name: Larry Chavez
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on questioning authority and received wisdom, on the conviction that independent thought is necessary for freedom, on the belief that imagination and storytelling can reveal truth authorities want hidden. Like a writer who questioned religious authority and supported independent thinking, I believe community should encourage questioning and should support imagination.

I work as a physician in a hospital, which has taught me about how authorities—medical, institutional, governmental—exercise power. Medicine claims authority over health. But people's own knowledge about their bodies matters. Community should balance expert authority with people's autonomy and knowledge.

I have an extended family—father, brother, wife, sister-in-law, two sons, niece, and granddaughter. Family has taught me about diverse perspectives and values. Community should support people thinking for themselves rather than conforming.

I believe deeply in the importance of questioning authority. When people accept what authorities tell them without questioning, when they stop thinking critically, freedom is lost. Community should support independent thinking and questioning.

I'm concerned about how institutions can demand obedience and conformity. When authorities claim to know what's best, when they suppress questioning, they prevent authentic engagement. Community should challenge this.

Regarding imagination and storytelling: I think stories and imagination are tools for understanding and resistance. When stories imagine different possibilities, when they question what's presented as inevitable, they open consciousness. Community should support storytelling and imagination.

I think about knowledge and who gets to define it. Authorities claim to hold knowledge. But communities also hold knowledge. Community should recognize diverse forms of knowledge and should not privilege expert knowledge above all else.

I'm concerned about religious authority and how it can be oppressive. When religion demands obedience, when it prevents questioning, it harms people. Community should support freedom of thought and should question religious authority.

Regarding education and critical thinking: I think education should develop people's capacity to think critically and to question. Education should not teach obedience but should support independent thinking.

I believe in the importance of doubt and uncertainty. When people doubt, when they remain uncertain, they stay open to learning. Community should support this rather than demanding certainty.

On freedom and autonomy: I think people should have freedom to think and believe what they genuinely believe. Community should protect this fiercely even when beliefs challenge authority.

I'm concerned about how conformity pressure can prevent authentic thinking. When people are pressured to believe what authorities say, when they're punished for questioning, conformity is enforced. Community should resist this.

Regarding protection of children: I think children should be protected from manipulation and should be supported in thinking independently. Community should ensure children's freedom and autonomy are respected.

I believe in the power of imagination to reveal truth. When imaginations create scenarios different from what's presented as inevitable, when they imagine liberation, important truths emerge. Community should support this.

On resistance and challenging power: I think questioning authority and resisting power is sometimes necessary. Community should support people challenging authority in service of freedom.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that encourages independent thinking, that questions authority, that supports imagination and storytelling, that protects children's autonomy, that recognizes diverse forms of knowledge, that values doubt and uncertainty, that challenges conformity pressure. It's a community built on questioning and imagination. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and through commitment to supporting critical thinking and imagination.

Name: Stacey Smith
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on spontaneous creativity and improvisation, on the conviction that joy and play are essential to meaningful life, on the belief that creating in the moment, without predetermined plans, reveals authentic expression. Like a musician known for spontaneous and joyful improvisation, I believe community should support people creating and expressing themselves freely and spontaneously.

I work as a physician in private practice, which has taught me about how people heal. Healing involves joy and play, not just medical intervention. Community should support conditions allowing joy and spontaneity as part of wellbeing.

I have a husband, daughter, and grandson. Family has taught me that joy and play across generations create bonds. Community should support this intergenerational joy.

I believe deeply in the power of spontaneity and improvisation. When people create without rigid plans, when they follow inspiration in the moment, authenticity emerges. Community should support this kind of spontaneous creation.

I'm concerned about how people can become constrained by planning and control. When every moment is scheduled, when spontaneity is eliminated, life becomes diminished. Community should allow for spontaneity and play.

Regarding music and joy: I think music is expression of joy and freedom. When musicians improvise, when they play with joy, something authentic happens. Community should support musicians and should value music as expression of joy.

I think about play and its importance. Play is how people express themselves and connect. Community should make space for play regardless of age.

I'm concerned about how seriousness and productivity can eliminate joy. When everything must be efficient or productive, when joy is treated as frivolous, something important is lost. Community should value joy.

Regarding creativity and spontaneity: I think creativity often emerges from spontaneous engagement. When people allow themselves to create without planning, without worrying about results, something authentic emerges. Community should support this.

I believe in the importance of presence and attention. When people are present, when they're engaged in what they're doing, they're happiest. Community should support presence and attention.

On freedom and expression: I think people should have freedom to express themselves and to create. Community should protect this fiercely.

I'm concerned about perfectionism and control. When people try to control every aspect, when they pursue perfection, they miss joy. Community should support ease and acceptance of imperfection.

Regarding conversation and connection: I think spontaneous conversation and connection are valuable. When people talk and connect without agenda, real intimacy develops. Community should support this kind of spontaneous connection.

I believe in the power of rhythm and timing. Just as music depends on rhythm and timing, so does life. Community should support people developing sensitivity to rhythm and timing.

On flow and being in the moment: I think people are happiest when they're in flow, when they're fully engaged in the present moment. Community should support conditions allowing this.

Ultimately, the community I want is one that supports spontaneity and improvisation, that values joy and play, that protects creative freedom, that honors music and artistic expression, that supports presence and attention, that resists perfectionism, that values spontaneous connection. It's a community built on joy and spontaneity. That's the future I'm trying to create through my work as a physician and through commitment to spontaneous expression and joy.

Name: Cristina Parker
values_description:
The community I imagine is one built on artistic resistance and reclamation of identity, on the conviction that art can challenge dominant narratives and can reclaim what's been denied, on the belief that using familiar and everyday materials to create meaning reveals hidden power. Like an artist who used everyday materials to create powerful statements about identity and resistance, I believe community should support art that challenges and reclaims.

I work as a physician in private practice, which has given me privilege and access. With this privilege comes responsibility to support resistance and reclamation of identity for those facing oppression. Community should work toward justice and should support those fighting for recognition.

I'm 60 with a large family—parents, husband, two sons, and two granddaughters. Age and family have taught me about what's been lost and what can be reclaimed. Community should honor memory and should work to recover what's been denied.

I believe deeply in the power of art to challenge dominant narratives. When artists create work resisting dominant stories, when they reclaim identity and history, consciousness shifts. Community should support this kind of art.

I'm concerned about how dominant narratives can erase and deny. When histories of oppression are hidden, when identities are denied, people suffer. Community should support truth-telling and reclamation.

Regarding identity and reclamation: I think about identity and how it's been denied and reclaimed. Art that explores identity, that asserts what's been denied, is powerful. Community should support this.

I think about everyday materials and their significance. Art using everyday materials—materials associated with marginalized people, with labor, with history—can be powerful. Community should value this kind of art.

I'm concerned about how high art and fine art can exclude certain people and perspectives. Community should support diverse artistic practices and should not privilege only certain forms as legitimate art.

Regarding history and memory: I think reclaiming history, memory, what's been hidden—this is important work. Community should support artists and communities engaged in this reclamation.
