I want to describe a community built on the recognition that we are all caught in systems, and those systems can be changed if we understand them and work together.

My vision of a good community is one where collective wellbeing is the measure of success, not individual accumulation. Right now, we organize work so that individuals compete, where some people's safety is sacrificed for others' wealth. I want a community where the health and safety of all workers is non-negotiable, where economic systems are designed to serve people rather than people being forced to serve economic systems. This community would be transparent about how decisions are made—how risk is calculated, who benefits and who bears the cost, how power flows. It would be democratic, with workers having real say in how their work is organized. It would believe that change is possible, that we don't have to accept the systems we inherit, that different ways of organizing work are feasible.

Freedom, as I understand it, means the real ability to shape conditions of your own life. But this isn't possible if you're desperate, if you have to accept dangerous work to feed your family. In my ideal community, people would have genuine freedom to choose their work, knowing they have alternatives. They could refuse unsafe conditions without losing their livelihood. They could voice concerns about how work is organized without fear of punishment. They could change their minds, leave situations that harm them, try different paths. Freedom also includes the freedom to understand how systems work—to have access to information about workplace safety, about how risks are calculated, about economic decisions that affect your life. Right now, much of this is hidden from workers. We decide policies in private and present them as inevitable. Real freedom means transparency and ability to contest those decisions.

How we care for each other is central to work. Right now, work is often organized in ways that isolate people—individual competition, hierarchy, secrets. I want a community where people who work together genuinely know each other and care about each other's wellbeing. This doesn't mean everyone has to be friends, but it means you work alongside someone and care whether they get home safe. It means collective responsibility for each other. If one person is struggling—with health, with family problems, with fatigue—others respond. If someone is injured, the community doesn't just replace them; it makes sure they're cared for. Care also means extending beyond your immediate workplace. Workers in other regions, other countries, deserve care too. Supply chains connect us; we should feel responsibility for people whose labor we benefit from.

Safety and basic stability are absolutely fundamental. Every worker should have guaranteed access to safe working conditions, healthcare, food, shelter, rest. Work should not destroy your body or mind. Factories should be designed with safety as a primary goal, not an afterthought. People should have clear understanding of risks and should have choice about accepting them. Risk calculations should be made transparently with worker input. Beyond physical safety, people need economic stability. Nobody should have to choose between safety and survival. The community should have clear agreements about minimum standards—for wages, for hours, for conditions. These should be set with worker input and should be adjusted as evidence about what's needed changes.

Justice means that those who profit from work should share that profit with those who do the work. Right now, workers are paid minimal amounts while owners accumulate enormous wealth from their labor. This is not justice. Justice means workers have fair share of what they produce. It also means addressing the history of workplace exploitation and discrimination. Women and migrants have been systematically paid less and exposed to worse conditions. Justice requires acknowledging this and actively changing it. When someone is harmed by unsafe conditions, they should be fully compensated, and the conditions should be changed so it doesn't happen to someone else. When systems have harmed people, we should work to restore them and transform the systems.

Redemption matters in workplaces too. People make mistakes in how they treat each other. Managers make poor decisions. Workers violate safety protocols. The response should be learning and change, not permanent exile. People should be able to acknowledge harm they've caused and work to do better. Systems should be redesigned so people aren't set up to fail. This requires believing that people can change and that better conditions make different behavior possible.

Authentic expression should be protected in workplaces. Workers should be able to voice safety concerns without fear of retaliation. They should be able to express concerns about how work is organized, about policies, about treatment of each other. They should be able to disagree with management and not be punished. This creates a culture where problems are addressed rather than hidden. It also means people can be genuinely themselves at work—not pretending to be more compliant or less knowledgeable than they are. When people are authentic, workplaces run better because problems are visible and solvable.

Protecting vulnerable workers is essential. Young workers need special protection—they're less likely to know their rights or speak up about problems. Disabled workers need accommodations and protection from discrimination. Migrant workers often have no legal standing and face severe exploitation. Families of injured workers need support. And we need to think about future workers. What kind of workplaces are we creating? What injuries are we normalizing? What labor practices are we establishing as acceptable? These decisions affect people not yet born.

Working together and collective decision-making should be foundational to how work is organized. Workers should have real power in decisions about their working conditions—through unions, through works councils, through direct democracy. Decisions should be transparent and explained. Sometimes individual preferences do need to yield to collective good, but workers should understand why and should be part of deciding when that happens. Resources generated by work should be managed collectively and fairly. The goal should be supporting everyone's wellbeing, not maximizing some people's profits.

Regarding spiritual and religious practice, workplaces should respect people's needs for meaning and community. If people's faith is important to them, they should have time and space to practice it. Different traditions should be honored. Work shouldn't be the only source of meaning; communities should support people's spiritual lives.

Digital rights and technology in workplaces are increasingly important. Workers' data shouldn't be extracted and sold. Surveillance systems shouldn't monitor workers without consent and transparency. Technology should serve workers' needs—making work easier or safer—not replace human judgment or enable control. Everyone should have access to technology needed for work. Digital systems should be governed with worker input, not controlled only by management.

I feel real tension between collective good and individual need. When someone's individual choice—to take risks, to work beyond safe hours—harms themselves and affects the collective, what do we do? I think community should work to understand why someone is making that choice, address the underlying conditions, and then trust them to make better choices. Another tension is between business survival and worker safety. If a business genuinely cannot survive while meeting safety standards, do we let it fail or do we support it? I think we should support transition and transformation, not let workers suffer.

What I believe most deeply is that work is collective, that we depend on each other, and that systems are changeable. Workers have more power than they often realize. When we understand how we're connected, when we organize collectively, when we insist on transparency and democracy in workplaces, we can create different conditions. My daughters deserve to inherit a working world that is built on mutual care and democratic participation.

Name: Jeremy Burns
values_description:
I am an agricultural worker, and I have made mistakes that haunt me. Years ago, I was arrested for drug possession—a moment of desperation that branded me as criminal. Later, I was cyberharassed, targeted online, publicly shamed for things I had said. I have two sons and a daughter, and a grandson now. I want to describe a community that gives people like me—people who have made mistakes, been broken by the system, been humiliated—a genuine path back. Betty Friedan wrote about liberation from limiting roles, and I think that applies to my situation too. I was trapped in a role—the criminal, the delinquent, the target—and community seemed designed to keep me there permanently. I want a community that, like Friedan's feminism, insists that people are not fixed categories but are capable of change, growth, and full participation. I want a community that doesn't accept what seems inevitable about who people are and what they can become.

My vision of a good community is one that believes in genuine redemption and transformation. I have changed. I am not the person I was when I made those mistakes. But systems are built to assume I haven't changed, to mark me as permanently suspect. I want a community that looks at people like me and sees possibility, not just history. This community would be organized around the idea that people matter—not because of what they've done or achieved, but because they exist, because they're human. It would believe that people can change fundamentally if circumstances and support are right. It would make space for people to contribute, to learn, to become different. It would not give up on anyone.

Freedom, to me, means being freed from limiting categories. Right now, I carry a label—'ex-offender'—that determines opportunities available to me. I cannot get certain jobs because of that arrest decades ago. I cannot vote in some places. I am forever marked as untrustworthy by background checks. This is not freedom. In the community I want, people should be free to change, to escape the categories applied to them, to have their growth recognized. Freedom also means freedom from shame and permanent punishment. I should be able to make a mistake without my entire life being determined by it. Shame is a tool of control, a way to keep people in the roles assigned to them. Communities should be able to say: you made a mistake, you've made amends, now you're part of us again. People should be free to make their own choices about their lives and bodies without judgment or punishment if those choices don't harm others.

How we care for each other is about seeing people fully. When I was harassed online, the community that mattered most was the people who knew me, who could say 'we know who you really are.' That's what care looks like—knowing someone beyond their mistakes or their worst moments. I want a community where people know each other genuinely, where people don't reduce each other to categories. Care means understanding that people have complex histories, that harm and pain and struggle shape us, that everyone is more than their worst moment. It means accepting people even when we disagree with their choices. It means having each other's backs—knowing that you won't be abandoned or permanently exiled if you fall. My grandson will grow up alongside people who care what happens to him, who look out for him, who believe in him.

Safety and stability are essentials. Everyone needs guaranteed access to food, shelter, healthcare, work. Without these, you cannot think about becoming better or contributing. Right now, the moment you're labeled criminal or untrustworthy, these things become harder to access. I have had trouble finding housing because of my record. I have had trouble getting work. This pushes people back toward the mistakes that got them labeled in the first place. Communities should guarantee basic stability for everyone—not conditional on good behavior, but guaranteed. Everyone should also be safe from violence, cruelty, and abandonment. And people should have clear understanding of rules and expectations, with the ability to challenge them if they seem unfair. The rules shouldn't be designed to trap people permanently.

Justice means giving people what they actually need to flourish, not just what's equal on paper. It means recognizing that I've been harmed by systems and working to repair that harm. Justice also means when I have caused harm, the community's response should be focused on restoration—on repairing damage, on my changing behavior, on integration back into community. Not permanent punishment. I spent time dealing with legal consequences. I have felt shame and public humiliation. That should have been enough to teach me, to change me, to bring me back. Instead, systems continue to treat me as suspect. This isn't justice; it's perpetual punishment. Justice means giving people real second chances, removing barriers that prevent change, actively supporting transformation.

Redemption and second chances are maybe the most important thing to me. I believe people can change. I believe I have changed. I want a community built on this belief. When someone makes a mistake, community should focus on: what led to this mistake? What conditions made this possible? Can we change those conditions? Can this person change their behavior? Can we support them in becoming different? The goal is restoration to community, not exile. This applies broadly—to people with criminal records, to people struggling with addiction, to people who have been abusive and want to change. It also applies to social redemption. My past shouldn't prevent my full participation in community. My voice shouldn't carry less weight because I once made bad choices. I should be able to contribute fully, to be trusted, to be part of decisions that affect all of us.

Authentic expression should be protected, even when it's difficult. I should be able to express my views, my concerns, my doubts without fear that it will be used against me later or used to define me permanently. People should have space to be messy, to change their minds, to express real complexity. Communities shouldn't demand that people be simple or consistent. We should trust that people can hold contradictions, can be wrong sometimes, can learn. This is how real people are. This is how change happens.

Protecting the vulnerable is essential. Children, especially, need protection from being labeled and condemned. If a young person makes mistakes, the response should be support and guidance, not branding them as criminal. Disabled people need protection and support. Families affected by economic hardship need genuine help, not judgment. And I think about my grandson. What kind of community will he inherit? Will he be safe? Will there be space for him to make mistakes and recover? Will he be valued for his potential, not diminished by his failures?

Working together means people like me get to be part of decisions. Right now, people with criminal records are excluded from jury duty, from voting, from having voice. This is wrong. All community members should have say in how things are organized. Decisions should be made together, explained transparently, open to challenge. Resources should be managed to support everyone's wellbeing.

Spiritual and religious practice should be supported. Faith has been crucial for my transformation. Community should honor people's spiritual paths and create space for them.

Digital rights matter increasingly, especially given my experience with cyberharassment. People should have some protection from harassment and public shaming online. Personal data should be protected. Technology should serve human connection and flourishing, not enable targeting and humiliation. Everyone should have access to technology and digital tools.

Where I feel tension is between accountability and redemption. If someone has caused serious harm, does understanding them as a person who can change mean we don't hold them accountable? I think both are necessary. People should be accountable for harm they've caused, and also should be genuinely welcomed back into community if they change. Another tension is between protecting vulnerable people and trusting that people can change. If I was genuinely dangerous, protecting others would matter more. But I wasn't genuinely dangerous, and I was treated as if I was. How do we distinguish between real ongoing threat and people whose circumstances have changed?

What I believe most deeply is that people are not their worst moments, not their worst mistakes. We are capable of extraordinary change when given support and belief. Communities that write people off, that treat them as permanently marked, create the very problems they claim to be solving. Communities that believe in transformation, that make space for people to become different, that integrate people fully—those communities are stronger and better. My children and my grandson deserve that kind of community.

Name: Miyu Kobayashi
values_description:
I am a physician in hospital medicine, and I have spent my career inside the intersection between modern medical science and something deeper—the ways that healing happens through relationship, through trust, through understanding what people actually need rather than what systems say they should need. As I think about this, Pat Buchanan comes to mind—not for his political positions, but for his commitment to preserving and honoring what is particular, what is rooted, what connects communities to their past and gives them identity. I have three adult children and a granddaughter now, and I am acutely aware that medicine is becoming increasingly abstracted, technological, disconnected from the human relationships that actually make healing possible. I want to describe a community where medicine serves healing—real human flourishing—rather than merely managing disease, and where cultural and relational knowledge is honored alongside scientific knowledge.

My vision of a good community is one where diverse ways of knowing and healing are genuinely respected and integrated. Right now, biomedicine dominates, often dismissing other traditions and ways of understanding health. I want a community where my granddaughter can benefit from both modern medicine and traditional healing wisdom, where these are not seen as competing but as complementary. Community would be rooted in particular places and cultures—healing practices would be adapted to local contexts, would honor local traditions, would integrate healing with community meaning-making. At the same time, community would be able to reach out and learn from other traditions, other cultures, other ways of being. It would be humble about the limits of what any single tradition knows. It would believe that real healing happens through relationship—between doctor and patient, between community members, between people and the natural world.

Freedom in medicine means having genuine choice about your own healthcare. People should be able to refuse treatments, choose alternative approaches, make decisions based on their values rather than medical authority. But real freedom requires good information. People should understand what's being recommended and why, should understand alternatives, should be able to make decisions based on their own values and understanding of what matters for their life. Freedom also includes freedom to practice your own traditions—whether that's spiritual healing, herbal medicine, traditional practices—without medical judgment or interference. But it also includes freedom for communities to establish agreements about safety. If something genuinely harms people, community can establish boundaries. The key is doing this together, with understanding, not through unilateral medical authority.

How we care for each other should be rooted in genuine relationship. In hospitals, I see how medicine fragments care—specialists who see you for procedures, doctors who don't know your history, systems that treat your body as a machine with separate parts. Real care is different. It knows you as a person with a story, understands how your health is connected to your relationships and your community, sees your whole being. Care means taking time, asking real questions, listening to answers. It means understanding what health means to you, not imposing what I think health should mean. It also means extending care across cultural and social difference. I should care about someone's health whether they are wealthy or poor, educated or not, similar to me or fundamentally different. Care requires genuinely knowing people across difference. My family includes diverse traditions and ways of being, and that has taught me that care looks different in different contexts. What heals one person might not heal another.

Safety and stability are foundational. Everyone should have guaranteed access to healthcare, to food, to shelter, to rest and recovery when ill. These should not depend on wealth or status. Regarding medical safety specifically, people should know they won't be harmed by treatment, that their bodies will be respected, that they can trust medical systems. Right now, marginalized groups have reason not to trust—history of medical abuse, ongoing discrimination, exploitation. Building trust requires acknowledging this history and genuinely changing practices. People should have clear understanding of medical decisions being made, should be able to question them. The community should have agreements about standards of care, but should also be willing to change them as evidence changes.

Justice requires equal access to healing and equal respect in medical systems. Right now, wealthy people receive better care, more time, better outcomes. This is not justice. Everyone should receive the same quality of care and the same respect. Justice also means addressing the history of medical harm to particular groups—experimentation without consent, forced sterilizations, dismissal of women's and minorities' health concerns. Justice requires acknowledging this and actively changing. It also means that when medical harm happens, it should be fully addressed—compensation, treatment of harm, systematic change so it doesn't happen again. When someone has harmed patients, the focus should be on their understanding what they did wrong and changing behavior, not just punishment.

Redemption and second chances matter in healthcare. Doctors make mistakes. Sometimes these harm patients. The response should help the doctor understand and change, not permanent exile. Patients sometimes don't follow medical advice or harm themselves through their choices. The response should be understanding—why is this person making this choice?—and support, not judgment and abandonment. We should believe people can change and that different support and understanding can enable change.

Authentic expression should be protected. Medical professionals should be able to voice concerns about treatments, about harmful practices, about what modern medicine gets wrong. Patients should absolutely be able to express what they believe, what matters to them, what they're afraid of. When someone's authentic belief doesn't match medical recommendations, we should engage with that belief, not dismiss it. If someone doesn't trust modern medicine, that's real information about why, and we should understand it rather than condemn it. Creating space for authentic conversation makes healing possible.

Protecting the vulnerable is essential. Children need protection from over-medicalization and from genuine medical neglect. Elderly people need care and respect, not dismissal. Disabled people need medicine that enables their flourishing, not medicine aimed at normalizing them. And I think deeply about my granddaughter and what kind of healthcare system she'll inherit. Will it respect her autonomy? Will it honor her culture and values? Will it have space for all the ways of healing, not just pharmaceutical interventions? Will it see her as a whole person, not a collection of symptoms?

Working together and sharing decisions is important in healthcare. Patients should have real say in treatment decisions, not just be told what to do. Communities should have voice in how healthcare is organized—whether resources go to prevention or treatment, whether traditional medicine is supported, whether research respects ethical boundaries. Healthcare workers should have say in how medicine is practiced. Decisions should be made together and explained transparently.

Spiritual and religious practice are inseparable from healing. People need meaning, connection, hope. Different traditions provide these. Healthcare should absolutely create space for spiritual practice and should support people's spiritual needs. This is not separate from medicine; it's central to what makes healing possible.

Regarding digital rights and technology, I have concerns about how technology distances us from each other. Medical information should absolutely be private and controlled by individuals. Medical technology should serve healing and relationship, not replace the doctor-patient relationship. Telemedicine, for instance, has some value but loses essential human connection. Everyone should have access to necessary medical technology. Digital systems should be governed with physician and patient input, not controlled only by corporations.

I feel real tension between honoring tradition and embracing beneficial innovation. Some traditional practices are harmful; some modern interventions are genuinely lifesaving. How do we discern? I think together, with humility, listening to each other. Another tension is between individual choice and community good. If someone refuses vaccination and spreads disease, what then? I think individual autonomy should usually win, but genuine public health crises create real tension. I'm thinking carefully about how to hold both.

What I believe most deeply is that healing is fundamentally relational. It happens between people who know and trust each other, in communities that honor diverse ways of being. Modern medicine has tremendous power, but power without relationship and cultural understanding can harm as much as help. My granddaughter deserves to inherit a healthcare community that integrates scientific knowledge with relational wisdom, that honors multiple traditions, that sees people fully as human beings with stories and values and communities.

Name: Heather Reyes
values_description:
I work in industrial production, where I have learned to see how things fit together—how materials come in, how they're transformed through collective work, how products emerge. Juan Gris was a Cubist painter who understood that reality could be understood through geometric relationships, through how elements fit together to create something new, through finding order in complexity. I see my work similarly—production is not individual achievement but collective coordination. I have a large family—my brother and sister, my father, my husband, nieces and nephews, and two daughters—and managing a household is much like managing a production floor. Everyone has a role, everyone contributes, and the whole works because of how we coordinate and support each other. I want to describe a community built on the understanding that we are fundamentally interdependent, that things work when all the parts function well, and that this kind of coordination and care is valuable and should be honored.

My vision of a good community is one organized around collective wellbeing and coordinated care. Right now, we celebrate individual achievement and isolate people into nuclear families or isolated workers. I want a community more like my extended family or my production team—where people understand they're part of something larger, where coordinating with others is natural, where no one person is expected to be self-sufficient. This community would value the work of holding things together—caregiving, organizing, maintaining, coordinating—as much as it values individual achievement. It would be organized so that people can contribute according to their abilities and receive according to their needs. It would understand that coordination and mutual dependence make things work, not competition and individual striving.

Freedom in such a community looks different than isolated individual choice. I don't want freedom to be entirely separate from others; I want freedom within relationship. People should be free to choose their work, to pursue what interests them, but knowing that they're part of something larger. They should be free to refuse work that harms or exploits them. They should be free to voice concerns about how things are organized. But they should also understand that their freedom exists within the freedom of others, and sometimes you have to coordinate. In my household, nobody is free to work in a way that completely destabilizes others' lives. My freedom is bound up with my family's stability. That's healthy, not oppressive. The community should create conditions where people are genuinely free to make choices, but always within relationships of mutual responsibility.

How we care for each other is central. In production, you work alongside people day after day, and you learn each other's strengths and needs. You learn who gets tired, who needs support, who's having difficulty at home. A good workplace culture is one where people actually care what happens to each other. Beyond work, families matter. I grew up in a large extended family, and that shaped how I understand community. You know your nieces and nephews, you're involved in their lives, you step in when they're struggling. Extended family provides a network of care. I want community organized so that more people have that extended network. People should know each other, should naturally care about each other's wellbeing, should be willing to help when someone is struggling. This extends beyond close family—people should care about those unlike them too, but rooted in genuine relationship.

Safety and stability are foundational. Everyone needs guaranteed access to food, shelter, healthcare, work. Right now, some people live in constant precarity while others hoard security. This creates desperation and prevents caring for others. Everyone should know their basic needs will be met. Regarding safety specifically, people should be safe from violence, from arbitrary cruelty, from abandonment. People should have stable housing, not constant threat of homelessness. Work should be stable and sufficient to live on. People should have time and energy for rest and family. The community should have clear agreements about how these things are provided and protected. These agreements should be made together and adjusted when needed.

Justice means distributing resources and opportunities fairly. Everyone should have fair access to good work, to education, to healthcare. If outcomes differ, it should be because of effort and genuine difference in ability, not because of discrimination or starting inequality. Justice also means addressing ongoing exploitation. Women have been expected to do care work for free while men were paid for work. This is not just. Migrant and immigrant workers are exploited. This is not just. Justice requires acknowledging these harms and changing the systems that created them. When someone causes harm, the community response should focus on restoration—on them changing behavior, on repairing relationships, on integration. Not permanent punishment.

Redemption and second chances are important. People should be able to make mistakes and change. In production, if someone doesn't do their job well, the response is understanding why—do they lack training? Are they struggling with something? Can we support them?—and helping them improve. Communities should work the same way. If someone has caused harm, the question should be: can they understand what they did wrong? Can they change? Can we support that change? If so, they should be welcomed back. The goal is not permanent exile but restoration.

Authentic expression should be protected. People should be able to voice concerns about how things are organized, about treatment, about unfairness. This makes things work better—problems are addressed rather than hidden. People should be able to express who they really are without pretense. When people are authentic, communities run better because you're dealing with real people, real concerns, real possibilities. I should be able to say what I think without fear of punishment or permanent marking. My daughters should grow up able to express themselves without being condemned.

Protecting the vulnerable is essential. Children need protection and care that allows them to develop. Disabled people need support and inclusion, not segregation or dismissal. Elderly people deserve respect and care. People in precarious situations need community support. And I think about the future. What kind of production and work are we normalizing? What kind of community are we building for my daughters and the next generation? Are we depleting resources or managing sustainably? Are we creating good work or disposable people?

Working together and sharing decisions should be central. Major decisions should be made with input from those affected. In production, workers should have say in how work is organized. In communities, people should have say in shared decisions. Decisions should be transparent—explained so people understand. Sometimes individual interests must yield to collective good, but this should be clear and justified. People should feel their voice matters and that decisions are made together.

Spiritual and religious practice should be respected and supported. Different traditions should be honored. Whether someone finds meaning through religion, through family, through work, through community service, these matter and deserve space and respect.

Regarding digital rights and technology, I am concerned about how technology can isolate people. But technology can also connect and support collective work. Personal data should absolutely be controlled by individuals, not extracted and sold. Technology should serve human connection and collective work, not isolate or control. Everyone should have access to technology needed for work and connection. Digital systems should be governed democratically, not controlled only by corporations.

I feel real tension between individual need and collective good. When someone's individual desires threaten collective wellbeing, what prevails? In my family, we try to balance—sometimes someone's needs take priority, sometimes they yield. We negotiate. That's what community should be—constant negotiation about how to honor both individual flourishing and collective wellbeing. Another tension is between stability and change. I value stability—it allows caring and coordinated work. But sometimes systems need to change. How do we change without destabilizing everything? Carefully, together, with attention to everyone's welfare.

What I believe most deeply is that we are fundamentally coordinated beings. We work, we live, we flourish through coordination with others. Communities that understand this, that value the work of coordination and care, that genuinely distribute labor and resources, that make decisions together—those communities work better and everyone flourishes more. Like in production, the best output comes when all the parts work well together. My daughters deserve to inherit a community built on this understanding of our mutual dependence and collective power.

Name: Andrew Chavez
values_description:
I am a physician working in hospital medicine, and this work has taught me that healing is fundamentally about service—about understanding what someone actually needs and dedicating yourself to meeting that need with humility and care. George Herbert wrote about devotion, about serving God through service to others, about finding meaning in small acts of attention and care. This resonates deeply with how I understand medicine. I have two sons, and I want them to grow up in a community where service is honored, where caring for others is seen as meaningful work, where people understand that we are all interconnected and that taking care of each other is central to what makes community work. I want to describe a community built on the recognition that healing—whether physical, emotional, or communal—happens through sustained attention, genuine care, and understanding what people actually need.

My vision of a good community is one where people fundamentally understand themselves as servants of something larger than themselves. This doesn't mean submissiveness or lack of individual value. It means recognizing that your life gains meaning through how you contribute to others' wellbeing, how you show up for people, how you are faithful to relationships and commitments. In community, people would naturally care about each other's wellbeing, would be present in each other's struggles, would find purpose in being useful to others. This community would honor caregiving work—nursing, teaching, parenting, elder care—as much as it honors more visible or economically rewarded work. It would understand that behind every person who is healthy or educated or safe is someone who cared for them. We would acknowledge this gratefully and organize community to support this caring work.

Freedom, in my understanding, is not unlimited individual choice. It is the freedom to live according to your values, to serve what you believe is important, to commit to people and communities you care about. Real freedom includes constraints—the constraints of responsibility to others, the constraints of commitment. I am most free when I am faithfully showing up for my patients, for my family, for my community. This is not oppressive; it's liberating. It releases me from the exhausting project of constantly asserting myself and proves me toward meaning. In the community I want, people would be free to choose what they serve, who they commit to, what communities they belong to. But they would understand that freedom and responsibility are bound together. You cannot have genuine freedom without also having commitment to something beyond yourself.

How we care for each other is the core of community. Care is not sentimental. It is concrete, consistent, attentive. It looks like a nurse holding someone's hand while they're scared. It looks like a mother staying up all night with a sick child. It looks like a neighbor noticing someone is struggling and showing up with food. It looks like taking time to really listen to someone, not just waiting for your turn to talk. Care means knowing people—really knowing them, understanding their history and their struggles and what matters to them. It means extending care to those who are not like us, not just to our in-group. In medicine, I see how care heals in ways that medication alone cannot. When someone feels genuinely cared for, something shifts. Community should cultivate this quality of care everywhere—in workplaces, in neighborhoods, in institutions. Care also includes setting boundaries and sometimes saying no, but always with genuine concern for the other person.

Safety and stability create the conditions where people can flourish and can care for others. Everyone needs guaranteed access to food, shelter, healthcare, and rest. Without these basics, people are in survival mode and cannot focus on anything beyond immediate needs. Beyond material basics, people need emotional and relational safety—to know they belong, that they will be cared for if they fall, that they are valued for who they are beyond what they produce. In hospitals, I see how trauma and chronic instability damage people deeply. Community should provide genuine safety and predictability. This includes clear agreements about how people will be treated, how disputes will be resolved, how vulnerable people will be protected. These agreements should reflect that people matter, that their dignity is non-negotiable.

Justice is about restoring people to wholeness and dignity. When someone is sick or injured or in crisis, justice means they receive the care they need regardless of their ability to pay, regardless of their status. Right now, healthcare is organized around profit and status in ways that are deeply unjust. Wealthy people receive better care while poor people suffer. This violates the fundamental principle that all human beings have equal worth. Justice also means addressing the history of how medicine has harmed people—through experimentation without consent, through racism in diagnosis and treatment, through dismissal of women's and minorities' experiences. Justice requires acknowledging this history and genuinely transforming practices. When someone has been harmed, the focus should be on healing them—physically, emotionally, relationally. Justice is about restoration, not just punishment of wrongdoers.

Redemption and second chances are central to how I understand community. People make mistakes. People struggle with addiction, with mental illness, with desperation that leads them to harm others. The response should be compassionate and focused on healing and change, not judgment and permanent exile. I believe people are capable of tremendous change when given support, understanding, and genuine belief that they can become different. Medical practice shows this—someone in crisis can become stable; someone with addiction can recover; someone broken can heal if they receive sustained care and community support. Communities should operate on this belief. When someone has caused harm, the goal should be their understanding what they did, their genuine change, and their restoration to community. This is harder than punishment but ultimately more healing.

Authentic expression is important but should be balanced with responsibility to community. People should be able to express their genuine concerns, their doubts, their struggles without fear of judgment or punishment. In healthcare, I need my colleagues to be able to voice concerns about how we're practicing, about treatments that might not be serving patients well. Patients need to be able to express their real fears and values. But authentic expression is not unlimited—you cannot use it as justification for harm. People should express themselves thoughtfully, with consideration for how their words affect others. Communities should create space for difficult conversations, for disagreement, for people to be fully themselves. But also with the understanding that we are accountable to each other for what we say and do.

Protecting the vulnerable is a core responsibility. Children need protection, nurturing, education that helps them develop their full humanity. Sick and disabled people need support and inclusion, not segregation or abandonment. Elderly people deserve respect and care. And I think about my sons and the world they'll inherit. What kind of community are we creating? Are we caring for people through their lifespan? Are we addressing what makes people vulnerable in the first place? Are we building systems that support wellbeing or that exploit vulnerability? Healthcare shows us clearly—preventing disease through decent living conditions is far more effective than treating disease. Communities should invest in prevention, which means ensuring everyone has food, housing, education, meaningful work.

Working together and making decisions collaboratively is important, but the focus should be on building genuine community rather than on procedural democracy. Yes, decisions should be made together, but the deeper goal is that people develop genuine relationships, understand each other, care about each other. When people genuinely care about each other's wellbeing, decision-making becomes easier because the focus is naturally on what serves everyone, not on winning for your side. Communities should create conditions where people actually know each other, work together, experience interdependence. This is harder than voting but more durable.

Spirituality and religious practice are essential to community wellbeing. People need sources of meaning that go beyond survival and work. Different spiritual traditions should all be honored. Whether someone finds meaning through organized religion, through nature, through contemplation, through service to others, these sources of meaning matter. Communities should make space for spiritual life and should understand that spiritual wellbeing and physical health are not separate.

Regarding digital rights and technology, I am cautious about technology replacing human connection. In medicine, technology is valuable—diagnostic tools, communication across distance, access to knowledge. But it cannot replace the doctor-patient relationship, the human connection that is essential to healing. Personal health data should absolutely belong to individuals and be protected. Technology should serve human wellbeing and human connection, not replace it. Everyone should have access to necessary technology. Digital systems should be governed with consideration for human flourishing, not just for corporate profit.

Where I feel tension is between individual freedom and collective responsibility. Sometimes people's choices harm the community. How much do we constrain individual choice for collective good? I think the answer lies in building genuine relationships where people naturally care about each other's wellbeing and freely choose to limit their choices out of care. Another tension is between accepting people as they are and calling them to something better. My faith tradition teaches both radical acceptance and the belief that people can and should grow. Both are true. We should love people unconditionally while also believing they can become more fully human.

What I believe most deeply is that community is built through small acts of faithful service. When people show up consistently, honestly, caringly—in their relationships, their work, their community—something sacred happens. This is how healing occurs, how trust develops, how community becomes real. My sons deserve to inherit a community where service is honored, where people understand that their meaning comes through how they care for each other, where devotion to each other's wellbeing is the foundation.

Name: Shawn Chung
values_description:
I work as a shift supervisor in industrial production, and I have spent my career managing complex human situations—keeping people coordinated, safe, and working together. Kara Walker creates silhouettes that reveal hidden violence and racism in American history, using the beautiful and artistic form of silhouettes to expose what is usually hidden, made invisible, or aestheticized away. I think about my work in similar terms. The production floor looks efficient and clean on the surface, but underneath are exploitations, discriminations, harms that are often invisible unless you look carefully. I have a granddaughter now, and I want her to grow up in a community that doesn't hide its difficult histories and ongoing injustices, that is willing to look at the silhouettes—at what is shadowed or obscured—and names what it sees. I want a community committed to transparency about power, about who benefits and who bears costs, about how systems that seem neutral actually privilege some and harm others. I want to describe a community built on the commitment to seeing clearly and naming honestly.

My vision of a good community is one that is radically honest about its own history and ongoing practices. We tend to hide things—to have public narratives of fairness and inclusion while practicing discrimination and exploitation. I want a community that stops hiding. This means examining who gets paid what, why some people's work is valued and others' is not, what discriminations run through institutions. It means acknowledging historical harms—colonialism, slavery, exploitation—and genuinely working to transform the systems those harms created. It means creating space where people who have been excluded or harmed can speak, and where those communities genuinely listen. This community would believe that transparency and honesty, even when uncomfortable, are essential to justice and healing.

Freedom means having genuine power and agency, not just formal rights. Right now, I supervise workers, and I see how many have limited freedom—they cannot refuse unsafe work without losing their jobs, cannot speak up about problems without retaliation, cannot make real choices about their futures because they are desperate. Formal freedom doesn't matter when you are economically desperate. Real freedom requires material security and genuine voice. In the community I want, people would have enough security that they could refuse harmful situations, could speak honestly, could pursue what matters to them. They would have real power in decisions that affect them. This is different from just voting on something—it's having genuine ability to shape your conditions, your work, your life. Freedom also includes freedom from surveillance and control, freedom to be yourself without constant monitoring or performance.

How we care for each other is about seeing each other fully, including seeing how we harm each other. In workplaces and communities, we often develop relationships while ignoring systemic harms we participate in. We are friends with someone while the systems we both operate in exploit their labor. We care about our in-group while ignoring those excluded. Real care means being willing to see this, to acknowledge it, to change. Care means recognizing that people have different experiences based on their position—based on race, gender, class, immigration status—and that these differences matter. I cannot truly care for someone while ignoring how systems harm them. Care also means being accountable for harm I cause or participate in, and being willing to change. In my role as supervisor, I care about my workers, but I also need to recognize how production systems can exploit them and work to change that.

Safety and stability are non-negotiable. Everyone needs guaranteed access to food, shelter, healthcare, meaningful work. Without these, people are desperate and easily exploited. Beyond material safety, people need safety from violence and discrimination. Right now, marginalized people face constant threat—threat of violence, threat of police, threat of discrimination in employment and housing. Community should guarantee actual safety, not just rhetorical commitment to it. This means addressing the systems that create differential threat for different people. It also means having clear agreements about how people will be treated and what happens when those agreements are violated. These agreements should be transparent and should address power imbalances—people with less power need stronger protections.

Justice requires addressing root causes of harm and inequality, not just treating symptoms. If someone is sick from poverty, justice is not charity; it is ensuring they have resources and meaningful work. If someone is incarcerated because of systemic racism, justice is not a fair trial within a racist system; it is transforming the system. Justice means redistributing power and resources so that those who have been excluded and exploited have genuine power and are no longer exploited. It also means addressing the people who have benefited from exploitation. This is uncomfortable. I benefit from systems that exploit others. Justice requires I acknowledge this and work to change it, even at cost to myself. When harm happens, the response should focus on stopping the harm, understanding how systems created it, and transforming those systems.

Redemption is complicated by power. I believe people can change, but I also believe that sometimes people benefit from exploitation and don't want to change. Communities need to address both—creating conditions where people can change and be restored, but also not giving endless chances to those who refuse to stop causing harm. For people genuinely working to change—to understand what they've done wrong and become different—community should absolutely welcome them back. But this has to be real change, not performative change. And for those causing ongoing harm, community has responsibility to protect those being harmed.

Authentic expression is essential but should be coupled with accountability. People should be able to voice concerns about injustice, about harm they see, about how systems affect them. But this expression should be coupled with willingness to hear how your own actions cause harm. Authentic expression is not just saying whatever you want without responsibility; it's being honest about what you see and being willing to be honest about yourself. In workplaces and communities, we need people who will name what is being hidden, who will point out the silhouettes, who will say what everyone is pretending not to see.

Protecting the vulnerable is essential, but it requires understanding that vulnerability is often created by systems, not inherent. Children are vulnerable and need protection. Disabled people face vulnerability from inaccessible systems. Poor people are vulnerable to exploitation. Rather than just offering charity to vulnerable people, justice requires changing the systems that create vulnerability. My granddaughter should inherit a community that works to eliminate the conditions that create vulnerability in the first place.

Working together should be genuinely democratic, with particular attention to power imbalances. In production, workers should have real say in decisions that affect them—not just consultation where management ignores them, but genuine democracy. Communities should make decisions together, but should pay attention to who is speaking and who is being silenced. Marginalized people often are not heard even when they speak. We need to actively work to center voices that are usually excluded. Shared resources should be managed fairly, with transparency about how decisions are made and whose interests are served.

Spirituality and religious practice should be respected, but I'm cautious about spirituality being used to justify inaction about injustice. Yes, people need meaning and connection. But meaning should not come at the cost of justice. Communities should honor spiritual traditions while also being willing to critique traditions that are used to justify harm and exploitation.

Regarding digital rights and technology, I'm concerned about surveillance and control. Workers are increasingly monitored electronically. Personal data is harvested and exploited. Technology should serve human freedom and connection, not enable control. Everyone should have access to technology. Digital systems should be governed democratically, not controlled by corporations seeking profit. And people should have protection from surveillance and data extraction.

Where I feel real tension is between addressing ongoing harms and maintaining relationships. If I acknowledge that a system I've benefited from is unjust and harmful, it changes my relationship to it and to people who have benefited from it. This is uncomfortable. But avoiding the discomfort means perpetuating the harm. Another tension is between believing in people's ability to change and protecting those being harmed by people who aren't changing. These have to be balanced carefully.

What I believe most deeply is that communities can only be just and healthy when they are willing to look at what they have been hiding, to see the silhouettes, to name the shadows. This is not comfortable, but it is necessary. My granddaughter deserves to inherit a community that is honest about its history and present, that names injustices clearly, and that is actively working to transform them.

Name: Jessica Wallace
values_description:
I work as a shift supervisor in industrial production, managing people and processes in an environment where precision, responsibility, and understanding human nature are essential. Dorothy L. Sayers was a writer and thinker who insisted on intellectual rigor, who refused simplistic answers to complex questions, who believed that good craft and careful thinking were forms of integrity. She also fought for women's right to meaningful work and intellectual engagement. I have three sons, and I want them to grow up in a community where work is seen as meaningful, where careful thinking and responsibility matter, where excellence is pursued not for status but for the integrity of doing something well. I want to describe a community built on the understanding that work is how we express our values, how we contribute to something beyond ourselves, how we develop as human beings. I want people to take their work seriously—whether that's raising children, making products, caring for others—and to believe that doing things well matters morally.

My vision of a good community is one where work is honored and understood as an expression of character and commitment. Right now, we treat work as merely instrumental—something you do to get money so you can do what you really want. But humans spend enormous time working, and that time shapes who we become. Good community would understand work as a place where you develop virtue, where you take responsibility, where you contribute to something beyond yourself. Work should be structured so that people can do it well, with care and attention. This means work that is not so exploitative or exhausting that you have no energy for excellence. It means apprenticeship and learning, so people develop genuine skill. It means communities where people take pride in their work and are held accountable for quality.

Freedom means having genuine opportunity to develop your abilities and exercise your judgment. In production, I see how much worker autonomy has been stripped away—jobs so simplified and controlled that people cannot exercise judgment or develop skill. I want a community where people are trusted to do their work well, where they have room to think and problem-solve, where their judgment is valued. This applies broadly—children should have freedom to develop their abilities, not be constrained by others' limited vision of what they can become. Women should absolutely have freedom to do meaningful work and to develop intellectually, not be confined to narrow roles. Freedom also means freedom from desperation—you cannot exercise genuine judgment when you are desperate. Everyone should have secure enough position that they can make real choices.

How we care for each other is about taking each other seriously and wanting each other to become fully developed persons. I care about my workers not in a sentimental way but in the way you might respect a craftsperson—you want them to be excellent, to develop their abilities, to take responsibility. Care means holding people to high standards while also supporting them in meeting those standards. It means believing people can do more than they currently do, and creating conditions for growth. In families, this kind of care is crucial. Parents should want their children to develop fully, not just to be obedient. Communities should care about people becoming their best selves, not just about compliance or contentment. This extends across difference—I should care about opportunities for those unlike me, should believe they can develop and contribute, should support their growth.

Safety and stability create conditions where people can focus on doing things well. Everyone needs guaranteed access to food, shelter, healthcare, education, meaningful work. Without these, people are in survival mode and cannot focus on excellence or development. Beyond material basics, people need safety from arbitrary cruelty or judgment. But safety should not mean protection from legitimate consequences of poor work. If you do something poorly or carelessly, there should be consequences, because consequences teach responsibility. The community should have clear standards about what is acceptable and what is not. These standards should be maintained consistently, not applied arbitrarily.

Justice is about fair treatment and about each person receiving what they actually need to develop and flourish. Everyone should have fair access to education and meaningful work. But fairness is not simple sameness—people have different needs and abilities. Justice means addressing real inequalities that prevent people from developing fully. It means ensuring that barriers based on gender, race, or background don't prevent people from flourishing. It also means holding people responsible for their choices and actions. Justice requires that when someone does poor work or treats others badly, they face consequences that teach them to do better. When someone has been wronged, the focus should be on repairing the damage and preventing future harm. Punishment divorced from restoration is not justice.

Redemption and second chances matter, but they should be coupled with genuine effort to change. If someone has done poor work or caused harm, the question should be: can they understand what they did wrong? Will they genuinely work to do better? If so, they deserve another chance. But the chance should come with clear expectations and accountability. This is how people learn and develop. Communities should believe people can become better, can develop new skills, can change their character. But this belief should be coupled with real standards and real consequences.

Authentic expression should be coupled with responsibility and rigor. People should be able to express their genuine views and concerns, but they should be prepared to defend those views with reason and evidence. In workplaces, people should be able to voice concerns about how things are done. But they should also be willing to understand the reasoning behind current practices before assuming they should be different. In communities, people should be able to express themselves fully. But they should also take responsibility for what they say and should be willing to engage seriously with critique. I want my sons to be able to express themselves authentically and to engage rigorously with ideas and challenges.

Protecting the vulnerable is important, but I'm concerned about protection that enables passivity. Children should be protected from genuine harm while also being challenged to grow. Disabled people should have support and access, but should also be believed capable of developing and contributing. Vulnerable people should be protected from exploitation, but should also be treated as capable and responsible. Protection without belief in capability creates infantilization. My sons should be protected from genuine harm but should also be expected to develop strength and capability.

Working together should involve genuine deliberation and responsibility-taking. Decisions should be made carefully, with input from those affected. But once decisions are made, people should take responsibility for implementing them well. In communities, people should deliberate together about important matters. But the goal should be making wise decisions and then executing them with excellence, not just achieving consensus or democracy for its own sake. Shared resources should be managed carefully and well. People should be held accountable for stewardship of shared things.

Spirituality and religious practice matter as sources of meaning. Different traditions should be honored. But spirituality should not be used as excuse for avoiding responsibility or rigorous thinking. I respect people's spiritual commitments and think communities should make space for them. But spiritual belief should be held alongside intellectual integrity and genuine accountability.

Regarding digital rights and technology, I think technology should serve human capacity and development, not replace it. Personal data should be protected. Technology should enable people to do their work better, not surveil or control them. Everyone should have access to technology needed for meaningful work. Digital systems should be governed with attention to human flourishing, not just corporate profit. And people should develop understanding of how to use technology well—it should enhance human judgment, not replace it.

Where I feel real tension is between holding high standards and accepting human limitation. Not everyone can be excellent at everything. How do we pursue excellence without creating despair? I think the answer is that excellence should be pursued in different domains—everyone should develop something to excellence, even if different people develop different things. Another tension is between individual development and collective good. Sometimes developing yourself fully means choosing a path that doesn't serve the collective as efficiently. I think both matter, and both should be honored.

What I believe most deeply is that work is sacred—it's how we express our character, develop our capacities, contribute to something beyond ourselves. Communities that understand this, that create conditions for people to do work well, that hold people to high standards while supporting them, that believe in people's capacity to develop and excel—those communities are healthier and people are more fulfilled. My sons deserve to inherit a community where excellence is pursued, where work is honored, where people are believed capable of developing fully.

Name: Brent Tucker
values_description:
I have worked in production supervision for decades, and I have learned through that work that communities function best when people understand their roles clearly, do what they commit to do, and work together with discipline and good humor toward shared goals. Larry Miller was a comedian and observer of human nature who understood absurdity and found humor in human situations while never losing sight of what matters—dignity, decency, fairness. I think about my work in similar terms. The production floor has inherent absurdities and frustrations, but what matters is that people are treated fairly, that work is organized rationally, that everyone understands what's expected and why. I have aging parents who I care for, which has deepened my understanding of how important it is to have clear agreements about responsibility and care. I want to describe a community built on mutual accountability, on people taking their commitments seriously, on everyone contributing according to their ability, and on managing resources responsibly.

My vision of a good community is one based on mutual obligation and clear expectations. Right now, many communities are built on vague good intentions and unstated assumptions. People don't clearly understand what's expected of them or what they can count on from others. I want a community where people make clear commitments to each other and follow through on those commitments. It's not romantic, but it's reliable. People would understand their roles, would know what they need to do, and would do it. Resources would be managed efficiently and fairly, without waste or favoritism. Decisions would be made clearly, explained rationally, and implemented responsibly. This community would have a basic competence about how things work and a commitment to doing things right.

Freedom means having clear boundaries and the responsibility to work within them. Some people think freedom is unlimited choice, but that doesn't make sense in community. When many people are depending on each other, freedom must be balanced with responsibility. I am most free when I know where I stand, when I understand what I'm committing to and what others are committing to me. I'm not free if I cannot count on people, if rules are arbitrary, if responsibility is unclear. In the community I want, people would have genuine choice about their work and their lives, but would also understand that choice comes with responsibility. You choose to commit to something, and then you follow through. This is not oppressive—it's liberating because you know where you stand.

How we care for each other is through reliable presence and follow-through. I care about my parents by making sure they are cared for as they age, by being present consistently, by doing what I commit to do. I care about my coworkers by being someone they can depend on, by doing my job well so they can count on me, by treating them fairly and with respect. Care is not just sentiment; it's action and commitment. In community, people should care for each other by being reliable, by following through on commitments, by treating each other fairly. Care also means noticing when someone is struggling and helping them, but always in the context of also expecting them to do their part. It means extending that care across difference—you should be reliable and fair to people unlike you as well as to those close to you.

Safety and stability come from clear agreements and responsible management. Everyone should have guaranteed access to basic needs—food, shelter, healthcare, meaningful work. But beyond that, safety comes from knowing what to expect, from having clear rules that apply consistently, from being treated fairly. People should be able to count on each other. When someone makes a commitment, they should follow through. When there are rules, they should be applied fairly to everyone. When resources are managed, they should be managed responsibly. In production, this means clear processes, trained people, equipment that works. In community, it means similar things—systems that work, people who take responsibility, resources managed well.

Justice is about fair treatment and equal application of rules. Everyone should have fair access to work and to resources. Rules should apply equally to everyone; I have no patience with favoritism or arbitrary treatment. When someone does wrong, the consequences should be proportionate and should be applied consistently. Justice also means that when people are harmed, they should be made whole to the extent possible. But justice should be balanced with mercy. If someone genuinely changes and shows they will not repeat harm, they should be able to move on. Permanent punishment doesn't serve anyone. The goal should be people learning and changing and becoming responsible contributors.

Redemption and second chances are important. People make mistakes. If they understand what they did wrong and genuinely work to not repeat it, they should be welcomed back and given opportunity. But this has to be real change. You can't just say you'll do better; you have to show through consistent action that you have changed. In production, someone might do poor work at first but learn and become reliable. That's good—that's how people develop. Similarly, in communities, people who have made mistakes should have opportunity to show they've changed. But the opportunity comes with the expectation that they will follow through.

Authentic expression is important but should be balanced with responsibility. People should be able to speak up about problems, to say what they actually think, to disagree with leadership. But they should do this respectfully and should be willing to listen to reasoning. I don't expect people to pretend to agree with me when they don't. I expect them to be honest. But I also expect them to be professional about it—to express concerns in appropriate ways, to consider that there might be reasons for things being the way they are. People should be able to be themselves, but should also be accountable for how their authenticity affects others.

Protecting the vulnerable is a responsibility. Children need protection and guidance. Elderly people like my parents deserve care and respect. Disabled people need support and access. But protection should not mean people are infantilized or kept from contributing. My parents are aging and need care, but they are also intelligent and should be treated with respect. Vulnerable people should be protected from exploitation but should also be believed capable of contributing and taking responsibility.

Working together should involve clear communication and shared commitment. Decisions should be made by those responsible for implementing them or should be made in consultation with them. People should understand why decisions are being made. But once decisions are made, people should commit to executing them well. It's not productive to constantly rehash decisions that have been made. Shared resources should be managed carefully—without waste, without favoritism, with attention to making sure everyone is treated fairly. People should be held accountable for how they manage shared resources.

Spirituality and religious practice should be respected. People need meaning and sources of community beyond work. Different traditions should be honored, and people should have time and space to practice their faith. But spirituality should not be used as excuse for avoiding responsibility or treating people unfairly.

Regarding digital rights and technology, I think technology should serve human work, not replace human judgment. Personal data should be protected. Technology can improve efficiency and communication, but should not be used for surveillance or control. Everyone should have access to technology needed for their work. Systems should be managed responsibly and governed fairly.

Where I feel real tension is between efficiency and considering individual circumstances. In production, there's a right way to do things that makes everything work well. But individual people sometimes need accommodation or flexibility. How much flexibility can you have without things falling apart? I think the answer is that you build some flexibility into your systems from the start, so people aren't always choosing between the system and their individual needs. Another tension is between believing in people's capacity to change and protecting yourself from people who won't change. Some people just won't do their part. You have to be willing to address that, even though it's difficult.

What I believe most deeply is that communities work when people understand their commitments and follow through on them. When people are treated fairly and know where they stand. When resources are managed responsibly. When everyone contributes according to their ability. It's not glamorous or revolutionary, but it's how things actually function. My parents and everyone in the community deserve to live in a place where things work, where people can be counted on, where responsibility is clear and honored.

Name: Lynn Phillips
values_description:
I work as a receptionist in a spa hotel, and my work puts me at a particular threshold—between the outside world and the private space where people come to rest and be cared for. King Oliver was a musician who understood how to create space for others to develop and shine, how to lead collaboratively, how to listen and respond. He was a master of creating the conditions where music—beauty, communication, spontaneity—could happen. I think about my work similarly. A good receptionist is not just processing transactions; I am creating the atmosphere, setting the tone, helping people transition from their stressed or private worlds into a space where they can relax and be cared for. I have two sisters, a mother and father, and a nephew and daughter, and this extended family has taught me how much our wellbeing depends on attention, on noticing how people are, on creating space for different people to thrive. I want to describe a community built on the recognition that what happens between people matters, that creating welcoming and caring space is important work, that attention and responsiveness are gifts we offer each other.

My vision of a good community is one where people genuinely welcome each other, where there is grace and generosity in how we greet people and invite them in. Right now, so much of community life is transactional and impersonal. People rush past each other, treat each other as obstacles or functions rather than as full persons. I want a community where people slow down enough to really see each other, where there is warmth in how you greet someone, where people make space for each other. This community would value hospitality not as a service economy thing but as a genuine practice of welcoming people. It would have space for beauty, for relaxation, for people to be cared for. It would understand that how we treat each other in small moments shapes everything. A simple greeting done with genuine care can change someone's day. A space organized with attention to comfort can help someone relax. Community should cultivate this quality of attention and care.

Freedom means having space to be yourself and to develop according to your own values and interests. In my work, I see how much people need permission to slow down, to rest, to be cared for. In communities, people should feel free to be themselves—to express their interests, to pursue what matters to them, to develop in their own direction rather than following someone else's plan. This doesn't mean unlimited freedom; it means freedom within relationships and community. You are free to pursue your path, knowing that you're also part of something larger, that you have responsibilities to others. It also means freedom from being constantly evaluated or judged. People should be able to be imperfect, to be in process, to be developing, without constant critique.

How we care for each other is through attention, presence, and genuine interest. In the spa, we practice a kind of caring that is concrete and attentive—we notice what temperature someone likes, what kind of massage helps them relax, what they need. This kind of caring can extend throughout community. It means noticing how someone actually is, asking genuine questions and listening to answers, being present with people even when they're struggling. Care means extending this attention across difference. I should care about my neighbors, about people I work with, about people unlike me, about distant people whose labor and lives affect me. Care also means sometimes challenging people to become their best selves, to develop more fully, not just accepting them as they are.

Safety and stability create the conditions where people can relax and flourish. Everyone needs guaranteed access to food, shelter, healthcare, rest. Right now, too many people are constantly in survival mode, always stressed, never able to truly relax. This damages people. Communities should ensure that everyone has security—material security so they're not desperate, also emotional security so they know they're cared for and won't be abandoned. Beyond basic needs, people need safety from violence, from being treated poorly, from unpredictable cruelty. Clear agreements about how people will be treated help create this safety.
